Riverbend Juices is a partnership making cold-pressed fruit drinks for health food stores. Monthly cash inflows average $65,000, but harvest-month outflows reach $95,000 due to upfront fruit purchases. Opening cash balance is $15,000 and trade receivables total $90,000.

Current liabilities are $130,000, including $85,000 payables due in 30 days and a $45,000 bank overdraft. To overcome a $30,000 cash flow deficit, the partners are weighing a larger overdraft against cutting customer credit terms from 60 to 30 days.

questions.question_text: Calculate the Net Cash Flow for a month where cash inflows are $65,000 and cash outflows are $95,000, and calculate the resulting closing bank balance given an opening balance of $15,000.
questions.model_answer: Net Cash Flow = Cash Inflows ($65,000) - Cash Outflows ($95,000) = -$30,000 [k]. This $30,000 deficit means cash outflows exceed inflows during harvest months, draining the opening balance [app]. Closing Bank Balance = Opening Balance ($15,000) + Net Cash Flow (-$30,000) = -$15,000 [k]. The business would therefore start the next period $15,000 overdrawn, matching the projected deficit in the forecast [app].

scenario_stem:
Medivance Instruments PLC is a public limited company producing specialized surgical instruments. Revenue is $10,000,000 with gross profit of $6,000,000 and operating profit of $1,800,000 (18% net profit margin). Current assets of $2,500,000 comprise $1,400,000 inventory, $800,000 receivables and $300,000 cash; current liabilities are $1,000,000 ($700,000 payables, $300,000 overdraft).

Non-current liabilities are $2,000,000; capital employed $8,000,000, shareholders' funds $6,000,000. Analysing liquidity ratios, management must choose between new share capital and another bank loan to fund a $1,500,000 robotic facility.

questions.question_text: Calculate the Return on Capital Employed (ROCE) for this medical device manufacturer. Show your working.
questions.model_answer: ROCE = (Operating Profit / Capital Employed) x 100 = ($1,800,000 / $8,000,000) x 100 = 22.5% [2].

questions.question_text: Calculate the Acid-Test Ratio for this medical device business and explain what this result indicates about liquid solvency.

This indicates the business has $1.10 of liquid assets (cash and receivables) for every $1.00 of current liabilities [app], showing satisfactory immediate solvency to clear $700,000 trade payables and $300,000 overdraft [app]. An acid test above 1.0 suggests the company can meet immediate debts without selling inventory [k].

scenario_stem:
The healthcare software corporation is a public limited company developing electronic health records. Operating profit is $3,500,000 (25% margin), giving 35% ROCE on $10,000,000 capital employed. Current assets $4,000,000 include $500,000 inventory; current liabilities $2,500,000 comprise $1,800,000 payables and a $700,000 overdraft. Bank loans total $3,000,000.

A 1.40 acid-test supports liquidity, yet directors compare an additional 6-year bank loan at 6% interest with issuing new PLC shares to fund a $2,500,000 cybersecurity expansion.

questions.question_text: Calculate the Return on Capital Employed (ROCE) for this healthcare software company. Show your working.
questions.model_answer: ROCE = (Operating Profit / Capital Employed) x 100 = ($3,500,000 / $10,000,000) x 100 = 35% [2].

knowledge_max_2: (Operating Profit / Capital Employed) x 100 formula
ROCE measures how effectively long-term capital generates operating profit

questions.question_text: Calculate the Acid-Test Ratio for this company and explain what this result indicates about liquid solvency.
questions.model_answer: Acid-Test Ratio = (Current Assets - Inventory) / Current Liabilities = ($4,000,000 - $500,000) / $2,500,000 = 1.40 : 1 [k]. The acid-test ratio shows whether liquid assets cover short-term liabilities without selling inventory [k]. This result shows $1.40 of liquid assets per $1.00 owed [app], indicating healthy solvency to settle $1,800,000 trade payables and the $700,000 overdraft [app].

scenario_stem:
Ironvale Fasteners Co is a private limited company making steel bolts and nuts, employing 96 workers. Output hit 1.8 million units, up 12%. Pay is $9.50 hourly, yet 34% of bolts failed March checks and two line supervisors resigned over overtime.

Manager Priya Nair must decide in 6 weeks: Option A, a $0.09 piece rate for 60 line workers under Taylor's scientific management, or Option B, an $18,000 recognition scheme with a $150 team bonus.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'Maslow's hierarchy of needs'.
questions.model_answer: Maslow's hierarchy of needs is a theory that arranges human needs in five levels — physiological, safety, social, esteem and self-actualisation — where lower-level needs must be met before higher-level needs can motivate employees [2].

knowledge_max_2: Needs are arranged in a hierarchy or levels (physiological to self-actualisation)
Lower-level needs must be satisfied before higher-level needs motivate

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why a well-motivated workforce is important to Ironvale Fasteners Co.
questions.model_answer: A well-motivated workforce matters because motivated workers produce more output per hour, raising productivity so Ironvale can grow beyond 1.8 million units with the same 96 workers [k]. Higher productivity spreads fixed costs over more bolts, lowering the average cost per unit and protecting the margin needed to fund the $18,000 scheme [app]. Second, motivated workers take greater care and make fewer mistakes [k]. Fewer errors mean the 34% defect rate seen in March should fall, so fewer bolts are scrapped and Ironvale's reputation with its new contract customer is protected [app].

knowledge_max_2: Motivated workers are more productive / higher output per worker
Motivated workers make fewer errors / take greater care
application_max_2: Reference to 1.8 million units output / 96 workers
Reference to 34% defect rate in March / scrap and reputation

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Ironvale Fasteners Co might face if it introduces the piece rate (Option A).
questions.model_answer: First, a problem is that piece rate can reduce quality [k]. Paying $0.09 per approved bolt pushes workers to produce bolts as fast as possible, so defect rates could climb above the 34% recorded in March [app], and higher defects would damage Ironvale's standing with clients, leading to lost orders and rework costs [an]. Second, piece rate rewards individual speed, not teamwork [k]. Taylor's scientific management treats each worker separately, so experienced staff may refuse to help the slower of the 60 line workers [app], and the friction could trigger more disputes like the one that cost the factory two supervisors, raising labour turnover [an].

knowledge_max_2: Piece rate can push workers to rush / quality may fall
Piece rate rewards individual effort / weakens teamwork
application_max_2: Reference to $0.09 per approved bolt / 34% defect rate in March
Reference to Taylor's scientific management / 60 line workers / two supervisors resigned
analysis_max_2: Chain from rushing to more defects to lost orders / rework costs
Chain from individual reward to friction to disputes / higher labour turnover

questions.question_text: Do you think Ironvale Fasteners Co should switch to the piece rate (Option A)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A follows Taylor's scientific management: paying $0.09 per approved bolt links pay directly to output, so the 60 line workers would be driven to maximise production and Ironvale could lift output above 1.8 million units [k]. Because only approved bolts are paid, workers also carry the quality risk themselves, creating a direct incentive to avoid the defects that reached 34% in March [app]. Higher throughput would spread fixed costs over more units, improving efficiency and competitiveness [an]. However, Option B targets Herzberg's theory and Maslow's esteem needs [k]. Monthly certificates and a $150 team bonus reward the whole team for the lowest defect rate while keeping the $9.50 per hour base pay unchanged, so the $18,000 cost is predictable [app]. This addresses the overtime dispute and low morale directly, whereas piece rate could inflame them further [an]. Overall, I think Option B is the better choice [eval] because Ironvale's central problem is quality — a 34% failure rate — and Herzberg shows pay alone does not remove dissatisfaction; recognition and team effort do [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Taylor's scientific management: pay linked to output motivates effort
Herzberg: motivators (recognition) / hygiene factors (pay) distinction
application_max_2: Reference to Option A: $0.09 per approved bolt / 60 line workers / 1.8 million units
Reference to Option B: $18,000 scheme / $150 team bonus / $9.50 per hour
analysis_max_2: Chain from piece rate to throughput to lower fixed cost per unit / efficiency
Chain from recognition scheme to morale / quality improvement vs overtime dispute
evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear justified recommendation between Option A and Option B
Weighs both options using stem evidence (34% defects and morale vs higher output)

Reason 2: Organ building relies on highly skilled craftspeople with specialist voicing and joinery skills [k]. scenario_stem:
Copperfield Electronics Assembly is a public limited company making circuit boards, with 210 workers and 18 quality inspectors. Revenue is $26 million, but turnover on the assembly line hit 22% as 58 workers left in 12 months. The $1,450 salary feels repetitive.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'Taylor's scientific management'.
questions.model_answer: Taylor's scientific management is the theory that workers are motivated principally by money, using time-and-motion studies to find the one best way to do each job and paying a piece rate linked to how much each worker produces [2].

Repeating the same assembly stations all day adds no variety or new skills, removing Herzberg's motivators such as responsibility, so the 210 production-line workers drift towards quitting — 58 left in the last 12 months [app]. A second reason is that pay does not reward effort [k]. A salary of $1,450 per month is paid regardless of output, so productive and unproductive workers earn the same, and turnover has hit 22% [app].

A second benefit is greater flexibility [k]. Time-and-motion studies and a 10-week training programme would also standardise methods for new hires, helping stabilise a workforce that lost 58 workers in 12 months [app]. Retention of skilled assemblers also protects quality, which the 18 inspectors police on every board before it reaches home-appliance clients [an]. scenario_stem:
Calver Caravans Ltd is a private limited company making recreational caravans in a large factory where 42 workers operate one flow line. Workers idle 11% of the time, complaints cost $18,000 last year, and 380 caravans were built at $9,800 each.

questions.question_text: Define 'cell production'.
questions.model_answer: Cell production is a method of production where the process is split into groups (cells) of workers, each responsible for completing a whole product or a major part of it [1]. Each cell is self-managing and responsible for quality at its own stage [1]. [2]

Advantage 2: Communication within a small cell is easier [k]. A 7-person cell can spot and fix wiring and panel faults immediately instead of passing defects down the line [app].

A second reason is that accidents destroy productivity and cost money [k]. scenario_stem:
Clearway Glassworks is a private limited company making glass tubing, with 52 glass-blowers and 14 packers. Output averages 9,500 metres at a defect rate of 4%. Blowers earn a $1,380 salary, but quit rates reach 15% yearly; Helena Ortiz blames low pay.

Helena chooses: Option A, profit sharing - 3% of annual profit, $70,000, split among 66 staff - or Option B, an individual bonus of $60 while the defect rate stays under 2%, for 5 months yearly.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'teamworking'.
questions.model_answer: Teamworking is organising employees into groups that share responsibility for a task or goal, pooling skills, supporting one another and taking collective ownership of the result [2].

questions.model_answer: One way is to meet safety needs [k]. Glass-blowing involves molten glass, so better heat-resistant gloves and face protection would reduce the 15% annual quit rate among young blowers by making the workshop feel safe [app]. A second way is to meet esteem needs [k]. Recognising blowers whose defect rate is under 2% with a certificate would make them feel respected and valued, matching the pride Herzberg says esteem-level recognition creates [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two drawbacks of Option B (an individual bonus of $60 per month for defects under 2%).
questions.model_answer: One drawback is weakened teamwork [k]. Paying $60 only for personal sub-2% months rewards individual effort over group success [app], so experienced blowers may stop helping juniors whose defect rates run closer to 4%, eroding the shared skills the workshop needs [an]. A second drawback is the temptation to hide defects [k]. Blowers chasing $60 could pass flawed tubes on to the 14 packers for shipment [app], and faulty laboratory tubing reaching hospitals would mean returns, lost contracts and a damaged reputation far costlier than the bonus pool [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Clearway Glassworks should choose Option A? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A is straightforward and equal: 3% of annual profit, about $70,000 this year, split equally among all 66 staff, gives blowers and packers the same stake [k]. On Herzberg's view, financial reward is a hygiene factor — a profit share will not by itself create lasting drive — but it signals the firm values everyone and costs nothing until profits exist [app]. Equal sharing, however, links blower effort only weakly to the payout: each of the 66 staff receives roughly $1,060 whether or not their own defects fell [an]. Option B ties $60 per qualifying month directly to quality: under 2% defects, up to 5 months a year, worth $300 extra for top blowers [k]. It attacks the actual 4% defect rate with a clear personal target and leaves the $1,380 salary untouched [app]. But it ignores the packers entirely, may breed rivalry among the 52 blowers, and does not address why quit rates hit 15% a year [an]. Overall, I think Clearway should choose Option A first, then layer Option B on next year [eval] because equal profit sharing builds firm-wide loyalty at predictable cost, while the individual bonus can be added once defect data is reliable [eval].

Raising wages to $10.61 per hour stops dissatisfaction but soon becomes the expected norm, so the extra motivation fades after the first few pay packets [app]. A second limitation is that pay does not change behaviour at the machine [k]. Workers can be paid 5% more yet still watch waste run at 8.5% of raw material, because money adds no authority to stop the line or set quality checks [app].

Money alone does not give authority to change working methods
application_max_2: Reference to $10.61 per hour / 5% pay rise / $10.10 per hour

questions.question_text: Explain two arguments in favour of Option A (the job enrichment programme).
questions.model_answer: One argument is responsibility and ownership [k]. Letting line teams decide on quality checks and stop the line meets Herzberg's responsibility motivator and gives crews real authority over defects [app], so problems are fixed at source and the 8.5% fibre waste figure should fall sharply [an]. A second argument is shared visibility of results [k]. A weekly feedback board shows waste and output figures to all 118 workers, turning improvement into a shared challenge [app], and shared visibility plus ownership should cut waste per 1.4 million square metres produced each quarter [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Redbank Paper Mill should choose Option A? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A gives teams the authority and the information to act [k]. Stop-the-line power and a weekly feedback board target the actual problem — 8.5% fibre waste — and add Herzberg motivators such as responsibility, achievement and recognition rather than a one-off wage bump [app]. Cutting waste by even a couple of percentage points across 1.4 million square metres per quarter would save far more than a 5% pay rise costs [an]. Option B is simpler and universal [k]. A 5% rise to $10.61 per hour rewards all 118 workers equally, is easily understood and looks decisive before the June shareholders' meeting [app]. However, Herzberg warns pay is only a hygiene factor, so workers may welcome $10.61 briefly then coast, and the higher wage bill is permanent with no guaranteed fall in waste [an]. Overall, I think Option A is the better choice [eval] because the mill's central problem is waste, not pay — enrichment fixes it at source and builds a quality culture within the 3 weeks available [eval].

scenario_stem:
Northpeak Outdoor, a private limited company, makes hiking jackets. Its Northpeak Pro sells 8,500 units at $145, with 45% reordering from 40 specialist outdoor shops across the highlands, built on durability and a premium image.

A budget rival entered at $95 and sales fell 18% last quarter. Directors debate cutting the Northpeak Pro to $110 or holding $145 and spending $60,000 on athlete sponsorship and a 'buy once, last forever' campaign defending the premium image.

Problem 2: It removes margin per unit [k], because each jacket earns $35 less than at $145 [app], which across 8,500 units a year strips about $297,500 of revenue [an].

scenario_stem:
CaseCraft Ltd is a private limited company moulding phone cases under contract for 2 smartphone brands. It adopted just-in-time, holding almost no stock, and orders moulded parts from one overseas supplier with a 12-week lead time and no local alternative.

Two supplier failures halted assembly for 3 days each, costing $96,000 and forcing air-freighted parts at $18,000 per emergency shipment, while net-30 terms squeeze cash flow. The manager debates rebuilding a 3-week stock for $120,000 or keeping just-in-time and qualifying a second supplier.

questions.question_text: Outline two disadvantages of just-in-time production.
questions.model_answer: If suppliers fail to deliver on time, production must stop because there is no stock to fall back on [1]. The business becomes heavily dependent on reliable suppliers, and any disruption can halt output completely [1]. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Supply delays halt / stop production with no stock fallback
Heavy dependence on reliable suppliers

questions.question_text: Explain two risks of just-in-time shown by CaseCraft's experience.
questions.model_answer: Risk 1: Just-in-time leaves no stock to absorb supplier disruption [k]. Both halts followed supplier failures, and with a 12-week lead time CaseCraft could not quickly replace moulded parts from scratch [app]. Risk 2: A single overseas supplier creates dangerous dependence [k]. The need to air-freight parts at $18,000 per emergency shipment shows how one failing source can sharply raise costs and stress the two smartphone brands [app].

knowledge_max_2: Supply disruption halts production when no stock is held
Dependence on a single/unreliable supplier is risky
application_max_2: 12-week lead time; line halted for 3 days each time
Air-freighted parts at $18,000 per emergency shipment

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of qualifying a second overseas supplier while keeping just-in-time.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: A second supplier reduces the chance of a halted line [k]. If one supplier fails, CaseCraft can switch orders across, avoiding 3-day stoppages like the two that cost $96,000 in lost output [app], protecting the two smartphone contracts and future renewals [an]. Benefit 2: A second supplier keeps the benefits of just-in-time [k]. Just-in-time still avoids the $120,000 needed to rebuild a 3-week stock, plus storage costs [app], so the firm keeps its lean cash flow while gaining resilience [an].

knowledge_max_2: Multiple suppliers reduce risk of stoppage / increase resilience
Qualifying a second supplier preserves low-stock / lean advantages
application_max_2: Two halts cost $96,000; avoiding repeat losses protects contracts
Avoids $120,000 3-week stock and storage costs
analysis_max_2: Protects the two smartphone contracts and reputation
Maintains low working capital and lean cash flow

questions.question_text: Do you think CaseCraft Ltd should abandon just-in-time? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Arguments for abandoning: two supplier failures in 8 months stopped the line for 6 days in total and cost $96,000 in lost output plus $18,000 air-freight bills [k]. Rebuilding a 3-week stock of parts costing $120,000 would let the line run through most disruptions and protect the two smartphone contracts [app]. Predictability and customer trust may outweigh stock-holding costs [an]. Arguments against abandoning: a 3-week stock ties up $120,000 that could be used elsewhere and adds storage costs, eroding the savings just-in-time created [k]. Qualifying a second overseas supplier attacks the same risk at lower cost while keeping working capital free [app]. Large stock also raises obsolescence risk for phone-specific parts [an]. Overall, abandoning just-in-time entirely is not justified; qualifying a second supplier plus a small emergency stock of critical parts is cheaper and safer than either extreme [eval]. However, if no second supplier can be qualified within 3 months, rebuilding the 3-week stock is a necessary stopgap [eval].

Stock holding costs: capital tied up, storage, obsolescence

$120,000 3-week stock; 12-week lead time; 8 months experience

Second supplier preserves lean benefits at lower cost; obsolescence risk of stock
evaluation_max_2: Justified conditional judgement favouring second supplier / small emergency stock
Stated fallback if supplier cannot be qualified quickly

scenario_stem:
Anchorline Hotel is a private limited company with 48 guest rooms. Revenue was $1,150,000, profit after tax $230,000, and occupancy averaged 74%. The board paid a dividend of $85,000 and holds $96,000 of retained profit brought forward.

The hotel wants to refurbish the kitchen for $140,000 and replace its shuttle vans for $54,000. The finance manager proposes funding the kitchen from retained profit and selling 2 vans for $14,000, but shareholders are divided between higher dividends and investment.

questions.question_text: Calculate the retained profit Anchorline Hotel added this year. Show your working.
questions.model_answer: Retained profit = Profit after tax − Dividends paid = $230,000 − $85,000 = $145,000 [2].

knowledge_max_2: correct formula: profit after tax − dividends

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of using retained profit to fund the kitchen refurbishment.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Retained profit is an internal source of finance [k], so the hotel avoids interest charges on the $140,000 kitchen cost [app]. Advantage 2: Reinvesting retained profit keeps ownership unchanged [k]; no new shares need to be issued and existing shareholders retain full control [app].

knowledge_max_2: internal source: no interest or repayment required
ownership and control remain unchanged
application_max_2: no interest on the $140,000 kitchen cost
no new shares issued; control stays with current shareholders

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages of relying only on retained profit to fund both projects.
questions.model_answer: Disadvantage 1: The two projects total $194,000 [k], more than this year's $145,000 retained profit [app], so the hotel must draw on its $96,000 brought-forward balance, leaving nothing in reserve for next year [an]. Disadvantage 2: Retained profit is finite and may disappoint shareholders [k]; the board already paid $85,000 [app], and shareholders expecting an increase may resent an unchanged or lower dividend while funds are locked into the kitchen and vans [an].

knowledge_max_2: retained profit is limited in amount and may be insufficient
using retained profit may reduce or prevent a dividend
application_max_2: projects total $194,000 vs $145,000 retained profit this year
existing $85,000 dividend already paid and shareholders divided
analysis_max_2: drawing on the $96,000 brought-forward leaves no reserve for next year
shareholder dissatisfaction could damage relations with owners

questions.question_text: Do you think Anchorline Hotel should fund both projects from retained profit or pay a higher dividend? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Funding both projects from retained profit [k] gives the hotel a refurbished kitchen and new shuttle vans, protecting the $1,150,000 revenue from its 48 rooms [app]; the projects cost $194,000 and this year's retained profit is $145,000, so the $96,000 brought forward would comfortably cover the gap [an]. Paying a higher dividend [k] would reward shareholders who backed a 74% occupancy year and satisfy those shareholders wanting immediate returns [app]; however, it would leave the kitchen and vans unfunded, pushing the board towards borrowing or delaying investment that grows future profits [an]. On balance, the projects should be funded from retained profit [eval], because the refurbishment and vans should raise future earnings more than a one-off dividend rise would satisfy owners [eval].

knowledge_max_2: reinvestment strengthens future earning capacity
dividends reward shareholders in the short term
application_max_2: projects cost $194,000; $145,000 retained profit plus $96,000 brought forward covers it

analysis_max_2: $96,000 brought forward comfortably covers the shortfall on both projects
delaying or borrowing increases cost and slows investment for future profit
evaluation_max_2: overall justified recommendation balancing reinvestment against dividends
judgement weighs long-term earnings growth against immediate shareholder return

scenario_stem:
Ashford Grain Co-operative is a primary sector partnership of 14 wheat farmers in industrialising Country X. They sell 9,000 tonnes of wheat yearly to exporters at $240 per tonne. Manufacturing grew 8.2% last year, and domestic bakeries import $30 million of flour annually.

The farmers consider a $500,000 co-operative flour mill selling flour at $360 per tonne, keeping $120 per tonne of added value. The mill needs government approval and a trained miller, and would run two shifts.

questions.question_text: Outline why the primary sector's share of employment falls as a country develops.

scenario_stem:
Westbrook Industrial Coatings is a private limited company painting steel tanks and beams, with 58 spray-painters and 8 QA inspectors on 2 lines. Revenue is $5.6 million; 6% rejections cost $340,000. Painters earn $11.90, but staff turnover is 20%.

Ten coach painters lead daily briefings and approve first-off checks — Herzberg's responsibility and recognition motivators in action [app], and coach-led checks catch spray faults early, helping to cut the 6% rejection rate on tanks and beams [an]. scenario_stem:
Calloway Rods is a sole trader workshop run by Sam Whitaker, building bespoke trout and salmon rods. Each takes about 7 days, sells at $340, and 260 rods were made last year with a 6-week waiting list.

Discounted cork grips and local angling shops wanting 3 standard models create a choice: keep job production, switch those models to batches of 40 alongside bespoke work, or go fully batch and drop custom orders, with an answer due in 3 months.

questions.question_text: Outline two advantages of batch production.
questions.model_answer: Batch production allows a range of different products to be made on shared machines, keeping some flexibility between runs [1]. Unit costs are lower than job production because larger quantities spread fixed and setup costs [1]. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Different products made in batches on shared machinery / flexibility of range
Lower unit cost than job production / setup costs spread over batch

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why batch production might help Calloway Rods.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Batch production lowers unit costs for standard lines [k]. Making 3 standard models in batches of 40 would spread labour and machine time across 120 rods, cutting average cost per rod compared with one-off builds [app]. Reason 2: Batch production can supply local angling shops reliably [k]. Stocking 3 standard models in predictable batches of 40 matches exactly what the shops have asked for and relieves the 6-week waiting list [app].

knowledge_max_2: Lower unit cost from larger runs / shared fixed costs
Predictable stock supply for retailers
application_max_2: 3 standard models x 40 = 120 rods per batch cycle
Angling shops asked for 3 standard models; 6-week waiting list

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Calloway Rods could face if it switched fully to batch production.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Unique bespoke work would disappear [k]. Dropping custom orders means giving up the $340 bespoke trout and salmon rods and the loyal customers behind the 6-week waiting list [app], shrinking the firm's premium reputation with serious anglers [an]. Problem 2: Batch production risks unsold stock [k]. If the 3 standard models do not sell in batches of 40, capital is tied up in rods that angling shops cannot shift [app], raising storage costs and waste if designs fall out of fashion [an].

knowledge_max_2: Loss of custom/bespoke work and premium reputation
Risk of unsold stock / capital tied up in batches

3 standard models in batches of 40 held as stock

questions.question_text: Do you think Sam should switch the three standard models to batch production alongside the bespoke work? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Arguments for switching: producing 3 standard models in batches of 40 spreads setup costs, frees capacity for bespoke rods and shortens the 6-week waiting list [k]. Supplier discounts on identical hand-built cork grips ordered in batches cut material costs further [app]. The angling shops' request widens the market beyond the 260 rods sold last year [an]. Arguments against: splitting production could dilute the bespoke reputation that supports $340 pricing [k]. Batch runs of 40 unsold models tie up cash, and savings only materialise if grips are ordered for proven demand [app]. Overproducing one design would leave expensive unsold stock [an]. Overall, adding 3 standard batch models alongside bespoke work captures shop demand and supplier discounts without abandoning the firm's identity, so the partial switch is justified [eval]. However, Sam should keep batches small and monitor sell-through before expanding, protecting workshop flexibility [eval].

scenario_stem:
Foxglove Lodge is a partnership guest house with 14 letting rooms, founded by Mark and Leanne Doyle. Revenue was $310,000. Bookings peak in summer. They want a self-catering annexe costing $120,000, adding 8 family rooms, and must repair the kitchen roof for $26,000 while keeping $9,400 a month for wages.

Internal sources are $74,000 of retained profit, an unused minibus worth $22,000, and $30,000 of personal savings. Both owners work full-time and must decide which project to fund first and from which source.

questions.question_text: Identify two needs for finance that Foxglove Lodge has.
questions.model_answer: Capital expenditure for the annexe and the kitchen roof repair [1] and working capital to pay the monthly wages [1].

knowledge_max_2: capital expenditure (annexe / roof repair)
working capital for day-to-day costs such as wages

questions.question_text: Explain two internal sources of finance available to Foxglove Lodge.
questions.model_answer: Source 1: Retained profit [k]; the lodge has accumulated $74,000 from past profits, which could pay the $26,000 roof repair in full and still leave $48,000 towards the annexe [app]. Source 2: Sale of the unused minibus [k] would raise $22,000 towards the project without borrowing or repaying interest [app].

knowledge_max_2: retained profit — internal reinvestment of past earnings
sale of existing assets — selling unused property or equipment
application_max_2: $74,000 covers the $26,000 roof and leaves $48,000
minibus valued at $22,000 sold to fund part of the annexe

questions.question_text: Explain two problems the owners face when choosing between these sources.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Each source is finite [k]; internal sources total $126,000 but the annexe and the roof cost $146,000 together, a shortfall of $20,000 [app], so something must be delayed, reduced or financed from outside the business [an]. Problem 2: Using personal savings carries a heavy opportunity cost [k]; the $30,000 is also the family's safety cushion [app], and spending it on the annexe would leave them exposed if bookings fell or another repair was needed [an].

personal savings involve opportunity cost and lost security

Delaying the annexe and repairing only the roof [k] would protect the $30,000 personal savings and keep wages of $9,400 a month secure [app]; however, the lodge would forfeit a full summer of extra family-room income and might lose guests to rival guest houses [an]. On balance, the Doyles should build the annexe now [eval], using retained profit, the minibus sale and savings, and covering the $20,000 gap with a small short-term bank loan only if strictly needed [eval].

scenario_stem:
Harwick Appliances Ltd is a private limited company manufacturing washing machines and ovens for retailers and export customers in 6 countries, employing 210 workers. Revenue rose from $16.1 million to $18.5 million; wages rose 7%.

The economy is close to full employment; corporation tax has risen from 21% to 25% and skilled workers are scarce. The directors must decide whether to spend $1.5 million automating 2 production lines, cutting the need for 30 assembly workers, or keep manual lines and accept slower output.

questions.question_text: Define 'full employment'.
questions.model_answer: Full employment is a situation in which everyone who is willing and able to work at the prevailing wage rate can find a job, i.e. unemployment is kept at a very low level. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies that everyone willing and able to work can find a job
Identifies that unemployment is kept very low

questions.question_text: Explain two effects on Harwick Appliances Ltd of the economy being close to full employment.
questions.model_answer: Effect 1: Skilled assembly workers are hard to find, so Harwick cannot recruit the workers it needs and output cannot grow; it already employs 210 workers at one factory. [k] [app] Effect 2: Wages across the economy are rising fast — Harwick's wages have risen 7% this year — pushing up costs and squeezing profit after the 25% corporation tax. [k] [app]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies labour shortages/recruitment difficulty near full employment
Identifies upward pressure on wages (and costs)
application_max_2: References 210 workers at one factory / inability to recruit assembly workers
References the 7% wage rise or the 25% corporation tax

questions.question_text: Explain two problems of automating the 2 production lines at a cost of $1.5 million.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: The $1.5 million investment must come from profit or borrowing, so cash is tied up and financial risk rises. [k] With corporation tax now at 25%, profit retained after tax is lower, making the $1.5 million harder to fund internally. [app] High upfront costs must be recovered through higher output, so the automated lines need to run at high capacity for years. [an] Problem 2: Automation would cut the need for 30 assembly workers, causing possible redundancies and lower morale among the remaining 210 workers. [k] Cutting jobs could damage Harwick's reputation as a stable employer in the 6 countries where it sells. [app] Low morale and industrial relations problems could disrupt production and offset the wage savings from automation. [an]

Identifies redundancies/low morale/reputation risk from automation

References the 30 assembly workers, 210 workers or 6 countries

Explains how job losses/morale problems can offset automation savings

questions.question_text: Do you think Harwick Appliances Ltd should automate the 2 production lines? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Yes: automating solves the underlying problem — near full employment means labour is scarce and Harwick's wages have risen 7% this year. [k] Harwick employs 210 workers, cannot recruit assembly staff and faces 25% corporation tax, so cutting unit labour costs protects profit. [app] The $1.5 million spent on 2 lines would stabilise output of washing machines and ovens and remove the 30 hard-to-fill vacancies. [an] However, $1.5 million is a major commitment and automating may cut jobs and lower morale among the workforce. [k] Keeping manual lines preserves all 210 jobs and avoids upfront debt, but slower output and rising wages would hold Harwick back while revenue grows from $16.1 million to $18.5 million. [app] Redundancies could also hurt the brand's reputation in 6 markets, though retraining affected workers onto the new lines would soften this. [an] Overall, Harwick should automate the 2 lines, because chronic labour shortages near full employment make the current approach unsustainable. [eval] This is justified by 7% wage growth and the recruitment gap; spending $1.5 million now is cheaper long-term than permanent wage inflation, provided some workers are retrained. [eval]

scenario_stem:
Kestrel Construction Ltd is a private limited company building houses and warehouses in Marlow. It owns one plot near the ring road large enough for either 12 houses or a single distribution warehouse. The houses would earn $900,000 over 18 months; the warehouse $650,000 over 14 months.

With only $120,000 saved for materials, Daniel must choose, since land prices have risen 20% since 2023 and delays could raise costs 15%. Scarcity means every choice carries an opportunity cost.

questions.question_text: Define 'land' as a factor of production.
questions.model_answer: Land refers to all natural resources used to produce goods and services, such as the plot near the ring road in Marlow and materials like timber and sand. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Land = all natural resources used in producing goods and services, e.g. the building plot, timber, sand or land itself
Reward any example of a natural resource input used to make goods or services (2 marks for a clear definition with reference to nature)

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why land is important to Kestrel Construction Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Land is a basic factor of production that provides natural resources for making goods [k]. Kestrel's only plot near the ring road is large enough for either 12 houses or a single distribution warehouse worth $900,000 or $650,000 of revenue [app]. Reason 2: Without suitable land the business cannot produce or sell anything [k]. With no plot to build on, the $900,000 house scheme and the $650,000 warehouse scheme would both be impossible and Kestrel would earn nothing [app].

knowledge_max_2: Land provides natural resources / site / raw materials needed for production
Without land the firm cannot produce or generate sales revenue
application_max_2: Reference to the single plot being large enough for 12 houses or the warehouse
Reference to the $900,000 (houses) and $650,000 (warehouse) revenue figures / the Marlow site

questions.question_text: Explain two ways in which opportunity cost affects Kestrel Construction Ltd's decision.
questions.model_answer: Point 1: Opportunity cost is the next best alternative forgone when a choice is made [k]. By choosing the 12 houses, Kestrel gives up the chance to earn $650,000 from the warehouse, so the true cost of the houses includes the lost warehouse revenue [app]. This means Daniel must compare both revenue streams carefully before spending the $120,000 of scarce materials money [an]. Point 2: Scarcity of the single plot means the land cannot serve both projects [k]. Committing the plot to the housing scheme removes the chance to use it for the warehouse, so every scarce input carries a sacrifice [app]. This forces Daniel to recognise that scarcity creates opportunity cost in all of his decisions, not only in this one [an].

knowledge_max_2: Opportunity cost = next best alternative forgone when a decision is made
Scarcity = limited resources vs unlimited wants, forcing economic choices
application_max_2: Reference to forgoing the $650,000 warehouse revenue if the 12 houses are chosen (or vice versa)
Reference to the single plot / the $120,000 materials finance as scarce resources
analysis_max_2: Analysis of how foregone revenue or profits changes the true cost of each option
Analysis chain linking scarcity -> choice -> sacrifice -> better decision-making

questions.question_text: Do you think Kestrel Construction Ltd should build the 12 houses rather than the warehouse? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Argument for the houses: Building 12 houses suits Kestrel's construction skills and could earn $900,000 in revenue [k]. That is $250,000 more than the warehouse's $650,000, even though it takes 18 months rather than 14 [app]. However, the scheme ties up $120,000 of scarce materials money and any delay could raise costs by 15%, squeezing the margin for error on a fixed plot [an]. Argument for the warehouse: The warehouse earns $650,000 within 14 months, releasing cash faster for future projects [k]. Land prices have risen 20% since 2023, so completing quickly protects the value of the Marlow plot [app]. But $650,000 is $250,000 less revenue and would leave Kestrel dependent on a single buyer in a weaker warehouse market [an]. Overall, on the stem's figures the housing project offers the higher revenue of $900,000 and matches Kestrel's house-building specialism, so it should proceed only if Daniel secures firm buyer contracts and a contingency for the 15% cost risk [eval]. Otherwise the quicker, lower-risk warehouse would be the wiser choice for a business holding just $120,000 in materials finance [eval].

Warehouse gives faster cash return (14 vs 18 months) and matches 20% land price rise

scenario_stem:
Queensbridge Deli & Rotisserie, a family-run deli, serves about 420 roast-chicken meals weekly. Each costs $8 and, with 25% cost-plus pricing, sells at $10, giving $4,200 revenue and $840 weekly mark-up profit.

A new supermarket deli nearby charges $9.50, attracting price-sensitive shoppers. The owner must keep 25% cost-plus pricing and promote quality, or adopt competitive pricing at $9.50, reviewing the decision in September after 8 weeks.

questions.question_text: Define 'mark-up'.
questions.model_answer: A mark-up is the amount added to the cost of a product to arrive at its selling price, usually expressed as a percentage of cost; for example, adding 25% to the $8 cost gives a price of $10 [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages to Queensbridge Deli & Rotisserie of keeping cost-plus pricing.

Problem 2: No signal from the market [k], as cost-plus only covers the $8 cost plus 25% and ignores what shoppers will pay [app], so falling demand may go unnoticed until the September trading review [an].

scenario_stem:

scenario_stem:
Silverbirch Aerospace Plc is a public limited company making small aircraft components in Country X, with 240 workers and revenue of $18 million last year. It wants a $6.5 million plant to cut delivery times and meet overseas orders.

The Board is choosing between issuing 2.5 million new shares at $2.60 each and a bank loan of $6.5 million over 8 years at 8.5%, costing $552,500 yearly. Its 40 million existing shares make shareholders fear dilution of control.

questions.question_text: Define 'issue of shares' as a source of finance.
questions.model_answer: An issue of shares is the sale of shares (small ownership stakes) in a company to investors in exchange for capital. It is a long-term source of external finance available to limited companies, and the money raised does not have to be repaid. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Sale of shares (ownership stakes) to investors for capital
Money raised does not have to be repaid; long-term external finance for limited companies

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of issuing new shares rather than taking a bank loan to finance the new plant.
questions.model_answer: First advantage: issuing shares provides the $6.5 million of capital without adding fixed repayments, so $552,500 a year of interest is saved and cash flow is eased while the 240 workers are paid [k], which suits a company whose revenue is already $18 million and whose overseas orders are rising [app]. Second advantage: shares carry no obligation to repay the capital, unlike the 8-year bank loan at 8.5%, so the risk of insolvency is reduced if profits fall [k], and the $2.60 issue price means 2.5 million new shares raise exactly the $6.5 million needed without increasing the company's debt [app].

knowledge_max_2: No repayment obligation and no interest to pay on share capital
Reduces insolvency risk compared with fixed loan repayments
application_max_2: $6.5 million raised matches the cost of the new plant
$552,500 per year of interest avoided
2.5 million shares at $2.60 equals $6.5 million

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages of issuing new shares for the existing shareholders of Silverbirch Aerospace Plc.
questions.model_answer: First disadvantage: existing shareholders' ownership would be diluted, because issuing 2.5 million shares to new investors reduces the percentage held by the owners of the existing 40 million shares [k], meaning each share receives a smaller slice of any future dividends and has weaker voting power over how the new $6.5 million plant is run [app], so existing investors may resist the issue or demand a higher share price [an]. Second disadvantage: control of the company could change hands, because new shareholders voting at the AGM may outvote current holders on key decisions [k], for example whether the $6.5 million raised is reinvested to cut delivery times or paid out as dividends [app], so the original owners risk losing their ability to steer the company's long-term strategy [an].

Possible loss of control; weaker voting power over decisions

Dividend per share and voting strength reduced for current holders

analysis_max_2: Dilution leads to smaller dividends and weaker influence, causing shareholder resistance
Loss of control means original owners cannot direct company strategy

questions.question_text: Do you think Silverbirch Aerospace Plc should issue new shares rather than take the 8-year bank loan to finance the new plant? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Issuing shares would raise the full $6.5 million needed for the plant without creating fixed repayments, saving $552,500 a year of interest and keeping cash flow healthy while orders grow [k], and because revenue is already $18 million with 240 workers, the company can afford to dilute the 40 million existing shares by issuing 2.5 million new ones at $2.60 [app], so the business avoids the risk of defaulting on the loan if overseas demand weakens [an]. However, the bank loan would keep ownership and control unchanged and protect the existing 40 million shares from dilution, costing only $552,500 per year of interest, which a business with $18 million revenue could comfortably cover [k], and loan interest is tax-deductible whereas share dividends are not, and unlike share issues the loan does not permanently reduce shareholders' claim on profits [app], so the loan is less damaging to owners in the long run [an]. Overall, I think the company should issue the new shares, because eliminating $552,500 of annual interest and avoiding 8 years of fixed repayments outweighs the dilution from a 2.5 million share issue when the plant will cut delivery times and win more overseas orders [eval]. The decision would change only if the current owners refused any loss of control, in which case the bank loan would be the safer choice [eval].

Loan preserves existing ownership and control; interest is tax-deductible

analysis_max_2: No fixed repayments reduce default risk during demand fluctuations
Dilution reduces owners' claim on profits and control
evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation weighing interest saving against dilution

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Coppermill Furniture Ltd is a private limited company making oak dining tables and chairs. It made $2.6 million sales; a 2023 $400,000 loan at 5% leaves $300,000 outstanding.

The base rate has risen from 5% to 9%, adding $12,000 yearly. Priya Raman wants a $180,000 second workshop via a 10% loan costing $18,000 yearly. The order book is full, but customers may spend less if rates stay high; she must decide whether to expand now or wait.

questions.question_text: Identify two effects of a rise in interest rates on a business with a bank loan.
questions.model_answer: One effect is higher interest payments on the outstanding loan, which reduce profit. A second effect is less cash available to fund other spending or expansion, which may force the business to delay plans. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Higher interest payments on an existing loan reduce profit
Higher borrowing costs make new loans more expensive

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the interest rate rise on Coppermill Furniture Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Higher interest costs: the rise from 5% to 9% on the $300,000 outstanding balance adds $12,000 a year, which will reduce Coppermill's profit [k], and this extra cost arrives while the machinery loan taken out in 2023 is still being repaid [app]. More expensive expansion finance: the proposed second workshop would need a further loan at 10%, costing about $18,000 a year in interest [k], which may make the $180,000 expansion hard to justify if customers spend less while rates stay high [app].

knowledge_max_2: Interest payments on an existing loan increase when rates rise
New borrowing becomes more expensive when rates rise
application_max_2: The outstanding balance is $300,000, so the rise from 5% to 9% adds $12,000 a year
The proposed $180,000 workshop loan at 10% would cost about $18,000 a year in interest

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why rising interest rates might reduce demand for Coppermill's furniture.
questions.model_answer: Higher mortgage and loan payments: rising interest rates increase the cost of borrowing for households [k], so buyers of oak dining furniture already stretched by higher monthly repayments have less money to spend [app]. As buyers postpone big-ticket purchases, Coppermill's order book may shorten from its current 6 months, cutting future revenue [an]. Attractive savings returns: higher rates make saving more rewarding, so households save rather than spend [k], meaning demand for non-essential items like oak furniture falls [app], which would leave Coppermill with unsold stock and lower cash inflow [an].

knowledge_max_2: Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive for consumers
Higher interest rates make saving more attractive than spending
application_max_2: Coppermill makes big-ticket items such as oak dining tables, which are often financed by borrowing
Coppermill fears customers may spend less if rates stay high
analysis_max_2: Higher mortgage and loan repayments reduce disposable income and big-ticket demand
More saving means less spending on non-essential furniture, cutting future sales

questions.question_text: Do you think Priya Raman should proceed with the $180,000 expansion now? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Proceeding now would let Coppermill open the second workshop while its order book is full for the next 6 months [k], spreading the $18,000 a year interest on a $180,000 loan across higher sales [app], so profit could rise and the firm could win customers from rivals [an]. However, the rise from 5% to 9% already adds $12,000 a year to existing loan costs, and customers may spend less so demand could drop below the order book's promise [k], leaving the new loan hard to repay on only $2.6 million of sales [app], and serving two loans at once could push the business into debt it cannot service [an]. On balance, Priya should proceed but with caution, for example by confirming orders before signing the loan [eval], because the order book is full and waiting could mean missing the selling season when rates fall [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Expansion can increase output and sales while demand is strong
Higher interest rates increase repayment burdens and financial risk
application_max_2: The order book is full for the next 6 months at time the 9% rate takes effect
Existing loan balance of $300,000 now costs $12,000 a year extra; expansion loan would cost $18,000 a year
analysis_max_2: New capacity could lift output and win market share before demand falls
If sales fall, the business may be unable to service the additional loan
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation (proceed with caution or confirm orders first)
Judgement weighs short-term opportunity against borrowing risk

scenario_stem:
Willow & Pine Furniture Ltd is a private limited company handcrafting oak dining tables. It employs 14 carpenters paid $38,000 yearly and 3 apprentices at $16,000 each, producing 900 tables sold at $520. Wages cost $580,000 annually.

The sisters consider division of labour, reorganising into 4 stations so each worker specialises. Trials show a table takes 6 hours instead of 11, lifting output to 1,240 tables yearly, but carpenters fear narrower skills. Quality complaints must stay below 3%.

questions.question_text: Define 'labour' as a factor of production.
questions.model_answer: Labour refers to the human effort, both physical and mental, used to produce goods and services, such as the 14 carpenters and 3 apprentices working in the Willow & Pine workshop. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Labour = human effort used in producing goods and services
Reward references to physical/mental effort, or workers such as carpenters, apprentices or staff

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why labour is important to Willow & Pine Furniture Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Labour performs the skilled work needed to create the product [k]. Willow & Pine employs 14 carpenters at $38,000 per year plus 3 apprentices, whose hands craft the 900 tables sold at $520 each [app]. Reason 2: Without labour the business cannot turn timber into furniture [k]. If the carpenters and apprentices stopped work, the $580,000 wage bill would produce nothing and the 900-table output could not be reached [app].

knowledge_max_2: Labour does the physical/mental work of production
Without labour, production is impossible / no goods and services made
application_max_2: Reference to 14 carpenters and 3 apprentices / $38,000 and $16,000 pay
Reference to 900 tables a year at $520 / $580,000 wage bill

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of division of labour for Willow & Pine Furniture Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Point 1: Division of labour means workers specialise in one repeated stage of production [k]. Trials show specialised staff can finish a table in 6 hours instead of 11, lifting potential output to 1,240 tables a year [app]. This raises productivity so the $580,000 wage bill is spread over more units and average labour cost per table falls [an]. Point 2: Specialised workers become faster and more skilled at their single stage [k]. Each of the 4 stations such as cutting or finishing would develop deep expertise, keeping quality complaints below the 3% target [app]. This improves customer satisfaction, protects the brand and supports repeat orders from the Fenwick workshop [an].

knowledge_max_2: Specialisation in one repeated task / stage of production
Workers become quicker and more expert through repetition
application_max_2: Reference to 6 hours vs 11 hours build time and 1,240 tables a year
Reference to 4 stations and the 3% quality complaint threshold
analysis_max_2: Analysis that higher output per worker lowers average cost / raises profit margin
Analysis that fewer errors improve quality, reputation and repeat sales

questions.question_text: Do you think Willow & Pine Furniture Ltd should introduce division of labour in its workshop? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Argument for division of labour: Specialisation would cut build time from 11 hours to 6 hours per table and could lift output to 1,240 tables a year [k]. Average labour cost per table would fall and revenue could rise sharply if demand holds for oak tables at $520 each [app]. However, gains depend on staff accepting repetitive jobs across 4 stations and on quality complaints staying below 3% [an]. Argument against: Whole-table crafting preserves the craft skills that justify premium pricing and keeps workers engaged [k]. Forcing specialisation could trigger boredom and resignations, risking the loss of experienced $38,000-a-year carpenters [app]. This risk is manageable through job rotation and careful deployment of the 3 apprentices, but it cannot be ignored [an]. Overall, division of labour is the better choice because saving 5 hours per table and the chance to reach 1,240 tables a year clearly outweigh the morale risk, provided the Ashbys consult staff and monitor the 3% quality threshold closely [eval]. Otherwise output gains could be cancelled out by turnover, rework and quality claims [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Division of labour cuts build time (11 to 6 hours) and can raise output (1,240 tables)
Whole-table crafting preserves skill, variety and worker engagement
application_max_2: Uses 6 hours vs 11 hours, 1,240 tables, 4 stations and $580,000 wage figures from the stem
Reference to monotony fears and the 3% quality complaints target
analysis_max_2: Analysis of productivity/cost per unit versus motivation and turnover risks
Analysis of quality outcomes and how they affect revenue and reputation
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation supporting specialisation (or retention) conditional on consultation and quality monitoring
Balanced judgement weighing output gains against craft-skill loss and boredom

scenario_stem:
Copperpot Coffee House is a sole trader cafe chain with 4 shops, 17 part-time baristas and 3 managers. Monthly revenue is $54,000, with $4.60 average spend. Turnover reached 33%, and milk and pastry wastage runs at 9% of stock.

Priya Nair decides before the festive rush: a $150 bonus for baristas in shops beating $14,500 sales with wastage under 8%, or rotating baristas between counter, espresso and baking, with latte art training and promotion after 12 months.

questions.question_text: Define 'bonus'.
questions.model_answer: A bonus is an extra payment made to employees in addition to their basic pay, usually linked to reaching targets or strong performance [2].

knowledge_max_2: extra payment on top of basic pay
linked to targets or performance

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of the monthly bonus proposal for Copperpot Coffee House.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Clear target focus [k], as every barista in a shop beating $14,500 in sales with wastage below 8% earns the $150 bonus [app]. Advantage 2: Higher productivity and less waste [k], as staff concentrate on upselling above the average customer spend of $4.60 and reducing milk and pastry waste from 9% [app].

knowledge_max_2: focus on agreed targets
higher productivity and lower wastage
application_max_2: $150 bonus
8% wastage
$4.60 spend
9% stock waste

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of the non-financial approach for this business.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Greater flexibility and skill coverage [k], as rotating baristas between counter, espresso and baking duties lets the 4 shops cover absences [app], keeping service fast during the festive rush [an]. Benefit 2: Improved retention and loyalty [k], as fortnightly latte art training and a lead barista promotion after 12 months give staff a career path [app], reducing the 33% turnover rate and hiring costs [an].

retention and loyalty through career progression

questions.question_text: Do you think Copperpot Coffee House should introduce the $150 monthly bonus rather than the non-financial approach? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The bonus scheme links pay directly to results [k], rewarding baristas when their shop beats $14,500 in sales with wastage below 8% [app], which should lift the average $4.60 spend and trim the 9% wastage [an]. The non-financial approach instead builds lasting commitment [k]: rotating duties, fortnightly latte art training and a lead barista promotion after 12 months give the 17 part-time baristas variety and progression [app], tackling the 33% turnover that drives recruitment costs [an]. Overall, the non-financial approach is the better choice for Copperpot [eval], because its problems are skills, variety and retention rather than effort; however, the owner could keep a modest version of the bonus as a short-term festive incentive on top of the rotation plan [eval].

non-financial builds commitment and retention

scenario_stem:
Bluewater Frozen Foods, a discount retailer, opened 3 stores with $900,000 capital. Its frozen vegetables sell at $3.50 using penetration pricing, against $6.00 at the national chain; $2.75 unit costs leave $0.75 per bag, and first-month sales hit 9,000 bags.

The board is choosing whether to hold $3.50 for 6 months to build 15% local share or switch to competitive pricing at $5.25, trusting local sourcing. With 68% of shoppers citing price, they meet in 3 weeks.

questions.question_text: Define 'market share'.
questions.model_answer: Market share is the proportion of total sales in a market held by one business or brand, usually expressed as a percentage of total market sales; it shows how well a business is performing against its rivals [2].

knowledge_max_2: the proportion of total market sales held by one business or brand
usually expressed as a percentage of total market sales

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages to Bluewater Frozen Foods of holding the $3.50 penetration price.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Rapid share growth [k], as $3.50 continues to undercut the national chain's $6.00, drawing the 68% of shoppers who switched for price and lifting the 3 stores toward the 15% local market share target [app]. Advantage 2: High volume drives store traffic [k], as 9,000 bags sold in month 1 means more shoppers also buy other groceries on the same trip [app].

knowledge_max_2: builds market share quickly
high sales volume increases store traffic and basket size
application_max_2: $3.50 price versus the national chain's $6.00; 68% switched for price
9,000 bags sold in month 1 across 3 stores; 15% share target

questions.question_text: Explain two problems of Bluewater Frozen Foods holding the $3.50 penetration price.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Very thin margins [k], as the unit cost is $2.75, so each bag earns only $0.75 [app], which delays recovery of the $900,000 of owners' capital for longer [an]. Problem 2: Risk of a price war [k], as holding a deep discount invites rivals to match $3.50 [app], leaving Bluewater with thinner margins and no lasting share gain [an].

knowledge_max_2: penetration prices give very low profit margins
rivals may match the low price, triggering a price war
application_max_2: unit cost $2.75 gives only $0.75 margin per bag
$900,000 owners' capital; $3.50 launch price

questions.question_text: Do you think Bluewater Frozen Foods should hold the $3.50 penetration price rather than switch to competitive pricing at $5.25? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Holding $3.50 keeps the volume engine running [k]: $3.50 against the national chain's $6.00 pulled in 9,000 bags in month 1, and 68% of surveyed shoppers switched for price, supporting the push to 15% local market share [app], which builds scale, buying power and brand presence for future growth [an]. However, switching to $5.25 protects profit [k]: lifting the price into the competitive zone raises the margin from $0.75 to $2.50 per bag [app], turning thin trading into healthier cash to fund more stores [an]. Overall, Bluewater should hold $3.50 only until the 15% share target is met, then move towards $5.25 [eval], because penetration pricing is a launch tactic rather than a permanent strategy, and share won cheaply now must eventually convert into profit [eval].

knowledge_max_2: low penetration price wins volume and share quickly
switching to competitive pricing restores unit margin
application_max_2: $3.50 versus $6.00; 9,000 bags in month 1; 68% switched for price
$5.25 switching raises margin from $0.75 to $2.50

extra $1.75 per bag funds expansion and healthier cash flow
evaluation_max_2: recommends time-limited price hold then switch to competitive pricing
recognises penetration pricing is a launch tactic, not permanent strategy

scenario_stem:
Cinderford Brickworks is a private limited company supplying facing and engineering bricks to housebuilders, which spent $250,000 on a mechanised extrusion machine and automatic wire-cutter. The yard employs 74 workers, 30 of whom run the machines.

Output rose from 140,000 to 210,000 bricks per week and rejects fell from 7% to 3%, but clay prices climbed 12%. With $11.50 hourly wages tempting recruitment of 6 more workers, kilns are now the bottleneck and a wage rise is delayed to repay the loan.

questions.question_text: Define 'mechanisation'.
questions.model_answer: Mechanisation is the use of machines to carry out work that was previously done by hand, with workers still operating or controlling the machines [2].

knowledge_max_2: Use of machines to replace or assist manual labour
Human operators still control or supervise the machines

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Cinderford Brickworks introduced mechanised machines.
questions.model_answer: First, to raise output [k]; the mechanised extruder and wire-cutter lifted production from 140,000 to 210,000 bricks per week [app]. Second, to cut waste [k]; reject bricks fell from 7% to 3% after the machines were installed [app].

knowledge_max_2: To increase output/productivity
To reduce waste, rejects and human error
application_max_2: Production rose from 140,000 to 210,000 bricks per week
Reject bricks fell from 7% to 3%

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Cinderford Brickworks may face from its mechanisation.
questions.model_answer: First, dependence on skilled operators [k]: the business relies on 30 of its 74 workers to run the machines at $11.50 per hour [app], so any absence or breakdown could stop extrusion and widen the kiln bottleneck [an]. Second, rising input costs [k]: clay prices have climbed 12% [app], squeezing margins and making it harder to recover the $250,000 outlay without raising brick prices for builders [an].

knowledge_max_2: Dependence on specialist operators and machine breakdowns
Higher costs or repayment burden after investment
application_max_2: 30 of 74 workers run the machines at $11.50 per hour
Clay prices have climbed 12% after $250,000 was spent
analysis_max_2: Absences or breakdowns halt output and delay deliveries to builders

questions.question_text: Do you think Cinderford Brickworks should now invest in mechanising the kilns as well? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Yes, mechanising the kilns would attack the bottleneck [k]; the yard already lifted output from 140,000 to 210,000 bricks per week and cut rejects from 7% to 3% by mechanising extrusion [app]; applying the same approach to firing could raise capacity and stabilise quality while builder demand keeps growing [an]. However, machines reduce rather than increase labour needs [k]; the business has already spent $250,000 and pays operators $11.50 per hour amid a 12% clay price rise [app], and another large outlay plus recruiting 6 more workers risks overstretching cash if the housing market slows [an]. Overall I recommend phased kiln mechanisation funded largely from retained profit, because the proven 50% output gain outweighs the cost risk, provided the new recruits are trained to operate the machines before phase two begins [eval]; if clay costs keep climbing, phase two should be delayed rather than debt-financed [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Mechanisation raises capacity and reduces rejects
High capital cost and cash-flow strain

Conditional decision supported by stem figures

scenario_stem:
Bramblehurst Joinery Co is a private limited company making bespoke fitted kitchens and bedroom furniture, with revenue of $3.2 million and profit of $290,000. It needs $850,000 for a CNC routing machine to reduce production from 9 days to four per kitchen.

The owners weigh a bank loan of $850,000 over 5 years at 9%, costing $76,500 yearly and $382,500 in total interest, against issuing new shares to the founding families, reducing their holding from 75% to 60%.

questions.question_text: Define 'bank loan' as a source of finance.
questions.model_answer: A bank loan is a sum of money borrowed from a bank or other lender for an agreed period, to be repaid with interest in instalments. It is a long-term external source of finance commonly used to purchase fixed assets such as machinery. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Borrowing from a bank or lender for an agreed period

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the bank loan may be attractive to Bramblehurst Joinery Co.

Second reason: although the $76,500 annual interest is a fixed cost, the machine should cut cutting times from 9 days to 4 days per kitchen and win more orders, lifting revenue above $3.2 million so the interest is comfortably covered [k], and the 5-year term spreads repayment instead of demanding one large up-front sum the business cannot fund from profit of $290,000 alone [app].

Cutting time reduced from 9 days to 4 days per kitchen

questions.model_answer: First risk: the loan creates fixed repayments of about $76,500 per year plus principal for 5 years, regardless of profits [k], so if revenue falls below $3.2 million or a major kitchen contract is lost, the business could fail to pay and the bank could demand repayment or seize the CNC routing machine offered as security [app], meaning the business faces a real risk of insolvency during a downturn [an]. Second risk: interest of $382,500 over the 5 years is a direct cost that reduces net profit [k], so profit of $290,000 last year would drop sharply once interest is paid, leaving little retained profit for dividends or expansion [app], which limits the business's ability to fund future growth from internal sources [an].

knowledge_max_2: Fixed repayments must be made regardless of profit; default risk
Interest is a direct cost that reduces net profit and retained profit

Profit of $290,000 would be heavily reduced by interest
CNC routing machine may be used as security
analysis_max_2: Fixed repayments in a downturn lead to insolvency risk
Higher interest charges leave less retained profit for future expansion

questions.question_text: Do you think Bramblehurst Joinery Co should take the bank loan rather than issue shares to the founding families? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Taking the bank loan keeps the founding families in complete control, with their holding at 75% instead of falling to 60% [k], and it provides the $850,000 for the CNC routing machine immediately so cutting times fall from 9 days to 4 days per kitchen and orders can rise [app], meaning the loan could pay for itself from extra revenue within a few years [an]. However, the loan adds fixed repayments of $76,500 a year plus interest totalling $382,500, which is heavy compared with profit of $290,000 last year [k], so a bad year could push the business into cash-flow difficulty, whereas issuing shares to the families would bring cash with no interest and no repayment deadline [app], although dilution to 60% would weaken the families' control over the business [an]. Overall, I think the business should take the bank loan, because keeping 100% family control and the prospect of faster production and higher revenue outweigh the $76,500 annual interest, provided the families are confident orders will grow [eval]. If sales were likely to fall, the share issue would be the safer option because it carries no repayment obligation [eval].

application_max_2: Holding stays at 75% versus 60% under share issue

Fixed repayments create cash-flow risk in bad years versus dilution risk of shares
evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation supported by stem figures
Acknowledges conditions under which the decision would change

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Halden Motors is a sole trader car dealership selling new and used family cars. It earned $4.3 million revenue; 70% of buyers use finance packages, with new cars averaging $19,000.

The base interest rate fell from 6% to 3%; weekly finance applications rose from 18 to 29, and rival dealers are expanding. Mr Whitmore must choose: borrow $250,000 for 40 additional new cars before the peak sales season, or keep 90 cars and rely on used vehicles.

questions.question_text: Outline what is meant by the 'base rate' of interest.
questions.model_answer: The base rate is the interest rate set by a country's central bank. It influences the rates commercial banks charge on loans and pay on savings, so a cut makes borrowing cheaper. [2]

knowledge_max_2: The base rate is set by the central bank
The base rate influences commercial bank lending and saving rates

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the interest rate cut may increase Halden Motors' car sales.
questions.model_answer: Cheaper borrowing for buyers: cutting the base rate from 6% to 3% reduces monthly finance payments on cars [k], and with 70% of Halden's buyers using finance packages, more customers can afford a new $19,000 car [app]. Borrowing is now more attractive than saving: lower rates make saving less rewarding and credit cheaper [k], which is why weekly finance applications have jumped from 18 to 29 [app].

knowledge_max_2: Lower interest rates reduce the cost of borrowing
Lower interest rates reduce the reward for saving
application_max_2: Around 70% of Halden's buyers use finance packages and the average new car costs about $19,000
Weekly finance applications have risen from 18 to 29 since the cut from 6% to 3%

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Halden Motors of borrowing $250,000 to buy 40 additional new cars.
questions.model_answer: Meeting rising demand: sales applications have risen from 18 to 29 a week and rival dealers are expanding their forecourts [k], so having 40 extra cars ready before the peak sales season would let Halden capture sales rather than lose buyers to competitors [app]. More cars in stock lifts potential revenue by roughly 40 x $19,000 = $760,000 [an]. Economies of bulk buying: ordering 40 cars at once may earn volume discounts from manufacturers [k], reducing the cost of each additional car [app], and with finance demand this strong the extra stock should sell quickly, protecting cash flow [an].

scenario_stem:
Hartley & Rye Artisan Bakery runs 2 shops in a market town, with 14 bakers and 1,100 loyal weekly customers. It sells a staple cottage loaf at $3.20 and a premium heritage-grain sourdough at $5.50.

questions.question_text: Define 'price elasticity of demand'.

scenario_stem:

Second, how each is increased [k]; production can be raised by adding workers or overtime, while productivity rose because 96 workers replaced 120 after the new machines arrived [app].

Second advantage: debenture holders are not owners, so control of the company remains with the existing shareholders, and the 10-year repayment profile is gentler than repaying over 5 years [k], giving Drummond Alloys a longer, steadier repayment window for a $2 million furnace that will transform alloy output [app].

questions.model_answer: Two reasons are that internal sources such as retained profit may be insufficient to fund a large investment, and that external finance can provide the full sum needed more quickly than the business can build up reserves. Second advantage: new public shareholders bring permanent capital and may support future rapid growth across the 3 countries [k], and dividends are paid only if the Board declares them, unlike mandatory loan interest of $660,000 every year even in weak years [app], giving the Plc flexibility if the $5.5 million export contracts deliver slowly [an].

scenario_stem:
Clearbrook Logistics is a private limited company operating a distribution depot for supermarket customers. It earned $5.2 million and delivers 1,900 tonnes weekly. Regional unemployment is 2.1%, yet it has 25 unfilled driver vacancies after advertising for 4 months, and rivals have raised wages 8%.

questions.question_text: Identify two problems a very low unemployment rate can cause a business.

Rivals are competing for the same workers: two rival firms have already raised wages by 8% [k], so Clearbrook's current pay is no longer competitive [app].

Grows a committed workforce: training 25 local people with no prior driving experience builds loyalty [k], and they arrive without holding rival offers created by the 8% wage rises elsewhere [app], reducing the risk of trained drivers simply leaving for competitors [an].
