scenario_stem:
BrightPath Logistics is a private limited company parcel depot with 78 staff: 50 full-time on $15 an hour, 28 part-time on $12 an hour. Volumes rise 45% in the 10-week peak to 9,600 parcels weekly; 140 were damaged last year.

The manager must hire 20 additional part-time for the peak or 10 full-time at $31,200 with 6 weeks' training. Part-timers cannot drive heavy vehicles or forklifts. Advertising costs $180 per vacancy; the budget is $4,000.

questions.question_text: Define 'part-time employment'.
questions.model_answer: Part-time employment is a job in which the employee works fewer hours per week than a full-time employee, often on flexible or reduced shifts, and is paid for the hours worked. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Works fewer hours per week than a full-time employee
Paid for the hours worked, often on flexible or reduced shifts

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages to BrightPath Logistics of hiring 20 additional part-time workers for the peak.
questions.model_answer: Part-time workers are paid only for the hours they work [k], so during the 10-week pre-Christmas peak, when volumes rise by 45% to 9,600 parcels a week, the depot pays extra wages only when the extra capacity is actually needed [app]. Additional part-time staff reduce the overload on the existing 78 staff [k], helping to prevent repeats of the 140 damaged and 12 lost parcels that occurred last year [app].

knowledge_max_2: Pay only for the hours worked; labour cost flexes with demand
Extra staff relieve pressure and reduce errors/losses
application_max_2: 10-week peak; volumes rise 45% to 9,600 parcels a week; $12 an hour
140 damaged and 12 lost parcels last year; 78 existing staff

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of employing 10 additional full-time staff all year.
questions.model_answer: Full-time staff can be trained and trusted with demanding tasks [k]. The 50 current full-time drivers and operatives already handle heavy vehicles and forklifts, and new full-time hires would receive 6 weeks of training [app], widening the pool of skilled staff available all year, not just in December [an]. Full-time staff remain after the peak, giving the depot stable capacity [k]. Ten full-time salaries cost $312,000 a year (10 x $31,200), but these staff can cover quieter months and stand in for absences [app], reducing reliance on agency cover and repeated seasonal recruitment every December [an].

knowledge_max_2: Full-time staff can receive full training and handle more demanding tasks
Full-time staff provide year-round stable capacity and continuity
application_max_2: 6 weeks of training; heavy vehicles and forklifts; 50 current full-time staff
10 x $31,200 = $312,000 a year; stays after the peak ends
analysis_max_2: Wider skilled pool all year reduces bottlenecks and dependence on December cover
Year-round presence lowers agency costs and re-recruitment effort

questions.question_text: Do you think BrightPath Logistics should hire 20 additional part-time workers for the peak or 10 additional full-time staff all year? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Hiring 20 part-time workers is cheaper and more flexible [k]. At $12 an hour part-timers cost less than the $15 full-time rate and are paid only for hours worked, and 20 vacancies at $180 each total $3,600, still inside the $4,000 recruitment budget [app]. Bringing in extra hands should stop the 140 damaged and 12 lost parcels that overstretched staff caused last year [an]. However, part-time staff cannot drive heavy vehicles or operate forklifts [k], so the depot would still rely on its 50 full-time staff for the hardest tasks and might repeat the same overload in January returns or other peaks [app]. Full-time hires at $31,200 each would stay year-round, receive 6 weeks of training and cut the need to re-recruit every December [an]. Overall, the depot should hire the 20 part-time peak workers because demand is temporary and $312,000 of annual salary for year-round cover is hard to justify for a peak that lasts 10 weeks [eval]. If volumes stayed high all year, or forklift-certified full-time staff were urgently needed, the full-time option would become worth the extra cost [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Part-time: flexible, cheaper per hour, suits short peaks
Full-time: permanent, trained, versatile but costly year-round
application_max_2: $12 vs $15 an hour; $180 per vacancy; 20 vacancies = $3,600 inside $4,000 budget
10 x $31,200 = $312,000; 10-week peak; 9,600 parcels; 140 damaged and 12 lost
analysis_max_2: Cheap flexible capacity matched to a known 10-week peak reduces overload and parcel losses
Full-time gives year-round skill and stability but overspends for a temporary need
evaluation_max_2: Clear overall judgement justified by the temporary nature of the peak and the cost arithmetic
Recognises the circumstances in which the full-time option would be preferable

scenario_stem:
Northgate Electrical is a family-run partnership with 2 stores in Country X, 26 staff and $2.4 million sales. It stocks 1,800 product lines, mainly televisions and washing machines. Since a national chain opened nearby, sales fell 9% and footfall keeps dropping.

The owners must choose: use market research to identify local demand for smart home devices and restructure the range, or keep the range and cut prices 15% to match the national chain. Unsold televisions fill the shelves.

questions.question_text: Define 'market-orientated business'.
questions.model_answer: A business that bases its decisions on the needs and wants of customers identified through market research, rather than on what it currently produces [2].

knowledge_max_2: bases decisions on customer needs and wants
uses market research to guide decisions

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Northgate Electrical of being a market-orientated business.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Products would better match local customer needs [k], so stock such as smart home devices would appeal to country town buyers [app]. Benefit 2: Customer satisfaction and loyalty would improve [k], helping the 2 stores win back sales lost since the national chain opened [app].

knowledge_max_2: products match customer needs
higher customer satisfaction and loyalty
application_max_2: smart home devices as example stock
2 stores recovering from the 9% sales fall

questions.question_text: Explain two difficulties Northgate Electrical might face in becoming more market-orientated.
questions.model_answer: Difficulty 1: Market research costs money and staff time [k], so interviewing customers across both stores takes staff off the shop floor [app], leaving less cash for new stock purchases [an]. Difficulty 2: Customer tastes change quickly [k], so research done this year may not show what customers want next year [app], meaning the restructured range of 1,800 lines could still miss demand [an].

knowledge_max_2: market research costs money and time
customer tastes change quickly
application_max_2: interviewing customers across both stores
restructured range of 1,800 lines
analysis_max_2: less cash left for new stock purchases
range could still miss future demand

questions.question_text: Do you think Northgate Electrical should restructure its range based on market research rather than cut prices by 15%? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Market research would identify exactly what local customers want [k], letting Northgate stock profitable lines such as smart home devices instead of unsold televisions [app], differentiating the 2 stores from the national competitor and protecting margins [an]. However, cutting prices by 15% would produce an immediate sales boost [k], tempting country town customers to return [app], but it would slash profit on every one of its 1,800 product lines [an]. Overall, restructuring the range is the stronger strategy [eval] because differentiation builds loyalty that a price cut cannot [eval].

knowledge_max_2: market research identifies local customer wants
price cut gives immediate sales boost
application_max_2: smart home devices replacing unsold televisions
15% price cut on 1,800 product lines
analysis_max_2: differentiation protects margins against the national chain
price cut slashes profit on every line
evaluation_max_2: weighs differentiation and loyalty against short-term sales boost
justified recommendation to restructure the range

scenario_stem:
Driftwood Toy Co is a private limited company owned by Daniel Reyes, designing wooden trains and puzzles. With 68 workers it made 900,000 units exported to 6 countries for $7.2 million; paint-defect returns hit 5%.

One retailer threatened to cancel a $400,000 order. Within eight weeks Daniel chooses Total Quality Management — every worker responsible, weekly meetings and a suggestion scheme, costing $30,000 in training — or keeps four end-of-line inspectors, costing nothing but leaving returns unchanged.

questions.question_text: Outline what is meant by 'Total Quality Management (TQM)'.
questions.model_answer: Total Quality Management is a business-wide approach in which every employee is responsible for quality, with continuous improvement of processes and products until zero defects are achieved [2].

knowledge_max_2: Every employee in the business is responsible for quality
Continuous improvement aiming for zero defects

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Driftwood Toy Co of producing high-quality toys.
questions.model_answer: First, high quality builds reputation and customer loyalty [k]. Export retailers in 6 countries rely on safe, well-made toys, so a good record would help secure the $400,000 order now at risk of cancellation [app]. Second, high quality reduces returns and rework costs [k]. With paint defects causing 5% of shipments to be returned, better quality would cut replacement costs and protect the $7.2 million revenue [app].

knowledge_max_2: Quality builds reputation and customer loyalty
Quality reduces returns, rework and replacement costs
application_max_2: Reference to 6 export countries / $400,000 order at risk
Reference to 5% paint defect returns / $7.2 million revenue

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of introducing Total Quality Management (Option A) at Driftwood Toy Co.
questions.model_answer: First, TQM makes every worker responsible for quality [k]. Under weekly improvement meetings, all 68 workers can spot paint defects during production rather than after dispatch [app]. Catching faults at source reduces waste and rework, lowering production costs and raising profit margins [an]. Second, TQM encourages continuous improvement and employee involvement [k]. The suggestion scheme lets workers closest to the toys propose fixes, improving morale and ownership [app]. A motivated workforce checks its own work more carefully, so the 5% return rate falls and the $400,000 retailer order is protected [an].

knowledge_max_2: Every employee is responsible for quality; faults found at source
Continuous improvement / employee involvement through suggestions
application_max_2: Reference to 68 workers / weekly improvement meetings
Reference to suggestion scheme / 5% returns / $400,000 order
analysis_max_2: Chain from shared responsibility to fewer faults to lower waste and rework costs
Chain from employee involvement to morale to fewer returns and a secured order

questions.question_text: Do you think Driftwood Toy Co should introduce Total Quality Management (Option A)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A costs $30,000 to train all 68 workers, but TQM builds quality into every stage, so paint defects would be prevented before toys reach export markets [k]. This directly addresses the root cause of the 5% return rate and would reassure the retailer ahead of the $400,000 order review [app]. Preventing defects also cuts rework and scrap, improving profit over time rather than just inspecting faults after they occur [an]. However, Option B keeps 4 end-of-line inspectors at no extra cost, so Daniel could redeploy the $30,000 to sales or new toy designs [k]. Inspection does catch faulty toys before dispatch, but returns would likely stay at 5% and the retailer could still cancel the $400,000 order [app]. Losing that order would cost far more than $30,000, and it does nothing to fix the paint process itself [an]. Overall, I think Daniel should choose Option A [eval] because $30,000 is small next to the $400,000 order and the $7.2 million revenue at stake; prevention beats detection [eval].

knowledge_max_2: TQM builds quality into each stage / all employees responsible
End-of-line inspection detects faults but does not prevent them
application_max_2: Reference to Option A: $30,000 / 68 workers / weekly meetings / suggestion scheme
Reference to Option B: no extra cost / 4 inspectors / 5% returns / $400,000 order
analysis_max_2: Chain from TQM prevention to fewer returns to protected profit and contract
Chain from inspection-only to persistent 5% returns to risk of losing $400,000
evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B
Weighs both options using stem figures ($30,000 vs $400,000, 5% returns, $7.2 million revenue)

scenario_stem:
Halvern Castings Ltd is a private limited company casting iron brackets for farm machinery. At 30 June, current assets were $286,000, comprising inventories $150,000, trade receivables $96,000 and cash $40,000, against current liabilities of $104,000.

The steel supplier offers a 2% cash discount to settle the $60,000 debt early instead of usual 60-day terms. Marcus must decide whether to take a 90-day bank loan at 1.5% interest to pay early, or wait and risk upsetting the supplier before steel prices rise next quarter.

questions.question_text: Define 'current ratio'.
questions.model_answer: The current ratio measures whether a business can meet its current liabilities with its current assets, calculated as current assets divided by current liabilities; Halvern Castings holds $286,000 of current assets against $104,000 of current liabilities, a ratio of 2.75:1. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Current ratio = current assets / current liabilities
It shows the liquidity of the business, i.e. its ability to pay short-term debts

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Marcus should check the current ratio before taking the loan.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: the current ratio shows whether current assets cover current liabilities [k]; Halvern's $286,000 of current assets against $104,000 of current liabilities is 2.75:1, indicating comfortable cover today before taking on a 90-day loan [app]. Reason 2: the current ratio helps Marcus see whether paying $60,000 early still leaves the business able to meet its remaining bills [k]; paying early would use the $40,000 cash plus part of the $96,000 trade receivables, so he must confirm cover stays above 1:1 through the 90 days [app].

knowledge_max_2: Current ratio shows whether current assets cover current liabilities
Current ratio indicates the liquidity buffer available before taking on new short-term debt
application_max_2: Applies the $40,000 cash and $96,000 trade receivables against the $60,000 early payment

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of using the current ratio alone for this decision.
questions.model_answer: Limitation 1: the current ratio treats all current assets as equally quick to convert into cash [k]; Halvern holds $150,000 of inventories, the slowest asset, so excluding them (the acid test ratio) gives a more cautious picture of ($286,000 minus $150,000) divided by $104,000, about 1.31:1 [app][an]. Limitation 2: the current ratio is a single snapshot at 30 June and ignores timing [k]; if $96,000 of trade receivables pay slowly, Halvern may not have the $60,000 in cash even though the 2.75:1 ratio looks strong, so cash-flow timing must also be checked [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: Current ratio assumes all current assets convert to cash equally fast
Current ratio is a static snapshot and ignores cash-flow timing
application_max_2: Applies the $150,000 inventories exclusion giving an acid test of about 1.31:1
Applies the $96,000 trade receivables timing and the 2.75:1 snapshot
analysis_max_2: Explains inventories are the slowest asset so the current ratio overstates true liquidity
Explains that a strong snapshot figure can still hide a cash-timing shortfall in the 90 days

questions.question_text: Do you think Marcus should take the 90-day bank loan to pay the supplier early? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Marcus could take the loan because a strong steel supplier supports reliable deliveries for the farm-machinery brackets his factory casts [k]. The 2% discount on the $60,000 saves $1,200 against $900 of interest (1.5% for 90 days), a net gain of $300, and the current ratio of 2.75:1 plus an acid test of about 1.31:1 shows he can cover a short 90-day loan from $286,000 of current assets [app][an]. However, the cash buffer is only $40,000 and the $96,000 of trade receivables must convert to cash within 90 days, so if customers pay late the loan rolls over with fresh interest and the net gain turns into a loss [app][an]. Conversely, waiting for the normal 60-day settlement costs nothing but forfeits the $1,200 discount and leaves the supplier waiting [k][eval]. Overall, Marcus should take the loan only if receivables have a strong payment record and the supplier confirms the terms in writing; the acid test of about 1.31:1 supports it, but with only a $300 net saving he should walk away if any part of the arrangement looks uncertain [eval].

knowledge_max_2: 2% discount on $60,000 = $1,200 saved; 1.5% for 90 days = $900 interest; net $300
Current ratio 2.75:1; acid test about 1.31:1; cash buffer only $40,000
application_max_2: Applies the $1,200 saving versus $900 interest and net $300 gain
Applies the $40,000 cash and $96,000 receivables against the 90-day repayment window
analysis_max_2: Explains receivables converting on time is essential or the loan rolls over costing more
Explains the liquidity ratios support a short-term loan from current assets
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation tied to written confirmation, receivables' payment record and the thin $300 net benefit

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Foxglove Denim Co is a private limited company weaving denim at its Glendale mill. It imports 30 tonnes of cotton monthly from Country Z; a 15% depreciation lifts the cost from $120,000 to $138,000 a month, or $4,600 per tonne. 40% of jeans are exported.

Prices must be set by 1 August. Option A raises jeans from $45 to $48, passing on the $18,000 monthly rise. Option B keeps $45 and absorbs $216,000 a year, hoping cotton costs fall or Country Z sales grow.

questions.question_text: Outline what is meant by 'depreciation'.
questions.model_answer: Depreciation is a fall in the value of one currency compared with other currencies, so the currency buys less foreign currency than before [2].

knowledge_max_2: A fall in the value of a currency
Compared with other currencies / buys less foreign currency than before

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the 15% depreciation on Foxglove Denim Co.
questions.model_answer: First, depreciation raises the cost of imported cotton [k]. Cotton now costs $4,600 per tonne, so the monthly bill has jumped from $120,000 to $138,000, an extra $18,000 a month [app]. Second, depreciation makes Foxglove's jeans cheaper for overseas buyers [k]. With 40% of jeans exported to Country Z, the finished garments cost Country Z retailers fewer Country Z units, so export orders may rise and partly offset the higher cotton bill [app].

knowledge_max_2: Depreciation raises the dollar cost of imports
Depreciation makes exports cheaper abroad
application_max_2: Reference to $4,600 per tonne / $138,000 vs $120,000 / $18,000
Reference to 40% exported to Country Z

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Foxglove Denim Co might face if it chooses Option B.
questions.model_answer: First, absorbing the increase squeezes profit margins on every pair of jeans [k]. The extra $216,000 a year must come out of the margin on jeans sold at $45, leaving less for repairs, machinery or wages at the Glendale mill [app]. Lower retained profit means less money available for future investment, such as replacing weaving looms, which weakens competitiveness [an]. Second, Foxglove cannot know when cotton costs will fall back [k]. If the Country X dollar keeps depreciating beyond 15%, the $138,000 monthly cotton bill could rise further, so a fixed $45 price leaves the firm exposed to open-ended cost growth [app]. Continued absorption would eventually push certain lines into loss-making months, forcing emergency price changes or borrowing [an].

knowledge_max_2: Absorbing costs squeezes profit margins
Currency costs may keep rising / future is uncertain
application_max_2: Reference to $216,000 a year / $138,000 monthly / $45 price
Reference to Glendale mill / further depreciation beyond 15%
analysis_max_2: Chain from absorbed costs to lower retained profit to weaker investment capacity
Chain from ongoing depreciation to open-ended cost growth to losses and forced price changes

questions.question_text: Do you think Foxglove Denim Co should raise its wholesale jean price from $45 to $48 (Option A)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A raises the price by $3 to $48, passing the $18,000 monthly cotton increase on to retailers [k]. This restores margins without raising Foxglove's costs, which matters because depreciation lifted its bill from $120,000 to $138,000 a month [app]. Protecting $216,000 a year of margin lets Foxglove keep upgrading the Glendale mill and keeps its export pricing stable in Country Z terms [an]. However, Option B keeps prices at $45 [k]. Holding price may retain retailer loyalty and sales volume at home, and with 40% of jeans exported, stronger export volumes could offset the $216,000 absorbed [app]. The risk is that cotton costs keep rising if the dollar weakens further, so $45 may become unsustainable [an]. Overall, I think Foxglove should choose Option A [eval] because a $3 rise is only about 6.7% on a wholesale price and is caused by an external currency movement, so retailers are likely to accept it rather than lose supply; it should review the price each season in case cotton costs fall back [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Option A: pass on cost via $3 rise to $48
Option B: hold $45 to protect loyalty and volume
application_max_2: Reference to $18,000 monthly increase / $216,000 a year / $45 to $48
Reference to 40% exports to Country Z / $120,000 to $138,000
analysis_max_2: Chain from price rise to restored margin to sustained investment
Chain from held price to volume retention but open-ended cost exposure
evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B
Weighs both options using stem figures ($45 vs $48, $216,000, 40%)

scenario_stem:
Saffron Thread Textiles is a private limited company founded by the Rahman family, weaving cotton for garment exporters. It employs 85 factory workers, made $420,000 profit, and its 400,000 shares are held by 12 family members.

The family wants 2 weaving machines costing $1,800,000 for a large export order. Directors debate staying private and paying from retained profit over years, or becoming a public limited company, selling shares on the Stock Exchange to raise $2,500,000.

questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: The family keeps full control [k], as the 400,000 shares are held by only 12 family members who decide every major issue [app]. Advantage 2: Retained profits can be reinvested [k], so the $420,000 made last year can build toward the $1,800,000 machines without paying interest to a bank [app].

retained profit reinvested without interest payments

Disadvantage 2: Shares cannot be traded on the Stock Exchange [k], making it slow and difficult for the family to raise cash by selling shares [app], restricting future growth options [an].

scenario_stem:
Meadowbrook Day Nursery is a sole trader nursery for 48 children, with 9 full-time practitioners on $26,000 and 5 part-time assistants. One resigned; the $250 advert drew 30 applications in 3 weeks for autumn term.

Of these, 18 enclosed a curriculum vitae and 12 completed the application form with 8 standard questions; CVs vary in layout, forms give consistent data. Panels cost $120 per candidate; the budget is $800. The owner must shortlist by CV or form.

questions.question_text: Define 'application form'.
questions.model_answer: An application form is a standard document produced by the business that applicants complete to provide details such as personal information, qualifications and experience, allowing the employer to compare candidates fairly. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Standard document produced by the employer for applicants to complete
Gathers consistent information (qualifications, experience, personal details) to aid fair comparison

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Meadowbrook Day Nursery might prefer the application forms when shortlisting.
questions.model_answer: Application forms present every candidate's information in the same format [k]. With 30 applications received in 3 weeks, the owner can scan the 12 completed forms quickly against the 8 standard questions instead of comparing 18 different CV layouts [app]. Forms ensure the nursery gets the specific information it needs [k]. The form's questions on qualifications, experience and childcare training directly test whether applicants meet the requirements for caring for children aged 2 to 5 [app].

knowledge_max_2: Forms give a consistent, directly comparable format
Forms gather specific job-relevant information the employer chooses
application_max_2: 30 applications in 3 weeks; 12 forms versus 18 CVs; 8 standard questions
Qualifications, experience and childcare training questions; children aged 2 to 5

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of inviting shortlisted candidates for an interview.
questions.model_answer: Interviews let the owner probe claims made on the forms or CVs [k]. With $120 of staff time per candidate and a total budget of $800 (minus $250 already spent on the advertisement), the nursery can interview only the strongest candidates and check their claims face to face [app], which reduces the risk of hiring unsuitable staff for the 48 children [an]. Interviews also give candidates the chance to ask questions about the role [k]. Discussing the $26,000 full-time salary, the 9 existing full-time practitioners and daily duties helps both sides judge fit before the autumn term [app], lowering the chance of an early resignation and the $120 per-interview cost being wasted [an].

knowledge_max_2: Interviews verify/probe candidate claims and reveal interpersonal qualities
Interviews allow two-way communication; candidates can ask questions and judge fit
application_max_2: $120 per candidate; $800 budget; $250 spent on the advertisement
$26,000 salary; 9 full-time colleagues; autumn term deadline
analysis_max_2: Better screening reduces risk of unsuitable hires around young children
Two-way fit assessment lowers early turnover and wasted recruitment spend

questions.question_text: Do you think Meadowbrook Day Nursery should shortlist using the CVs or the application forms? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Application forms give consistent information the nursery can compare quickly [k]. The 12 completed forms answer the 8 standard questions directly, so the owner can shortlist confidently before paying $120 per interview from the remaining budget [app]. This reduces the risk of hiring someone unsuitable to work with the 48 children aged 2 to 5 [an]. However, CVs reveal more about personality, motivation and experiences such as first-aid courses, and the 18 CVs received may contain stronger candidates than the forms show [k]. A detailed CV might reveal qualities the standard form cannot capture, and rejecting them all could leave the nursery choosing only from the form-fillers [app]. Over-reliance on the form alone could cause the nursery to miss the most enthusiastic applicant for the role [an]. Overall, the nursery should shortlist using the application forms because consistency and the 8 targeted questions suit a safeguarding-critical childcare role, and the budget does not stretch to interviewing widely from an unverified CV pool [eval]. scenario_stem:
Silverpine Youth Hostels is a private limited company with 14 hostels in Country X and 38,000 guests a year. The manager wants to survey 400 guests on a proposed $250,000 dormitory refurbishment adding bunk pods and study corners.

Guests aged 16-24 are 55% of bookings. The options are random sampling from the guest list or quota sampling by age and gender until 400 responses are gathered. Accuracy depends on sample size, wording of the questions and possible bias.

questions.question_text: Define 'random sampling'.
questions.model_answer: A sampling method in which every member of the population has an equal chance of being selected, usually using a random number generator [2].

knowledge_max_2: every member of the population has an equal chance
selection is random, for example using random numbers

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages to Silverpine Youth Hostels of using random sampling for its guest survey.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Every guest on the full list has an equal chance of selection [k], so the 400 respondents are likely to represent the 38,000 guests fairly [app]. Advantage 2: It reduces the risk of bias [k] compared with hand-picking guests from just one hostel [app].

knowledge_max_2: equal chance of selection for all
reduces risk of bias
application_max_2: 400 respondents representing 38,000 guests

questions.model_answer: Factor 1: Sample size [k] - surveying only 40 guests instead of 400 would poorly represent the 16-24 group that makes up 55% of bookings [app], producing unreliable results and a wasted $250,000 refurbishment [an]. Factor 2: Wording of the questions [k] - leading or confusing questions would bias answers about dormitory facilities [app], so the chain builds features guests do not want [an].

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Timberline Joinery of winning the housebuilder contract.

The housebuilder requires evidence of consistent quality, and a 12-month certificate from external auditors satisfies that demand without repeated checks for every order [app]. Securing this independent approval makes the $900,000 contract far more likely, lifting revenue by a quarter [an]. Second, external audits identify weaknesses in production processes [k]. scenario_stem:
Tidewater Leisure Pools Ltd is a private limited company operating 2 swimming and fitness venues. In the year to 31 August, profit was $180,000 and capital employed $900,000; last year profit was $135,000 on capital employed $900,000. A competitor's ROCE is 12%.

Rachel must decide whether to build a third venue costing $400,000 from retained profit, adding $52,000 in year one but $112,000 once established, or raise annual dividends of $60,000. She will announce this at the September annual general meeting.

questions.question_text: Calculate the Return on Capital Employed (ROCE) for Tidewater Leisure Pools. Show your working.
questions.model_answer: ROCE is the percentage return a business earns on the capital invested in its operations, calculated as profit divided by capital employed multiplied by 100; Tidewater Leisure Pools earns $180,000 divided by $900,000 multiplied by 100 = 20.0% this year, up from 15.0% last year ($135,000 divided by $900,000 multiplied by 100). [2]

knowledge_max_2: ROCE = profit / capital employed x 100
It shows how effectively capital is used to generate profit

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why ROCE is the key figure for the board's decision.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: ROCE shows how much profit each dollar of capital employed generates [k]; Tidewater's ROCE improved from 15% last year ($135,000 divided by $900,000) to 20% this year ($180,000 divided by $900,000), well above the competitor's 12%, evidence that the existing venues earn strong returns [app]. Reason 2: ROCE lets the board compare the $400,000 third venue with leaving retained profit idle or paying dividends [k]; if the new venue lifts annual profit towards $292,000 in its third year, ROCE would reach about 22.5% ($292,000 divided by $1,300,000), beating the competitor and justifying the build [app].

knowledge_max_2: ROCE shows the return generated on capital employed
ROCE allows investment options to be compared on a percentage return basis
application_max_2: Applies 20.0% this year ($180,000 / $900,000) versus 15.0% last year and 12% competitor
Applies the $400,000 venue cost, $1,300,000 resulting capital employed and the $292,000 third-year profit potential

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of using ROCE for this decision.
questions.model_answer: Limitation 1: ROCE is based on historic figures and profit only, not on how long the $400,000 takes to recover [k]; the venue adds only $52,000 in its first year, giving a first-year ROCE of about 17.8% on capital employed of $1,300,000, so early years dilute the ratio before the full benefit appears [app][an]. Limitation 2: ROCE ignores the other factors affecting the 2 existing venues [k]; occupancy, local competition and the $60,000 dividend expectation do not appear in the ratio, so customer demand and team capacity must also guide the board [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: ROCE is historic and does not show how an investment recovers its cost over time
ROCE ignores non-financial and contextual factors
application_max_2: Applies the $52,000 first-year contribution and the $1,300,000 resulting capital employed (about 17.8%)
Applies the $400,000 cost, $60,000 dividends and the 2 existing venues context
analysis_max_2: Explains that first-year returns dilute ROCE so the ratio looks worse than the long-run position
Explains that ROCE cannot capture demand, competition or shareholder expectations

questions.question_text: Do you think Rachel should build the third venue? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Rachel could approve the build because the business currently earns an ROCE of 20% ($180,000 divided by $900,000) against a competitor's 12%, proving the 2-venue model works well [k][app]. The third venue should add $52,000 in year one and $112,000 at maturity, lifting capital employed to $1,300,000 and reaching an ROCE of about 22.5% in year three, while also defending the venues' position in Country X [an]. However, first-year ROCE falls to about 17.8% ($232,000 divided by $1,300,000), and paying $400,000 from retained profit reduces dividends below the $60,000 shareholders currently expect [app][an]. Conversely, paying larger dividends rewards shareholders now but leaves $400,000 barely generating anything and loses the chance to outgrow the 12% competitor [k][eval]. Overall, Rachel should approve the third venue but phase the spending, because a long-run ROCE above the competitor matters more than short-term dilution, provided membership numbers stay strong and some dividend is maintained during construction [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Current ROCE 20% ($180,000 / $900,000); competitor 12%; last year 15%
Third venue: $52,000 year one, $112,000 at maturity; capital employed rises to $1,300,000
application_max_2: Applies the 20% current ROCE versus the competitor's 12% as evidence the model works
Applies the first-year 17.8% ROCE ($232,000 / $1,300,000) and the dividend cut below $60,000
analysis_max_2: Explains that maturity-phase profit lifts ROCE to about 22.5% and defends market position
Explains that short-term dilution and dividend cuts are the main shareholder costs
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation tied to long-run ROCE superiority, dividend affordability and membership strength

scenario_stem:
Ridgemont Electronics Ltd is a private limited company assembling smartphone accessories at its Darnwell factory with 85 workers. It imports circuit boards from Country W, paying €90,000 a month. The rate moved from $1.30 to $1.45 per euro, raising dollar costs.

A decision is due before the October contract is signed. Option A switches to a Country X supplier at $135,000 a month in dollars, fixed for 12 months. Option B keeps importing from Country W at $130,500 a month, hoping the rate reverses.

questions.question_text: Calculate the dollar cost of the monthly €90,000 payment before and after the rate change.
questions.model_answer: Before: €90,000 x $1.30 = $117,000. After: €90,000 x $1.45 = $130,500. The depreciation raises the monthly cost by $13,500 [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the exchange-rate movement on Ridgemont Electronics Ltd.
questions.model_answer: First, the depreciation of the dollar raises the cost of imported circuit boards [k]. The monthly bill has increased from $117,000 to $130,500, an extra $13,500 a month that Ridgemont must absorb or pass on to customers [app]. Second, the movement reduces the reliability of Ridgemont's cost planning [k]. If the rate moves beyond $1.45 per euro, the $130,500 monthly import cost rises further, so the firm cannot confidently fix prices in its October supply contract [app].

knowledge_max_2: A weaker dollar makes imports dearer
Rate uncertainty makes cost planning difficult
application_max_2: Reference to October supply contract / $130,500 vs $135,000

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Ridgemont Electronics Ltd might face if it chooses Option B.
questions.model_answer: First, the import cost is unpredictable month to month [k]. If the dollar weakens past $1.45 per euro, the €90,000 payment will exceed the current $130,500 and could approach the $135,000 charged by the Country X supplier [app]. Open-ended cost growth makes it hard to quote firm prices to customers, risking lost orders [an]. Second, continued importing keeps Ridgemont dependent on one foreign supplier and its lead times [k]. Any delay or disruption at the Country W factory would halt the Darnwell line that employs 85 workers [app]. A line stoppage would push up costs and damage reputation with accessory customers [an].

knowledge_max_2: Import costs can keep rising beyond current levels
Single foreign supplier creates dependency and lead-time risk
application_max_2: Reference to $1.45 per euro / $130,500 vs $135,000
Reference to Darnwell factory / 85 workers / October supply contract
analysis_max_2: Chain from further depreciation to import cost above $135,000 to eroded margin and lost orders
Chain from single-source dependency to line stoppage to costs and reputation damage

questions.question_text: Do you think Ridgemont Electronics Ltd should switch to the Country X supplier (Option A)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A switches to a local supplier charging $135,000 a month with a 12-month fixed price in dollars [k]. For roughly $4,500 a month more than the current $130,500, Ridgemont buys certainty: its October supply contract can be priced firmly and its 85 Darnwell workers face no supply interruption [app]. Locking $135,000 removes the risk that the dollar weakens to $1.50 per euro, at which point €90,000 would cost $135,000 anyway [an]. However, Option B keeps the lower import price [k]. If the rate swings back towards $1.30 per euro, the import bill returns to $117,000, saving Ridgemont $13,500 a month, or $162,000 a year, against the fixed contract [app]. The saving is not guaranteed and costs remain unpredictable in the meantime [an]. Overall, I think Ridgemont should choose Option A [eval] because fixed costs remove the guesswork from the October contract and a domestic supplier also shortens lead times; it can revisit the decision when the 12-month contract expires [eval].

Option B: keep cheaper import at $130,500 / $117,000 if rate returns to $1.30

Chain from swinging rate to possible $162,000 annual saving forgone
evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B

scenario_stem:
Tekworks Electronics is a private limited company repairing computers at 2 workshops with 64 people, producing 1,100 repaired devices at $190. A new client needs 12 electronics assemblers in 6 weeks.

questions.question_text: Define 'interview' in the context of selection.

questions.question_text: Do you think Tekworks Electronics should use practical assessments or panel interviews to select the 12 assemblers? Justify your answer.

scenario_stem:
Redfern Farm Kitchen Ltd is a private limited company making pasta sauce and pesto. Year to 30 April: revenue $610,000, gross profit $183,000, expenses $103,700, profit $79,300; last year revenue $520,000, expenses $88,400, profit $83,200.

Revenue rose $90,000 yet profit fell. The value range, launched 18 months ago, is now 60% of jars sold. Colin Marsh must decide whether to discontinue it and focus on premium sauces, or keep it for volume and shelf space in 3 chains.

questions.question_text: Calculate the profit margin for Redfern Farm Kitchen. Show your working.
questions.model_answer: Profit margin (net profit margin) is the percentage of revenue remaining as profit after all expenses are deducted, calculated as profit divided by revenue multiplied by 100; Redfern Farm Kitchen earned $79,300 divided by $610,000 multiplied by 100 = 13.0% this year, down from 16.0% last year ($83,200 divided by $520,000 multiplied by 100). [2]

knowledge_max_2: Profit margin = profit / revenue x 100
It shows the percentage of each dollar of revenue left as final profit after expenses

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Colin should study the profit margin before discontinuing the value range.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: the profit margin shows the percentage of revenue left after all expenses, revealing whether the value range is truly profitable [k]; the margin fell from 16.0% last year ($83,200 divided by $520,000) to 13.0% this year ($79,300 divided by $610,000), a drop of 3 percentage points despite revenue growing by $90,000 [app]. Reason 2: the profit margin shows whether the value range dilutes overall profitability [k]; with the value range making 60% of jars sold and expenses rising from $88,400 to $103,700, overhead growth is eating into final profit even though gross profit held near 30% [app].

knowledge_max_2: Profit margin shows final profitability after expenses

application_max_2: Applies the 60% value-range share of jars and expenses rising from $88,400 to $103,700

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of using profit margin to judge the value range.
questions.model_answer: Limitation 1: the profit margin is a single blended figure that cannot split value-range performance from premium-sauce performance [k]; without product-level accounts, the 13.0% margin could hide a strong premium line subsidising a weak value line, so discontinuing the wrong lines would remove volume without lifting profit [app][an]. Limitation 2: the profit margin ignores the strategic value the range brings [k]; 60% of jars sold means the value lines fill factory capacity and support the $90,000 of revenue growth, and dropping them could strand overheads while gross profit margin stays at 30% [app][an].

questions.model_answer: Colin could keep the range because it accounts for 60% of jars sold and helped revenue grow by $90,000 (from $520,000 to $610,000), filling factory capacity and widening brand reach in Country X [k][app]. scenario_stem:
Carrowmore Cider Co is a private limited company pressing craft cider in Country X. Of 150,000 cases a year, half are exported to Country W at €20 each, invoiced in euros. The rate moved from $1.45 to $1.30 per euro, strengthening the dollar.

January export prices are due. Option A cuts the Country W price by 10% to €18 a case to defend 75,000 cases yearly. Option B holds €20 and accepts orders falling to 60,000, focusing on domestic farm shops and supermarkets.

questions.question_text: Calculate the dollar value of the annual export payments before and after the rate change.
questions.model_answer: Annual exports: 75,000 cases x €20 = €1,500,000. Before: €1,500,000 x $1.45 = $2,175,000. After: €1,500,000 x $1.30 = $1,950,000. The appreciation cuts dollar export revenue by $225,000 [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the exchange-rate movement on Carrowmore Cider Co.
questions.model_answer: First, the appreciation cuts the dollar value of Carrowmore's euro export sales [k]. The same 75,000 cases at €20 now convert to $1,950,000 rather than $2,175,000, so dollar export revenue falls by $225,000 [app]. Second, the appreciation makes it harder to recover that revenue by raising the export price [k]. Lifting the €20 price to claw back the shortfall would make Country W buyers switch to cheaper local cider, so Gareth must plan marketing carefully [app].

knowledge_max_2: Appreciation lowers the dollar value of euro receipts
Raising foreign prices to recover revenue weakens competitiveness

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Carrowmore Cider Co might face if it chooses Option B.
questions.model_answer: First, holding price means giving up export volume [k]. Orders fall from 75,000 to 60,000 cases, so euro export revenue drops from €1,500,000 to €1,200,000, a loss of €300,000 a year [app]. Lower export volume may leave cider stockpiled for the domestic market, forcing farm-gate discounting [an]. Second, Option B shrinks Carrowmore's presence in Country W [k]. Once listings are lost to Country W rivals, winning them back is expensive, and farm shops and supermarkets at home may not absorb the extra 15,000 cases [app]. Domestic sales growth could lag, leaving the pressing plant underused and unsold stock [an].

scenario_stem:
Thorne & Vale Toys Ltd is a private limited company running a toy shop. At 31 October, current assets were $340,000: inventories $224,000, trade receivables $88,000, cash $28,000, against current liabilities of $160,000. Last year's acid test ratio was 0.95:1; festive sales are 45% of annual sales.

Beth must choose between a full $180,000 festive stock order, backed by her forecast, or a reduced $120,000 order, waiting on December trading before reordering. Supplier prices rise 6% in November.

questions.question_text: Define 'acid test ratio'.
questions.model_answer: The acid test ratio measures whether a business can meet its current liabilities using only its quick assets (excluding inventories), calculated as (current assets minus inventories) divided by current liabilities; Thorne & Vale Toys has ($340,000 minus $224,000) divided by $160,000 = $116,000 divided by $160,000 = 0.725:1, down from 0.95:1 last year. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Acid test ratio = (current assets - inventories) / current liabilities
It measures immediate liquidity without relying on selling inventories

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Beth should consider the acid test ratio before placing the festive order.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: the acid test ratio shows whether liquid assets alone can cover current liabilities, without counting inventories [k]; Thorne's quick assets are only $116,000 ($88,000 receivables plus $28,000 cash) against $160,000 of current liabilities, giving 0.725:1, down from 0.95:1 last year [app]. Reason 2: the acid test ratio signals whether the full $180,000 stock order would stretch the business through the festive peak [k]; festive sales make up 45% of annual toy sales, so stock must be right, but committing $180,000 against a $44,000 shortfall exposes the shop to supplier-payment risk [app].

knowledge_max_2: Acid test ratio shows liquidity excluding inventories
Acid test ratio indicates the risk of committing to large stock purchases on credit

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of using the acid test ratio for this decision.
questions.model_answer: Limitation 1: the acid test ratio assumes inventories cannot be sold quickly, which is rarely true in a busy toy shop in December [k]; festive stock turns over fast, so excluding all $224,000 of inventories may understate Thorne's ability to generate cash from the 45% of annual toy sales that arrive in the season [app][an]. Limitation 2: the acid test ratio is a single snapshot and ignores the effect of order size on December sales [k]; a reduced order of $120,000 protects cash but could leave shelves empty in the peak fortnight when 45% of annual toy sales are made, losing revenue and emptying shelves [app][an].

Conversely, a reduced order of $120,000 saves $60,000 of cash and protects the shop if festive sales disappoint, though re-ordering mid-season may delay delivery and cost late-December sales [k][eval]. Overall, Beth should place a staged order: most of the $180,000 now with a top-up in early December once first-week festive cash arrives; this balances the 0.725:1 acid test against the 45% of annual toy sales at stake [eval].

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Wren & Willow Fashion is a private limited company running 6 shops selling womenswear across Country X, with 34 full-time and part-time staff. It imports 4,000 winter coats a year from Country W at €40 each. Appreciation from $1.45 to $1.30 per euro cuts coat costs from $58 to $52.

questions.model_answer: First, each imported coat now costs $52 instead of $58, saving $6 [k]. On 4,000 winter coats a year the total saving is $24,000, which can fund refurbishment or wage rises [app]. Second, cheaper coats let Wren & Willow compete on price without cutting its margin [k]. Passing on the $6 would keep relative value attractive to Country X shoppers while protecting the mark-up the shops need to pay 34 staff for 6 stores [app].

questions.model_answer: First, cutting the ticket price sacrifices margin headroom [k]. Passing on the entire $6 import saving leaves no extra profit from the appreciation, so the $24,000 stays locked in lower prices rather than funding refurbishment of 2 shops [app]. If sales do not rise enough to offset the lower price, the business forgoes profit the currency change already delivered [an]. Second, price promotions can be matched by rival shops [k]. Competing Country X retailers importing from Country W will also face a $6 cost fall, so all may cut ticket prices together, leaving Wren & Willow with lower prices but little extra footfall [app]. Market-wide price cuts reduce revenue per coat and can squeeze cash flow during the crucial winter season [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Wren & Willow Fashion should cut the ticket price of the imported coats by $6 (Option A)? Justify your answer.

scenario_stem:
Fenland Woollens Ltd is a private limited company making woollen blankets. Year to 30 June: city mill revenue $540,000, gross profit $167,400, profit $59,400, capital employed $594,000; rural branch revenue $300,000, gross profit $66,000, profit $9,000, capital employed $225,000.

The board may close the rural branch if figures confirm this, yet it supplies the city mill with specialist yarn and employs 15 local weavers, affecting the community. The managing director must recommend at next month's board meeting.

questions.question_text: State two limitations of ratio analysis.
questions.model_answer: Two limitations of ratio analysis are firstly that ratios are based on historic figures and may not reflect future performance, and secondly that ratios ignore qualitative factors such as staff morale, customer loyalty and community impact, so they cannot tell the whole story about a business. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Ratios use historic data, so they may not predict future performance
Ratios ignore qualitative and non-financial factors

questions.question_text: Explain two ways the board has used ratio analysis on the two mills' figures.
questions.model_answer: Use 1: ratio analysis lets the board compare the two mills on a common basis [k]; the city mill produced a 31% gross profit margin ($167,400 divided by $540,000) against the rural branch's 22% ($66,000 divided by $300,000), showing the rural branch is weaker at the making or buying stage [app]. Use 2: ratio analysis highlights where profit leaks after expenses [k]; the rural branch returned only a 3% profit margin ($9,000 divided by $300,000) on capital employed of $225,000 (an ROCE of 4%) versus 11% and 10% for the city mill, flagging underperformance for the board [app].

knowledge_max_2: Ratio analysis enables comparison of different parts of a business on a common basis
Ratio analysis identifies weaknesses in profitability and efficiency
application_max_2: Applies 31% vs 22% gross profit margins ($167,400/$540,000 vs $66,000/$300,000)
Applies 3% vs 11% profit margins and 4% vs 10% ROCE ($9,000/$225,000 vs $59,400/$594,000)

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of ratio analysis that apply to this closure decision.
questions.model_answer: Limitation 1: ratios ignore the qualitative factors behind the figures [k]; the rural branch supplies specialist yarn to the city mill, so closing it could disrupt the city mill's 31% gross profit margin in ways that appear nowhere in the rural branch's own 3% profit margin [app][an]. Limitation 2: ratios are calculated from one year's figures and give no reasons for the poor result [k]; one weak year of $9,000 profit does not prove the branch cannot improve with new equipment or markets, and the value of 15 local weavers' skills to the Country X community is invisible to the ratios [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: Ratios ignore qualitative and interconnected business factors
Ratios are historic single-year snapshots with no explanation of causes
application_max_2: Applies the rural branch's yarn supply role versus the city mill's 31% gross profit margin
Applies the 15 local weavers, $9,000 profit and single-year data
analysis_max_2: Explains closure could damage the profitable city mill despite good city ratios
Explains that ratios cannot explain or reverse the underlying causes of weak performance

questions.question_text: Do you think the managing director should recommend closing the rural branch? Justify your answer.

However, the branch supplies specialist yarn to the city mill; closure could raise city mill's costs and endanger its 31% gross profit margin, and making 15 local weavers redundant damages the yarn supply and community goodwill [app][an]. Conversely, keeping the branch open preserves the yarn supply and the weavers' skills, but it consumed management time for only $9,000 profit, while the same $225,000 employed in the city mill would earn about 10% [k][eval]. Overall, the director should not close the branch outright; she should set a 12-month turnaround plan targeting yarn costs and sales, because the supply dependency outweighs one year of weak ratios, but closure must follow if branch profit stays below, say, $30,000 [eval].

scenario_stem:
Greenacres Garden Centre is a family-run sole trader with 22 staff selling plants and tools. Spring drives 60% of sales: 1,800 plants weekly at $9 over a 13-week season.

For March to May the owner needs 3 extra weekend assistants and must choose advertising: $400 for a local newspaper read mainly by those over 55, or $150 online with younger reach but no local targeting. A print advert drew 40 phone enquiries; the budget is $600.

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Greenacres Garden Centre should include clear details in its job advertisement for the 3 weekend assistants.
questions.model_answer: Clear details attract applicants who can actually do the job [k], so stating the 13-week March to May weekend pattern and duties such as helping customers and loading purchases filters out anyone wanting permanent, full-time work [app]. Precise details reduce wasted applications [k], meaning the $150 online or $400 print advert pulls in relevant candidates the first time rather than forcing a costly re-advertisement [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of choosing the $150 online advert.
questions.model_answer: The online advert costs far less than print [k], saving $250 against the $400 newspaper advert and leaving $450 of the $600 budget for other recruitment tasks [app], which improves value for money across just 3 seasonal posts [an]. Online adverts also reach younger, mobile-first audiences quickly [k], going beyond the over 55 newspaper readership that dominated the last print campaign [app], which raises the chance of filling all 3 weekend roles before the 13-week season starts [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Greenacres Garden Centre should place the $400 newspaper advert or the $150 online advert? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The online advert is cheaper and reaches a broader, younger audience [k]. At $150 it leaves $450 of the $600 budget intact, and younger weekend applicants are more likely to be flexible, often browse mobile job sites and may know garden tools and tills, fitting a plant retail environment selling at an average of $9 [app]. Choosing online reduces cost per effective applicant and should fill the 3 roles before the 13 weeks begin [an]. However, the local newspaper is read mainly by residents over 55, who are the garden centre's core plant-buying customers and may be the most credible, knowledgeable weekend assistants [k]. The centre's last print advert generated 40 phone enquiries, proving its local pull, whereas the online advert offers no guaranteed local targeting [app]. Print might produce fewer but far better-suited local candidates, some with real horticultural knowledge for questions about 1,800 plants sold in a peak week [an]. Overall, the centre should place the online advert because it can be launched quickly, costs $250 less, and 3 seasonal roles can be filled from a wider pool without breaking the $600 budget [eval]. If the online response produces too few strong local candidates, a small print boost can follow, using the savings to reinforce the local message [eval].

scenario_stem:
Ferndale Tiles is a private limited company making ceramic wall and floor tiles with 85 workers. It produced 2.2 million tiles at $2 each for $4.4 million; two containers cracked in transit and 4% failed finish inspection.

A hotel group offers $600,000 for proven quality. In six weeks the owners choose $45,000 for an external audit and 12-month certification, or building their own quality assurance system for clay preparation, glazing, firing and packing at $22,000 plus $5,000 yearly.

questions.question_text: Outline the difference between quality control and quality assurance.
questions.model_answer: Quality control checks finished products at the end of production and removes faulty items [1]. Quality assurance builds quality into every stage of production so faults are prevented before they occur [1]. [2]

Quality assurance = builds quality into every stage / prevents faults

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Ferndale Tiles of obtaining external certification (Option A).
questions.model_answer: First, certification proves quality objectively to buyers [k]. The hotel group offering $600,000 wants proof before placing orders, and an external audit provides independent evidence [app]. Second, certification strengthens reputation and competitiveness [k]. Winning the $600,000 contract would lift revenue above the $4.4 million earned last year and open further large hotel projects [app].

Stronger reputation / competitive advantage
application_max_2: Reference to $600,000 hotel group contract
Reference to $4.4 million revenue / 2.2 million tiles

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Ferndale Tiles of building its own quality assurance system (Option B).
questions.model_answer: First, quality assurance prevents faults at source [k]. Checking clay preparation, glazing, firing and packing would catch the flaws causing tiles to crack, rather than discovering them after dispatch [app]. Preventing the 4% finish failures would cut returns and rework, raising profit [an]. Second, a documented system makes quality consistent and trainable [k]. Written procedures let all 85 workers follow the same checks every shift, so quality does not depend on memory [app]. Consistent routines lower waste and help Ferndale keep the hotel contract worth $600,000 year after year [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Ferndale Tiles should pay for external certification (Option A) rather than build its own quality assurance system (Option B)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A costs $45,000 and provides independent, audit-verified certification that the hotel group can trust as proof of consistent quality [k]. Because the hotel wants quality proven, the 12-month certificate converts directly into the $600,000 contract and renews credibility with other large buyers [app]. Securing $600,000 of annual revenue against $45,000 spent is a strong commercial return [an]. However, Option B costs $22,000 plus $5,000 a year and tackles the actual causes of the 4% finish failures and cracked tiles, rather than just reporting on them [k]. Owning the system keeps procedures for clay preparation to packing in-house permanently, and over three years Option B costs $37,000, less than the first $45,000 year of Option A [app]. Building internal capability also raises staff ownership of quality, not just audit paperwork [an]. Overall, I think Ferndale Tiles should choose Option B [eval], because it prevents faults permanently and costs less, unless the hotel group rejects uncertified systems, in which case Option A is a necessary $45,000 investment to secure the $600,000 contract [eval].

scenario_stem:
Marrow Lane Catering Ltd is a private limited company providing event catering. At 30 September, current assets were $408,000, comprising cash $240,000, trade receivables $108,000 and inventories $60,000, against current liabilities of $120,000; last year's current ratio was 2.1:1.

A $300,000 bank loan carries 7% interest. Shareholders want Tom to repay $240,000 early from cash to save interest, or keep the cash as a buffer for a spring wedding contract needing $90,000 of supplies paid upfront by February.

questions.question_text: Calculate the current ratio for Marrow Lane Catering. Show your working.
questions.model_answer: The current ratio measures current assets against current liabilities, calculated as current assets divided by current liabilities; Marrow Lane Catering holds $408,000 divided by $120,000 = 3.4:1, up from 2.1:1 last year. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Current ratio = current assets / current liabilities
Expressing the answer as a ratio such as 3.4:1

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of a strong current ratio for the wedding contract.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: a strong current ratio shows Marrow Lane can pay its short-term obligations as they fall due [k]; with $408,000 of current assets against $120,000 of current liabilities (3.4:1), the business can comfortably cover the $90,000 of up-front wedding supplies and normal monthly bills [app]. Benefit 2: a healthy current ratio reassures suppliers and the lender of creditworthiness [k]; paying the $90,000 of catering supplies up front is easy when cash alone is $240,000, and the ratio gives the bank confidence about the $300,000 loan [app].

knowledge_max_2: A strong current ratio indicates the business can meet short-term obligations
A healthy current ratio strengthens credibility with suppliers and lenders
application_max_2: Applies $408,000 / $120,000 = 3.4:1 against the $90,000 up-front wedding supplies
Applies the $240,000 cash and the $300,000 bank loan context

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of a very high current ratio.
questions.model_answer: Limitation 1: a very high current ratio can mean resources are idle rather than productive [k]; $240,000 of cash earning nothing while the $300,000 loan still costs 7% interest ($21,000 a year) represents an opportunity cost shareholders rightly question [app][an]. Limitation 2: the current ratio hides what the assets actually are [k]; if most of the $408,000 were slow-moving inventories or unpaid trade receivables of $108,000 rather than cash, the 3.4:1 ratio would overstate true short-term strength [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: A high current ratio may indicate idle, unproductive resources
The current ratio does not show the composition or quality of current assets

Applies the $60,000 inventories and $108,000 trade receivables composition of the $408,000

Explains the ratio can flatter liquidity if assets are slow-moving

questions.question_text: Do you think Tom should repay $240,000 of the loan early? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Tom could repay the $240,000 because it would save $16,800 of annual interest at 7%, directly lifting profit, and shareholders would see disciplined use of cash instead of a 3.4:1 idle balance [k][app]. The reduced current ratio of 1.4:1 ($168,000 divided by $120,000) still covers current liabilities, and the loan balance would fall to $60,000, lightening the balance sheet and reducing risk [an]. However, using all $240,000 of cash leaves nothing as a buffer if the spring wedding contract needs $90,000 of supplies up front or if receivables of $108,000 pay late, and Tom could face emergency borrowing at higher cost [app][an]. Conversely, keeping the cash protects the wedding contract and day-to-day operations, but shareholders would question why a 7% loan stays outstanding while cash sits idle [k][eval]. Overall, Tom should repay $180,000 now and keep $60,000 plus receivables as a buffer; this saves about $12,600 of interest, keeps the current ratio near 1.9:1 ($228,000 divided by $120,000), and still funds the wedding supplies, balancing shareholder pressure against operational safety [eval].

scenario_stem:
Thistledown Coffee Roasters is a private limited company importing and roasting green coffee from Country W for independent cafe chains. It buys 80 tonnes a year at €2,800 a tonne. Appreciation from $1.45 to $1.30 per euro cuts the bill from $324,800 to $291,200, saving $33,600.

Beans must be chosen. Option A signs a 12-month fixed-price contract at €2,800 a tonne with the Country W supplier. Option B buys monthly at spot rates, saving more if the dollar reaches $1.25 per euro ($280,000).

questions.question_text: Define what is meant by a 'stronger currency'.
questions.model_answer: A stronger currency is one that has risen in value against other currencies, so it buys more foreign currency than before [2].

knowledge_max_2: Currency has risen in value
Buys more foreign currency than before

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of the appreciation for Thistledown Coffee Roasters.
questions.model_answer: First, the appreciation cuts the annual green coffee bill [k]. At the new rate, 80 tonnes cost $291,200 rather than $324,800, saving $33,600 a year [app]. Second, the cheaper euros give Thistledown more room to compete and invest [k]. The $33,600 saving can be kept as extra profit or reinvested in roasting capacity without raising bean prices for cafe customers [app].

knowledge_max_2: Import bill falls in the home currency
Savings can be kept as profit or reinvested
application_max_2: Reference to $291,200 vs $324,800 / $33,600 saving
Reference to 80 tonnes / €2,800 a tonne / cafe customers

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Thistledown Coffee Roasters might face if it chooses Option A.
questions.model_answer: First, the contract locks the cost even if the dollar keeps strengthening [k]. If the rate reaches $1.25 per euro, spot buyers would pay only $280,000 a year, so Thistledown would overpay by $11,200 against spot purchases [app]. Overpaying weakens the margin on every bag of beans and wastes funds that could finance growth [an]. Second, a 12-month fixed contract removes flexibility to switch suppliers [k]. If the Country W supplier's quality or reliability slips, Thistledown cannot easily move its 80 tonnes to a rival roaster without renegotiating, and it is exposed for a full year [app]. Being locked in limits negotiating power on quality, delivery and payment terms during the peak season [an].

Chain from reduced flexibility to weaker negotiating power and supplier risk

questions.question_text: Do you think Thistledown Coffee Roasters should sign the 12-month fixed-price contract (Option A)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A signs a 12-month fixed-price contract at €2,800 a tonne [k]. This locks the bill at $291,200 equivalent regardless of rate movements, so planning, pricing and cash flow are predictable for the whole year [app]. Certainty matters because the bean bill is Thistledown's biggest cost, and locking it protects margin if the dollar weakens back towards $1.45, which would lift the bill to $324,800 [an]. However, Option B keeps monthly spot buying [k]. If the dollar strengthens to $1.25 per euro, the annual bill falls to $280,000, saving $11,200 more than the contract, and buying monthly avoids being locked into one supplier [app]. The trade-off is exposure to sudden reversals, which could add tens of thousands of dollars of cost overnight [an]. Overall, I think Thistledown should choose Option A [eval] because predictable input costs protect the business's narrow roaster margins and support firm pricing with cafe customers; the $11,200 possible extra saving is not worth the risk of a reversal [eval].

scenario_stem:
Northgate Coach Travel is a private limited company running 24 daily routes between 5 cities: 44 drivers on $34,000 a year and 26 staff. It won an airport shuttle contract needing 8 drivers in 8 weeks.

The director chooses two-round interviews - a 15-minute telephone screening and a 30-minute panel at $140 - or a 20-minute informal chat. Drivers need a 5-year clean driving record. With $1,400, 40 drivers applied; screening took 10 hours.

questions.question_text: Outline two advantages of using interviews to select candidates.
questions.model_answer: Interviews let the panel assess communication and customer-service skills face to face, and allow candidates to explain their 5-year clean driving record and route knowledge. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Assesses communication and interpersonal skills directly
Allows candidates to explain experience and driving history

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of using two-round interviews to select the 8 airport drivers.
questions.model_answer: Telephone screening cheaply filters out unsuitable applicants [k], so the 15-minute first round can eliminate anyone lacking a valid licence or the 5-year clean record before staff time is spent, narrowing the 40 applicants to a serious shortlist [app]. Structured panel interviews give every shortlisted driver the same 30-minute question set [k], making customer-service answers directly comparable and enabling a fair choice of the strongest 8 within the $1,400 budget [app].

knowledge_max_2: Screening removes unqualified applicants early at low cost
Structured interviews make assessments fair and comparable

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Northgate Coach Travel might face with a single informal chat.
questions.model_answer: Informal chats follow no fixed agenda [k], so each of the 40 applicants may be asked different questions and answers cannot be compared consistently when picking the 8 airport drivers [app], raising the risk of a biased or lucky selection for a safety-critical role [an]. A single chat also reveals little depth [k]. In 20 minutes the owner cannot verify driving records, licences or claim histories before trusting drivers with passengers on 24 daily routes [app], risking poor service that could damage, or even lose, the new airport contract [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Northgate Coach Travel should use two-round interviews or a single informal chat to select the 8 airport drivers? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Two-round interviews cost a little but are far more reliable [k]. The 15-minute telephone screening clears the 40 applicants cheaply, and the $1,400 budget covers panel interviews for up to 10 finalists at $140 each (10 x $140 = $1,400), selecting the strongest 8 on merit [app]. Structured, recorded answers protect the company from unfair-selection claims and let panel members probe customer-service skills properly [an]. However, the 20-minute informal chat is free, fast and might secure drivers within days, which helps if routes must start within 8 weeks [k]. For internal candidates from the 44 existing drivers it could work, but it cannot test new applicants consistently against licence and the 5-year clean-record requirement [app]. Saving $1,400 means little if an unfit driver causes an incident on the 24 daily routes [an]. Overall, the company should run two-round interviews because the airport contract demands verified records and strong customer-service skill, and the process fits the $1,400 budget exactly [eval]. The informal chat could follow the panel decision as a courtesy introduction, but never as the selection method [eval].

scenario_stem:
Amberleigh Dairies is a private limited company processing 90,000 litres of milk weekly, supplying 40 shops and 8 cafes. Last year revenue was $2.9 million; three deliveries contained sour milk and 2% of yoghurt pots were underweight.

Its largest customer, a 10-shop chain, is reviewing suppliers. In 5 weeks the owners choose 2 inspectors testing finished batches at packing for $30,000 a year, or quality assurance covering pasteurisation checks, calibrated fillers and hygiene training for $40,000 once.

questions.question_text: Define 'zero defects'.
questions.model_answer: Zero defects is the quality target that every product produced should have no faults, so production is right first time [2].

knowledge_max_2: Producing goods with no faults at all
Being right first time / continuous effort to eliminate errors

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why quality is important to Amberleigh Dairies.
questions.model_answer: First, quality is vital for food safety [k]. Sour milk in three deliveries last month risks making customers ill, which could lead to fines, product seizures and prosecution [app]. Second, quality protects customer relationships and sales [k]. The 10-shop chain, its largest customer, is reviewing suppliers, and repeated faults would push it to switch to a rival dairy [app].

knowledge_max_2: Quality protects customer safety / avoids fines
Quality protects customer relationships and sales
application_max_2: Reference to sour milk in three deliveries last month
Reference to 10-shop chain reviewing suppliers / $2.9 million revenue

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Amberleigh Dairies might face if it relies on inspection of finished batches alone (Option A).
questions.model_answer: First, checking finished batches detects faults only after they occur [k]. Pasteurisation errors and underweight filling happen upstream, so inspectors would find but not fix the 2% below-weight pots [app]. Scrapped pots waste milk already processed, raising costs [an]. Second, sampling at packing can miss faulty items in a large batch [k]. With 90,000 litres processed weekly, sour milk could still slip through in untested pots reaching 40 shops and 8 cafes [app]. One case of food poisoning could cost the dairy its 10-shop chain and permanently damage its reputation [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Amberleigh Dairies should choose quality assurance (Option B)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option B costs $40,000 once and prevents faults at source: pasteurisation temperature and time checks, calibrated filling machines and hygiene training remove the causes of sour milk and below-weight pots [k]. Preventing failures before packing protects the 40 shops, 8 cafes and the 10-shop chain whose review is due within 5 weeks [app]. Over two years Option B costs $40,000 while Option A costs $60,000, so prevention is both safer and cheaper [an]. However, Option A hires 2 inspectors for $30,000 a year and starts immediately, giving early warning on every finished batch as an independent checkpoint [k]. But Option A recurs at $60,000 over two years, detects rather than prevents, and leaves pasteurisation faults unchecked at source [app]. A single missed batch could still end the 10-shop chain relationship, threatening $2.9 million of revenue [an]. Overall, I think Amberleigh Dairies should choose Option B [eval] because it addresses root causes, costs $20,000 less over two years and directly defends the largest customer contract [eval].
