questions.question_text: Define 'electronic point of sale (EPOS)'.
questions.model_answer: Electronic point of sale is a computerised till system that scans barcodes, records each sale and updates sales and stock records automatically at the checkout. [2]

knowledge_max_2: EPOS = computerised till that records sales electronically
Linked to stock records so inventory updates automatically

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Ondara Convenience Stores of installing EPOS tills.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: EPOS records every sale instantly, so stock figures are always up to date [k]. Reordering would be automatic, replacing the 2 days per store monthly stock-take with a 4 hours per store task [app]. Benefit 2: EPOS creates a detailed sales record that helps ordering decisions [k]. Shrinkage of $84,000 a year would be expected to fall by 60%, saving about $50,400 a year [app].

knowledge_max_2: EPOS keeps stock records accurate and current in real time
Detailed sales data supports better ordering and pricing decisions
application_max_2: Monthly stock-take falls from 2 days to 4 hours per store
Shrinkage of $84,000 reduced by 60% (about $50,400 a year saved)

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Ondara Convenience Stores could face if it installs EPOS tills.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: EPOS requires a large upfront payment [k]. Option B costs $260,000, a big outlay for a business earning $9.6 million a year [app]. If the system underperforms, the money is hard to recover and cash flow suffers [an]. Problem 2: Staff must learn to use the new system [k]. With 58 staff across 4 stores, training and early till errors could frustrate customers [app]. Poor training could slow service and lose regular shoppers [an].

knowledge_max_2: EPOS needs a large upfront capital payment
Staff require training to operate EPOS correctly
application_max_2: Option B costs $260,000 against $9.6 million annual revenue
58 staff across 4 stores need retraining and support
analysis_max_2: High fixed investment reduces liquidity and financial flexibility
Disruption and customer frustration during changeover could offset savings

questions.question_text: Do you think Ondara Convenience Stores should install EPOS tills rather than hire stock clerks? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Case for EPOS: EPOS automates sales recording and reordering [k]. It would cut shrinkage by 60% (about $50,400 a year from $84,000) and turn the 2 days per store stock-take into a 4 hours per store task, while 4 clerks would cost $76,000 a year (4 x $19,000) [app]. Accurate, live stock data would help Ondara avoid empty shelves across its 4 stores [an]. Case for clerks: Option A avoids the $260,000 outlay and keeps records checked by people who know each store [k]. Four part-time clerks at $19,000 a year each would cost $76,000 a year and could also serve customers, but would not cut shrinkage or speed up tills [app]. Clerks alone leave the shrinkage problem and the 2-day stock-takes untouched [an]. Overall, Ondara should install EPOS because the $50,400 shrinkage saving plus avoided clerk costs of $76,000 a year (about $126,400 in total) recovers the $260,000 outlay in roughly 2 years [eval]. If staff are unsure about the system, the owners could trial EPOS in 1 store first [eval].

knowledge_max_2: EPOS automates sales recording and stock reordering
Manual clerks keep records but cannot prevent shrinkage electronically
application_max_2: 60% shrinkage cut (~$50,400 of $84,000), stock-take falls from 2 days to 4 hours per store
4 clerks at $19,000 each = $76,000 a year vs Option B $260,000 outlay
analysis_max_2: Live stock data reduces stockouts and over-ordering across stores
Clerks retain old problems (shrinkage, slow stock-takes), weakening the manual option
evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation using stem figures (save ~$126,400 a year, recovery in about 2 years)
Suggestion to de-risk the decision (trial in one store first)

scenario_stem:
Greyfin Fisheries Ltd is a private limited company processing fish in Country X. It employs 26 workers, has sales revenue of $520,000 and holds $35,000. Owner Marco Dene wants a $60,000 cold-storage room after the old one failed twice.

Marco compares a $30,000 government grant with micro-finance. The grant needs audited accounts, completion within 18 months and no spending on wages. A $45,000 micro-finance loan charges 11% over 4 years, costing $4,950 a year and $19,800 total interest.

questions.question_text: Define 'grant'.
questions.model_answer: A grant is a sum of money given to a business, often by a government, to support a specific purpose, which does not have to be repaid, normally subject to conditions. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Sum of money given to a business (often by government)
Does not have to be repaid / usually has conditions and a specific purpose

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of the government grant for Greyfin Fisheries Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: A grant does not have to be repaid [k], so Greyfin could fund half the $60,000 cold-storage room from the $30,000 grant and keep its $35,000 cash reserves intact [app]. Advantage 2: The grant pays towards a specific project the business wants to complete [k]; Greyfin can replace the cold-storage room that failed twice last year and protect its 26 jobs and $520,000 annual sales revenue [app].

knowledge_max_2: No repayment / non-repayable finance
Supports a specific purpose/project chosen by the business
application_max_2: $30,000 towards the $60,000 cold-storage unit; $35,000 reserves intact
26 workers / $520,000 annual sales revenue / failed cold-storage room

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages of micro-finance for Greyfin Fisheries Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Disadvantage 1: Interest and repayments must be made [k]; the $45,000 loan at 11% costs $4,950 a year and $19,800 in total interest [app], reducing the profit and cash available for other needs such as repairs or new equipment [an]. Disadvantage 2: Missing payments can damage the business [k]; with the cold-storage room unreliable, revenue could slip and Greyfin could struggle to meet the annual repayments of $4,950 [app], harming its credit record with lenders [an].

knowledge_max_2: Interest must be paid on the loan
Loan must be repaid on schedule / repayment risk
application_max_2: $45,000 loan / 11% / $4,950 a year / $19,800 total interest
4 years repayment period / unreliable cold-storage room
analysis_max_2: Interest reduces profit and available working capital
Default risk damages credit record and future borrowing

questions.question_text: Do you think Greyfin Fisheries Ltd should accept the grant or take the micro-finance loan? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The grant is free money: $30,000 towards the $60,000 project, so with $35,000 of cash reserves Greyfin could fund the $30,000 balance without borrowing a penny [k] [app]; the project would cost nothing beyond the stated conditions [an]. However, the grant is not guaranteed until the audited accounts are assessed, the work must finish within 18 months, and the money cannot be used to pay wages [an]. Micro-finance is larger and faster ($45,000), giving Greyfin more headroom, but it costs $19,800 in total interest over 4 years and must be repaid even if fish sales dip [k] [app]. Overall, I think Greyfin should apply for the grant first [eval], using its $35,000 reserves to bridge any timing gap; it should take the micro-finance loan only if the grant is refused, delayed or insufficient [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Grant: non-repayable but conditional and not guaranteed
Micro-finance: smaller loans with interest and fixed repayment
application_max_2: $30,000 grant + $35,000 reserves vs the $60,000 cost
$45,000 loan / $19,800 total interest / 4 years
analysis_max_2: Grant: zero interest and cash preserved vs risk of delay/refusal/conditions
Micro-finance: certainty/speed/headroom vs interest burden and repayment risk
evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation weighing both sources with stem figures
Sensible fallback/sequencing argument or recognition of grant conditions / justified overall judgement

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Marne Valley Dairies is a sole trader dairy farm in Country X selling milk to a processing plant. It earned $820,000 revenue and $46,000 profit, having borrowed $400,000 at a variable interest rate of 4% to replace its milking parlour.

The base rate rose to 7%, lifting annual interest from $16,000 to $28,000, an extra $12,000, while milk prices stayed flat and feed and energy costs rose. The owner must decide whether to switch to a fixed rate.

questions.question_text: Calculate how much more interest the farm pays each year at 7% compared with 4% on its $400,000 loan.
questions.model_answer: At 4% the annual interest is $16,000 and at 7% it is $28,000 [1]; the difference is $28,000 - $16,000 = $12,000 extra a year [1]. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Difference = $12,000 additional interest per year

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why a rise in interest rates increases the financial pressure on businesses with loans.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Higher rates directly raise the cost of borrowing [k]. Marne Valley's annual interest on its $400,000 loan has risen from $16,000 to $28,000, an extra $12,000 a year [app]. Reason 2: Higher interest payments reduce profit and cash flow [k]. The farm's profit was only $46,000 last year, so the extra $12,000 removes over a quarter of its profit before tax or reinvestment [app].

knowledge_max_2: Interest costs rise when variable rates rise, increasing fixed financial commitments
Higher interest payments reduce profit and cash available for investment
application_max_2: Interest risen from $16,000 to $28,000 on the $400,000 variable-rate loan
Profit of $46,000; the extra $12,000 is over a quarter of annual profit

questions.question_text: Explain two ways Marne Valley Dairies could respond to the extra $12,000 annual interest cost.
questions.model_answer: Way 1: Cut production costs [k]. Feed and energy costs have already risen even though milk prices have stayed flat [app], so the farm could trim waste and renegotiate supplier prices to restore the margin [an]. Way 2: Renegotiate the loan with its bank [k]. The $400,000 outstanding loan could be stretched over a longer repayment period or converted to a fixed rate [app], which spreads the cost more evenly and removes the risk of rates rising again [an].

knowledge_max_2: Reducing costs offsets higher interest without cutting sales
Refinancing or renegotiating can spread repayments or fix the rate
application_max_2: Feed and energy costs have risen while milk prices have stayed flat
Variable-rate loan of $400,000; base rate raised to 7%; interest now $28,000 a year
analysis_max_2: Lower costs rebuild the profit margin absorbed by the extra $12,000
A longer term or fixed rate smooths cash flow and caps future repayments

questions.question_text: Do you think Marne Valley Dairies should switch its loan to a fixed rate now? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Switching to a fixed rate would give the farm certainty [k]: at 7.5% the annual interest would be $30,000, only $2,000 more than the $28,000 it pays now [app], so the business can budget with confidence if the base rate rises again [an]. However, a fixed rate removes the benefit if rates fall [k]: if the base rate returns to 4%, the farm would still pay $30,000 instead of $16,000, an extra $14,000 a year [app], which would hurt a farm whose profit is only $46,000 [an]. Overall [eval], with profit so thin and rates already well above the 4% at which the loan was taken, the farm should fix the rate to protect cash flow [eval], accepting a small premium for certainty.

knowledge_max_2: Fixed rate gives certainty of repayments regardless of rate movements
Fixed rate removes the benefit if market interest rates fall
application_max_2: Fixed at 7.5% = $30,000 a year vs $28,000 now, only $2,000 more
If the rate fell back to 4% the farm would pay $14,000 a year extra; profit only $46,000
analysis_max_2: Certainty helps budgeting and protects against further rises
Being locked into a high fixed rate wastes money if rates fall
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options using stem figures before deciding
Reaches a justified, qualified recommendation (fix to protect thin profit and cash flow)

scenario_stem:
Brackmoor Haulage Co is a road freight partnership in Fenwick running 28 HGVs on the northern industrial corridor. Its 34 drivers take 2 weeks of training and specialise on 3 fixed routes, carrying 1,900 tonnes monthly.

Fuel use has fallen 14% since fixed routes began. Tom Brady must decide whether to keep the 3 fixed routes or switch to flexible scheduling. Two supermarket contracts require delivery within 90 minutes of schedule, with $1,200 penalties per late load.

questions.question_text: Define 'specialisation'.
questions.model_answer: Specialisation is when a worker, business or region focuses on one product or one task, such as Brackmoor's drivers each specialising on one of the 3 fixed routes. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Specialisation = concentrating on one product, service or task
Workers or firms focus on what they do best (allow fixed-route driver examples)

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why specialisation benefits Brackmoor Haulage Co.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Specialisation lets drivers become expert on particular routes, saving time and fuel [k]. Since drivers were assigned fixed routes, fuel use per kilometre has fallen 14%, and the company carries 1,900 tonnes a month [app]. Reason 2: Specialisation builds experience and knowledge that reduce mistakes [k]. Drivers receive 2 weeks of route-specific training before their first trip, and the 3 fixed routes help supermarket contracts arrive within the 90-minute window [app].

knowledge_max_2: Specialists become expert, faster and make fewer mistakes
Experience reduces waste of fuel, time and money
application_max_2: Fuel use per kilometre fell 14% after fixed routes were assigned
1,900 tonnes a month; 2 weeks route-specific training; 90-minute delivery windows; 3 fixed routes

questions.question_text: Explain two risks of specialisation for Brackmoor.
questions.model_answer: Risk 1: Relying on a few drivers per route creates dependency if a specialist is absent [k]. With only 34 drivers covering 3 fixed routes, illness or resignation could leave a route uncovered [app]. A missed supermarket delivery would cost $1,200 in penalties per late load, directly hitting profit [an]. Risk 2: Specialisation reduces flexibility when demand changes [k]. If one route's volume falls while another rises, fixed assignments could leave Brackmoor with unused capacity on one route and overtime on another [app]. Rigid schedules may make it harder to win new contracts outside the northern industrial corridor, limiting growth [an].

knowledge_max_2: Dependency on specialist staff / capacity lost if they are absent
Inflexibility when demand patterns change
application_max_2: 34 drivers across 3 fixed routes; 2 national supermarket contracts with 90-minute windows
$1,200 penalty per late load
analysis_max_2: A single absence can trigger $1,200 penalties and damage supermarket relationships
Rigid routes limit the ability to respond to demand changes or win work outside the corridor

questions.question_text: Do you think Brackmoor should keep its 3 fixed routes rather than switch to flexible scheduling? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Argument for keeping fixed routes: specialisation has cut fuel use per kilometre by 14% since drivers were assigned fixed routes [k]. Fixed routes also support the 90-minute delivery windows in the 2 national supermarket contracts, where each late load costs $1,200 [app]. Dropping fixed routes would risk late deliveries, penalties and losing these contracts [an]. Argument for flexible scheduling: flexible cover would help if a specialist driver is ill and would let Brackmoor respond when volumes change between the 3 fixed routes [k]. It could also let the firm take on work outside the northern industrial corridor, using its 28 HGVs more fully [app]. However, flexible drivers would need retraining and fuel savings would likely fall below the 14% already achieved [an]. Overall, on the stem's figures, keeping the 3 fixed routes is the safer choice because the 14% fuel saving and the $1,200-per-load penalties tied to 90-minute windows outweigh the flexibility benefit while the supermarket contracts run [eval]. If a key driver resigns or a major client leaves, Brackmoor should review the decision and consider partial flexibility [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Fixed routes underpin specialisation gains such as fuel savings
Flexible scheduling improves staff cover and adaptability
application_max_2: 14% fuel saving; 90-minute windows; $1,200 penalties; 2 national supermarket contracts
28 HGVs; 34 drivers; 3 fixed routes
analysis_max_2: Losing the fuel saving and risking penalties would damage profit and contracts
Flexibility has value for cover and new markets but dilutes driver expertise
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation favouring fixed routes while contracts run
Balanced judgement recognising partial flexibility if circumstances change

scenario_stem:
Wexmoor Care Homes Ltd is a private limited company with 240 carers, 9 care managers and a head of care. Each home has 2 management levels below the head of care. Turnover is 26%, and 41% of leavers cited no progression.

The board weighs a senior carer grade, adding a third level and promotion for 36 experienced carers at $2,400 each, costing $86,400 a year, against keeping 2 levels with a 4% pay rise costing $151,000. The head of care favours promotion.

questions.question_text: Define 'hierarchy'.
questions.model_answer: Hierarchy is the levels of authority and responsibility in a business, from senior managers at the top to junior staff at the bottom, such as Wexmoor's carers reporting through care managers to the head of care. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Hierarchy = levels of authority/responsibility in an organisation
Staff at higher levels hold more authority over those below

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why a clear hierarchy is important to Wexmoor Care Homes Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: A hierarchy clarifies who is responsible for what [k]. Wexmoor's 240 carers report through 9 care managers to one head of care, so each home knows its lines of authority [app]. Reason 2: A hierarchy should give staff a promotion path [k]. With only 2 management levels, 41% of leavers cited no career progression, so clearer levels could help retain carers [app].

knowledge_max_2: Hierarchy defines responsibilities and lines of authority
Hierarchy provides promotion paths that aid retention and motivation
application_max_2: 240 carers report through 9 care managers to one head of care across 6 homes
Only 2 management levels; 41% of leavers cited no career progression

questions.question_text: Explain two drawbacks of adding a third level (senior carer grade) to Wexmoor's hierarchy.
questions.model_answer: Drawback 1: Adding a level lengthens the chain of command and can slow decisions [k]. A third level would sit between the 240 carers and the head of care, adding another step for approvals and information to travel [app]. Longer lines could delay responses to care-home incidents where minutes matter [an]. Drawback 2: A new grade raises payroll costs [k]. The senior carer grade would cost $86,400 a year (36 experienced carers at $2,400 extra each) [app]. If the grade does not cut the 26% turnover, Wexmoor would carry higher wages without the promised savings [an].

knowledge_max_2: Extra levels lengthen the chain of command and slow decisions
Extra levels add management cost and may narrow spans further
application_max_2: A third level would sit between 240 carers and the head of care
$86,400 a year for 36 experienced carers at $2,400 extra each
analysis_max_2: Longer decision lines could delay urgent care responses, risking resident safety
If turnover stays at 26%, the $86,400 grade cost is paid without retention benefits

questions.question_text: Do you think Wexmoor should create the senior carer grade rather than give all carers a 4% pay rise? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Argument for the senior carer grade: it adds a third level to the hierarchy and creates a visible promotion path [k]. 36 experienced carers would gain $2,400 a year extra each, costing $86,400 a year, and 41% of leavers cited no career progression as the reason for leaving [app]. A targeted grade could lift retention of the most skilled carers and protect care quality [an]. Argument for the 4% pay rise: it rewards all carers fairly rather than a chosen few [k]. The 4% rise across 240 carers costs $151,000 a year, nearly double the grade's $86,400, but it avoids resentment among carers passed over for senior posts [app]. However, a flat rise does not fix the missing progression that drives leavers, so turnover may stay near 26% [an]. Overall, on the stem's figures, Wexmoor should create the senior carer grade because 41% of leavers point to missing progression and $86,400 a year is cheaper than $151,000; it should be paired with clear selection criteria to limit resentment [eval]. If turnover does not fall within a year, the 4% rise for all carers should be reconsidered [eval].

knowledge_max_2: A promotion grade motivates and retains high performers
A flat pay rise rewards everyone equally but may ignore progression needs
application_max_2: $2,400 extra each for 36 experienced carers = $86,400 a year
4% rise for 240 carers costs $151,000 a year; 41% of leavers cite no career progression; turnover 26%
analysis_max_2: Targeted grade tackles the stated reason for leaving and should lift retention
Flat rise is costlier and may not fix progression, so turnover could persist
evaluation_max_2: Recommends the senior carer grade at $86,400 a year, with clear selection criteria
Reconsider the 4% rise if turnover does not fall within a year

scenario_stem:
Bramfield Supermarket is a private limited company in Country X with 6 branches and 480 staff, earning $14.6 million. Breakfast cereals are 11% of sales. Annual marketing is $210,000, with $60,000 allocated to cereal promotions as discounters cut staple prices.

The manager wants cereal sales up 20%. Options: a BOGOF offer on 14 cereal brands or a 15% price reduction on the same 14 brands. Suppliers have agreed to fund half of the cost this quarter.

questions.question_text: Define 'sales promotion'.
questions.model_answer: Short-term incentives used to encourage customers to buy a product or to boost sales of it, such as discounts or special offers [2].

knowledge_max_2: short-term incentives to buy
used to boost sales of a product

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages to Bramfield Supermarket of using a BOGOF offer on cereal.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: BOGOF can rapidly increase sales volume [k], helping the supermarket reach its target of a 20% rise in cereal sales across the 6 branches [app]. Advantage 2: BOGOF attracts customers into the supermarket [k], where they may buy other products alongside the 14 cereal brands [app].

knowledge_max_2: rapidly increases sales volume
attracts customers into the store (footfall)
application_max_2: 20% rise in cereal sales
6 branches
14 cereal brands
breakfast cereals

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Bramfield Supermarket of the suppliers funding half the promotion.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Funding halves the supermarket's net cost of the promotion [k], so the $60,000 allocation stretches further whichever option is chosen [app], keeping money available within the wider $210,000 marketing budget [an]. Benefit 2: Suppliers fund the activity because higher sales also benefit their own brands [k], so they share the risk on the 14 cereal brands [app], which strengthens the long-term trading relationship [an].

knowledge_max_2: reduces supermarket's net promotional cost
shared risk with suppliers seeking higher sales
application_max_2: $60,000 allocation
$210,000 marketing expenditure
14 cereal brands
fund half of the cost
analysis_max_2: keeps budget available for other marketing
strengthens supplier relationships and cooperation

valid_app_words: Suppliers have agreed to fund half

questions.question_text: Do you think Bramfield Supermarket should use the BOGOF offer or the 15% price reduction on its cereal brands? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The BOGOF offer creates a strong short-term incentive, because shoppers pay full price for one box and receive a second box free [k], which could push cereal sales up sharply towards the 20% target across all 14 brands [app], clearing stock quickly and drawing in price-conscious families [an]. However, the 15% price reduction is simpler for staff and customers to understand [k], lowering the shelf price of every box without giving away extra units [app], protecting margins if BOGOF would halve the value of each sale at higher volume [an]. Overall, Bramfield should choose BOGOF because the suppliers fund half the cost either way, making the free extra units affordable [eval], and a dramatic offer is more likely to achieve a 20% quarterly uplift than a modest 15% discount during rival price cuts [eval].

knowledge_max_2: BOGOF: strong instant incentive, drives volume
price reduction: simple, protects unit margins/understanding
application_max_2: 20% target across 14 brands
suppliers funding half of either option
$60,000 allocation
rival discounters cutting prices
analysis_max_2: clears stock quickly, attracts price-sensitive shoppers
simpler administration and preserves margins per unit
evaluation_max_2: weighs dramatic volume-driving offer against simpler discount
justified choice given shared funding and rival price pressure

scenario_stem:
Breckfield Pump Works, a private limited company, makes water pumps for farms. With 85 workers it produces 1,400 pumps a month and earns $11.2 million a year. Design errors mean 8% of pumps need reworking before dispatch.

Option A keeps separate CAD/CAM machines and 2 inspection stations. Option B spends $2.4 million on a CIM system linking design, 6 CNC machines, scanners and stock control, cutting rework from 8% to 3% and lifting output to 1,750 pumps a month; training 12 staff costs $36,000.

questions.question_text: Define 'computer-integrated manufacturing (CIM)'.
questions.model_answer: Computer-integrated manufacturing is the linking of all production stages - design, machining, quality inspection and stock control - into one computer-controlled system that shares information automatically. [2]

knowledge_max_2: CIM links design, production, inspection and stock in one computer system
Information flows automatically between stages without manual paperwork

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Breckfield Pump Works of installing a CIM system.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: CIM shares design data directly with the machines, removing manual re-entry [k]. Rework would fall from 8% of pumps to 3%, saving materials and labour [app]. Benefit 2: Linking all stages in one system speeds up the whole production flow [k]. Output would rise from 1,400 pumps a month to 1,750 pumps a month, a 25% increase [app].

knowledge_max_2: CIM removes manual data transfer errors between design and production
An integrated flow speeds up the process from planning to dispatch
application_max_2: Rework falls from 8% to 3% of pumps
Output rises from 1,400 to 1,750 pumps a month (a 25% increase)

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Breckfield Pump Works could face if it installs a CIM system.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: CIM costs a great deal of money up front [k]. Option B requires $2.4 million plus $36,000 to train 12 staff [app]. Borrowing that sum would add interest payments and raise financial risk for the company [an]. Problem 2: CIM depends on all its linked parts working together [k]. A fault in 1 of the 6 CNC machines or in the shared database could stop the whole line [app]. One breakdown could halt deliveries to farm customers and breach supply commitments [an].

knowledge_max_2: CIM requires very high capital investment and training spend
Integrated systems can fail as a whole if one component breaks
application_max_2: Option B costs $2.4 million plus $36,000 to train 12 staff
6 CNC machines and one shared database are all linked together
analysis_max_2: High borrowing increases interest burden and financial risk
A single-point failure could stop production and lose farm customer contracts

questions.question_text: Do you think Breckfield Pump Works should install the CIM system rather than keep the separate machines? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Case for CIM: CIM links design, machining, inspection and stock in 1 system [k]. It would cut rework from 8% to 3% and raise output from 1,400 to 1,750 pumps a month, a 25% increase on $11.2 million of revenue [app]. Fewer errors and higher output would raise profit and let Breckfield take on more farm contracts [an]. Case for keeping separate machines: Option A avoids the $2.4 million cost and the $36,000 training bill [k]. The existing CAD and CAM machines and 2 inspection stations already work, so there is no disruption or retraining [app]. Staying with separate machines keeps the 8% rework rate and the 1,400 pumps a month output limit [an]. Overall, Breckfield should install CIM, because cutting rework from 8% to 3% and lifting output by 25% outweighs the upfront cost over time [eval]. The directors could phase the system in over 12 months to limit disruption [eval].

knowledge_max_2: CIM integrates all stages to cut errors and speed flow
Separate machines avoid capital cost and retraining
application_max_2: Rework falls from 8% to 3%; output rises from 1,400 to 1,750 pumps (+25%) on $11.2 million revenue
Option A avoids $2.4 million and $36,000 training; 8% rework and 1,400 pumps limit remain
analysis_max_2: Lower rework and higher output raise profit and capacity for farm contracts
Keeping separate machines preserves status quo inefficiencies and output ceiling
evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation using stem figures (rework and 25% output gain outweigh cost)
Practical phasing suggestion to reduce risk (12-month phased rollout)

scenario_stem:
Kitebridge Apps Ltd is a private limited company developing a budgeting app for students in Country X. The app has 4,200 downloads and revenue of $38,000. The founders need $35,000 for marketing and a freelance illustrator before launching a premium version.

They compare a $20,000 micro-finance loan at 9% over 3 years, costing $1,800 a year, with reward-based crowdfunding targeting $35,000. Unmet targets return all pledges; the platform takes a 4% success fee of $1,400.

questions.question_text: Define 'micro-finance'.
questions.model_answer: Micro-finance is the provision of small loans and other financial services to small businesses or entrepreneurs, usually by specialist lenders, often for those unable to obtain ordinary bank finance. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Small loans (and other financial services) to small businesses/entrepreneurs
Offered by specialist lenders, often to those excluded from ordinary bank finance

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of crowdfunding for Kitebridge Apps Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: No interest or repayments are owed [k]; if the campaign reaches $35,000, backers fund the marketing budget and the premium launch without Kitebridge taking on debt [app]. Advantage 2: A campaign generates publicity and feedback [k], helping Kitebridge promote the app to a far wider audience than its current 4,200 downloads and build an engaged community of early users [app].

knowledge_max_2: No interest or repayment if target reached
Marketing/publicity and feedback from backers
application_max_2: $35,000 target funding marketing and the premium version
4,200 downloads / student audience / freelance illustrator

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages of micro-finance for Kitebridge Apps Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Disadvantage 1: The loan is smaller than the amount needed [k]; at $20,000 it leaves a $15,000 shortfall against the $35,000 required [app], so the premium version and its marketing could be delayed, frustrating growth [an]. scenario_stem:
Vanguard Fleet Haulage Ltd is a private limited company providing regional logistics with 18 trucks in Country X. It employs 34 drivers and staff, with $2.4 million revenue. It can buy 4 electric trucks costing $120,000, cutting diesel costs by $15,000 a year.

Under a green-freight subsidy, the government pays $40,000 and Vanguard funds the remaining $80,000 from reserves, with trucks operational within 9 months. Alternatively, a factoring company advances 75% of $150,000 of outstanding customer invoices ($112,500) for a 3.5% fee ($5,250).

questions.question_text: Define 'capital expenditure'.

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of the green-freight subsidy for Vanguard Fleet Haulage Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: It does not have to be repaid [k]; the $40,000 subsidy cuts Vanguard's net cost of the four electric trucks by one-third, to $80,000 from its reserves [app]. Advantage 2: It lowers the risk of a large investment [k]; Vanguard can modernise its 18-truck fleet, meet clean-air rules and protect annual sales revenue of $2.4 million [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages of factoring of debts for Vanguard Fleet Haulage Ltd.

Disadvantage 2: The factor takes over collection of the debts [k], dealing with Vanguard's customers about the $150,000 owed [app], which can strain relationships built over years and push clients towards rival hauliers [an].

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Rowanbrook Ice Cream Co is a private limited company producing premium ice cream and exporting to two neighbouring countries. It made $2.8 million sales amid strong demand and 4.5% growth.

With inflation at 6.5% against a 2% target, the central bank raised its base rate from 3% to 6%. Profitable and debt-free, the firm plans a $900,000 factory extension, a bank loan costing $54,000 interest yearly at 6%, and 26 new production jobs. Should it proceed now?

questions.question_text: Define 'boom'.
questions.model_answer: A boom is a phase of the business cycle in which the economy is growing rapidly, with high consumer spending, low unemployment and rising incomes and output. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Phase of the business cycle with rapid economic growth
High spending, low unemployment and rising incomes/output

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the central bank may raise interest rates during a boom.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: To control inflation [k]. Inflation has reached 6.5%, well above the government target of 2%, so higher interest rates should cool spending and slow price rises [app]. Reason 2: To reduce excessive borrowing [k]. The economy is growing at 4.5% a year and the base rate was raised from 3% to 6%, so higher rates discourage households and businesses from taking on more debt [app].

knowledge_max_2: Raise rates to bring inflation back towards its target
Raise rates to curb excessive borrowing and credit growth
application_max_2: Inflation at 6.5% compared with the 2% target
Economy growing at 4.5% a year; base rate raised from 3% to 6%

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Rowanbrook Ice Cream Co of the current boom.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Strong sales demand supports growth [k]. The economy is growing by 4.5% a year and Rowanbrook generated $2.8 million in sales last year, exporting some of its output to two neighbouring countries [app], so demand may support the planned factory extension [an]. Benefit 2: Profits can partly fund expansion [k]. The company is profitable and carries no debt apart from the planned loan [app], so it can use retained profit to cover part of the $900,000 cost and borrow less [an].

knowledge_max_2: Strong consumer demand lifts sales and output
Healthy profits and cash flow enable self-financing of investment
application_max_2: Economy growing at 4.5% a year; sales of $2.8 million; exports to two neighbouring countries
Profitable business with no debt apart from the planned loan for the $900,000 extension
analysis_max_2: Strong demand supports the case for extra capacity
Retained profit cuts the amount borrowed and the interest bill

questions.question_text: Do you think Rowanbrook Ice Cream Co should proceed with the $900,000 factory extension now? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Proceeding would capture strong demand at the right time [k]: the economy is growing at 4.5% a year and Rowanbrook sold $2.8 million of ice cream last year [app], so extra capacity would lift output and spread fixed costs, raising the profit on each tub [an]. However, borrowing now is expensive [k]: the base rate was raised from 3% to 6% to cool inflation of 6.5%, and the loan would cost $54,000 a year in interest [app], so if the boom cools the new factory may run below capacity while the interest still has to be paid [an]. Overall [eval], the extension is justified if Rowanbrook fixes the loan rate before it rises further [eval], since strong demand, profitability and no existing debt give the business scope to service the repayments; it should delay only if orders soften before the 26 new jobs are hired.

knowledge_max_2: Investing in capacity during strong demand maximises returns
Borrowing at higher rates increases fixed financial commitments
application_max_2: Economy growing at 4.5% a year; sales of $2.8 million; extension costing $900,000
Base rate raised from 3% to 6%; loan costing $54,000 a year in interest at 6%
analysis_max_2: Extra capacity spreads fixed costs and lifts output and profit
If demand cools, fixed interest must still be paid on below-capacity output
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options using stem figures
Conditional, justified recommendation (proceed with a fixed rate, delay if orders soften)

scenario_stem:
Northchill Cold Chain Ltd is a private limited chilled-storage business in Kellby, holding frozen fish, meat and dairy for 72 food clients across 3 warehouses with 6,800 pallet spaces. Demand has grown 25% in 2 years, but land is scarce.

Ruth Adeyemi must decide how to use 400 spare pallet spaces at Kellby No. 2: sublet them to an exporter at $18 per pallet monthly, earning $86,400 a year, or reserve them for existing clients expecting 30% growth.

questions.question_text: Define 'scarcity'.
questions.model_answer: Scarcity is the situation in which resources are limited but wants are unlimited, forcing choices, such as Northchill having only 6,800 pallet spaces while demand for chilled space has grown 25% in 2 years. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Scarcity = limited resources versus unlimited wants
Choices must be made because resources cannot satisfy all wants

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why scarcity of chilled space matters to Northchill.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Scarce capacity forces Northchill to choose between competing uses [k]. It has only 400 spare pallet spaces at Kellby No. 2, while demand has grown 25% in 2 years [app]. Reason 2: Scarcity means an opportunity cost arises whichever option is picked [k]. Reserving the spaces for existing clients excludes the income from subletting to the new exporter at $18 per pallet per month [app].

knowledge_max_2: Scarcity forces choices between competing uses of limited resources
Every choice made under scarcity carries an opportunity cost
application_max_2: 400 spare pallet spaces; demand up 25% in 2 years
$18 per pallet per month sublet option; Kellby No. 2 warehouse

questions.question_text: Explain two ways Northchill could respond to the scarcity of its chilled capacity.
questions.model_answer: Way 1: Northchill could raise prices to ration scarce space to the highest-paying users [k]. With demand up 25% in 2 years and occupancy near capacity, higher rental rates would balance supply and demand [app]. This would increase revenue per pallet and send scarce space to the clients who value it most [an]. Way 2: Northchill could invest in expansion, such as a 4th warehouse, if suitable land and capital allow [k]. Suitable land is scarce and expensive, so expansion would take planning and money [app]. Extra pallet spaces would remove the bottleneck, increasing capacity so existing clients' growth can be served without subletting to exporters [an].

knowledge_max_2: Rationing via higher prices
Expanding capacity through investment
application_max_2: Demand up 25% in 2 years; suitable land is scarce
72 food clients; 6,800 pallet spaces; 400 spare pallet spaces
analysis_max_2: Higher prices raise revenue per pallet and allocate space efficiently
Expansion removes the bottleneck and protects service to existing clients

questions.question_text: Do you think Northchill should sublet the 400 pallet spaces rather than reserve them for existing clients? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Argument for subletting: subletting the 400 spaces to the new frozen-food exporter at $18 per pallet per month earns $86,400 a year with no capital outlay [k]. That is certain, immediate income on otherwise idle capacity in a business serving 72 food clients [app]. The cash could fund the next warehouse phase or cover rising running costs [an]. Argument for reserving: existing clients expect orders to expand 30% next year, and demand has already grown 25% in 2 years [k]. If Northchill sublets the 400 spaces, existing clients may face shortages next year, damaging loyalty and risking business moving to rivals [app]. Losing anchor clients would cost far more than $86,400 a year and would undermine Northchill's role as a reliable cold-chain partner [an]. Overall, on the stem's figures, reserving the spaces for existing clients is the wiser choice because loyal clients with 30% expected growth protect Northchill's long-term capacity use and revenue, while $86,400 is modest against the risk of losing major cold-chain contracts [eval]. Northchill should revisit subletting only if existing clients confirm their 30% expansion is genuinely committed [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Subletting gives certain immediate income from idle capacity
Reserving protects relationships and expected future demand
application_max_2: 25% demand growth in 2 years; 30% expected expansion; 72 food clients
analysis_max_2: $86,400 a year is a one-off style gain that could fund expansion or running costs
Losing loyal clients risks long-term capacity use and exceeds $86,400
evaluation_max_2: Recommends reserving the spaces, conditional on clients confirming their 30% expansion
Weighs certain $86,400 income against the risk of losing long-term client relationships

scenario_stem:
Pembroke Castings Co is a private limited company in Grasmere, Country X, casting iron parts for 40 engineering firms with 130 staff. Three urgent orders worth $1.4m are due in 6 weeks, but its 4 CNC machines are booked for 8 weeks.

Production director Gary Swinnerton can buy a machine for $210,000, hire capacity at $18,000 a month for 3 months, or pay triple time for 6 weekends. He must organise job bags and inspections so 3 orders ship without disrupting the 40 customers.

questions.question_text: Define 'organising' as a role of management.
questions.model_answer: Organising is arranging resources such as staff, materials and equipment so that work can be carried out, such as Gary organising job bags, tooling and inspections so the 3 urgent orders ship on time. [2]

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why organising resources effectively is important to Pembroke Castings Co.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Organising ensures the right resources are in the right place at the right time [k]. The machining department has only 4 CNC machines, all booked solid for 8 weeks, so without reorganising, the 3 urgent orders worth $1.4m cannot ship [app]. Reason 2: Organising prevents clashes between urgent work and regular customers [k]. The board wants the 3 orders shipped on time without disrupting the 40 existing customers, which only careful allocation can achieve [app].

knowledge_max_2: Organising matches resources to tasks and deadlines

application_max_2: Only 4 CNC machines, all booked solid for 8 weeks; 3 urgent orders worth $1.4m due in 6 weeks

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Pembroke of buying the used CNC machine for $210,000.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Buying the machine gives permanent capacity inside Pembroke [k]. For $210,000 the business would own a 5th CNC machine instead of paying an outside rival foundry $18,000 a month [app]. Extra capacity would let Pembroke quote for more urgent orders after the 3 current ones, raising long-term revenue from its 40 engineering firms [an]. Benefit 2: Owning capacity removes dependency on a competitor [k]. Hiring from a rival means sharing designs, schedules and margins with a direct competitor [app]. Keeping work in-house protects Pembroke's confidential drawings and quality standards for the $1.4m of urgent orders [an].

Owning capacity reduces dependency on outsiders/competitors
application_max_2: $210,000 used machine vs $18,000 a month rival hire ($54,000 over 3 months)
3 urgent orders worth $1.4m; 4 CNC machines currently booked solid; 40 engineering firm customers
analysis_max_2: Extra capacity lets Pembroke chase further urgent orders, raising long-term revenue
In-house work protects confidentiality and quality versus outsourcing to a rival

questions.question_text: Do you think Pembroke should buy the used CNC machine rather than hire capacity from a rival foundry? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Argument for buying: buying builds permanent capacity [k]. A used CNC machine at $210,000 would give the machining department a 5th machine rather than paying $18,000 a month for 3 months ($54,000 total) for outside help [app]. Extra capacity supports the $1.4m of urgent orders and future work from the 40 engineering firms [an]. Argument for hiring: hiring is cheaper short term [k]. At $18,000 a month for 3 months, hiring costs $54,000, only about a quarter of the $210,000 purchase, and brings no maintenance or breakdown risk [app]. However, hiring shares confidential work with a rival foundry and delays capacity if the rival is busy, risking the 6-week deadline on the 3 orders [an]. Overall, on the stem's figures, Pembroke should hire capacity from the rival foundry first, because the orders are due in 6 weeks and $54,000 is far cheaper than $210,000; it can buy the machine later if urgent orders keep arriving [eval]. If the rival cannot guarantee dates or the machine proves reliable, buying it after the orders ship would be the better next step [eval].

evaluation_max_2: Recommends hiring first given the 6-week deadline and $54,000 cost versus $210,000

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Fernwood Café Ltd is a private limited company running a café in Marrowgate with 12 staff. Revenue fell from $420,000 to $330,000 over 18 months after two factories closed, costing 240 jobs.

Unemployment rose from 4% to 9%, and the central bank cut its base rate from 6% to 3.5%, but footfall stays weak and January meal deals had little effect. The owner is considering a $150,000 second outlet or trimming staff hours at the single site.

questions.question_text: Define 'recession'.
questions.model_answer: A recession is a phase of the business cycle in which economic activity falls, usually shown by two consecutive quarters of negative GDP growth, with rising unemployment and falling consumer spending. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Period of falling economic output/negative GDP growth
Rising unemployment and weak consumer spending

questions.question_text: Explain two ways the cut in interest rates from 6% to 3.5% could help Fernwood Café.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Customers can afford to borrow and spend more [k]. Lower rates reduce the cost of personal loans and overdrafts, so office workers and families may return to the café at lunchtimes and weekends [app]. Reason 2: The café could finance a second outlet more cheaply [k]. With the base rate cut to 3.5%, a loan for the $150,000 neighbouring-town outlet would carry much lower interest [app].

knowledge_max_2: Lower rates increase disposable income and the incentive to spend
Lower rates reduce the cost of business borrowing
application_max_2: Base rate cut from 6% to 3.5%; café serves office workers and families
A second outlet costing $150,000 in a neighbouring town

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Fernwood Café may still struggle despite cheaper credit.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Consumer confidence is low and unemployment is high [k]. Local unemployment has risen from 4% to 9% after two local factories closed with the loss of 240 jobs [app], so even cheap credit may not persuade cautious households to eat out [an]. Reason 2: The café's revenue has already collapsed [k]. Revenue fell from $420,000 to $330,000 over the last 18 months [app], so fixed costs such as rent and the wages of 12 staff are spread over far fewer customers, squeezing profit [an].

knowledge_max_2: Low confidence and high unemployment suppress spending regardless of rates
Falling revenue against unchanged fixed costs erodes profit
application_max_2: Unemployment rose from 4% to 9%; two factories closed with 240 jobs lost
Revenue fell from $420,000 to $330,000 over 18 months; 12 staff
analysis_max_2: Fearful households save rather than spend, so the rate cut has limited effect
Fixed costs spread over fewer sales reduce margin and risk losses

questions.question_text: Do you think Fernwood Café should open the second outlet now? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Opening now would give Fernwood a foothold in a neighbouring town before the market recovers [k]: a loan at the cut base rate of 3.5% would be relatively cheap for the $150,000 cost [app], and capturing customers early could help rebuild revenue towards the $420,000 it earned before the closures [an]. However, the café is already weakened by the recession [k]: revenue has fallen from $420,000 to $330,000 and local unemployment has risen to 9% with 240 jobs lost in two factory closures [app], so taking on $150,000 of new commitments while one site struggles could magnify losses and threaten the original café [an]. Overall [eval], Fernwood should wait rather than open now [eval], because opening in a recession with weak footfall and collapsed revenue risks compounding losses; it should hold the $150,000 and focus on restoring sales at the existing site.

knowledge_max_2: Early expansion can secure a new market when credit is cheap
Expanding while loss-making multiplies financial risk
application_max_2: Base rate cut from 6% to 3.5%; second outlet costing $150,000
Revenue fell from $420,000 to $330,000; unemployment rose to 9%; 240 jobs lost
analysis_max_2: Early mover advantage could rebuild revenue towards pre-closure levels
New fixed commitments in a downturn magnify losses at the existing site
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options using stem figures
Clear, justified recommendation (wait; restore the existing site first)

scenario_stem:
Windover Housebuilding Ltd is a private limited housebuilder with 2 active sites and 38 skilled workers, building 46 houses a year on $16m turnover. It bought a 7-hectare greenfield plot for $3.4m, planning 120 houses over 5 years.

Director Ben Hollis must choose between that plot and an inner-city brownfield site at $5.9m, which saves 18 months of planning. Greenfield needs $700,000 of new road access, while brownfield may need $850,000 of contamination clean-up.

questions.question_text: Define 'land' as a factor of production.
questions.model_answer: Land is all natural resources used to produce goods and services, including the 7-hectare greenfield plot Windover bought for $3.4m and the raw materials taken from building sites to make homes. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Land = natural resources / raw materials used in production
Reward examples such as building plots, minerals, timber or land itself

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why land is important to Windover Housebuilding.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Land provides the natural space and raw materials needed for building [k]. Windover owns 2 active sites and recently bought a 7-hectare plot for $3.4m to build 120 houses [app]. Reason 2: Without land Windover cannot produce or sell homes [k]. The planned 120-house development over 5 years depends entirely on securing suitable building land [app].

knowledge_max_2: Land = site and natural resources needed for building
Without suitable land, production is impossible
application_max_2: 2 active sites; 7-hectare plot bought for $3.4m; 38 skilled workers
46 houses a year; 120 houses planned over 5 years

questions.question_text: Explain two drawbacks of the greenfield plot compared with the brownfield site.
questions.model_answer: Drawback 1: The greenfield plot needs new road access, adding $700,000 to costs [k]. Together with the $3.4m purchase, Windover would commit $4.1m before construction, while the brownfield site already sits within existing roads and utilities [app]. Higher upfront costs reduce early cash flow and squeeze returns on the 120 planned houses [an]. Drawback 2: Greenfield development may face a longer planning process [k]. The brownfield site would save 18 months of planning time and sit closer to buyers' workplaces, advantages the greenfield plot lacks [app]. Extra delay would push back sales and tie up Windover's $16m turnover and 38 skilled workers for longer [an].

knowledge_max_2: Greenfield land needs extra infrastructure such as roads
Greenfield development often faces a longer planning process than brownfield
application_max_2: $700,000 road access; $3.4m purchase = $4.1m committed
18 months planning saved on brownfield; closer to buyers' workplaces
analysis_max_2: Higher upfront cost reduces cash flow and returns on the 120 houses
Longer delay ties up capital and workers and delays sales

questions.question_text: Do you think Windover should buy the inner-city brownfield site rather than proceed with the greenfield plot? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Argument for brownfield: the brownfield site costs $5.9m plus $850,000 of contamination clean-up, so $6.75m in total, but it saves 18 months of planning and sits closer to buyers' workplaces [k]. Faster sales of part of the 120 houses would bring in revenue sooner and cut holding costs [app]. Earlier revenue would also improve cash flow and reduce the need to borrow during construction [an]. Argument for greenfield: at $3.4m plus $700,000 road access, the greenfield plot costs $4.1m in total, $2.65m less than brownfield, and offers open space for all 120 houses [k]. With $16m annual turnover, Windover can fund the cheaper greenfield route, although greenfield may face longer planning [app]. However, delay would tie up capital and the 38 skilled workers and could strain cash before first sales [an]. Overall, on the stem's figures, Windover should proceed with the greenfield plot because at $4.1m it is $2.65m cheaper than brownfield at $6.75m, and the saving outweighs 18 months provided planning approval is likely for a 7-hectare plot outside the city [eval]. If planning is refused or buyers strongly prefer inner-city homes, the brownfield option becomes the better choice [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Brownfield: faster approval, closer to buyers, higher total cost
Greenfield: cheaper, more open space, longer planning risk
application_max_2: Greenfield $3.4m + $700,000 road = $4.1m; brownfield $5.9m + $850,000 = $6.75m
18 months planning saved; 120 houses over 5 years; $16m turnover
analysis_max_2: The $2.65m saving outweighs 18 months if approvals are obtainable
Inner-city location may boost sales but costs $2.65m more
evaluation_max_2: Recommends greenfield based on the $2.65m saving, conditional on planning approval
Recognises brownfield becomes preferable if planning is refused or demand shifts

scenario_stem:
Brightmoor Events Co is a private limited company in the capital of Country X managing conferences for 60 clients a year with 24 staff, including 8 event managers. Turnover was $3.6m. A conference on 18 September hosts 1,400 delegates at 3 venues.

Caterers, AV contractors and hotels report to different event managers; double-booked AV equipment once delayed a wedding 45 minutes. The board must appoint one senior event manager for the September conference or keep separate reporting lines.

questions.question_text: Define 'coordinating' as a role of management.
questions.model_answer: Coordinating is making sure different departments and people work together towards the same goal, such as Brightmoor ensuring the catering team, AV contractors and hotel partners all deliver for the 18 September conference. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Coordinating = linking departments/teams so they work together smoothly
Ensures consistency of effort and avoids duplication or clashes

questions.question_text: Explain two problems caused by poor coordination at Brightmoor Events Co.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Poor coordination causes clashes and mistakes between teams [k]. At a wedding last month, double-booked AV equipment delayed speeches by 45 minutes because no one aligned the suppliers [app]. Problem 2: Poor coordination wastes time and damages service quality [k]. The catering team, AV contractors and hotel partners each report to different event managers, so delays surface too late to fix before clients notice [app].

knowledge_max_2: Poor coordination causes clashes, duplication and mistakes
Poor coordination wastes time and harms service quality
application_max_2: Double-booked AV equipment delayed wedding speeches by 45 minutes
Catering team, AV contractors and hotel partners report separately to different event managers

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Brightmoor of appointing one senior event manager to coordinate all suppliers for the September conference.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: One coordinator avoids clashes and duplication between suppliers [k]. A single senior manager overseeing catering, AV contractors and hotel partners would prevent repeats of the double-booked AV equipment that delayed wedding speeches by 45 minutes [app]. Fewer clashes mean a smoother 18 September conference for the 1,400 delegates [an]. Benefit 2: One coordinator gives clear accountability [k]. With everyone reporting to one senior manager, problems surface early across the 3 venues and decisions are taken faster [app]. Faster decisions protect Brightmoor's reputation with 60 clients a year and its $3.6m turnover [an].

knowledge_max_2: Single coordinator prevents clashes and duplication
Single coordinator gives clear accountability and faster decisions
application_max_2: One senior manager to oversee catering, AV contractors and hotel partners for the 18 September conference
1,400 delegates across 3 venues; avoid repeat of the 45-minute AV delay
analysis_max_2: Clash-free delivery protects the conference experience for 1,400 delegates
Clear accountability speeds decisions, protecting reputation and $3.6m turnover

questions.question_text: Do you think Brightmoor should appoint one senior event manager to coordinate all suppliers rather than keep separate reporting lines? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Argument for one coordinator: coordinating means making teams work together towards one goal [k]. A senior event manager overseeing catering, AV contractors and hotel partners would prevent a repeat of the double-booked AV equipment that delayed speeches by 45 minutes at a wedding last month [app]. Clear ownership across the 3 venues would raise the odds of a flawless 18 September conference for 1,400 delegates [an]. Argument for separate reporting lines: separate lines keep event managers specialised and close to their own clients [k]. Each of the 8 event managers focuses on their own relationships, and adding a coordinator layer costs senior time for one event rather than the whole year [app]. However, different managers each optimising their own area created the supplier clash that caused the 45-minute delay, and a 1,400-delegate conference has no room for that [an]. Overall, on the stem's figures, Brightmoor should appoint the senior event manager for the September conference, because the 45-minute AV failure and 1,400 delegates across 3 venues show separate lines are not working at this scale [eval]. If the coordinator role creates bottlenecks or slows small events, it should be limited to large conferences only [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Coordinating = linking teams towards one goal
Specialist reporting lines keep managers close to their clients
application_max_2: One senior event manager vs 8 event managers with separate supplier reporting lines
45-minute AV delay at a wedding; 1,400 delegates across 3 venues on 18 September; $3.6m turnover
analysis_max_2: Single ownership prevents clashes and protects the conference for 1,400 delegates
Separate lines suit small events but fail at multi-venue conference scale
evaluation_max_2: Recommends appointing the coordinator for the September conference based on the AV failure evidence
Limit the role to large conferences if it creates bottlenecks on small events

scenario_stem:
Bramble & Ink Books is a sole-trader bookshop in Country X opened by Hugo Lindgren in a market town of 28,000. With 5 staff and books averaging $14, it earned $390,000. Chains and online retailers undercut by 10 to 20%, and footfall fell 15%.

online shop is open around the clock

scenario_stem:
Ferrymead Packaging Ltd, a private limited company, makes printed cardboard boxes for toy makers with 44 workers and $6.1 million revenue. Hand-drawn designs and test prototypes take 3 weeks; 7% fail customer tests, wasting about $45,000 a year.

Option A keeps hand-drawn in-house prototypes. Option B spends $220,000 on CAD design plus CAM driving a cutting table, cutting prototype time from 3 weeks to 3 days and failures from 7% to 2%, letting customers approve designs on screen; running costs are $38,000 a year.

questions.question_text: Define 'production'.
questions.model_answer: Production is the process of converting inputs such as land, labour, capital and enterprise into goods and services that can be sold to customers. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Production = turning inputs/resources into goods and services
It combines the factors of production to create output

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Ferrymead Packaging Ltd of using CAD and CAM.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: CAD lets designs be edited on screen and approved instantly [k]. Prototype time would fall from 3 weeks to 3 days and customers can approve designs on screen [app]. Benefit 2: A CAM cutting table follows the CAD design exactly [k]. Prototype failures would fall from 7% to 2%, saving about $32,000 a year in wasted board and printing [app].

knowledge_max_2: CAD allows instant digital editing and customer approval of designs
CAM reproduces CAD designs exactly, reducing errors
application_max_2: Prototype time falls from 3 weeks to 3 days
Failures fall from 7% to 2%, saving about $32,000 a year of $45,000 waste

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Ferrymead Packaging Ltd could face if it adopts CAD and CAM.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: CAD and CAM cost money to buy and run [k]. Option B needs $220,000 up front plus $38,000 a year in licences and running costs [app]. These fixed set-up costs reduce profit in the early years on $6.1 million of revenue [an]. Problem 2: Workers must learn new skills [k]. The 44 workers, used to hand-drawing, would need training on CAD software and the CAM cutting table [app]. Training time and early mistakes could delay orders for toy-maker customers [an].

knowledge_max_2: CAD/CAM needs capital outlay plus annual licences and running costs
Staff need training to use CAD and CAM effectively

questions.question_text: Do you think Ferrymead Packaging Ltd should adopt CAD and CAM rather than keep hand-drawn designs? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Case for CAD and CAM: CAD lets designs be edited, stored and shared digitally [k]. Prototype time would fall from 3 weeks to 3 days, failures from 7% to 2% and waste from $45,000 to about $13,000 a year [app]. Faster approval cycles would help Ferrymead win repeat orders from toy makers beyond the current $6.1 million revenue [an]. Case for hand-drawing: Option A avoids the $220,000 investment and the $38,000 yearly licence costs [k]. Existing hand skills keep prototypes flexible for unusual one-off boxes with no computer dependence [app]. Hand-drawing keeps the 3-week prototype cycle and the $45,000 a year waste burden [an]. Overall, Ferrymead should adopt CAD and CAM, because prototypes cut from 3 weeks to 3 days and about $32,000 a year waste saving outweigh licence costs [eval]. In quiet seasons the firm could run fewer CAM hours to keep costs down [eval].

knowledge_max_2: CAD/CAM gives fast digital design, approval and exact cutting
Hand-drawing avoids capital and licence costs and keeps flexibility

scenario_stem:
Stanway Uniform Co is a private limited company making school and hospital uniforms in Country X. It employs 30 full-time production workers, with monthly wages of $28,000. Clients buy on 75-day credit and owe $84,000. Ruth Calloway needs $58,000 embroidery machines to keep a $120,000 hospital contract.

A factoring company advances 90% of invoices ($75,600) for a 2% fee ($1,680) and takes over credit control. A $25,000 micro-finance loan charges 13% over 3 years, costing $3,250 a year and $9,750 total interest.

Bought on credit / payment not yet received

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of factoring of debts for Stanway Uniform Co.

Advantage 2: The factor takes over collecting the debts [k], removing the chasing workload from Ruth Calloway's 30 workers and helping to safeguard the hospital contract worth $120,000 a year [app].

Factor takes over debt collection/credit control

Disadvantage 2: Interest is expensive relative to the amount borrowed [k]; 13% costs $3,250 a year and $9,750 over 3 years [app], a heavy strain alongside monthly wages of $28,000 [an].

knowledge_max_2: Loan size limited / below requirements
Interest must be paid / cost of borrowing
application_max_2: $25,000 vs $58,000 needed / $33,000 shortfall

questions.question_text: Do you think Stanway Uniform Co should use factoring of debts or micro-finance? Justify your answer.

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Corvale Deliveries Ltd is a private limited company providing parcel and grocery delivery. It employs 29 staff, serves 300 business customers with 8 diesel vans bought with a $240,000 loan, and earned $1.9 million.

As the base rate rose from 3% to 6%, interest rose from $7,200 to $14,400 yearly, an extra $7,200. Inflation reached 7%, lifting diesel and wage costs, with fuel up $38,000, yet customers resist surcharges. Should the owner raise prices 8% across all contracts?

questions.question_text: Define 'inflation'.
questions.model_answer: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level of goods and services, which reduces the purchasing power of money over time. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Sustained rise in the general price level
Reduces the purchasing power of money (each unit buys less)

questions.question_text: Explain two problems rising inflation causes for Corvale Deliveries.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Diesel and wage costs rise faster than revenue [k]. Inflation has reached 7%, the fuel bill rose by $38,000 last year, and wages must keep pace to retain the firm's 29 staff [app]. Reason 2: Pressure on margins because customers resist surcharges [k]. Interest on the $240,000 van loan is also up $7,200 a year after the base rate rose from 3% to 6%, so the gap between costs and revenue keeps widening [app].

knowledge_max_2: Inflation raises input costs such as fuel and wages
Inflation forces higher prices or squeezes profit margins
application_max_2: Inflation at 7%; fuel bill rose by $38,000; 29 staff

An 8% increase across all contracts would recover some of the extra $7,200 a year of interest and the $38,000 fuel increase [app], though the firm risks losing rounds to cheaper rivals [an]. Way 2: Improve route efficiency and cut empty miles [k]. Combining parcel routes across its 300-plus business customers would cut diesel use per drop [app], lowering costs without raising prices [an].

knowledge_max_2: Passing costs on through higher prices restores margin
Efficiency improvements reduce cost per unit delivered

questions.question_text: Do you think Corvale Deliveries should raise its delivery prices by 8% across all contracts? Justify your answer.

However, a flat 8% rise risks losing price-sensitive contracts [k]: customers resist surcharges and rivals that hold prices could win the firm's rounds [app], so Corvale could lose more revenue than it recovers [an]. Overall [eval], Corvale should raise prices by a smaller, cost-linked amount rather than a flat 8%, or add a transparent fuel surcharge [eval], because recovering proven cost increases is fairer and less likely to drive away the 300-plus business customers it serves.

Losing contracts could outweigh the recovered costs
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options using stem figures
Justified, qualified recommendation (smaller cost-linked rise or fuel surcharge)

scenario_stem:
Valecrest Logistics Ltd is a private limited delivery company in Ridgeline running 36 vans and 9 HGVs for 130 retail and e-commerce clients. Last year's fleet completed 48,000 deliveries, up 16%, but 2 HGVs need replacing at $110,000 each.

Managing director Sara Iqbal is choosing between a $720,000 same-day deal needing 4 dedicated vans and a 4-hour delivery window, and 3 bulk contracts worth $540,000 using existing vehicles. She has a $250,000 bank credit limit.

questions.question_text: Define 'wants'.
