questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why customer wants matter to Valecrest Logistics.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Customer wants show what services the business should offer [k]. Clients expect guaranteed 4-hour same-day delivery, so Valecrest is considering a national same-day deal worth $720,000 a year [app]. Reason 2: Meeting wants keeps customers loyal and generates repeat business [k]. Valecrest already serves 130 retail and e-commerce clients and completed 48,000 deliveries last year [app].

knowledge_max_2: Wants indicate what customers demand
Satisfying wants builds loyalty and repeat business
application_max_2: 4-hour same-day deal; $720,000 a year
130 retail and e-commerce clients; 48,000 deliveries; 16% growth

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Valecrest of the same-day delivery deal.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: The same-day deal would raise revenue per contract [k]. At $720,000 a year it is $180,000 more than the 3 bulk supply contracts worth $540,000 in total [app]. Higher revenue would lift profits and help fund the 2 HGVs due for replacement at $110,000 each [an]. Benefit 2: The deal would strengthen Valecrest's reputation in e-commerce [k]. Deliveries grew 16% last year, so offering 4-hour same-day delivery matches market trends [app]. A reputation for speed would win further clients and defend Valecrest against rival couriers [an].

knowledge_max_2: Higher-value contracts raise revenue and profit
Reputation for speed attracts e-commerce clients
application_max_2: $720,000 a year versus $540,000 for the 3 bulk contracts
16% delivery growth; 4-hour window; 2 HGVs at $110,000 each
analysis_max_2: The extra $180,000 a year helps fund the $220,000 HGV replacements and raises profit
A reputation for speed wins further clients and defends against rivals

questions.question_text: Do you think Valecrest should accept the $720,000 same-day deal rather than the 3 bulk contracts worth $540,000? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Argument for the same-day deal: the deal pays $720,000 a year, $180,000 more than the $540,000 total for the 3 bulk contracts [k]. It also matches strong e-commerce growth, with deliveries up 16% last year, and the 2 HGVs due for replacement cost $220,000 for both (2 x $110,000), leaving headroom within the $250,000 credit limit [app]. Committing 4 dedicated vans to a guaranteed 4-hour window would squeeze capacity but build a formidable reputation [an]. Argument for bulk: the 3 bulk contracts use existing vehicles with flexible timing, avoiding the need for 4 dedicated vans and keeping deliveries manageable within current fleet capacity [k]. They carry lower delivery risk and could be handled without breaching the $250,000 credit limit, although annual income would be $180,000 lower [app]. Choosing bulk also preserves capacity for ad-hoc retail clients [an]. Overall, on the stem's figures, Valecrest should accept the $720,000 same-day deal if 4 dedicated vans are available, because the extra $180,000 a year and the 16% e-commerce growth outweigh the tighter 4-hour window risk [eval]. If van availability is tight or credit is needed for the HGV replacements, the 3 bulk contracts are the safer choice [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Same-day = higher revenue but tighter delivery requirements
Bulk = lower risk, existing vehicles, flexible timing
application_max_2: 4 dedicated vans; 4-hour window; 16% growth; $250,000 credit limit; $220,000 for 2 HGV replacements
analysis_max_2: The extra $180,000 a year funds fleet replacement and raises profit
Bulk preserves capacity and avoids credit strain
evaluation_max_2: Recommends same-day deal, conditional on van availability and credit headroom
Bulk becomes preferable if fleet or credit constraints tighten

scenario_stem:
Sansome Pharmacies Ltd is a private limited company with 9 pharmacies in 2 towns in Country X and 72 staff. Revenue is $17m. Yet 4 of the 9 branches have missed the 20-minute waiting target for 3 consecutive months.

Operations director Alice Brennan proposes dashboards reviewed each Friday, costing $31,000, or free weekly spot checks by managers. Two branch managers admit estimating rather than measuring. She must strengthen control before targets slip further.

questions.question_text: Define 'controlling' as a role of management.
questions.model_answer: Controlling is monitoring performance against targets and taking corrective action when standards are not met, such as Sansome tracking prescription turnaround, stock loss and waiting-time targets each month. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Controlling = monitoring/measuring performance against standards or targets
Involves corrective action when performance falls short

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why controlling is important to Sansome Pharmacies Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Controlling checks that actual performance matches targets [k]. Each month head office sets targets for prescription turnaround, stock loss and waiting time, yet 4 of the 9 branches have missed the 20-minute target for 3 months [app]. Reason 2: Controlling allows corrective action before problems grow [k]. Without monitoring, missed 20-minute targets would keep driving customers to rival pharmacies in the 2 towns [app].

knowledge_max_2: Controlling compares actual performance with targets/standards
Controlling enables corrective action before problems worsen
application_max_2: Monthly targets for turnaround, stock loss and waiting time; 4 of 9 branches missing the 20-minute target for 3 months
2 towns; 9 pharmacies; missed targets risk losing customers to rivals

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Sansome of installing the electronic dashboards costing $31,000.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Dashboards give accurate, real-time data instead of estimates [k]. Two branch managers admit they usually estimate rather than measure, so live waiting times would replace guesswork with facts in all 9 branches [app]. Reliable data lets Alice take corrective action on the 4 branches missing target before customers defect [an]. Benefit 2: Dashboards make performance visible and create accountability [k]. Weekly Friday reviews of live waiting times would show each of the 9 branch managers exactly where they stand [app]. Visible scorecards motivate managers to close the gap to the 20-minute target and protect $17m of annual revenue [an].

knowledge_max_2: Accurate real-time data improves control and decisions
Visible performance creates accountability and motivation
application_max_2: Live waiting times reviewed each Friday in every branch; replaces estimates admitted by 2 branch managers
4 of 9 branches missing the 20-minute target for 3 months; $17m annual revenue
analysis_max_2: Reliable data enables early corrective action on the 4 failing branches before customers leave
Visible scorecards motivate managers to hit the 20-minute target and protect revenue

questions.question_text: Do you think Sansome should install the electronic dashboards rather than use weekly spot checks by branch managers? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Argument for the dashboards: controlling means monitoring performance and taking corrective action [k]. Electronic dashboards would show live waiting times in every branch, reviewed each Friday, at a cost of $31,000 [app]. Real-time data would replace the estimates 2 branch managers admit to, letting Alice fix the 4 branches that missed the 20-minute target for 3 months [an]. Argument for spot checks: weekly spot checks cost nothing [k]. Branch managers phoning in results each week avoid the $31,000 outlay and keep control in their hands at no cost to Sansome [app]. However, spot checks rely on self-reporting, the exact weakness the 2 branch managers confessed to, so Alice would be controlling estimates, not reality [an]. Overall, on the stem's figures, Sansome should install the dashboards, because 4 of 9 branches have already missed target for 3 months and self-reporting has proven unreliable; $31,000 is small against $17m of revenue [eval]. If the dashboards show honest measurement returns and waiting times hit 20 minutes, the checks could be scaled back [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Controlling = monitoring performance and correcting deviations
Self-reported checks are cheaper but less reliable than independent systems
application_max_2: $31,000 dashboards; live waiting times reviewed each Friday in all 9 branches
4 of 9 branches missed the 20-minute target for 3 months; 2 branch managers admit estimating; $17m revenue
analysis_max_2: Real-time independent data enables corrective action on the 4 failing branches
Spot checks cost nothing but rely on dishonest self-reporting
evaluation_max_2: Recommends dashboards given sustained misses and unreliable self-reporting, cost justified by $17m revenue
Scale back checks if dashboards prove targets are met honestly

scenario_stem:
Embergate Cinema is a sole-trader 4-screen cinema in Country X owned by Marcus Whitfield, selling 95,000 tickets at $11 for $1.045 million plus $260,000 from food. Monday to Thursday attendance fell 28% and weekday screenings are half-empty.

For January, the manager chooses: a 25% price reduction on Monday to Thursday tickets to $8.25 with $12,000 advertising, or free large popcorn with each weekday ticket and a monthly competition for a season pass, costing $9,000 over three months.

questions.question_text: Define 'promotional pricing'.
questions.model_answer: Setting a temporarily reduced price, often below the normal price, in order to boost sales during a specific period [2].

knowledge_max_2: temporarily reduced price
used to boost sales over a specific period

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages to Embergate Cinema of offering a 25% price reduction on Monday to Thursday tickets.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Cutting the ticket price to $8.25 makes cinema-going cheaper [k], encouraging price-sensitive customers to visit on quieter weekdays [app]. Advantage 2: Lower prices can fill the half-empty weekday screenings [k], using spare capacity across the 4 screens to grow ticket sales [app].

knowledge_max_2: lower price attracts price-sensitive customers
fills spare capacity and lifts sales volume
application_max_2: Monday to Thursday
half-empty
4 screens

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Embergate Cinema of the free popcorn and competition promotion.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Free large popcorn adds perceived value without cutting the ticket price [k], making the $11 Monday to Thursday ticket more attractive [app], which can also lift food and drink sales worth $260,000 a year [an]. Benefit 2: A monthly competition to win a season pass creates excitement [k], giving regular weekday cinema-goers a reason to return month after month [app], strengthening loyalty and repeat visits [an].

knowledge_max_2: free gift adds perceived value without cutting price
competition creates excitement and repeat visits
application_max_2: Monday to Thursday
season pass
analysis_max_2: lifts food and drink income
converts one-off visits into repeat loyalty

questions.question_text: Do you think Embergate Cinema should use the 25% price reduction or the free popcorn and competition promotion for January? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The 25% price reduction to $8.25 directly attacks the 28% Monday to Thursday attendance fall [k], using a simple, visible discount that price-sensitive customers instantly understand [app], which should fill the 4 half-empty screens and protect contribution above variable costs [an]. However, the popcorn-and-competition offer costs only $9,000 and keeps the $11 price intact [k], preserving the $1.045 million ticket revenue base and protecting the $260,000 food and drink spend [app], while the season pass competition builds repeat visits and loyalty [an]. Overall, Embergate should choose the free popcorn and competition because it protects margins better than a 25% price cut would [eval], and it builds lasting weekday habits rather than training customers to wait for discounts [eval].

knowledge_max_2: price reduction: simple, effective volume lever on weak days
popcorn and competition: value-add that keeps price intact
application_max_2: 28% attendance fall
$9,000 promotion cost
$1.045 million ticket revenue
analysis_max_2: fills screens and boosts weekday sales
protects revenue base and builds repeat loyalty
evaluation_max_2: weighs discounting volume against value-add and loyalty
justified choice given margin protection and habit formation

scenario_stem:
Norbury Fasteners Co, a private limited company, makes steel bolts and rivets for bridge builders with 70 workers across 3 shifts, producing 18 million fasteners a year. Inspectors hand-check 10% of bolts, missing 3% of faults.

Option A hires 4 inspectors at $24,000 a year each to raise checks to 20%. Option B spends $650,000 on automated optical inspection checking 100% of fasteners at 2,000 per minute, cutting faults from 3% to 0.5%, replacing 5 inspector jobs ($130,000 a year) and costing $60,000 a year.

questions.question_text: Define 'efficiency'.
questions.model_answer: Efficiency is the ability to produce the maximum output from the resources used, minimising waste of time, materials and effort. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Efficiency = most output from given resources with least waste
Higher efficiency lowers unit costs and raises competitiveness

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Norbury Fasteners Co of installing automated optical inspection.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: The system checks every fastener rather than a sample [k]. Inspection would rise from 10% of bolts to 100% of output, at 2,000 per minute [app]. Benefit 2: Automated optics are far more reliable than the human eye [k]. Escape faults would fall from 3% to 0.5%, protecting bridge-builder customers [app].

knowledge_max_2: Automated inspection checks 100% of output, not samples
Machine vision is more accurate and consistent than humans
application_max_2: Inspection rises from 10% of bolts to 100% at 2,000 per minute
Escape faults fall from 3% to 0.5% across 18 million fasteners a year

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Norbury Fasteners Co could face if it installs the automated system.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: The system is a major purchase [k]. Option B costs $650,000 plus $60,000 a year in maintenance [app]. Heavy fixed costs reduce profit if fastener demand from bridge projects weakens [an]. Problem 2: 5 inspector jobs would be replaced [k]. Making 5 of 70 workers redundant costs redundancy payments and may cause disputes [app]. Losing experienced inspectors could hurt quality if the system needs recalibration [an].

knowledge_max_2: Automated systems need large capital and maintenance spend
Automation replaces existing worker jobs
application_max_2: Option B costs $650,000 plus $60,000 a year in maintenance
5 of 70 workers (inspector jobs worth $130,000 a year) would be replaced
analysis_max_2: High fixed costs increase financial risk when demand is weak
Redundancies cost money and risk skill loss for recalibration and edge cases

questions.question_text: Do you think Norbury Fasteners Co should install the automated inspection system rather than hire 4 more inspectors? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Case for the automated system: automation replaces human checks with machine precision [k]. It would inspect 100% of 18 million fasteners at 2,000 per minute and cut escape faults from 3% to 0.5%, while saving $130,000 a year in inspector wages [app]. Reliable quality would protect contracts with bridge builders and cut rejects and returns [an]. Case for hiring inspectors: Option A avoids the $650,000 outlay and adds only $96,000 a year in wages (4 workers at $24,000) [k]. Manual checking would rise to 20% of output, yet 80% of fasteners would still go unchecked [app]. Extra inspectors keep human judgement for difficult cases but leave escape faults far above 0.5% [an]. Overall, Norbury should install the automated system, because checking 100% of output and cutting escape faults sixfold outweigh the $650,000 cost over time [eval]. If a major bridge contract is won or lost, the directors could lease the system [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Automation checks every unit with machine precision
Manual hiring is cheaper upfront but samples only
application_max_2: 100% inspection at 2,000 per minute; faults 3% to 0.5%; $130,000 a year wage saving
Option A: $650,000 avoided; 4 inspectors at $24,000 = $96,000 a year; only 20% checked
analysis_max_2: Full-output inspection secures bridge-builder contracts and cuts return costs
Manual option leaves 80% of output unchecked and high escape faults
evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation (100% inspection and sixfold fault cut outweigh cost)
Practical condition for the alternative (lease the system if demand is uncertain)

scenario_stem:
The Glasshouse Community Venue Ltd is a private limited company running an events hall. It hosts 140 events yearly, employs 12 staff and earns $330,000. A worn kitchen and closed terrace mean the board wants $30,000 for refurbishment, allowing 40 extra events.

'Save the Glasshouse' crowdfunding targets $35,000 with a 5% fee ($1,750); rewards include a name on the wall and free dinners. A community regeneration subsidy offers $20,000, with $10,000 from the venue, giving local groups two free days monthly for 3 years.

questions.question_text: Define 'cash flow'.
questions.model_answer: Cash flow is the movement of money into and out of a business over a period of time; the difference between cash inflows and cash outflows. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Movement of money into and out of a business
Over a period of time / difference between inflows and outflows

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of crowdfunding for The Glasshouse Community Venue Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: No interest or repayments are owed [k]; if the 'Save the Glasshouse' campaign reaches $35,000, the kitchen and terrace are funded by the community rather than by borrowing [app]. Advantage 2: The campaign raises publicity and loyalty [k]; reward donors, with their names on the wall and free dinners, are likely to become regulars, supporting the 140 events a year and $330,000 revenue [app].

knowledge_max_2: No interest or repayment obligation
Publicity/marketing benefit / community buy-in
application_max_2: $35,000 target funds the $30,000 kitchen and terrace
Name on the wall / free dinners / 140 events / $330,000 revenue

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages of the community regeneration subsidy for The Glasshouse Community Venue Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Disadvantage 1: Binding conditions are attached [k]; local groups must get two free days of hall hire per month for 3 years [app], which could displace paying events and reduce the income needed to cover the cost of the 40 extra events [an]. Disadvantage 2: Only part of the cost is covered [k]; the subsidy gives $20,000, leaving the venue to find $10,000 itself [app], and any delay in grant approval could postpone the kitchen and terrace rebuild [an].

knowledge_max_2: Conditions attached to the subsidy
Only part of the cost covered / balance self-funded

analysis_max_2: Free hire displaces paying bookings, cutting income
Funding gap/delay risks the rebuild timetable and extra events revenue

questions.question_text: Do you think The Glasshouse Community Venue Ltd should use crowdfunding or the subsidy? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Crowdfunding [k] could raise $35,000, more than the $30,000 project, with no repayment, and the campaign would rally the local community behind the venue; however, reaching the target is not guaranteed, the 5% fee is $1,750, and free dinners and wall plaques must be produced [app] [an]. The subsidy is certain at $20,000 and non-repayable [k], but leaves a $10,000 gap and requires two free days of hall hire per month for 3 years, which could cost far more in lost bookings [app] [an]. Overall, I think The Glasshouse should use crowdfunding [eval], because the community goodwill, full funding and avoidance of restrictive hire conditions outweigh the uncertain target, provided the board markets the campaign strongly; if it fails, the subsidy can be claimed as a backup [eval].

Subsidy: certain but part-funding with conditions

Fallback/sequencing argument or justified overall judgement

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Eldercombe Toys Ltd is a private limited company manufacturing toys with 41 staff. Sales fell from $3.4 million in a boom to $2.6 million in the slump, profit reaching $120,000, with a third exported.

After the base rate fell from 6% to 3%, the economy grew 2.8% a year. Christmas brings 55% of sales and retailers are rebuilding stock, so orders are rising. A $350,000 expansion would add a moulding machine and 6 jobs. Should it expand now?

questions.question_text: Define 'business cycle'.
questions.model_answer: The business cycle is the regular pattern of economic growth and decline over time, moving through phases of growth, boom, recession and slump. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Regular pattern of economic expansion and contraction
Phases include growth, boom, recession and slump

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why businesses may cut output and staff numbers during a slump.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Consumer demand and sales fall [k]. Eldercombe's sales fell from $3.4 million in the boom year to $2.6 million in the slump, so producing at full capacity would create unsold stock and waste [app]. Reason 2: Falling profits force cost-cutting [k]. Profit dropped to $120,000 in the slump, so reducing staff hours and output was necessary to avoid losses [app].

knowledge_max_2: A slump reduces consumer demand for goods
Falling profits force businesses to cut costs, including labour
application_max_2: Sales fell from $3.4 million to $2.6 million
Profit dropped to $120,000

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Eldercombe Toys of the economy moving from slump to recovery.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Rising orders as retailers rebuild stock [k]. The economy is growing at 2.8% a year and Christmas accounts for 55% of annual sales [app], so demand should rise sharply in the coming months and Eldercombe can sell more toys [an]. Benefit 2: Cheaper borrowing for expansion [k]. The base rate was cut from 6% to 3% [app], so financing even part of the $350,000 moulding-line expansion would cost less interest than before [an].

knowledge_max_2: Recovery increases consumer and retailer demand
Lower base rates reduce the cost of borrowing
application_max_2: Economy growing at 2.8% a year; Christmas accounts for 55% of sales; retailers rebuilding stock
Base rate cut from 6% to 3%; expansion costing $350,000
analysis_max_2: Higher demand spreads fixed costs and lifts output and profit
Cheaper credit reduces the interest cost of the expansion and improves returns

questions.question_text: Do you think Eldercombe Toys should expand its production capacity now? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Expanding now positions Eldercombe for the Christmas peak [k]: the economy is growing at 2.8% a year, orders are rising as retailers rebuild stock and Christmas accounts for 55% of annual sales [app], so the new moulding machine added by the $350,000 expansion could lift output, spread fixed costs and raise profit [an]. However, the recovery is not guaranteed [k]: in the last slump sales fell from $3.4 million to $2.6 million and profit dropped to $120,000 [app], so committing $350,000 before the recovery is confirmed could leave Eldercombe with idle capacity and 6 extra jobs it cannot sustain [an]. Overall [eval], Eldercombe should expand, but cautiously [eval], by fixing any finance at the current 3% base rate and timing the expansion to be ready before Christmas, because the recovery evidence and cheap credit outweigh the residual risk.

knowledge_max_2: Expanding into rising demand captures sales and market share
Committing capital before recovery is confirmed is risky
application_max_2: Economy growing at 2.8% a year; Christmas accounts for 55% of sales; retailers rebuilding stock; $350,000 expansion
Sales fell from $3.4 million to $2.6 million in the slump; profit dropped to $120,000
analysis_max_2: Extra capacity captures peak demand, raising output, resource utilisation and profit
Idle capacity plus 6 extra jobs in a renewed slump would erode profit
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options using stem figures
Justified recommendation (expand cautiously, timed for Christmas and fixed finance)

scenario_stem:
Cinderhill Deli Foods is a private limited company preparing chilled ready meals, employing 16 chefs and packers on $1.05 million revenue. It sells 2,400 trays a day to local shops, with each worker handling every stage from cooking to sealing.

Dana Whitmore must choose between a division-of-labour line with 4 specialist stations, needing 2 vacuum-sealing machines at $9,600 each to reach 3,400 trays a day, and keeping the flexible method, where training each chef on all 4 stages takes 9 days.

questions.question_text: Define 'division of labour'.
questions.model_answer: Division of labour is when the production process is split into separate tasks and each worker is assigned one specific task or a small group of related tasks. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Production process is split into separate tasks/stages
Each worker concentrates on one/a few tasks

questions.question_text: Explain two factors of production used by Cinderhill Deli Foods.
questions.model_answer: Factor 1: Labour is the human effort used in production [k]; Cinderhill employs 16 chefs and packers to prepare, cook, chill and seal each tray of meals [app]. Factor 2: Capital refers to man-made resources used to produce goods [k]; the 2 new vacuum-sealing machines at $9,600 each would add machinery to the kitchen [app].

knowledge_max_2: Labour is the human input/effort used in production
Capital is man-made resources such as machinery used to produce goods
application_max_2: 16 chefs and packers prepare, cook, chill and seal the meals
Vacuum-sealing machines are capital equipment bought/used for the kitchen

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of division of labour for Cinderhill Deli Foods.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Division of labour allows workers to specialise in one task, increasing speed and skill [k]; Cinderhill could lift output from 2,400 to 3,400 trays a day with its 4 specialist stations [app], which raises productivity so more meals are sold without hiring extra chefs [an]. Benefit 2: Repeating the same task helps workers make fewer errors [k]; specialist sealing-station staff would produce fewer rejected trays [app], reducing wasted ingredients and protecting the $1.05 million revenue [an].

knowledge_max_2: Specialisation in a task increases skill and speed
Repetition reduces errors/wastage and raises productivity
application_max_2: Output rises from 2,400 to 3,400 trays a day with 4 specialist stations
Specialist staff at the sealing station make fewer rejected trays
analysis_max_2: Higher productivity means more meals sold without extra wage costs
Fewer rejects protect revenue and reduce waste costs

questions.question_text: Do you think Cinderhill Deli Foods should introduce the division-of-labour line? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One case for the line is productivity: splitting work into 4 specialist stations would lift output from 2,400 to 3,400 trays a day [k], an extra 1,000 trays daily for Cinderhill's local shop customers [app], spreading the $19,200 cost of the 2 vacuum-sealing machines over far more meals [an]. However, division of labour can make work monotonous and reduces flexibility [k]; Dana's chefs currently cover every stage, so the kitchen keeps running if one person is absent [app], meaning a rigid line could halt production when specialist staff are sick [an]. Overall, the case for the line is strong because demand is steady and the gain of 1,000 trays a day outweighs the cost [eval], but Dana should keep some chefs trained on all stages to protect flexibility [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Division of labour can raise productivity/output and lower unit costs
Division of labour can cause boredom/monotony and inflexibility
application_max_2: Output rises from 2,400 to 3,400 trays a day (1,000 extra)
2 vacuum-sealing machines at $9,600 each cost $19,200; all-round chefs keep kitchen flexible
analysis_max_2: Higher output spreads fixed machine costs over more units, improving profit
Rigid specialisation risks production halting when a specialist is absent
evaluation_max_2: Weighs up both options using stem figures (extra 1,000 trays vs $19,200 cost)
Reaches a justified recommendation with a sensible caveat

scenario_stem:
Glenmore Dairy Co is a private limited company in Country X making milk and yoghurt for 9 chains. Ravi Menon leads 46 employees in pasteurising and packing, processing 18,500 litres daily; revenue was $1.32 million. A works council meets every Friday and staff shaped last year's new yoghurt flavour, lifting sales 12%.

A new contract needs 22,000 litres daily from January, requiring an $85,000 pasteuriser in 6 weeks. Ravi must choose autocratic leadership for speed or keep the democratic style.

questions.question_text: Define 'autocratic leadership'.
questions.model_answer: Autocratic leadership is a style of leadership where the leader makes decisions alone without consulting employees and issues clear, direct instructions that staff are expected to follow. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Leader makes decisions alone/without consulting employees
Clear one-way instructions/close control of subordinates

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of a democratic leadership style for Glenmore Dairy Co.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Democratic leadership involves employees in decision-making, so employee ideas are used [k]; Glenmore staff suggested the new yoghurt flavour, which lifted sales by 12% [app]. Advantage 2: Employees who are consulted often feel valued, raising morale and motivation [k]; the Friday works council keeps 46 employees engaged in daily operations [app].

knowledge_max_2: Employees are involved in/consulted about decisions
Involvement can raise motivation/morale/commitment
application_max_2: Staff-suggested new yoghurt flavour lifted sales by 12%
Friday works council keeps 46 employees engaged

questions.question_text: Explain two problems of Glenmore Dairy Co switching to an autocratic leadership style.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Autocratic leaders decide alone, so employees lose influence over decisions affecting their work [k]; Ravi's Friday works council, where the 46 employees currently influence decisions, would be pushed aside [app], which could lower morale and cause staff to resist the change [an]. Problem 2: Decisions made without consultation ignore useful employee input [k]; staff knowledge of pasteurising and packing shaped the yoghurt flavour that raised sales [app], so ignoring it risks weaker decisions on the new line and delays the ramp-up to 22,000 litres a day [an].

knowledge_max_2: Autocratic style means the leader decides alone/little employee input
Consultation brings useful employee knowledge/ideas
application_max_2: Friday works council where 46 employees influence decisions
Staff knowledge of pasteurising and packing shaped the yoghurt flavour
analysis_max_2: Lower morale, resistance to change, possible higher labour turnover
Weaker decisions/delays in ramping up to 22,000 litres a day

questions.question_text: Do you think Ravi should switch Glenmore Dairy Co to autocratic leadership for the new contract? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One reason for switching is speed: autocratic leadership means the leader decides alone and issues direct instructions [k]; the new contract requires 22,000 litres a day within 6 weeks and a pasteuriser costing $85,000, so fast unquestioned decisions could keep the launch on schedule [app], reducing the risk of late delivery penalties and protecting the $1.32 million revenue base [an]. However, Glenmore's democratic culture produced the staff-suggested yoghurt flavour, which lifted sales by 12%, and the Friday works council keeps 46 employees committed [k]; sidelining it now could lower motivation just when extra effort is needed for the ramp-up [app], so errors and staff turnover could rise precisely when reliability matters most [an]. On balance, a time-limited use of tighter direction during the 6-week launch makes sense, with democratic consultation restored once running [eval], because permanent autocratic control would damage the culture that made the yoghurt launch successful [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Autocratic leadership = quick unilateral decisions/direct instructions
Democratic leadership = consultation/employee involvement, stronger commitment
application_max_2: 22,000 litres a day within 6 weeks; pasteuriser costing $85,000
Yoghurt flavour lifted sales by 12%; Friday works council; 46 employees
analysis_max_2: Faster decisions keep launch on schedule/protect contract and revenue

scenario_stem:
Avenmere Scientific Ltd is a private limited company manufacturing water testing kits for farms and fisheries, with revenue of $300,000 and profit of $42,000. It needs $120,000 for automated laboratory equipment to test twice as many samples weekly.

A government grant offers $50,000 but requires 6 technicians at $1,500 monthly and a promise to publish its accounts for 5 years. A bank loan of $120,000 at 8% interest over 5 years costs $9,600 a year in interest.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'grant'.
questions.model_answer: Money given by the government or another body to a business which does not have to be repaid, usually to support a specific purpose [2].

knowledge_max_2: money given to a business that does not have to be repaid
usually provided to support a specific purpose or project

questions.question_text: Explain two factors Avenmere Scientific Ltd should consider when choosing between the grant and the loan.
questions.model_answer: Factor 1: The cost of the finance [k], because the grant gives $50,000 without interest, while the loan adds $9,600 a year over 5 years [app]. Factor 2: The conditions attached to each source [k], because the grant requires 6 technicians at $1,500 a month each and published accounts for 5 years [app].

knowledge_max_2: the cost of the finance and its interest charges
the conditions attached to receiving the finance
application_max_2: grant provides $50,000 interest free while the loan costs $9,600 a year
grant requires 6 technicians at $1,500 a month each and 5 years of published accounts

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages of accepting the government grant for the laboratory equipment.
questions.model_answer: Disadvantage 1: It commits the firm to big extra wages [k], because 6 technicians at $1,500 a month each add about $108,000 a year to costs, against revenue of only $300,000 [app], squeezing profit unless sample volumes double as planned [an]. Disadvantage 2: It reduces privacy and freedom [k], because Avenmere must publish its accounts for 5 years and meet the grant conditions [app], exposing figures to competitors and limiting the founders' decisions [an].

knowledge_max_2: grants create heavy ongoing commitments such as new jobs
grants require public disclosure and reduce freedom
application_max_2: 6 technicians at $1,500 a month each add about $108,000 a year
revenue of only $300,000 makes the added cost significant
analysis_max_2: squeezes profit unless sample volumes double as planned
exposes accounts to competitors and limits the founders' decisions

questions.question_text: Do you think accepting the $50,000 grant is a better choice than the $120,000 bank loan to fund the laboratory equipment? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The grant cuts the amount that must be borrowed [k], because $50,000 of the $120,000 equipment cost arrives without interest, saving up to $4,000 of interest a year at 8% [app], which protects the $42,000 profit while testing volumes build up [an]. However, the grant obliges Avenmere to hire 6 technicians at $1,500 a month each [k], adding about $108,000 a year to costs and opening its books to public scrutiny for 5 years [app], which could strain cash badly if testing demand does not double on schedule [an]. Overall, the grant is the better choice only if firm contracts from farms are signed first, because the $50,000 free funding outweighs $48,000 of simple interest on the loan [eval], and without those contracts the bank loan is the safer, cleaner option [eval].

knowledge_max_2: grants provide interest free finance for a specific purpose
grants carry conditions such as job creation and disclosure
application_max_2: $50,000 of the $120,000 cost arrives without interest, saving up to $4,000 a year
6 technicians at $1,500 a month each add about $108,000 a year to costs
analysis_max_2: protects the $42,000 profit while testing volumes build up
cash could be strained if testing demand does not double on schedule
evaluation_max_2: weighs the free $50,000 against $48,000 of simple interest on the loan
grant only preferable with firm contracts in place; otherwise the loan is safer

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Callowmere Supermarkets is a private limited company running 9 stores with 320 staff. Inflation climbed from 6.1% to 11.3%, food prices rose 14% but wages grew 6%. Revenue rose 9% to $48.5 million, yet items sold fell 4% as shoppers switched to own-label, now 44% of basket value.

The director must choose between holding own-label prices and absorbing supplier costs, or raising all prices by 8% and risking defection to discounters. Two rivals opened within 5 km.

questions.question_text: Define 'inflation'.
questions.model_answer: A sustained general rise in the price level of goods and services in an economy over time [2].

knowledge_max_2: a sustained rise in the general price level
prices of goods and services increase over time

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of rising inflation on Callowmere Supermarkets.
questions.model_answer: Effect 1: Supplier costs rise faster than wages [k], and with food prices up 14% against only 6% wage growth, Callowmere's shelf prices squeeze shoppers' real incomes [app]. Effect 2: Shoppers switch to cheaper alternatives [k], which is why the number of items sold fell 4% and own-label lines now reach 44% of basket value [app].

knowledge_max_2: inflation raises input and stock costs faster than wages
inflation reduces consumers' real purchasing power and shifts demand to cheaper goods
application_max_2: food prices rose 14% while average wages grew only 6%
items sold fell 4% and own-label basket share reached 44%

questions.question_text: Explain two problems for Callowmere of raising prices across the board by 8%.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Higher shelf prices accelerate shopper defections [k], and two rival discounters already opened within 5 km of the busiest store this year, so an 8% rise could push price-sensitive families to rivals [app], cutting sales volume further [an]. Problem 2: Raising prices when real wages grew only 6% outstrips pay rises [k], and shoppers already cut items purchased by 4% as inflation hit 11.3% [app], so basket values could shrink despite the 8% rise [an].

knowledge_max_2: price rises can drive customers to cheaper competitors
price rises exceeding income growth shrink real demand
application_max_2: two discounters opened within 5 km of the busiest store; Callowmere plans an 8% rise
items sold already fell 4% with inflation at 11.3% and wages up only 6%
analysis_max_2: lost volume to discounters compounds the 4% decline already seen
revenue may fail to cover the supplier cost increases the rise is meant to offset

questions.question_text: Do you think Callowmere Supermarkets should hold own-label prices rather than raise prices across the board by 8%? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Holding own-label prices defends Callowmere's value position [k]; with own-label at 44% of basket value and inflation at 11.3%, keeping these prices steady protects the shoppers most squeezed by the gap between 14% food inflation and 6% wage growth [app], so footfall and loyalty should hold even if own-label margins turn negative short term [an]. However, holding prices means absorbing supplier increases [k]; with revenue of $48.5 million up 9% only because of price rises, flat own-label prices could erase profit on high-volume lines just as two new discounters open within 5 km [app], so the board would need to fund the gap from higher-margin branded lines [an]. Overall, Callowmere should hold own-label prices [eval], because an across-the-board 8% rise clashes with items already falling 4%, while targeted rises on branded goods can recover margin without driving away the value shoppers Callowmere needs [eval].

knowledge_max_2: holding value prices protects price-sensitive customers during inflation
absorbing supplier rises squeezes margins when input costs outpace wages
application_max_2: own-label at 44% of basket value; inflation 11.3% vs wage growth of 6%
$48.5 million revenue up 9% on price rises; two discounters within 5 km
analysis_max_2: loyalty and footfall protection versus margin erosion on own-label lines
risk of losing volume to discounters if all prices rise 8%
evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation linked to the 4% decline in items sold
recommendation weighs targeted branded rises against across-the-board increases

scenario_stem:
Harvest Lane Print Co is a private limited company printing catalogues and posters, employing 12 print operators and 2 sales staff. Revenue was $880,000 and net profit $96,000, but an online rival undercuts it by 25% on catalogue work.

Owner Priya Nair must choose between a $240,000 automated digital press running crewless overnight to double output to 60,000 sheets a shift, making 3 roles redundant, and hiring 4 operators at $21,000 each, adding $84,000 a year in wages and training time.

questions.question_text: Define 'factors of production'.
questions.model_answer: Factors of production are the resources used to produce goods and services. They are land (natural resources), labour (human effort), capital (man-made resources) and enterprise (the risk-taking organiser). [2]

knowledge_max_2: Resources used to produce goods and services
Land, labour, capital and enterprise (any two correctly identified)

questions.question_text: Explain two factors of production used by Harvest Lane Print Co.
questions.model_answer: Factor 1: Labour is the human effort used in production [k]; Harvest Lane employs 12 print operators and 2 sales staff to run its presses and handle customer orders [app]. Factor 2: Enterprise is the risk-taking factor that organises the others [k]; owner Priya Nair organises the business and is deciding whether to invest in the new press [app].

knowledge_max_2: Labour is the human effort used in production
Enterprise is the risk-taking factor that organises land, labour and capital
application_max_2: 12 print operators and 2 sales staff run the presses and orders
Priya Nair organises the business and the investment decision

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of buying the automated digital press for Harvest Lane Print Co.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Automation increases output and lowers unit costs [k]; the press doubles output to 60,000 sheets a shift and runs crewless overnight [app], cutting the cost per sheet and helping Harvest Lane match the online rival's 25% lower prices [an]. Benefit 2: Consistent machine quality reduces errors [k]; overnight automated runs would reduce reprints on catalogue jobs [app], protecting the $96,000 profit from wasted paper and ink [an].

knowledge_max_2: Automation raises output and lowers unit costs
Automation gives consistent quality and fewer errors
application_max_2: Output doubles to 60,000 sheets a shift, running crewless overnight
Fewer reprints on catalogue jobs; saves paper and ink
analysis_max_2: Lower unit cost lets Harvest Lane compete with the online rival's prices
Fewer errors protect profit and meet delivery promises

questions.question_text: Do you think Harvest Lane Print Co should buy the automated digital press? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One case for the press is competitiveness: at $240,000 it is costly, but doubling output to 60,000 sheets a shift lets Harvest Lane cut unit costs and match the online rival's 25% lower prices [k], protecting the $880,000 revenue produced by its 12 operators [app], and the crewless overnight run raises capacity without raising wage costs [an]. However, the press makes 3 roles redundant and removes jobs from a small market town [k]; losing experienced operators may also weaken customer service offered by the 2 sales staff [app], and redundancies could damage morale among remaining workers [an]. Overall, buying the press is the stronger option because it secures price competitiveness, and Priya could redeploy the 3 affected workers to finishing and delivery [eval]; the decision therefore protects both the business and most jobs [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Automation can lower unit costs and improve competitiveness
Automation can create redundancies and morale/loyalty issues
application_max_2: Press costs $240,000; output doubles to 60,000 sheets per shift; 3 roles redundant
Alternative is hiring 4 operators at $21,000 each ($84,000 a year) keeping jobs
analysis_max_2: Lower unit costs let Harvest Lane compete on price and defend revenue
Redundancies reduce wage costs but risk morale, skills loss and town goodwill
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both the press vs extra hiring options using stem figures
Reaches a justified recommendation (e.g. buy press with redeployment plan)

scenario_stem:
Seaward Printworks is a private limited company in Country X producing brochures, packaging and catalogues for 25 business customers. Omar Haddad manages 22 printers; output was 940,000 printed items with $1.28 million revenue.

Omar's 5 senior designers are skilled, self-motivated and complain his daily checks slow them. He must choose laissez-faire, letting them set deadlines, or keep close control until a $95,000 digital press arrives at year-end.

questions.question_text: Define 'laissez-faire leadership'.
questions.model_answer: Laissez-faire leadership is a leadership style where the leader gives employees freedom to make their own decisions and organise their own work, with very little supervision or guidance. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Employees given freedom to make decisions/organise their own work
Little supervision/guidance from the leader

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of laissez-faire leadership for Seaward Printworks.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Laissez-faire leadership gives employees freedom to organise their own work [k]; Seaward's 5 senior designers could set schedules around each client brief instead of waiting for daily checks [app]. Advantage 2: Autonomy can raise motivation and creativity among skilled staff [k]; the designers would have freedom to propose layouts for the brochures and catalogues, where fresh ideas win print contracts [app].

knowledge_max_2: Freedom/autonomy to organise own work with minimal supervision
Autonomy can raise motivation/creativity
application_max_2: 5 senior designers could set schedules around client briefs
Design ideas for brochures and catalogues win print contracts

questions.question_text: Explain two drawbacks of Seaward Printworks adopting a laissez-faire style for the design team.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Laissez-faire leaders avoid close monitoring, so poor work can go unnoticed [k]; the 5 senior designers could miss deadlines on client jobs without Omar's daily checks [app], leading to late delivery to one of the 25 business customers [an]. Problem 2: Inconsistent standards can reduce quality [k]; with no review before files reach the press, errors could pass into production [app], wasting output and reprints against the $1.28 million revenue [an].

knowledge_max_2: Laissez-faire leaders avoid monitoring, so problems go unnoticed
Inconsistent standards reduce quality
application_max_2: 5 senior designers may miss client-job deadlines without daily checks
Errors could pass into production without review
analysis_max_2: Late delivery damages relations with the 25 business customers
Reprints/waste cut revenue of $1.28 million

questions.question_text: Do you think Omar should move the design team to laissez-faire working now? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Omar should give the design team laissez-faire freedom now because the 5 senior designers are highly skilled and self-motivated [k]; removing daily checks would let them meet client briefs faster and improve the brochures and catalogues behind the $1.28 million revenue [app], lifting motivation and the quality of creative work [an]. However, the $95,000 digital press arriving at year-end will change workflows and client expectations [k]; keeping close control until then would let Omar set standards consistently during the changeover [app], avoiding costly mistakes when the new press is commissioned [an]. On balance, a middle path of agreed weekly reviews instead of daily checks until the press is installed captures most of the motivation benefit while limiting risk [eval], and would still protect the 940,000 printed items during the transition [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Laissez-faire frees skilled, self-motivated staff to self-manage
Close control suits periods of change/new equipment installation
application_max_2: 5 senior designers highly skilled/self-motivated; daily checks slow them
$95,000 digital press at year-end; 940,000 printed items; $1.28 million revenue
analysis_max_2: Freedom lifts motivation, speed and design quality
Close control reduces errors during the press changeover
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options (freedom now vs control until year-end)
Justified recommendation (weekly reviews until press installed)

scenario_stem:
Hazeldean Deli is a sole-trader delicatessen in Country X selling honey-glazed ham to office workers. It sells 11,000 packs at $9.50 for $104,500, with 6 staff. Trading Standards tested 40 '500g' packs and found they averaged 460g, 8% underweight.

Given 60 days to fix this or face an $18,000 fine, the owner can buy a $7,500 digital checkweigher or hire an extra checker for $14,000 a year. Peak ham sales run 11am to 2pm.

questions.question_text: Define 'weights and measures'.
questions.model_answer: Weights and measures are the legal rules requiring pre-packed goods to contain the weight or quantity shown on the label, enforced through inspections and fines. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Legal requirement that packs contain the stated weight/quantity
Enforced by trading standards inspections, fines and prosecution

questions.question_text: Explain two ways weights and measures legal controls affect Hazeldean Deli.
questions.model_answer: Way 1: Every pre-packed item must contain the labelled weight [k]; the sample of 40 ham packs averaged 460g against a labelled 500g, so Hazeldean was 8% underweight [app]. Way 2: Failure to comply brings enforcement [k]; Trading Standards gave 60 days to fix the shortfall or face an $18,000 fine and possible prosecution [app].

knowledge_max_2: Pre-packed goods must match the stated weight
Trading standards can enforce with fines/prosecution
application_max_2: 40-pack sample averaged 460g vs labelled 500g (8% underweight)
60 days to comply or face $18,000 fine and possible prosecution

questions.question_text: Explain two problems if Hazeldean Deli ignores the 60-day notice.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: A heavy fine would follow [k]; the $18,000 fine equals about 17% of its $104,500 ham revenue from 11,000 packs a year [app], which could wipe out profit and force price rises [an]. Problem 2: It could be prosecuted [k]; ignoring Trading Standards can mean a court case or the shop being banned from selling pre-packed ham [app], destroying the deli's core trade and the jobs of its 6 staff [an].

knowledge_max_2: Non-compliance brings fines/prosecution
Enforcement can restrict or end trading in affected goods
application_max_2: $18,000 fine is about 17% of $104,500 ham revenue
6 staff jobs at risk if ham sales are banned
analysis_max_2: Fine directly reduces profit and cash flow
Prosecution/ban destroys the deli's main revenue line

questions.question_text: Do you think Hazeldean Deli should buy the $7,500 digital checkweigher or hire an extra checker at $14,000 a year? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The $7,500 checkweigher would weigh every pack automatically [k]; it fixes the 8% underweight problem at a one-off cost of $7,500, far less than the $18,000 fine risk and than a year of an extra checker [app], and it copes with peak sales from 11am to 2pm without delaying service [an]. However, hiring a checker at $14,000 a year also verifies pack weights and adds staff for customer service at busy times [k]; but it costs $14,000 every year, and manual checks are slower and more error-prone than automatic weighing [app], so in year 2 the manual option is already $6,500 worse off than the machine [an]. On balance, buying the checkweigher is the better option [eval], because it permanently solves the legal problem and protects Hazeldean's $104,500 ham revenue from the $18,000 fine [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Automatic checkweighing is faster and more consistent than manual checks
Labour is a recurring cost; capital equipment is one-off
application_max_2: $7,500 one-off vs $14,000 a year; $18,000 fine at risk
Peak sales 11am-2pm; 6 days a week
analysis_max_2: Machine avoids peak-time bottlenecks and recurring wage cost
Manual checking keeps yearly costs rising and may still err
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options (automation vs extra staffing)
Justified recommendation: buy the $7,500 checkweigher

scenario_stem:
Saltwick Electronics Ltd is a private limited company making electric fans. It made 15,000 fans, 200 fans per worker, with $1.5 million revenue, and sells through wholesalers. Imported motors have a 10-week lead time.

A 9,000 motors order costs $90,000 and earns a 12% discount, saving $10,800, but next year's models may use a redesigned motor, making stock obsolete. Storage is $640 per month, security $150 per month, and $90,000 of working capital would be tied up.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'production'.
questions.model_answer: The process of converting inputs such as labour, materials and machinery into goods or services that can be sold to customers [2].

knowledge_max_2: converting inputs into goods or services
inputs include labour, materials and machinery

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Saltwick Electronics Ltd might hold a large inventory of electric motors.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Motors ensure uninterrupted production [k], because with a 10-week lead time the factory cannot wait months if the overseas supplier is late or short of stock [app]. Reason 2: Motors help meet sudden demand [k], because if a hot summer drove orders above the 200 fans per worker expected output, fans could be assembled immediately from stock [app].

knowledge_max_2: ensures uninterrupted production
helps meet sudden demand
application_max_2: 10-week lead time
200 fans per worker
15,000 fans

questions.question_text: Explain two costs Saltwick Electronics Ltd would face if it held 9,000 motors.
questions.model_answer: Cost 1: Storage and security costs reduce profit [k]; the motors would cost $640 per month to store and $150 per month to secure, about $9,480 a year [app], which absorbs nearly all of the $10,800 discount on the $1.5 million fan business [an]. Cost 2: Obsolescence risk [k]; if next year's models use a redesigned motor, the 9,000 motors could become unsellable [app], forcing Saltwick to write off up to $90,000 of stock and erase the saving [an].

knowledge_max_2: storage and security costs
obsolescence risk on stock
application_max_2: $640 per month
$150 per month
9,000 motors
analysis_max_2: storage absorbs nearly all of the discount
write-off risk if the model is redesigned

questions.question_text: Do you think Saltwick Electronics Ltd should order the 9,000 motors to gain the 12% discount? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Ordering the 9,000 motors would secure supply and save money [k]; the 12% discount is worth $10,800 off the $90,000 order [app], covering roughly a year of storage ($9,480) and protecting fan output ahead of peak summer sales [an]. However, the order is risky [k]; storage and security cost $790 a month and next year's redesigned motor could make the whole stock obsolete [app], which would write off $90,000 for a saving of only $10,800 [an]. Overall, Saltwick should not place the full order [eval], because the downside is far larger than the upside - losing $90,000 outweighs the $1,320 net annual benefit after storage costs [eval].

knowledge_max_2: guaranteed supply and discount benefit
obsolescence risk is asymmetric
application_max_2: $640 per month
$150 per month
analysis_max_2: discount barely covers a year of storage ($9,480)
potential $90,000 write-off for a $10,800 saving
evaluation_max_2: asymmetric risk, reject the full order
justified overall recommendation with reference to figures

scenario_stem:
Thornwick Gifts Ltd is a private limited company running 3 gift shops selling toys, candles and cards, with revenue of $620,000, including $210,000 in November and December. Current assets are $95,000 against current liabilities of $70,000.

The directors want $45,000 for Christmas stock. They compare a bank overdraft at 11% interest, costing about $1,650 over 4 months, with extended 60 day trade credit from suppliers who normally require payment within 30 days but expect it before February.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'working capital'.
questions.model_answer: The finance used for day to day trading, calculated as current assets minus current liabilities [2].

knowledge_max_2: finance used for day to day trading
calculated as current assets minus current liabilities

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why short term finance is suitable for the Christmas stock.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: The need is temporary [k], because the $45,000 is tied up only from October until the stock is sold by the end of December [app]. Reason 2: Repayment matches seasonal cash flow [k], because about $210,000 of November and December revenue would pay off the overdraft or the suppliers before February [app].

knowledge_max_2: short term finance suits temporary needs
short term finance matches seasonal repayment cycles
application_max_2: $45,000 is tied up only from October until the end of December
about $210,000 of November and December revenue arrives before February

questions.question_text: Explain two problems of using a bank overdraft for the $45,000 Christmas stock.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Interest adds to seasonal costs [k], because 11% annual interest on $45,000 for 4 months costs around $1,650 [app], trimming the margin made on Christmas sales [an]. Problem 2: The overdraft can be withdrawn on demand [k], because the bank may reduce the limit and the shops hold only $95,000 of current assets against $70,000 of liabilities [app], pressuring the directors if December sales disappoint [an].

knowledge_max_2: overdrafts carry interest charges
overdrafts are repayable on demand
application_max_2: 11% on $45,000 for 4 months costs around $1,650
only $95,000 of current assets against $70,000 of liabilities
analysis_max_2: interest trims the profit margin on Christmas sales
a reduced limit would pressure the directors if December sales disappoint

questions.question_text: Do you think a bank overdraft is a better source than extended trade credit for the $45,000 Christmas stock? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Trade credit is interest free [k], so the shops avoid the $1,650 overdraft charge and keep the full margin on around $210,000 of seasonal sales [app], which suits the tight working capital of only $25,000 [an]. However, relying on extended 60 day credit is risky [k], because the two suppliers expect payment before February and may shorten terms or charge more if trading stays slow [app], straining the relationships behind 11 years of stock supply [an]. Overall, trade credit is the better, cheaper option for the Christmas stock because the zero interest cost directly helps profit [eval], but the overdraft should remain available as backup if December trading falls well short of $210,000 [eval].

knowledge_max_2: trade credit is interest free finance from suppliers
extended supplier credit carries a risk of tightened terms
application_max_2: avoids the $1,650 overdraft charge and keeps margin on $210,000 of seasonal sales
current assets of $95,000 against current liabilities of $70,000 leave tight working capital
analysis_max_2: zero interest directly protects profit and cash flow
strained supplier relationships could damage future stock supply
evaluation_max_2: recommends trade credit as the cheaper option for the Christmas stock
retains the overdraft as backup if December sales fall short

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Pennyroyal Café is an independent café serving breakfast, brunch and lunch with 14 staff. GDP grew 4.2%, unemployment fell to 3.8% and restaurant spending rose 11% over 2 years. Revenue reached $86,000 from $61,000; weekend waits average 25 minutes. Consumer confidence is at its highest for a decade.

The owners must choose between a second café in the retail park 3 km away, costing $240,000 and seating 55 customers, or refitting 40 seats at the current site, before the lease is allocated in 8 weeks.

questions.question_text: Define 'economic growth'.
questions.model_answer: An increase in the value of goods and services produced in an economy, measured by the rise in GDP [2].

knowledge_max_2: an increase in real GDP / output of goods and services
the economy produces more value over time

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Pennyroyal's revenue grew during the economic boom.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Rising GDP lifts household incomes [k], and with unemployment down to 3.8% and GDP up 4.2%, more customers treat café meals as everyday spending rather than a luxury [app]. Reason 2: Strong consumer confidence encourages spending on leisure [k], and with restaurant spending up 11% over 2 years, Pennyroyal's monthly revenue rose from $61,000 to $86,000 [app].

knowledge_max_2: economic growth raises household incomes and purchasing power
consumer confidence rises in a boom, boosting discretionary spending
application_max_2: GDP grew 4.2% and unemployment fell to 3.8%
restaurant spending rose 11% and monthly revenue climbed from $61,000 to $86,000

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Pennyroyal of opening the retail park café.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: A second site widens the catchment [k], tapping the growing industrial estate and retail park trade instead of only the current street [app], so total revenue could rise beyond $86,000 a month [an]. Benefit 2: Two venues share customer goodwill and catering costs [k], and with 55 customers seated the $240,000 build cost can be spread across higher combined volume [app], improving overall profit margins [an].

knowledge_max_2: a new location reaches new customers and widens the catchment
expansion spreads fixed costs and shared resources across sites
application_max_2: retail park near a growing industrial estate, 3 km from the current site
new site seating 55 customers for $240,000 versus refitting 40 seats
analysis_max_2: higher combined volume lifts total revenue above $86,000 a month
fixed costs spread over two sites improve margins if demand holds

questions.question_text: Do you think Pennyroyal Café should open the retail park café rather than extend the current site? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Opening the retail park site would capture the boom at its peak [k]; with GDP up 4.2%, unemployment at 3.8% and restaurant spending up 11%, a café seating 55 customers near the industrial estate could reach a new market while the original site keeps the loyal crowd causing 25-minute weekend waits [app], so revenue could grow well past $86,000 a month [an]. However, extending the current site by refitting 40 seats is cheaper and less risky [k]; it costs far less than $240,000 and keeps one 14-person team focused on one location [app], so profit per café rises without duplicated management or split oversight while the boom lasts [an]. Overall, Pennyroyal should open the retail park café [eval], because demand fundamentals (GDP +4.2%, confidence at its highest for a decade) support two locations, and waiting 8 weeks risks losing the lease to a rival [eval].

knowledge_max_2: opening a second site captures new markets during rapid growth
extending the existing site is cheaper and keeps management simple
application_max_2: $240,000 new site seating 55 customers near a growing industrial estate
current site refit of 40 seats; weekend waits of 25 minutes at $86,000 monthly revenue
analysis_max_2: two-site revenue growth and capacity relief versus $240,000 outlay and execution risk
single-site efficiency and lower risk versus missing the retail park lease deadline
evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation tied to the 8-week lease deadline and boom-stage demand
recommendation links back to confidence at its highest for a decade

scenario_stem:
Olive Branch Kitchen Co is a private limited company preparing ready-to-cook meal kits, selling 52,000 kits at $12 each for $624,000 revenue. Ingredients cost $5.50 per kit, leaving $6.50 of added value on every sale.

Founder Marcus Vale is deciding how to raise added value: pre-chop ingredients and add recipe cards with 14 extra hours of labour weekly, or rebrand with premium packaging costing $0.85 extra per kit to target busy professionals and support a $2 price rise.

questions.question_text: Define 'added value'.
questions.model_answer: Added value is the difference between the selling price of a product and the cost of the bought-in materials and components used to make it. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Difference between selling price and cost of bought-in materials/inputs

questions.question_text: Do you think Kilnworth Ceramics should form the Westmark joint venture or spend $900,000 on a second kiln at home? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The joint venture opens a new market and growth beyond Country X [k]; with $1.4 million of Kilnworth's $1.9 million retained profit and partner-supplied land and 300 workers, year-3 dividends of about $350,000 would comfortably exceed the return on a $900,000 kiln [app], and exports spread risk beyond a domestic market squeezed by cheaper imports [an]. However, the second kiln lifts annual output by 25% at home at $900,000 [k]; it stays fully under Kilnworth's control, with no partner conflict, and directly defends its $2.1 million domestic revenue against imported tiles arriving next year [app], though it does nothing to open new markets or spread risk [an]. On balance, the Westmark joint venture is the stronger move [eval], because it tackles both the import threat and the need for growth, while the kiln only defends the status quo [eval].

scenario_stem:
Kettleworth Canning Co is a company making tinned tomatoes and sweet corn. It produced 4.8 million tins, selling at $1.25 each to 9 supermarket chains. Its single tinplate supplier has a 12-week delivery lead time.

A 3-week supply interruption stopped line two, losing 40,000 tins worth $50,000. Raising the raw material reserve from 2 weeks to 6 weeks would cost $2,100 per month extra storage, $350 per month extra insurance and tie up $480,000 of working capital.

questions.question_text: Identify two reasons why businesses hold inventories.
questions.model_answer: To keep production running without interruption if supplies are delayed; to meet sudden or unexpected demand from customers [2].

knowledge_max_2: ensures uninterrupted production

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Kettleworth Canning Co should increase its raw material reserve to 6 weeks.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: A larger reserve prevents production stoppages [k], because the single tinplate supplier has a 12-week delivery lead time and one 3-week interruption already stopped line two [app]. Reason 2: A larger reserve protects revenue [k], because last winter's interruption cost 40,000 tins of lost output, worth $50,000 at $1.25 a tin [app].

protects revenue and output
application_max_2: 12-week delivery lead time

questions.question_text: Explain two costs of raising the reserve from 2 weeks to 6 weeks.
questions.model_answer: Cost 1: Extra storage costs reduce profit [k]; the 6-week reserve adds $2,100 per month of storage and $350 per month of insurance, about $29,400 a year [app], which is more than half of last winter's $50,000 loss repeated within a single year [an]. Cost 2: Capital tied up [k]; raising the reserve from 2 weeks to 6 weeks locks up $480,000 of working capital [app], which cannot be used for new lines or repairs and might have to be borrowed at interest [an].

However, the reserve is not free [k]; storage and insurance cost $2,450 per month and $480,000 of working capital would be tied up in tinplate and tomatoes [app], and the money could instead earn interest or fund line two while a second supplier is found [an]. Overall, Kettleworth should raise the reserve [eval], because one avoided stoppage saves $50,000 against $29,400 a year of holding costs, and with 12-week lead times another delay is likely, not rare [eval].

scenario_stem:
Sorrel Cottage Tailoring is a sole trader business making school uniforms and alterations, with revenue of $54,000. Priya wants $8,500 to buy two industrial sewing machines for a supermarket uniform contract, as her current machine often breaks down.

She has saved $5,000 and needs $3,500 more. Micro-finance offers $3,500 at 14% interest over 2 years, about $187 a month. Crowdfunding offers backers a discount voucher with no interest, but the $3,500 target may not be met.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'micro-finance'.
questions.model_answer: Small scale finance offered to small businesses or entrepreneurs who cannot access traditional bank loans, often through specialist lenders [2].

knowledge_max_2: small scale finance for small businesses or entrepreneurs
used when traditional bank loans are not available

questions.question_text: Explain two factors Priya should consider when choosing between micro-finance and crowdfunding.
questions.model_answer: Factor 1: The amount required is small [k], because only $3,500 is missing after her $5,000 savings towards the $8,500 machines [app]. Factor 2: The cost and certainty of the finance [k], because the micro-finance lender asks 14% interest and about $187 a month for 2 years, while crowdfunding costs nothing but may raise nothing [app].

knowledge_max_2: the amount needed influences the most suitable source
cost and certainty of the finance differ between sources
application_max_2: only $3,500 is missing after her $5,000 savings towards the $8,500 machines
micro-finance costs 14% interest at about $187 a month for 2 years; crowdfunding may raise nothing

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of micro-finance for Sorrel Cottage Tailoring.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: She gets the machines quickly [k], because the $3,500 can be agreed without a long bank process, letting the supermarket uniform contract start this term [app], lifting revenue above $54,000 a year [an]. Advantage 2: She keeps full ownership of her business [k], because micro-finance involves no shares or voting rights being handed to backers [app], so Priya alone decides about prices, designs and hours [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think micro-finance is a better option than crowdfunding for the $3,500 Priya needs? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Micro-finance is certain and fast [k], because the lender has agreed $3,500 at 14% over 2 years at about $187 a month, so Priya can order the two industrial sewing machines immediately [app], winning the supermarket uniform contract before rivals [an]. Crowdfunding costs nothing in interest [k], but it demands constant promotion, delivers discount vouchers that cut margins, and may raise nothing at all [app], delaying the machines and risking the contract [an]. Overall, micro-finance is the better option because guaranteed funding at $187 a month is affordable for a $54,000 a year business [eval], provided Priya budgets for the 14% interest cost and never falls behind on repayments [eval].

scenario_stem:
Rillwater Construction Ltd is a private limited company employing 78 construction workers. GDP grew 3.6%, unemployment fell to 4.1% and housebuilding approvals rose 17%. Its order book is worth $9.4 million, its fullest in 6 years, but it turned down 2 contracts worth $2.8 million for lack of bricklayers and electricians.

With wages up 12%, directors must choose: raise pay 10% across 78 workers to attract staff, or subcontract the 2 contracts, cutting margins from 9% to 5% with 25% deposits upfront.

questions.question_text: Define 'boom'.
questions.model_answer: A period of rapid economic growth when output, employment and confidence are high [2].

knowledge_max_2: a period of rapid economic growth
high output, high employment and strong demand

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of low unemployment on Rillwater.
questions.model_answer: Effect 1: Skilled labour becomes scarce [k], and with unemployment at just 4.1% and site wages up 12%, Rillwater turned down 2 contracts worth $2.8 million for lack of bricklayers and electricians [app]. Effect 2: Recruiting from rivals costs more [k], and with GDP growth of 3.6% and three new housing estates due to start, keeping the 78 workers it has is harder [app].

knowledge_max_2: low unemployment creates skills shortages
low unemployment pushes wages up and intensifies competition for staff
application_max_2: unemployment fell to 4.1% and site wages rose 12%
2 contracts worth $2.8 million turned down for lack of skilled trades

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Rillwater of raising wages by 10%.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Higher pay attracts scarce skilled labour [k], letting Rillwater take on the 2 contracts worth $2.8 million instead of losing them again [app], directly lifting revenue and workload [an]. Benefit 2: Better pay improves retention and morale [k], so the 78 workers are less likely to leave for rivals whose site wages already rose 12% [app], protecting site productivity and delivery dates [an].

knowledge_max_2: higher wages attract scarce skilled staff
higher wages improve retention and morale
application_max_2: 10% wage rise targets the 2 contracts worth $2.8 million
78 workers retained against rivals whose wages rose 12%
analysis_max_2: revenue and workload rise when the $2.8 million contracts are won
lower turnover protects productivity and on-time delivery

questions.question_text: Do you think Rillwater Construction should raise wages by 10% rather than subcontract the 2 contracts? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Raising wages by 10% retains and attracts the skilled trades Rillwater needs [k]; with unemployment at 4.1%, GDP growth of 3.6% and wages already up 12% in the region, higher pay is the realistic way to win the 2 contracts worth $2.8 million while keeping the $9.4 million order book on schedule [app], so revenue and reputation both benefit despite higher payroll costs [an]. However, subcontracting avoids permanent wage inflation [k]; paying 25% deposits upfront and accepting margins cut from 9% to 5% on the 2 contracts would still clear the workload if recruiting fails [app], so subcontracting protects cash while the labour market stays tight [an]. Overall, Rillwater should raise wages by 10% [eval], because subcontracting at 5% margin sacrifices profit on $2.8 million of work, whereas higher wages keep control of quality, schedules and the full 9% margin on the strongest order book in 6 years [eval].

knowledge_max_2: raising wages attracts and retains scarce skilled workers in a boom
subcontracting avoids permanent wage increases but erodes margins
application_max_2: 10% wage rise vs 2 contracts worth $2.8 million and a $9.4 million order book
subcontract margins cut from 9% to 5% with 25% deposits upfront
analysis_max_2: winning the contracts with permanent staff protects quality and schedule control
subcontracting clears workload but halves the margin and demands cash deposits
evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation tied to the 6-year-high order book of $9.4 million
recommendation weighs long-term capability against short-term cash protection

scenario_stem:
Alderline Print Works is a private limited company printing flyers and menus, employing 6 print operators and 1 apprentice on $310,000 revenue. Orders have risen 15% since a rival closed, and both presses are fully booked most Saturdays.

Difficulty 2: Competing against established stationery sellers is hard for a small local firm [k]; Alderline has no reputation in weddings compared with specialist sellers [app], so winning trust and enough sales to earn the expected $18,000 a year may take longer than planned [an].

questions.model_answer: One case for launching is growth: the $7,500 investment is modest for a business earning $310,000 a year, and a 25% mark-up could add $18,000 of annual profit [k], using the spare capacity created by the rival's closure and the 15% rise in orders [app], spreading press costs across another product line [an].
