scenario_stem:
Mallowgate Flour Ltd is a private limited company milling flour in Country X with 118 workers making 240 tonnes weekly, on $5.6 million revenue. The NMFWU represents 74 of the workers; 81% balloted for strike over the 40-minute unpaid lunch break.

Mallowgate offers 2.5%, the union demands 6% and paid breaks. Talks collapsed after 7 weeks and a 10-day strike starts 2 December, risking a $900,000 a year bakery contract. Should it concede?

questions.question_text: Define 'industrial action'.
questions.model_answer: Industrial action is action taken by employees, such as a strike or a work-to-rule, to pressure their employer during an industrial dispute, usually organised through a trade union. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Action by employees/workers against the employer (e.g. strike)
Taken to pressure the employer during a dispute, usually via a trade union

questions.question_text: Explain two effects industrial action could have on Mallowgate Flour Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Effect 1: Industrial action halts or slows production [k]; a 10-day strike would stop the mill producing its 240 tonnes of flour a week [app], so orders for the national bakery chain worth $900,000 a year may not be fulfilled. Effect 2: Industrial action damages reputation and customer confidence [k]; bakeries relying on weekly flour supplies may switch to rival mills during a 10-day stoppage [app], risking the loss of long-term customers and revenue.

knowledge_max_2: Industrial action stops/slows production
Industrial action damages reputation/customer confidence
application_max_2: 10-day strike would stop 240 tonnes a week of flour
Bakery chain contract worth $900,000 a year at risk

questions.question_text: Explain two effects a strike would have on the employees of Mallowgate Flour Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Effect 1: Striking workers lose pay for days not worked [k]; during a 10-day strike from 2 December the 74 union members would forfeit wages while the dispute continues [app], squeezing household budgets even though the 6% demand is the union's goal [an]. Effect 2: Industrial action shows solidarity and strengthens the union's bargaining position [k]; with 81% of voting members backing the strike, the union negotiates from a position of strength [app], increasing the chance the employer improves the 2.5% offer or grants paid breaks [an].

knowledge_max_2: Strikers lose pay for days not worked
Industrial action demonstrates solidarity/strengthens bargaining position
application_max_2: 10-day strike from 2 December; 74 union members would forfeit wages
81% of voting members backed the strike; 2.5% offer vs 6% demand
analysis_max_2: Financial hardship/loss of income for striking workers
Stronger position to win a better offer (6% or paid breaks)

questions.question_text: Do you think Mallowgate Flour Ltd should agree to the union's demands of a 6% pay rise and paid lunch breaks? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Agreeing would end the threat to stop production [k]; a settlement would protect the bakery-chain contract worth $900,000 a year and keep 240 tonnes a week flowing [app], avoiding the $5.6 million revenue base being disrupted by a 10-day stoppage [an]. However, conceding 6% is far above the 2.5% offered, and paid breaks add hours that currently go unpaid [k]; lifting the offer to 6% across 118 workers and adding paid breaks would materially raise the wage bill [app], which could force price rises or job cuts at the mill [an]. On balance, Mallowgate should negotiate a compromise, such as a phased rise reaching 6% over two years with a shorter paid break [eval], because outright refusal guarantees a 10-day stoppage while full capitulation sets a costly precedent [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Industrial action pressures the employer; settlement protects production
Concession raises wage costs and may set a precedent for future claims
application_max_2: $900,000 a year bakery-chain contract; 240 tonnes a week; 10-day strike risk
2.5% offer vs 6% demand; 118 workers; $5.6 million revenue
analysis_max_2: Settlement avoids stopped production, lost orders and lost revenue
Full concession strains margins and invites further claims
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options (concede fully vs refuse vs compromise)
Justified recommendation: negotiated compromise/phased settlement

scenario_stem:
Cilento Pasta Co is a private limited company in Country X making jarred pasta sauces, with 40 staff and $1.6 million domestic revenue. An importer in Ostresh wants to produce and sell Cilento sauces locally under licence, paying an 8% royalty.

questions.question_text: Define 'licensing'.

However, Cilento's own sales office keeps full control of recipes, quality and pricing [k]; it costs $180,000 in year 1 but captures the whole profit margin in Ostresh and builds direct customer relationships [app], delivering far more income long term if the market grows [an]. unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Skerry Bay Hotel is a 3-star hotel with 120 rooms and 64 employees. GDP fell 1.4%, unemployment reached 10.2% and holiday spending fell 16%. Revenue fell from $3.1 million to $2.4 million, occupancy from 71% to 58%, and international tourist numbers fell 9%. Corporate bookings, once 30% of revenue, have dried up completely.

The manager must choose between cutting room rates by 15% to attract domestic families, or keeping rates and closing the leisure wing, making 9 staff redundant. Rivals cut rates by 12%.

Reason 2: Weak confidence and incomes reduce business tourism [k], and with GDP down 1.4% and corporate bookings dried up completely, international tourist numbers also fell 9% [app].

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Bluefin Leisure Centres Ltd is a private limited company running 4 fitness clubs with 21,000 members and 96 staff. After 3 years of growth, GDP rose 0.4%, unemployment rose 4.9% to 5.3% and confidence fell from 112 to 104; gym visits fell 7%, revenue $8.9 million.

scenario_stem:
Torvion Helmets Ltd is a private limited company making reinforced cycling helmets at its Briarport factory. With 26 workers it made 40,000 helmets last year: fixed costs $240,000, variable cost $9, price $17, average cost $15.00.

Orders from European distributors exceed capacity. A $600,000 injection-moulding machine would lift capacity to 60,000 helmets, cut variable cost to $7.50 but raise fixed costs to $330,000. Alternatively, outsourcing up to 20,000 helmets costs $12 each. The board must choose.

questions.question_text: Define 'fixed costs'.
questions.model_answer: Fixed costs are costs that do not vary with the level of output in the short run, such as rent, insurance and lease payments, which must still be paid even if nothing is produced. [2]

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages Torvion Helmets Ltd would gain from buying the new machine.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: It creates technical economies of scale [k]. The machine cuts variable cost from $9 to $7.50 per helmet and lifts capacity to 60,000 helmets, so average cost falls from $15.00 to $13.00 [app]. Reason 2: It spreads fixed costs over more units [k]. Although fixed costs rise to $330,000, spreading them over 60,000 helmets gives $5.50 each instead of $6.00 at 40,000 helmets [app].

knowledge_max_2: Technical economies of scale: new machinery lowers unit production cost

application_max_2: Variable cost falls $9 to $7.50; average cost falls $15.00 to $13.00 at 60,000 helmets

Outsourcing at $12 each means Torvion pays only for the extra units actually needed, so it keeps $600,000 rather than borrowing for a machine [app], protecting cash flow while the European distributors' orders are uncertain [an]. Reason 2: It avoids the risk of excess fixed costs [k]. Fixed costs of $330,000 would still be due even if the 60,000-helmet capacity went unfilled [app], and underused machinery would push average cost back above $13.00, wiping out the expected saving [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Torvion Helmets Ltd should buy the new injection-moulding machine? Justify your answer.

scenario_stem:

questions.question_text: Do you think Solmara Herbal Teas should appoint the agent in Country Y? Justify your answer.

scenario_stem:
Marazzi Pasta Sauce Co is a private limited company producing tomato sauces and passata for 30 delicatessens. With 11 workers it makes 240,000 jars a year; variable costs are $1.10 per jar, including $0.50 tomatoes, fixed costs $66,000, selling at $2.00 per jar.

A growers' co-operative offers a two-year contract for 120 tonnes at $800 per tonne versus $1,000 per tonne weekly, saving $24,000 a year. Quarterly deliveries need cold storage at $10,000 a year, cutting the tomato portion from $0.50 to $0.40 per jar.

questions.question_text: Define 'variable costs'.
questions.model_answer: Variable costs are costs that change directly with the level of output, rising when more units are produced and falling when fewer are produced, such as raw materials, components and packaging. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Variable costs change with the level of output
Examples: raw materials, components, packaging, direct labour per unit

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits the co-operative tomato contract could bring Marazzi Pasta Sauce Co.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: It is a purchasing economy of scale [k]. Buying 120 tonnes at $800 per tonne instead of $1,000 saves $200 per tonne, worth $24,000 a year [app]. Reason 2: It lowers the variable cost of every jar [k]. The tomato portion falls from $0.50 to $0.40, so variable cost drops from $1.10 to $1.00 per jar and average cost falls from about $1.38 to about $1.32 [app].

knowledge_max_2: Bulk purchasing earns lower prices (purchasing economies of scale)
Lower variable cost per unit reduces average cost
application_max_2: $200 per tonne saving on 120 tonnes = $24,000 a year
Tomato portion of variable cost falls $0.50 to $0.40; variable cost $1.10 to $1.00 per jar; average cost about $1.38 to $1.32

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages of signing the two-year tomato contract.
questions.model_answer: Disadvantage 1: It adds a new fixed cost [k]. Leasing cold storage at $10,000 a year must be paid even if jar sales fall below 240,000 [app], so the net saving drops to $14,000 and average cost rises if output dips [an]. Disadvantage 2: It locks Marazzi into one supplier [k]. If spot prices fall below $800 per tonne or the co-operative's quality slips, Marazzi must still honour the two-year deal [app], risking higher costs or inconsistent sauces across its 30 delicatessen customers [an].

knowledge_max_2: New fixed commitments must be paid regardless of output
Long-term supply contracts remove flexibility if prices or quality change
application_max_2: $10,000 a year cold-storage lease; output currently 240,000 jars
Fixed price $800 per tonne for two years; supplies 30 delicatessens
analysis_max_2: Fixed lease is unavoidable, so falling sales raise average cost and shrink the saving to $14,000
Lock-in risks paying above market price or poor quality, harming margins and reputation

questions.question_text: Do you think Marazzi Pasta Sauce Co should sign the two-year tomato contract? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Signing brings clear purchasing economies of scale [k]: the $200 per tonne saving is worth $24,000 a year, more than covering the $10,000 cold-store lease, so net costs fall by $14,000 a year [app] and profit rises from $150,000 to about $164,000, with average cost dropping to about $1.32 [an]. However, the two-year commitment is risky [k]: if tomato prices fall below $800 per tonne or demand from the 30 delicatessens weakens, the fixed lease and price would become a burden [app], and bulk quarterly deliveries could raise wastage, eroding the $0.10 saving per jar [an]. Overall [eval], the contract is worth signing because the saving exceeds the lease cost by $14,000 a year — about 9% extra profit — provided Marazzi negotiates quality guarantees and an exit clause before committing [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Purchasing economies of scale reduce input and average costs
Fixed commitments and supplier lock-in create risk
application_max_2: $24,000 annual saving versus $10,000 lease; net $14,000 saving
Profit rises $150,000 to about $164,000; average cost falls to about $1.32 per jar
analysis_max_2: Net saving improves profit by about 9% and lowers variable cost per jar
Weak demand or falling spot prices could make the fixed lease and price uncompetitive
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options with stem figures and reaches a justified recommendation
Overall judgement with a clear condition (quality guarantee/exit clause)

scenario_stem:
Starbright Toys is a private limited company selling children's toys and games online and from one shop in Country X. Annual revenue is $420,000, with 55% earned in November and December. August inflows are $6,500 against $15,800 outflows; September inflows $7,200 against $15,100 outflows, from a $9,000 opening balance on 1 August.

Marcus must decide before 1 August whether to arrange a $20,000 bank overdraft or delay paying toy suppliers $14,000 until January, when festive takings arrive.

questions.question_text: Define 'overdraft'.
questions.model_answer: An overdraft is a bank facility that lets a business spend more money than it holds in its current account, up to an agreed limit, with interest paid on the amount used [2].

knowledge_max_2: overdraft allows spending beyond the current account balance
up to an agreed limit with interest on the amount used

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why festive toy retailers like Starbright prepare cash-flow forecasts before Christmas.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: A forecast shows the timing of cash movements [k], so Marcus can see that August inflows of $6,500 will not cover outflows of $15,800 [app]. Reason 2: A forecast identifies borrowing needs in advance [k], letting Marcus arrange the $20,000 overdraft before the balance falls below zero [app].

knowledge_max_2: forecast shows timing of cash inflows and outflows
forecast reveals when borrowing will be needed
application_max_2: August inflows of $6,500 against outflows of $15,800
the overdraft must be arranged before the balance falls below zero

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Starbright could face if it delays paying toy suppliers until January.

Problem 2: Suppliers may charge late fees or withdraw credit terms [k], and Starbright's forecast already shows August inflows of only $6,500 against outflows of $15,800 [app], so extra costs would deepen the shortfall [an].

late payment may trigger fees or refusal to supply

questions.question_text: Do you think Marcus should arrange the $20,000 overdraft rather than delay paying toy suppliers? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Arranging the overdraft would protect supplier relationships ahead of the festive peak [k], because Starbright depends on suppliers delivering festive stock against $14,000 of September invoices [app], so keeping trust secures stock this year and next [an]. However, overdraft interest will add cost [k], and inflows of $6,500 and $7,200 in August and September sit well below outflows of $15,800 and $15,100 [app], so the balance could reach about -$8,200 by the end of September before festive sales arrive [an]. Overall, Marcus should arrange the $20,000 overdraft [eval], because the interest cost is lower than the risk of empty shelves in the two months that generate 55% of annual revenue [eval].

supplier goodwill is vital to secure festive stock

scenario_stem:
Estwick Brick Co is a private limited company producing 9 million clay bricks yearly for housebuilders. It employs 74 workers, runs two kilns continuously and turns over $3.7 million. Estwick town, 500 metres away, has 9,000 residents downwind.

Doctors recorded 34 cases of childhood asthma; chimney particulates are 45% above the legal limit. The Agency may fine $1,500 daily or shut the oldest kiln. The board can fit $210,000 electrostatic filters, switch to low-sulphur gas at $28,000 a year, or appeal.

questions.question_text: Define 'externalities'.
questions.model_answer: Externalities are the effects of producing or consuming a good on third parties not involved in the transaction; they may be negative, such as pollution, or positive, such as jobs created for the local community. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Effects on third parties not involved in the transaction
Can be negative external costs or positive external benefits

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the Environment Agency intervenes in Estwick Brick Co's operations.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: To protect public health [k], since 34 cases of childhood asthma were recorded near the plant in the last year, linked to dust drifting over 500 metres into a town of 9,000 residents [app]. Reason 2: To enforce the law against pollution [k], because chimney particulates measured 45% above the legal limit, so fines of $1,500 per day are needed to force compliance [app].

knowledge_max_2: To protect public health from pollution
To enforce legal limits and standards
application_max_2: 34 cases of childhood asthma near the plant last year
Particulates 45% above the legal limit; fines of $1,500 per day

questions.question_text: Explain two effects on Estwick Brick Co of fitting the electrostatic filters costing $210,000.
questions.model_answer: Effect 1: Emissions fall and fines stop [k], as filters capture particulates so the output stays legal and the $1,500 daily fines are avoided [app], preventing penalties that could total over $540,000 a year [an]. Effect 2: A large short-term cost [k], as $210,000 must be spent immediately, equal to about 5.7% of annual turnover of $3.7 million [app], squeezing short-term cash flow and reducing profit for the year [an].

knowledge_max_2: Filters reduce emissions and end fines
Filters are a large one-off capital cost
application_max_2: Filters cost $210,000 and avoid $1,500 daily fines
$210,000 equals about 5.7% of $3.7 million turnover
analysis_max_2: Avoided fines could save over $540,000 a year
Short-term cash flow and profit are squeezed

questions.question_text: Do you think Estwick Brick Co should fit the $210,000 electrostatic filters? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One argument for fitting the filters is that they solve the legal problem permanently [k], removing the 45% excess particulates and stopping $1,500 daily fines while keeping both kilns running for its 9 million bricks [app], protecting turnover of $3.7 million, the jobs of 74 workers and relations with Estwick's 9,000 residents [an]. However, one argument against is the immediate cost [k], since $210,000 equals roughly 5.7% of annual turnover and the firm could instead switch to low-sulphur gas at just $28,000 a year extra, preserving cash for expansion [app], although switching fuel may not capture the heavier particulates and would delay compliance [an]. Overall, Estwick Brick Co should fit the electrostatic filters [eval], because fines of $1,500 a day would exceed the $210,000 installation cost in 5 months of breach, making compliance cheaper and safer for its licence to operate [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Filters deliver permanent legal compliance
Upfront cost versus cheaper but partial gas switching
application_max_2: $210,000 filter cost versus $28,000 extra per year for gas
45% excess particulates; fines of $1,500 per day
analysis_max_2: Compliance protects turnover, jobs and community relations
Gas switching is cheaper but may not capture heavier particulates
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both fitting filters and switching fuel or appealing
Reaches a justified judgement using stem figures

scenario_stem:
Hartfield City Hospital is a public corporation funded by the State, employing 900 staff and treating 140,000 patients a year on a $180 million budget. Waiting lists rose from 4,000 to 6,500 in 3 years.

Nearby Saracen Health is a private clinic with 120 staff charging $250 per consultation and $3,800 for minor surgery, making $4.5 million profit. The government is debating contracting it to clear Hartfield's list at 15% below public costs, or raising the hospital's budget.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'mixed economy'.
questions.model_answer: An economic system in which both private sector and public sector organisations operate side by side, with resources allocated by both markets and the State. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Both public and private sectors operate side by side
Resources are allocated by markets and by the State

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Hartfield City Hospital remains in the public sector.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: To provide free healthcare to all [k], the hospital treats 140,000 patients a year funded by a $180 million budget rather than charging fees [app]. Reason 2: To guarantee access for people who cannot pay [k], 6,500 patients are waiting, many of whom could not afford $250 private consultations at Saracen Health [app].

knowledge_max_2: Public provision gives free access regardless of ability to pay
Guarantees essential healthcare for the whole population
application_max_2: 140,000 patients a year on a $180 million budget

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of Hartfield City's mixed healthcare economy.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Waiting times may fall [k], because Saracen Health offers same-week appointments and could treat some of the 6,500 patients waiting at Hartfield [app], so patients receive care sooner and return to work faster [an]. Benefit 2: The public hospital can focus on complex cases [k], since routine treatment could move to Saracen Health, freeing 900 staff and the $180 million budget for serious illness [app], improving overall service efficiency [an].

Public sector frees resources for complex care

900 staff and the $180 million budget freed for serious illness

However, one argument against is that contracting private care [k] would divert public money to a firm that made a $4.5 million profit and charges $3,800 for minor surgery [app], meaning the $180 million budget grows the private sector rather than strengthening Hartfield's 900 public staff [an]. Overall, the government should agree a short-term contract [eval], because cutting the 6,500 waiting list quickly serves patients best, provided the 15% saving is properly costed and Hartfield keeps capacity for serious cases [eval].

scenario_stem:
Redmarsh Construction Ltd is building a 9-storey office block in Country X with 74 workers, including 26 contract migrants. Falls from height are the main risk and 2 scaffolders were injured. Rules use coloured posters and hazard signs plus a 20-minute weekly talk.

After 3 near-misses, the safety officer proposes toolbox talks with a translator at $60 each. The manager prefers multilingual signs for $4,800, noting accident rates fell 40% after multilingual signage elsewhere. Both start within 2 weeks.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'visual communication'.
questions.model_answer: Visual communication is the passing of information through images, such as signs, posters, charts, diagrams, photographs or videos, rather than through words alone. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Communication using images, symbols or diagrams
Examples include posters, signs, charts and videos

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of visual communication on the construction site.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Signs and posters communicate safety rules instantly without spoken language [k], which is vital because 26 contract migrants on site have a first language other than English [app]. Advantage 2: Visual warnings are permanent and cannot be forgotten [k], so coloured hazard signs around the site constantly remind the 74 workers of the dangers of working at height on the 9-storey block [app].

knowledge_max_2: Images communicate quickly without spoken language
Visual messages are permanent and always visible
application_max_2: 26 contract migrants have a first language other than English
Coloured hazard signs remind the 74 workers on the 9-storey block

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why visual communication alone may not be enough on the site.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Posters and signs cannot check understanding [k], so the 26 contract migrants might misread hazard warnings even in their own language [app], leaving the safety officer unable to tell whether workers understand the risks [an]. Reason 2: Visual methods cannot answer questions [k], so workers cannot clarify site rules beyond the 20-minute Monday talk without stopping work [app], meaning misunderstandings about falls from height and scaffolding could persist undetected [an].

knowledge_max_2: Visual methods are one-way and cannot check understanding
Visual methods cannot answer questions or give feedback
application_max_2: 26 contract migrants might misread existing coloured posters and hazard signs
Only the 20-minute Monday talk allows any spoken explanation of the rules
analysis_max_2: The safety officer cannot tell whether workers understand the risks
Unchecked misunderstandings about falls from height may go undetected

questions.question_text: Do you think the project manager should spend $4,800 on multilingual signs instead of hiring a translator for toolbox talks? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One argument for the multilingual signs is that they cost $4,800 once [k] and would be on display in all areas permanently, covering the 26 contract migrants and the other 48 workers [app], so safety instructions would always be visible where the danger actually occurs on the 9-storey block [an]. However, one argument against is that signs are one-way [k] and cannot check that workers understand, as shown by the 3 near-miss incidents in one month despite existing posters [app], whereas a translator at $60 per session would let migrants ask questions and get answers face to face [an]. Overall, the site should fund both, but if only one option is possible, the multilingual signs are the better spend [eval], because they protect every worker every day, matching the 40% fall in accident rates seen on similar sites after signage was introduced [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Visual methods are permanent, always visible and cheap over time
Verbal two-way methods check understanding and allow questions
application_max_2: $4,800 once for multilingual signs covering 26 contract migrants and 48 other workers
3 near-miss incidents in one month despite existing posters and signs
analysis_max_2: Permanent visible signs protect workers where the danger occurs
Existing one-way signs failed to prevent near misses, so interaction is needed
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both the signs and the translator-led toolbox talks
Reaches a justified recommendation using stem figures

scenario_stem:
Brancott Catering Co is a private limited company catering for weddings and corporate parties. Founded 4 years ago, it employs 8 staff and earned $322,000 from 46 events, averaging $7,000, with most bookings by word of mouth.

A hotel group offers wedding referrals for a 12% fee, adding 15 events at lower margins. Brancott could spend $7,500 on its own website, aiming for 2 extra corporate events monthly at $7,000 each.

questions.question_text: Define 'e-commerce'.
questions.model_answer: Buying and selling goods or services over the internet, for example through a website, app or online booking platform [2].

knowledge_max_2: buying and selling goods or services over the internet
carried out through a website, app or online platform

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why selling services directly to customers suits a service business such as Brancott Catering Co.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Services are intangible and cannot be stored or transported, so they are normally sold direct from provider to customer [k], matching how Brancott already wins most of its 46 events through word of mouth [app]. Reason 2: Selling direct lets Brancott meet clients personally to plan each event [k], so each $7,000 event can be tailored to the customer's menu, budget and schedule [app].

knowledge_max_2: services are intangible and cannot be stocked, so direct selling is typical
direct sale enables personal consultation and tailoring of the service
application_max_2: most of Brancott's 46 events already come through word of mouth

questions.question_text: Explain two drawbacks for Brancott Catering Co of relying on hotel-group referrals.
questions.model_answer: Drawback 1: The hotel group would take a 12% fee on every referred booking [k], so on 15 referred events a year at $7,000 each Brancott would pay about $12,600 in fees, cutting the margin left for ingredients and staff [app], weakening profit per event over time [an]. Drawback 2: Referred clients are effectively loyal to the hotel rather than to Brancott [k], so if the hotel ends the partnership or switches caterer, Brancott could lose those 15 events a year without owning the customer relationships [app], making future revenue less predictable [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Brancott Catering Co should rely on referrals from the hotel group? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Relying on the hotel group would bring about 15 extra events a year worth roughly $105,000 at $7,000 each, with almost no marketing effort from Brancott [k]. Even after paying the 12% fee of about $12,600 a year, the referred bookings would add useful volume while Brancott builds its pipeline [app], and hotel clients could introduce Brancott to premium wedding customers it could not reach alone [an]. However, the 12% fee would recur every year, costing far more than a one-off $7,500 website plus modest hosting [k], while the owner expects 2 extra corporate events a month from the website at about $7,000 each, roughly $168,000 a year with no commission taken [app]. Owning that channel gives Brancott customer data, direct repeat bookings and full margin [an]. Overall, Brancott should not rely on hotel referrals as its main channel; it should invest in the website and accept hotel referrals only as a short-term top-up while online enquiries build [eval], because owning its own marketing channel protects margins and customer relationships in the long run [eval].

scenario_stem:
Peregrine Outdoor Co is a private limited company designing rucksacks and hiking jackets. Sales were 90,000 units ($4.5 million); fixed costs $1.8 million, variable cost $22, average cost is $42. Its two largest customers want faster northern deliveries.

The board considers a second northern factory doubling capacity to 180,000 units. Fixed costs would rise to $3.24 million, but bulk fabric buying would cut variable cost to $20. Problems include slower communication, duplicated management and integration across two sites.

questions.question_text: Define 'economies of scale'.
questions.model_answer: Economies of scale are the cost advantages a business gains as it increases the scale of production, so that the average cost of each unit falls as output rises. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Average cost per unit falls as the scale/output of production increases
Examples: purchasing, technical, financial, marketing and managerial economies

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits Peregrine Outdoor Co would gain from economies of scale if it doubles capacity.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Purchasing economies would lower variable cost [k]. Bulk buying of fabric cuts variable cost from $22 to $20 per unit, saving $2.00 on each of 180,000 units — $360,000 a year [app]. Reason 2: Fixed costs are spread over more output [k]. Fixed costs rise only to $3.24 million, so the fixed cost per unit drops from $20 to $18 and average cost falls from $42 to $38 [app].

knowledge_max_2: Purchasing (bulk-buying) economies lower variable cost per unit
Spreading fixed costs over greater output lowers average cost

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Peregrine might face from operating two factories.

Slower communication between a northern site and head office, plus duplicated management, could delay decisions and cause errors [app], pushing average cost up instead of down [an]. Problem 2: Fixed costs nearly double [k]. Fixed costs rise to $3.24 million, so if demand fails to reach 180,000 units, the extra fixed cost is spread over fewer units [app], pushing average cost above $42 and reducing profit below $720,000 [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Peregrine Outdoor Co should open the second northern factory? Justify your answer.

However, the gains depend on filling the extra capacity [k]: at only 90,000 units a year, fixed costs of $3.24 million would push average cost to about $56 [app], and duplicated management across two sites could cause diseconomies of scale, with slower decisions eroding the saving [an]. Overall [eval], the expansion is justified if the two largest customers commit to northern volumes and faster deliveries, since the $4.00 unit saving and delivery advantage outweigh moderate diseconomy risk; Peregrine should sign those orders before committing to the factory [eval].

Clear overall judgement linked to securing customer commitments first

scenario_stem:
Bramble & Board Catering Co is a private limited company offering wedding and conference catering. Annual revenue is $680,000, with 65% arriving between May and September. Fixed costs are $17,500 monthly; wedding clients pay 25% on booking and the balance 14 days before the event.

January to April inflows of $9,000, $11,000, $13,500 and $18,000 face $21,000 monthly outflows. With a $14,000 opening balance, Lena chooses between a $20,000 loan at 9% (repayable in October) and asking suppliers to wait 60 days.

questions.question_text: Define 'cash-flow forecast'.
questions.model_answer: A cash-flow forecast is a document estimating a business's cash inflows, outflows, net cash flow and opening and closing balances for each future period [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why a catering company can be profitable yet still run out of cash.

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity

Kongwe Plantations Ltd is a private limited company growing oil palm across 2,600 hectares. It earns $4.6 million exporting 80% of its 7,400 tonnes of crude palm oil, used in 3,000 supermarket products.

scenario_stem:

scenario_stem:

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity

questions.question_text: Do you think Rusthaven Engineering Ltd should replace the agent with its own sales representative? Justify your answer.

scenario_stem:
Eastport Cannery Ltd is a private limited company canning baked beans and chopped tomatoes for two supermarket chains. It canned 3.6 million tins: fixed costs $540,000, variable cost $0.28, price $0.52, average cost $0.43.

An automated line costing $800,000 would lift capacity to 4.4 million tins, cut variable cost to $0.20 and raise fixed costs to $660,000. A bank loan could fund it during the spring shutdown, but larger orders from the two chains are unsigned.

questions.question_text: Define 'technical economies of scale'.
questions.model_answer: Technical economies of scale are the cost advantages gained from using larger or more advanced machinery and production processes, which lower the cost of producing each unit. [2]

Example: automation, mass production equipment, specialist machines

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of the new automated canning line.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: It cuts variable cost per tin [k]. Automation lowers variable cost from $0.28 to $0.20, saving $0.08 per tin — $352,000 a year at 4.4 million tins [app]. Reason 2: It spreads fixed costs over more output [k]. Capacity rises to 4.4 million tins, so average cost falls from $0.43 to $0.35 [app].

Risk 2: Extra capacity may go unfilled [k]. Neither supermarket contract is signed, so output could stay near 3.6 million tins [app], in which case fixed costs of $660,000 give an average cost of about $0.38 — better than $0.43 but not the targeted $0.35 [an].

scenario_stem:
The Fig & Fiddle Café is a partnership serving all-day breakfasts and home baking. Annual revenue is $460,000, with 45% earned in December and summer. Last January revenue was $18,500 against $26,000 fixed costs.

From a $5,400 opening balance, January inflows $18,500 and outflows $30,200 are followed by February inflows $21,000 and outflows $27,500. By 15 December they choose between a $15,000 overdraft and postponing the $12,000 kitchen upgrade until April's spring tourist trade.

questions.question_text: Define 'current assets'.
questions.model_answer: Current assets are items owned by a business that are expected to be converted into cash or used up within one year, such as inventories, debtors and cash at bank [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why The Fig & Fiddle Café can be profitable yet face a January cash shortfall.

Reason 2: January revenue of $18,500 is far below the tourist peak [k], so inflows cannot cover the $30,200 of January outflows [app].

Advantage 2: Upgrading in April lets the partners pay from spring tourist receipts [k], when revenue recovers towards the $460,000 annual level [app], so the equipment is funded from stronger inflows [an].

scenario_stem:
Brackenfeld Salmon Farm Ltd is a private limited company raising salmon in sea cages off Dunara Bay. It produces 1,700 tonnes yearly, earns $5.2 million in exports, and shares the bay with 60 local fishing boats and holiday cottages.

It proposes doubling output to 3,400 tonnes with 6 more cages, $2.8 million investment and 26 extra jobs. The Fishery Trust says waste feed and sea lice have cut wild fish 30%; new cages require a sustainability standard costing $120,000 a year.

questions.question_text: Define 'sustainable development'.
questions.model_answer: Sustainable development is meeting the needs of people today without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs, balancing economic growth with environmental protection. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Meeting present needs without compromising future generations
Balancing economic growth with environmental protection

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Brackenfeld must weigh environmental effects before expanding.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: The bay is already under pressure [k], because sea lice and waste feed from the current cages have reduced wild fish numbers by 30%, threatening the 60 local fishing boats [app]. Reason 2: The government controls further licences [k], since new cages are allowed only if farms meet a sustainability standard costing $120,000 a year [app].

knowledge_max_2: Existing pollution already harms the bay ecosystem
Government licences require a sustainability standard
application_max_2: Wild fish numbers down 30%; 60 local fishing boats affected

questions.question_text: Explain two problems for Brackenfeld if it must meet the sustainability standard.

Problem 2: Ongoing compliance burden [k], because feed sourcing, stocking density and water-quality monitoring must be maintained to keep the licence [app], risking fines or a refused licence if any check fails [an].

However, one argument against is the environmental damage [k], since the bay has already seen a 30% decline in wild fish numbers, and installing 6 more cages would add more waste feed and sea lice [app], so the sustainability standard must be met or the expansion licence will be refused anyway [an]. Overall, Brackenfeld should expand only by meeting the sustainability standard [eval], because certified growth to 3,400 tonnes keeps the licence, protects the bay's wild fish and lets the community share the benefits without repeating the 30% decline [eval].

scenario_stem:
Ruskin & Cole Department Store is a private limited company in Country X with 210 staff and $24 million sales. Head office sends every change by email and memo, with full meetings twice a year. A survey found 58% did not understand the last 3 changes and turnover hit 34%.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'two-way communication'.

scenario_stem:
Rowanhill Knitwear is a private limited company making wool sweaters and cardigans. Founded 8 years ago, it employs 40 staff and sells through 80 independent clothes shops and 2 department stores, with revenue of $2.4 million.

questions.question_text: Do you think the government should privatise the Country X National Theatre? Justify your answer.

However, one argument against is that private ownership [k] would end regional touring and the education scheme for 40,000 schoolchildren a year, and raise ticket prices from $28 to $40 [app], depriving lower-income audiences among the 900,000 annual visitors of affordable, high-quality theatre [an]. Overall, the government should keep CXNT in public ownership [eval], because arts and culture are public goods whose social value exceeds the $38 million cost, and CXNT already covers 38% of its costs from ticket sales [eval].

scenario_stem:
Wrenhill Toys Ltd is a private limited company selling the 'Sunshine Express' train set through 160 retailers in Country X; about 9,000 sold at $45 each. Loose magnets pose a choking risk and 340 sets were returned.

The marketer wants a press release and social media alert. The MD prefers phoning 160 retailers and writing to 2,100 registered buyers, costing $6,500 over 2 weeks; only retailers and media reach 6,900 unregistered buyers. A public campaign may alarm non-buyers.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'written communication'.
questions.model_answer: Written communication is the passing of information through written words, such as letters, emails, memos, reports, notices or text messages, producing a record that can be read and re-read. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Communication using written words
Examples include letters, emails, reports and notices; creates a record

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of written communication for the product recall.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Written messages give a permanent record [k], so the 160 retailers would have the recall instructions in writing to identify and return the unsafe Sunshine Express sets [app]. Advantage 2: Written communication suits messages sent to named individuals [k], so the 2,100 buyers who registered online would receive clear return instructions by letter [app].

knowledge_max_2: Written messages create a permanent, checkable record
Written messages suit sending the same message to named individuals
application_max_2: 160 retailers would have recall instructions in writing for the unsafe sets
2,100 registered online buyers would receive return instructions by letter

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of announcing the recall through a press release and social media.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Mass electronic channels reach far more people far faster [k], alerting the 6,900 unregistered buyers who never registered online [app], so unsafe Sunshine Express sets can be returned before more magnets are swallowed [an]. Advantage 2: Posting online costs almost nothing [k], compared with about $6,500 and 2 weeks for phone calls and letters to retailers and registered buyers [app], protecting public safety and the brand at minimal cost [an].

knowledge_max_2: Mass media and social media reach huge audiences quickly
Electronic public announcements cost very little
application_max_2: 6,900 unregistered buyers would be reached instantly
Compared with about $6,500 and 2 weeks for phone calls and letters
analysis_max_2: Faster alerts return unsafe sets before more injuries occur
Minimal cost protects both public safety and the brand's reputation

questions.question_text: Do you think Wrenhill Toys should rely on the press release and social media instead of phoning retailers and writing to registered buyers? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One argument for the press release and social media is speed and reach [k], which would instantly alert the owners of the remaining 6,900 unregistered units, including the 340 sets already proving defective [app], so children could be protected immediately at almost no cost [an]. However, one argument against is that mass media cannot guarantee every affected buyer acts [k], whereas phoning the 160 retailers and writing to the 2,100 registered buyers uses two-way and written channels with confirmed receipt, costing about $6,500 and 2 weeks [app], giving an auditable recall record for the safety regulator [an]. Overall, Wrenhill should use both: the press release immediately to protect children, followed by calls and letters to retailers and registered buyers to evidence the recall [eval], prioritising safety over the $6,500 cost [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Mass media is fast and wide-reaching but unverifiable
Two-way and written channels confirm receipt and create records
application_max_2: Press coverage reaches the 6,900 unregistered buyers instantly

analysis_max_2: Immediate public alert prevents further injuries from loose magnets

evaluation_max_2: Weighs both the public campaign and direct two-way contact

scenario_stem:
Tidemill Electrical is a private limited company running 2 independent electrical shops. Founded 15 years ago, it employs 26 staff and earned $1.8 million, but sales fell 12% as online discounters undercut prices; a rival sells a $700 television for $549.

A click-and-collect website costing $35,000 plus $1,500 a month could help compete. 70% of customers value expert advice and free installation of kitchen appliances, earning $300,000 a year; the directors weigh online investment against remaining specialists.

questions.question_text: Define 'click-and-collect'.
questions.model_answer: A service where a customer orders goods online and collects them in person from a shop or depot at a chosen time [2].

knowledge_max_2: order placed online, typically paid for in advance
goods collected in person from a shop or depot

questions.question_text: Explain two threats e-commerce poses to Tidemill Electrical.
questions.model_answer: Threat 1: Online discounters carry lower store overheads and can undercut high street prices [k], as the rival selling a $700 television for $549 shows, helping drive Tidemill's 12% sales fall over 2 years [app]. Threat 2: Customers who buy online skip the shop entirely [k], so Tidemill loses walk-in trade that supports its $300,000 a year of kitchen appliance installation business [app].

knowledge_max_2: online discounters can undercut physical shops because they have lower overheads
online buying removes the store visit, cutting walk-in trade for physical retailers
application_max_2: a $700 television sold online for $549 undercuts Tidemill's pricing
the 12% sales fall over 2 years and the $300,000 installation income both reflect store traffic

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits Tidemill Electrical could gain from a click-and-collect website.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Click-and-collect lets Tidemill sell online while still driving customers into its two country-town shops [k], protecting footfall and upselling the kitchen appliance installation that already earns $300,000 a year [app], defending revenue and margins [an]. Benefit 2: Click-and-collect removes home delivery costs and waiting times [k], making online buying attractive for heavy items such as televisions and washing machines at a running cost of only $1,500 a month [app], improving convenience and customer loyalty [an].

knowledge_max_2: click-and-collect combines online ordering with in-store collection
click-and-collect avoids home delivery costs and delays
application_max_2: in-store collection drives upselling of the $300,000 a year installation service
$1,500 a month running cost for heavy items such as televisions and washing machines
analysis_max_2: store visits protect add-on sales and margins that pure delivery would lose
convenience versus home delivery can win back price-checking customers and build loyalty

questions.question_text: Do you think Tidemill Electrical should invest in a click-and-collect website? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Investing in click-and-collect would let Tidemill compete online while keeping its two shops relevant [k]; at $35,000 build cost and $1,500 a month running cost, it is cheaper than losing 12% of a $1.8 million business, about $216,000 of revenue at risk [app], and it converts browsing into store visits where advice and installation can be sold [an]. However, Tidemill cannot match online prices such as $549 for a $700 television, so price-led buyers may still leave [k]; the website only works if stock is visible online and collection is easy, and at $18,000 a year running cost the system must win back meaningful volume [app], otherwise the investment becomes an expensive brochure [an]. Overall, Tidemill should invest, prioritising click-and-collect over price cuts because its differentiator, advice and installation valued by 70% of customers, cannot be copied by online rivals [eval], and it should review sales versus the $216,000 at risk after 12 months [eval].

knowledge_max_2: click-and-collect lets a physical retailer compete online while retaining store visits
however, the firm cannot match online discounters on price alone
application_max_2: $35,000 setup plus $1,500 a month ($18,000 a year) versus about $216,000 revenue at risk from a 12% fall on $1.8 million
the $549 rival television example shows price competition is unwinnable; advice and installation valued by 70% of customers is the firm's edge
analysis_max_2: click-and-collect protects footfall and installation upselling worth $300,000 a year
execution risk: poor stock visibility or collection experience would make it an expensive brochure
evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation to invest in click-and-collect rather than cut prices
balanced judgement requiring a 12-month review against the $216,000 revenue at risk

scenario_stem:
Kettle & Fern Tea Co is a private limited company grading and packing specialty teas. It blended 480 tonnes: fixed costs $1.44 million, variable cost $5,000 per tonne, average cost $8,000, price $9,000 per tonne.

A purpose-built plant costing $3 million would double capacity to 960 tonnes. Fixed costs rise to $2.4 million, cutting average cost to $7,500 per tonne, but confirmed orders are only 700 tonnes; beyond 1,200 tonnes poor communication and low morale push costs up.

questions.question_text: Define 'average fixed cost'.
questions.model_answer: Average fixed cost is the fixed cost of production divided by the number of units produced; it falls continuously as output rises because the same fixed costs are spread more thinly. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Average fixed cost = fixed costs / output
It falls as output increases because fixed costs are spread over more units

questions.question_text: Explain two ways the new plant would lower Kettle & Fern's average cost.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Fixed costs spread over more tonnes [k]. Average fixed cost falls from $3,000 per tonne at 480 tonnes to $2,500 per tonne at 960 tonnes [app]. Reason 2: Technical economies of scale from purpose-built machinery [k]. Doubling capacity to 960 tonnes cuts average cost from $8,000 to $7,500 per tonne [app].

knowledge_max_2: Spreading fixed costs over larger output lowers average fixed cost
Larger, modern machinery creates technical economies of scale
application_max_2: Average fixed cost falls $3,000 per tonne (480 tonnes) to $2,500 per tonne (960 tonnes)
Capacity doubles to 960 tonnes; average cost falls $8,000 to $7,500

questions.question_text: Explain two problems with building the new plant ahead of demand.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Confirmed demand is too low [k]. Orders total only 700 tonnes against capacity of 960 tonnes [app]; at 700 tonnes, average cost would be about $8,429 — higher than today's $8,000 — so the plant would lose money until sales grow [an]. Problem 2: Diseconomies of scale are threatened [k]. The economist warns that beyond 1,200 tonnes, poor communication and low morale push average cost back up [app], so costs could rise again just as the new plant reaches full capacity [an].

knowledge_max_2: Underused capacity raises average cost and erodes the benefit of expansion
Diseconomies of scale: poor communication and low morale raise average cost at large scale
application_max_2: Confirmed orders of only 700 tonnes versus 960 tonnes capacity
Economist warns of diseconomies beyond 1,200 tonnes
analysis_max_2: At 700 tonnes average cost rises to about $8,429, making current volume better served by the old plant
Rising costs beyond 1,200 tonnes would reverse the falling average cost curve

questions.question_text: Do you think Kettle & Fern Tea Co should build the new plant now? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Building now captures technical economies of scale [k]: average cost falls from $8,000 to $7,500 per tonne at 960 tonnes, and profit could rise from $480,000 to about $1.44 million [app], making the $3 million investment recoverable within a few years [an]. However, confirmed orders are only 700 tonnes [k]: at that volume average cost would be about $8,429, worse than today, and output beyond 1,200 tonnes risks diseconomies of scale such as poor communication and low morale [app], so building ahead of demand gambles $3 million on unsigned sales [an]. Overall [eval], Kettle & Fern should delay construction until signed orders exceed roughly 800 tonnes — the point where average cost matches today's $8,000 — and meanwhile secure national distribution agreements, because proceeding at 700 tonnes would destroy the expected saving [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Technical economies of scale lower average cost and raise profit
Diseconomies of scale and underused capacity threaten large investments
application_max_2: Average cost falls $8,000 to $7,500; profit could rise $480,000 to $1.44 million; $3 million cost
Only 700 tonnes confirmed; at 700 tonnes average cost is about $8,429; diseconomies beyond 1,200 tonnes
analysis_max_2: At full capacity the $500 per tonne saving adds about $480,000 of annual profit
At 700 tonnes the higher average cost erases the gain and strains cash for loan repayments
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both options with stem figures and reaches a justified, conditional recommendation
Clear overall judgement tied to achieving at least 800 tonnes of signed orders

scenario_stem:
Copperpipe Plumbing & Heating is a private limited company handling boiler repairs and installations. It employs 6 plumbers and 2 apprentices, earned $390,000 last year, and has $15,500 monthly fixed costs; winter jobs pay on completion, summer contracts after 60 days.

From a $17,200 opening balance, November inflows $48,500 and outflows $39,800 are followed by December inflows $56,000 and outflows $52,300. By 31 October Dan must choose between buying a $30,000 van now for the winter rush or waiting until spring.

questions.question_text: Define 'cash flow'.
questions.model_answer: Cash flow is the movement of money into and out of a business over a period, shown as inflows, outflows and the resulting net cash flow [2].

knowledge_max_2: cash flow is the movement of money in and out of the business
measured as inflows minus outflows, giving net cash flow

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why winter is both the busiest and the riskiest season for Copperpipe's cash flow.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Winter brings the highest job volumes [k], pushing inflows to $48,500 in November and $56,000 in December [app]. Reason 2: Winter jobs increase outflows for materials, parts and overtime [k], which explains November outflows of $39,800 and December outflows of $52,300 [app].

knowledge_max_2: peak season means high job volumes and high receipts
peak season also drives higher outflows for parts and labour
application_max_2: inflows of $48,500 in November and $56,000 in December
outflows of $39,800 in November and $52,300 in December

questions.question_text: Explain two ways Dan could cover the November shortfall if he buys the van now.
questions.model_answer: Way 1: Dan could arrange an overdraft with the bank [k], covering the forecast dip to about -$4,100 after paying $30,000 for the van [app], which lets the business complete winter jobs that would otherwise be turned away [an]. Way 2: Dan could delay non-essential equipment purchases [k], protecting the November balance of $25,900 before the van payment [app], so the cash gap stays smaller and interest costs are limited [an].

knowledge_max_2: an overdraft covers short-term shortfalls up to an agreed limit
delaying non-essential spending reduces outflows
application_max_2: forecast dip to about -$4,100 after paying $30,000 for the van
protecting the November balance of $25,900 before the payment
analysis_max_2: keeps capacity to complete winter jobs that would be turned away
smaller gap means lower interest costs

questions.question_text: Do you think Dan should buy the van in November rather than wait until spring? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Buying now captures the winter rush [k], when inflows of $48,500 and $56,000 in November and December justify extra capacity [app], and the new van could generate enough extra jobs to pay for itself [an]. However, paying $30,000 in November drops the balance from $25,900 to about -$4,100 [k], forcing reliance on the bank through December [app], so the shortfall would need covering before spring work restarts [an]. Overall, Dan should buy the van now [eval], because missing the winter peak would lose more revenue than the modest overdraft needed to bridge two months [eval].

knowledge_max_2: buying capacity ahead of peak season captures extra revenue
large one-off purchases can push cash negative in the short term
application_max_2: November and December inflows of $48,500 and $56,000 vs a $30,000 van
balance falls from $25,900 to about -$4,100 after purchase
analysis_max_2: extra capacity could pay for itself in the winter rush
reliance on the bank until spring receipts arrive
evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation comparing lost winter revenue against two months of overdraft

scenario_stem:
Hartham Ridge Wind Farm Ltd is a private limited company formed to build an 8-turbine, $14 million wind farm on moorland. It would generate 21 megawatts for 11,000 homes, creating 34 construction jobs and 9 permanent maintenance roles.

The site is 3 kilometres from Hartham (620 residents) and 900 metres from a walking trail. Hartham Ridge Action gathered 700 signatures; 45% oppose it, citing 38 decibels and visual impact. Consent needs a $120,000-a-year community scheme and closing 2 turbines during migration, cutting output 9%.

questions.question_text: Define 'environmental pressure group'.
questions.model_answer: An environmental pressure group is an organisation that campaigns to influence business and government decisions to protect the natural environment, using publicity, petitions and lobbying. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Organisation campaigning to protect the environment
Uses publicity, petitions and lobbying to influence decisions

questions.question_text: Explain two external benefits the wind farm would bring to Country X.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Clean electricity for homes [k], as the 8 turbines would generate 21 megawatts, enough to power 11,000 homes without burning fossil fuels [app]. Reason 2: Jobs for the local area [k], as 34 construction jobs and 9 permanent maintenance roles would be created over 14 months of building [app].

knowledge_max_2: Wind farms generate clean electricity without fossil fuels
Wind farms create jobs for local people
application_max_2: 21 megawatts, enough for 11,000 homes
34 construction jobs plus 9 permanent roles over 14 months

questions.question_text: Explain two external costs the Hartham Ridge wind farm may create.
questions.model_answer: Cost 1: Noise disturbance for villagers [k], since Hartham village, 3 kilometres away with 620 residents, faces turbine noise of about 38 decibels [app], which may disturb sleep and reduce house prices, costs falling on people who gain no direct electricity [an]. Cost 2: Harm to wildlife and the landscape [k], as shutting 2 turbines during bird migration shows a real collision risk, and the moorland skyline is a valued landscape [app], damaging a recreational asset used by walkers on the nearby trail [an].

Wind farms affect wildlife and valued landscapes

questions.question_text: Do you think Hartham Ridge Wind Farm Ltd should proceed under the council's conditions? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One argument for proceeding is the clean energy and jobs [k], as 21 megawatts would supply 11,000 homes while 34 construction jobs and 9 permanent roles are created [app], giving Country X lower-carbon electricity and lasting employment on the moorland [an]. However, one argument against is the impact on Hartham [k], since 45% of 620 residents oppose the farm over noise of about 38 decibels and visual impact on the valued skyline [app], and the $120,000-a-year community fund plus a 9% output cut from shutting 2 turbines eat into returns on the $14 million project [an]. Overall, Hartham Ridge Wind Farm Ltd should proceed under the council's conditions [eval], because clean power for 11,000 homes and 43 jobs outweigh the residual disruption, and the community fund plus migration shutdowns fairly compensate Hartham while keeping the wind farm viable [eval].

Resident opposition and compliance conditions erode returns

Compliance conditions reduce returns on the $14 million project
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both proceeding under conditions and resident opposition
Reaches a justified judgement using stem figures

scenario_stem:
Oakhurst Precision Tools is a private limited company making precision measuring instruments in Brannock, employing 45 production workers and generating $950,000 revenue. Its customers are engineering firms across Country X.

Directors want $220,000 automated calibration machines to raise output 30% and cut unit costs, shifting from steady profit to rapid growth. The union warns automation could eliminate 18 of 45 jobs; workers voted to oppose it, and the two owners disagree.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'stakeholder'.
questions.model_answer: Any individual, group or organisation that has an interest in, or is affected by, the activities and decisions of a business. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Any individual, group or organisation with an interest in a business
Affected by the business's activities and decisions

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the owners and the workers at Oakhurst may have conflicting objectives over the automation plan.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Owners want to reduce costs and increase output [k], because the $220,000 machines would raise output by 30% and could win larger orders from engineering firms across Country X [app]. Reason 2: Workers want job security and stable wages [k], because the union warns that 18 of the 45 production roles could disappear if automation goes ahead [app].

knowledge_max_2: Owners seek lower costs and higher profit or growth
Workers seek job security and fair treatment
application_max_2: $220,000 machines would raise output by 30%
18 of the 45 production roles at risk of elimination

questions.question_text: Explain two ways Oakhurst could manage the conflict between the owners and the workers.
questions.model_answer: Point 1: Oakhurst could consult with the workers and their union before deciding [k], for example holding meetings about the $220,000 plan and the 18 at-risk roles [app], so employees feel heard and may accept retraining instead of resisting the change [an]. Point 2: Oakhurst could retrain or redeploy affected workers into new roles [k], offering the 18 workers training to operate or maintain the new calibration machines [app], which would reduce redundancies and keep skilled staff available for the 30% output increase [an].

Retraining or redeployment of affected staff

Training to operate the new machines for the 30% output increase

questions.question_text: Do you think Oakhurst should approve the $220,000 investment in automated calibration machines? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One argument for approving the investment is that the new machines would raise output by 30% [k], cutting unit costs for Oakhurst Precision Tools and helping it win larger orders from toolmakers across Country X [app], which could protect the business's survival and fund future growth [an]. However, one argument against is that automation could eliminate 18 of the 45 jobs [k], harming employee morale and creating bitter conflict with the trade union [app], which may damage productivity and undermine the very growth the owners want [an]. Overall, Oakhurst should not approve the machines immediately [eval]; it should first negotiate retraining and redeployment with the union, then approve the $220,000 investment in a phased programme that keeps most staff while still achieving the 30% output target [eval].

evaluation_max_2: Weighs automation benefits against worker welfare
Reaches a justified judgement favouring a phased, negotiated approach

scenario_stem:
Hartham Bakery is a family-run private limited company in Bramfield, founded 2003, with 24 staff making artisan loaves for 3 retail outlets on $520,000 sales. Priya Raman must replace the production supervisor who ran the bakery floor for 9 years.

With a $4,500 budget and 8 weeks, she has two internal candidates, senior bakers of 6 and 4 years, plus an external applicant from a rival bakery. She must choose internal promotion or outside hire.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'job description'.

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Hartham Bakery should carry out a job analysis before recruiting the new production supervisor.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Job analysis identifies exactly what the job involves [k], for example the daily tasks of managing the bakery floor, stock control and 24 staff across 3 retail outlets [app]. Reason 2: Job analysis ensures the advert and selection criteria match the role [k], so Priya attracts suitable candidates within the $4,500 recruitment budget rather than wasting money on unsuitable applicants [app].

Job analysis ensures the advert and criteria match the role
application_max_2: Managing the bakery floor and 24 staff across 3 retail outlets
$4,500 budget and need for suitable applicants

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Hartham Bakery of producing a clear job description for the supervisor vacancy.

Benefit 2: A job description gives the interviewer a checklist for comparing candidates [k], allowing internal and external applicants to be scored against the same duties [app], making the final choice more objective and lowering the risk of a poor appointment [an].

Internal and external applicants scored against the same list

questions.question_text: Do you think Hartham Bakery should appoint the production supervisor from outside the business rather than promote internally? Justify your answer.

scenario_stem:
Hallowfen Bakery is a private limited company baking artisan sourdough loaves, founded in 2018. Loaves sell at $10.00 wholesale, with variable costs of $4.00 and monthly fixed costs of $9,000. Last month it sold 2,250 loaves, making $4,500 profit.

A rival is undercutting prices. The owners must choose between a cheaper flour blend, cutting variable cost to $2.50, or raising the price to $12.00. Dearer loaves could lose orders, but cheaper flour might weaken the artisan quality behind loyal customers.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'break-even output'.
questions.model_answer: The level of output at which total revenue exactly equals total costs, so the business makes neither a profit nor a loss. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Output where total revenue equals total costs
Neither profit nor loss is made at this point

questions.question_text: Calculate Hallowfen Bakery's break-even output in loaves per month. Show your working.
questions.model_answer: Contribution per loaf = $10.00 − $4.00 = $6.00 [k]. Break-even output = fixed costs ÷ contribution = $9,000 ÷ $6.00 = 1,500 loaves per month [app], the level at which total revenue equals total costs [k]. Revenue at break-even equals $15,000 and would exactly cover all fixed and variable costs [app].

knowledge_max_2: Break-even output = fixed costs ÷ contribution per unit
At break-even, total revenue equals total costs
application_max_2: Contribution of $6.00 per loaf ($10.00 − $4.00)

questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: It shows how many loaves must be sold before profit begins [k], which for Hallowfen is 1,500 loaves a month against actual sales of 2,250 loaves [app], so the owners can see the bakery has a 750-loaf cushion before falling into losses [an]. Benefit 2: It helps the owners judge price and cost changes safely [k], for example testing whether the cheaper flour or the $12.00 price rise would keep the margin of safety positive [app], which supports calmer decisions while a rival bakery undercuts on price [an].

scenario_stem:
Brackmere Paint & Decor is a sole trader paint and decorating-supplies shop with $680,000 annual revenue. Current assets are $92,000, including $38,000 owed by trade debtors, and current liabilities $74,000, including a $30,000 bank overdraft.

questions.question_text: Define 'working capital'.
questions.model_answer: Working capital is current assets minus current liabilities. It measures the cash and other short-term assets available to fund day-to-day trading after short-term debts are accounted for [2].

Reason 2: Working capital keeps a business trading while it waits for money it is owed to arrive [k], as $38,000 of Brackmere's $92,000 current assets is owed by trade debtors [app].

working capital funds day-to-day trading while awaiting payment from debtors

Benefit 2: Converting $38,000 owed by trade debtors into cash more quickly would strengthen Brackmere's position [k], where current liabilities of $74,000 already exceed the cash balance and current assets of $92,000 leave only $18,000 of working capital [app], easing pressure on day-to-day payments such as wages and suppliers [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Priya should ask existing debtors to pay sooner or arrange the $40,000 bank overdraft? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Asking debtors to pay sooner would inject cash without further borrowing [k], and it directly tackles the $38,000 owed by trade debtors that is straining Brackmere's cash while current liabilities stand at $74,000 [app]. scenario_stem:

questions.question_text: Define the term 'break-even chart'.

Boghall Mushroom Farm is a family business harvesting about 25,000 kg of oyster mushrooms a year. Annual fixed costs are $60,000 and variable costs are $4.00 per kg.

questions.question_text: Calculate the break-even output and the profit for each sales option. Show your working.

Option B (supermarket): contribution per kg = $7.00 − $4.00 = $3.00 [k]; break-even = $60,000 ÷ $3.00 = 20,000 kg a year, and profit at 25,000 kg = (25,000 × $3.00) − $60,000 = $15,000 [app].

scenario_stem:
Netherfield Farm is a family business running a pick-your-own strawberry field from June to August. It charges $9.00 per kg, with variable costs of $2.00 and seasonal fixed costs of $14,000. This year's harvest may reach 6,000 kg, but direct visitor sales may be only 4,500 kg.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'break-even analysis'.
questions.model_answer: Comparing fixed and variable costs with revenue to find the output at which no profit or loss is made, and to judge risk and profit at different outputs. [2].

questions.question_text: Calculate the break-even output for Netherfield Farm and the profit if 4,500 kg are sold this season. Show your working.
questions.model_answer: Contribution per kg = $9.00 − $2.00 = $7.00 [k]. Break-even output = $14,000 ÷ $7.00 = 2,000 kg of strawberries [app]. Profit if 4,500 kg are sold = (4,500 × $7.00) − $14,000 = $17,500 [app], before any surplus sales to the jam factory are counted [k].

Limitation 2: It assumes prices and costs stay fixed [k], but heat, rain or hail can ruin crop quality and force price cuts to clear fruit [app], so the real break-even can move sharply in a bad summer [an].
