scenario_stem:
Netherby Joinery Co Ltd is a private limited company making bespoke oak wardrobes. The income statement shows Revenue $385,000, Gross Profit $154,000, Expenses $98,000 and Profit for the year $56,000; Retained Profit is $36,000 after a dividend. The gross profit margin is 40%.

Directors weigh Option 1, raising prices by 5% to add about $19,000 of Revenue, against Option 2, cutting Expenses by $9,000 a year with energy-efficient saws and LED workshop lighting.

questions.question_text: Define 'expenses'.
questions.model_answer: Expenses are the indirect or running costs of a business, not directly tied to making or buying the goods sold, such as wages, rent, utilities, marketing and administration [2].

knowledge_max_2: Indirect or running costs of the business
Not directly linked to producing or buying the goods sold

questions.question_text: Explain two ways Netherby Joinery Co Ltd could improve its profit.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Raise selling prices, since a 5% increase should add about $19,000 of Revenue a year if volumes hold [k][app]. Reason 2: Reduce Expenses through efficiency, such as energy-efficient saws and LED workshop lighting saving about $9,000 a year on the $98,000 Expenses total [k][app].

knowledge_max_2: Increasing prices raises revenue and profit (if volumes hold)
Reducing expenses raises profit directly
application_max_2: 5% price rise should add about $19,000 of Revenue a year
Energy-efficient saws and LED lighting could save about $9,000 of the $98,000 Expenses

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Netherby Joinery Co Ltd of knowing the Expenses figure in its income statement.
questions.model_answer: Point 1: Knowing Expenses of $98,000 tells directors how much is consumed after the $154,000 Gross Profit [k], so they can target real savings like the $9,000 lighting and saws proposal instead of guessing [app][an]. Point 2: Expenses determine the gap between Gross Profit and Profit for the year ($56,000) [k], so tracking them helps directors spot overspending early and protect the $36,000 Retained Profit [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: Expenses show indirect costs after gross profit
Expenses create the gap between gross profit and profit for the year
application_max_2: $98,000 Expenses vs $154,000 Gross Profit
$56,000 Profit for the year and $36,000 Retained Profit at stake
analysis_max_2: Directors can target concrete savings rather than guessing
Early detection of overspending protects dividends and retained funds

questions.question_text: Do you think the directors should raise prices by 5% (Option 1) or cut expenses by $9,000 a year (Option 2)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option 1 should add about $19,000 of Revenue a year and, if volumes hold at a 40% gross profit margin, most of it should reach Profit for the year [k][app][an]. The risk is that bespoke furniture customers may trade down or delay purchases, hurting Revenue instead. Option 2 saves a guaranteed $9,000 a year on the $98,000 Expenses and does not risk alienating customers, but it is smaller and harder to repeat [k][app][an]. Overall, the directors should choose Option 1, because a price rise applies to every sale and homeowners in the capital region buying bespoke wardrobes are less price-sensitive; the $19,000 potential gain outweighs a guaranteed but smaller $9,000 saving, though Option 2 can also be done in parallel [eval][eval].

knowledge_max_2: Raising prices increases revenue and profit if demand holds
Cutting costs increases profit without needing higher sales
application_max_2: 5% rise worth about $19,000 on current Revenue at a 40% gross profit margin
$9,000 saving on $98,000 Expenses
analysis_max_2: Price rises risk losing price-sensitive customers
Cost cuts are guaranteed but smaller and can only be repeated so far
evaluation_max_2: For Option 1: bigger upside on every sale, low risk with bespoke buyers
Overall: Option 1 wins on value, though Option 2 can run alongside

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Dunwick Cannery Co is a private limited company in Country X canning mangoes and peaches. Its 74 workers process 2,600 tonnes yearly for $3.1 million revenue; sales come under two long-standing contracts.

A free trade agreement has abolished the 18% tariff on canned fruit between Country X and Country T. Country T's 60 million consumers import 40,000 tonnes a year. Two importers offer $900,000 if Dunwick meets safety standards; certification costs $220,000. It must choose: export deal or second domestic line.

questions.question_text: Define 'free trade'.
questions.model_answer: Free trade is the exchange of goods and services between countries without restrictions such as tariffs or quotas. [2].

knowledge_max_2: International trade without restrictions [1]
No tariffs or quotas between trading partners [1]

questions.question_text: Explain two ways in which the new free trade agreement could benefit Dunwick Cannery Co.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Removing tariffs makes exported goods cheaper and more competitive in foreign markets. [k] The abolition of the 18% tariff allows Dunwick's canned fruit to compete with Country T suppliers on price. [app] Reason 2: Free trade agreements open access to much larger markets. [k] Country T has 60 million consumers importing 40,000 tonnes of canned fruit a year, far bigger than Country X demand. [app]

knowledge_max_2: Removing tariffs makes exports more price-competitive [1]
Free trade agreements open access to larger foreign markets [1]
application_max_2: 18% tariff on canned fruit abolished on 1 June under the free trade agreement
Country T has 60 million consumers importing 40,000 tonnes a year

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits for Dunwick Cannery Co of accepting the Country T export contract.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: The contract creates a reliable new source of revenue. [k] The two Country T importers offer $900,000 a year, around 29% of last year's $3.1 million revenue. [app] This predictable income would cover the $220,000 certification cost within months and improve cash flow. [an] Benefit 2: Exporting diversifies the customer base and spreads risk. [k] Almost all sales currently go to Country X supermarkets under two long-standing contracts. [app] Adding Country T buyers reduces the danger that losing one domestic contract would seriously damage the business and its 74 workers. [an]

knowledge_max_2: Export contracts provide predictable revenue stream [1]
Diversifying customers spreads risk [1]
application_max_2: $900,000 a year offered, about 29% of last year's $3.1 million revenue
Almost all sales currently to Country X supermarkets under two long-standing contracts
analysis_max_2: Predictable income covers the $220,000 certification within months and eases cash flow
Less dependence on two domestic contracts protects the business and its 74 workers

questions.question_text: Do you think Dunwick should accept the Country T export contract? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Accepting the contract would lift revenue and profit. [k] The importers offer $900,000 a year, about 29% on top of last year's $3.1 million, helped by the 18% tariff saving. [app] Spreading sales across two countries would protect the 74 workers and reduce dependence on two domestic supermarket contracts. [an] However, the export route carries real costs. [k] Country T safety certification costs $220,000 and the contract depends on passing audits and meeting strict standards. [app] Building a second domestic production line would serve proven local demand with more certainty, and exchange-rate swings or importer failure could make the export deal less profitable than planned. [an] Overall, Dunwick should accept the export contract because Country T imports 40,000 tonnes a year and the $900,000 revenue would repay the $220,000 certification quickly. [eval] On balance, the strategic gain of an established Country T presence outweighs the safer second line, provided payment terms are agreed up front. [eval]

knowledge_max_2: Export contracts can raise revenue and reduce dependence on one market [1]
Exporting involves certification, compliance and currency risk [1]
application_max_2: $900,000 a year offer (about 29% on $3.1 million) with 18% tariff removed
$220,000 certification cost vs building a second domestic production line
analysis_max_2: Diversified revenue protects 74 workers and reduces reliance on two domestic contracts
Certification, audit and exchange-rate risks could erode the deal's returns vs the safer domestic line
evaluation_max_2: Accept the export contract (justified choice)
Weighs strategic Country T presence against certainty of domestic expansion

scenario_stem:
Aquajet Mobile Valeting is a sole trader start-up in Bracknell offering van-based car washing. Revenue fell from $9,800 to $6,300 monthly over 6 months while costs stayed $7,500. Danny has missed 2 van loan payments and lost a supplier.

The hardship scheme offers a one-off $5,000 grant and free budgeting training, but applicants must file a weekly cash-flow forecast for 6 consecutive months. Alternatively Danny could seek 45 days of supplier credit and raise prices 8%, though poor planning may be the cause.

questions.question_text: Define 'cash-flow forecast'.
questions.model_answer: A cash-flow forecast is a plan estimating the likely cash inflows and outflows of a business over a future period, showing the expected bank balance. [2]

knowledge_max_2: A forecast/estimate of future cash inflows and outflows
Shows expected bank balance / helps plan for cash shortfalls

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why many new businesses experience cash-flow problems.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Many new businesses fail to plan their cash needs, so inflows arrive later than bills [k]. Danny's revenue fell to $6,300 while costs stayed at $7,500, a gap of $1,200 a month that he apparently did not forecast [app]. Reason 2: Over-reliance on credit sales and suppliers can leave firms short of cash [k]. Danny missed 2 van loan payments and lost a supplier, showing his outflows are being called in faster than his inflows arrive [app].

knowledge_max_2: Poor planning / no cash-flow forecast
Timing mismatch between inflows and outflows / reliance on credit
application_max_2: Revenue $6,300 per month vs costs $7,500 per month (a $1,200 monthly gap)
2 missed van loan payments and a lost supplier

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits for Aquajet Mobile Valeting of producing a weekly cash-flow forecast.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: A weekly forecast shows Danny exactly when cash shortages will occur so he can act before bills go unpaid [k]. His costs of $7,500 exceed the $6,300 of revenue by $1,200 per month, so a forecast would expose the gap early enough to arrange credit or cut spending [app]. Acting early avoids more missed van loan payments and protects the business from collapse [an]. Benefit 2: The forecast is a required input for the hardship scheme, unlocking the $5,000 grant and free budgeting training [k]. Filing it for 6 consecutive months is mandatory, and the grant plus training would directly tackle his poor planning [app]. Better budgeting skills would stop the decline in revenue from $9,800 to $6,300 going unnoticed, restoring control over cash [an].

knowledge_max_2: Identifies shortages early / enables corrective action
Satisfies grant requirements and builds financial control
application_max_2: Costs $7,500 exceed revenue $6,300 by $1,200 per month; missed 2 van loan payments
Hardship scheme requires weekly forecast for 6 months; grant is $5,000
analysis_max_2: Early action prevents insolvency and protects the business
Better financial control slows/reverses the revenue decline, improving viability

questions.question_text: Do you think Danny should accept the hardship grant? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Danny could accept the hardship grant because the $5,000 one-off payment would cover more than 4 months of his $1,200 monthly cash gap and the free budgeting training targets his weak planning directly [k]. His revenue has fallen from $9,800 to $6,300 while costs stayed at $7,500, so cash support plus skills would address the root cause rather than the symptoms [app]. Fixing the planning weakness now tackles the real cause of failure instead of masking it [an]. However, the scheme demands a weekly cash-flow forecast for 6 consecutive months, plus follow-up checks, which adds administrative work while he is struggling to survive [k]. If he stops filing or forecasts poorly, the grant could be withdrawn and he gains nothing except extra pressure [an]. On the other hand, simply raising prices by 8% and asking for 45 days of credit would improve cash without conditions, though it may drive away price-sensitive households [app]. Overall, Danny should accept the hardship grant because it fixes both the finance and planning problems together, whereas credit terms merely delay the cash gap; the forecasting discipline he builds is exactly what a failing start-up needs [eval]. He should also raise prices gradually and confirm the credit deal in writing alongside the grant [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Grant provides emergency finance and training support
Grant conditions (weekly forecasts, compliance) impose burdens
application_max_2: $5,000 grant; revenue down from $9,800 to $6,300 vs costs of $7,500 (gap $1,200/month)
Alternative: 45 days credit and 8% price rise; 2 missed van loan payments
analysis_max_2: Grant plus training addresses root cause (poor planning), improving survival
Conditions add burden; failure to comply risks losing the grant
evaluation_max_2: Overall justified position weighing grant support against conditions
Evaluation tied to combining grant with price rise/credit and monitoring

scenario_stem:
Hathersage Garden Centre is a sole trader with 18 staff, busiest at weekends and in the spring planting season when customer numbers double. Weekend trade generates 60% of weekly revenue, while weekday mornings are quiet.

The owner must replace 4 full-time checkout employees. Option one: 8 part-time employees on Saturday, Sunday and Wednesday shifts at $11.50 an hour, saving $12,000 a year against $108,000 for 4 full-time replacements. Full-time staff offer consistent service and need less supervision.

questions.question_text: Define 'part-time employee'.
questions.model_answer: A part-time employee is a worker contracted for fewer hours per week than a full-time employee, for example weekend or reduced weekday shifts. Pay and benefits are usually calculated pro rata against full-time staff. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Works fewer hours per week than a full-time employee
Pay and benefits usually pro rata against full-time staff

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Hathersage Garden Centre of recruiting part-time employees.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Part-time staff can be rostered for the busiest periods, such as weekends when customer numbers double [k], matching labour to the pattern in which weekend trade now generates 60% of weekly revenue [app]. Benefit 2: Part-time employees at $11.50 per hour cost less than full-time replacements [k], saving an estimated $12,000 a year against the $108,000 full-time bill [app]. [4]

knowledge_max_2: Can be rostered to match peak trading periods
Lower total wage cost than full-time staff
application_max_2: Covers weekends when numbers double and 60% of revenue is earned
Saves about $12,000 a year versus the $108,000 full-time bill

questions.question_text: Explain two drawbacks to Hathersage Garden Centre of replacing the 4 full-time checkout employees with part-time staff.
questions.model_answer: Drawback 1: Replacing 4 full-time employees with 8 part-time workers doubles the number of people to train and supervise [k], increasing the workload for the owner of an 18-staff business [app], so induction and supervision costs could erode the projected $12,000 annual saving [an]. Drawback 2: Part-time staff often lack the product knowledge of full-time workers [k], so service quality during the spring planting season could slip [app], risking the garden centre's reputation and repeat custom [an]. [6]

knowledge_max_2: More part-time staff means more training and supervision
Part-time staff may lack full product knowledge
application_max_2: 8 part-time recruits to train versus 4 full-time at an 18-staff business
Service quality at risk during the spring planting season
analysis_max_2: Induction and supervision costs may offset the $12,000 saving
Poorer customer advice could reduce reputation and repeat sales

questions.question_text: Do you think Hathersage Garden Centre should recruit 8 part-time employees instead of replacing the 4 full-time checkout employees? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Hathersage Garden Centre should recruit the part-time employees because they can be concentrated on the weekend trade that generates 60% of weekly revenue [k], letting the centre serve doubled customer numbers without paying for idle hours on quiet weekday mornings [app]. The estimated $12,000 annual saving against the $108,000 full-time cost also protects margins [an]. However, 8 part-time workers mean more rotas, training and supervision than 4 full-time staff [k], and less experienced checkout staff may give poorer advice during the spring planting season rush [app], which could damage customer loyalty and reduce the very weekend sales that make the model work [an]. Overall, on balance the owner should recruit the part-time staff for Saturday, Sunday and Wednesday cover but retain one experienced full-time supervisor to train them [eval]. This captures the $12,000 saving and flexibility while limiting the risk of poorer customer service during the critical planting season [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Part-time staff can be rostered around peaks
More part-timers increase supervision and training needs
application_max_2: Targets 60% of weekly revenue at weekends
Saves about $12,000 a year versus the $108,000 full-time bill
analysis_max_2: Matching labour to demand protects margins and service at peaks
Inexperienced staff could reduce loyalty and weekend sales
evaluation_max_2: Balanced judgement favouring part-time cover with retained experience
Weighs wage saving against service risk in the planting season

scenario_stem:
Bumble & Bright Kidswear is a sole trader childrenswear retailer with 3 stores and 19 staff. Revenue is $410,000, with 70% from the 0-5 age segment. Research shows the 6-12 segment at 9% and teen streetwear aged 13-16 growing 25%, averaging $58 per purchase.

The owner must allocate a $30,000 marketing budget, choosing between a teen streetwear range for 13-16 year olds costing $28,000 and expanding the organic baby line for $15,000.

questions.question_text: Define 'demographic segmentation'.
questions.model_answer: Dividing a market into groups based on population characteristics such as age, gender, income or family status [2].

knowledge_max_2: dividing a market into groups
population characteristics such as age / income / family status

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Bumble & Bright Kidswear segments the childrenswear market by age.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Different age groups have different needs and tastes [k], shown by teens' average spend of $58 on streetwear compared with essentials for 0-5 year olds [app]. Reason 2: Targeted marketing is more cost-effective than one generic campaign [k], letting the retailer focus its $30,000 marketing budget on the 25% a year growth segment [app].

knowledge_max_2: different age groups have different needs and tastes
targeted marketing is more cost-effective
application_max_2: teens' average spend of $58
0-5 year olds
$30,000 marketing budget
25% a year growth segment

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Bumble & Bright Kidswear of launching the teen streetwear range.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Access to the fastest-growing segment [k], the 13-16 streetwear market expanding at 25% a year [app], which could lift total revenue above $410,000 [an]. Benefit 2: Higher average transaction values [k], with teens spending $58 per purchase against smaller baskets for baby basics [app], improving average profit per sale [an].

knowledge_max_2: access to the fastest-growing segment
higher average transaction values
application_max_2: 13-16 streetwear market expanding at 25% a year
teens spending $58 per purchase
analysis_max_2: could lift total revenue above $410,000
improves average profit per sale

questions.question_text: Do you think launching the teen streetwear range is a better decision than expanding the organic baby line? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The teen range taps a segment growing at 25% a year [k], diversifying beyond the 70% of revenue currently tied to 0-5s and capturing $58 average purchases [app], reducing reliance on a single age segment [an]. However, the organic baby line extends an established strength [k], refreshing the range that generates 70% of $410,000 revenue for only $15,000 [app], with lower risk than an untested teen offer [an]. Overall, launching the teen range is the better decision because 25% annual growth will likely outpace the mature baby segment [eval], provided the $28,000 launch is supported by the $30,000 marketing budget [eval].

knowledge_max_2: teen range taps fastest-growing segment / diversifies
baby line extends an established strength with lower risk
application_max_2: segment growing at 25% a year
70% of revenue currently tied to 0-5s
$58 average purchases
$410,000 revenue

lower risk than an untested teen offer
evaluation_max_2: weighs 25% annual growth against the mature baby segment
conditional on the $30,000 marketing budget supporting launch

scenario_stem:
Ambergate Stores Ltd is a private limited company operating 18 supermarkets in Country X. Revenue reached $34 million with $1.02 million profit, a 3% margin. After rapid growth decision-making slowed: pricing changes take 6 weeks to approve and 9% of staff left in 12 months.

It could buy 5 stores from Pellington Retail for $4.5 million, a horizontal integration adding eastern reach. Alternatively, grow organically, opening 2 stores yearly and spending $900,000 on faster stock systems.

questions.question_text: Define 'horizontal integration'.
questions.model_answer: Horizontal integration is when a business merges with or takes over another business at the same stage of the same industry, for example one supermarket buying another supermarket [2].

knowledge_max_2: merger/takeover of a business at the same stage of the same industry
e.g. a retailer buying a competing retailer

questions.question_text: Explain two problems slow decision-making causes Ambergate.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Lost competitiveness [k], because 6-week approval cycles mean Ambergate cannot react quickly to rival pricing or promotions, squeezing the already thin 3% margin [app]. Problem 2: Falling morale and rising turnover [k], because frustrated store teams wait for decisions that never come, reflected in 9% of staff leaving in the last 12 months [app].

knowledge_max_2: lost competitiveness vs faster rivals / slower reaction
low morale / high staff turnover
application_max_2: 6-week approval cycle for pricing changes
9% of staff left in 12 months / 3% margin

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Ambergate of buying the 5 Pellington stores.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Instant scale and market share [k], because the $4.5 million horizontal integration adds 5 operating stores to Ambergate's 18 for immediate reach in the eastern region [app], lifting revenue above the current $34 million [an]. Benefit 2: Economies of scale [k], as one head office, shared marketing and bulk purchasing across 23 stores would cut average costs [app], widening the 3% margin on $1.02 million profit [an].

knowledge_max_2: instant scale/market share (removes/ absorbs a competitor)
economies of scale (purchasing/marketing/managerial savings)
application_max_2: $4.5 million for 5 Pellington stores added to 18 stores
$34 million revenue / 3% margin on $1.02 million profit / 23 stores
analysis_max_2: immediate revenue growth without building stores from scratch
lower average costs from shared operations increase profit margin

questions.question_text: Do you think Ambergate should buy the 5 Pellington stores or grow organically? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Buying the stores would deliver instant growth and market share [k], because $4.5 million secures 5 trading stores and their eastern-region customers overnight, far faster than opening 2 new stores a year [app], lifting revenue beyond $34 million without delay [an]. However, organic growth avoids importing more problems [k], because integrating struggling stores onto a structure already slowed by 6-week approvals and 9% turnover risks compounding the failure before the $900,000 stock-system investment works [app], leaving the 3% margin even thinner [an]. Overall, I think Ambergate should grow organically [eval], because fixing slow decision-making first protects profits, whereas a $4.5 million takeover on top of broken processes would multiply diseconomies [eval].

knowledge_max_2: horizontal integration gives instant scale/share but carries integration risk
organic growth is slower but controlled and fixes internal problems first
application_max_2: $4.5 million for 5 Pellington stores / 18 supermarkets / 2 new stores a year
6-week approvals, 9% turnover, 3% margin, $900,000 stock systems
analysis_max_2: takeover accelerates growth and removes a failed rival quickly
internal fixes raise efficiency and margin before adding stores, reducing risk
evaluation_max_2: reasoned judgement on takeover vs organic growth, justified with stem figures

scenario_stem:
Ostler & Grey Printers Ltd is a private limited company printing wedding invitations and stationery. The income statement showed Revenue $460,000, Gross Profit $230,000 and Expenses $150,000; Profit for the year was $80,000, leaving Retained Profit of $48,000 after a $32,000 dividend.

An estate-agency chain offers a $120,000 contract at 30% gross profit, below the current 50%, with fixed Expenses unchanged. Option 2 is to keep focusing on wedding work and review prices.

questions.question_text: Define 'retained profit'.
questions.model_answer: Retained Profit is the profit kept in the business after dividends or other distributions have been paid, used to fund growth or build up reserves [2].

knowledge_max_2: Profit kept in the business after dividends are paid
Used to fund growth or build reserves

questions.question_text: Explain two ways directors can use the income statement to make decisions at Ostler & Grey Printers.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: It reveals which work earns the most, with wedding and stationery work at a 50% gross profit margin versus the contract's 30%, so directors can compare profit quality, not just Revenue [k][app]. Reason 2: It shows Retained Profit of $48,000 after the $32,000 dividend, telling directors how much could be reinvested without new finance [k][app].

knowledge_max_2: Shows profitability of different activities so better decisions can be made
Shows retained profit available for reinvestment without new finance
application_max_2: 50% gross profit margin on wedding work vs 30% on the estate-agency contract
$48,000 Retained Profit after the $32,000 dividend

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why gross profit matters more than Revenue when assessing the estate-agency contract.
questions.model_answer: Point 1: The contract adds $120,000 Revenue but only $36,000 of gross profit at 30% [k], so directors should weigh profit quality against headline Revenue rather than accept growth for its own sake [app][an]. Point 2: Current work earns $230,000 gross profit on $460,000 Revenue at 50% [k], so filling capacity with lower-margin contract work could dilute overall returns even while sales rise [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: Gross profit measures the return after direct costs, not just sales income
Profit quality matters more than headline revenue growth
application_max_2: 30% gross profit on the $120,000 contract = about $36,000
Current $230,000 gross profit on $460,000 Revenue at 50%
analysis_max_2: Revenue growth at a lower margin can weaken overall profitability
Directors should compare incremental gross profit, not just extra sales

questions.question_text: Do you think the directors should accept the estate-agency contract worth $120,000 a year at 30% gross profit (Option 1) or keep focusing on wedding work and review prices (Option 2)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option 1 uses the company's spare capacity and adds $120,000 of Revenue, about $36,000 of extra gross profit a year, with no change in fixed Expenses of $150,000 [k][app][an]. The risk is that it crowds out premium wedding orders and drags the blended margin from 50% towards 30% [app]. Option 2 protects the 50% margin and brand, and a price review could lift profit without extra workload [k][an]. Overall, the directors should accept Option 1 only if wedding bookings stay full, because the contract covers fixed Expenses and adds $36,000 of gross profit; they must cap contract volume so premium wedding work keeps priority [eval][eval].

knowledge_max_2: Contracts can absorb spare capacity and cover fixed costs
Premium positioning and price reviews can raise profit without extra volume
application_max_2: $120,000 extra Revenue at 30% gross profit = about $36,000
Fixed Expenses of $150,000 unchanged; current 50% margin vs 30%

evaluation_max_2: For Option 1: dependable volume and covers fixed costs

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Emberglaze Sauce Co is a sole trader making small-batch chilli sauce in Country X. Its 5 staff made 60,000 bottles at $6.50 each, earning $390,000; sales stayed flat until a cooking video reached 4.8 million views.

Distributors in Country N and Country R have offered to stock it in 400 shops; orders come from 30 countries via a global delivery firm. Foreign retailers pay after 60 days, copycat sauces appeared, and shipping costs $1.10 per bottle. Priya must choose exporting or domestic supermarket growth.

questions.question_text: Identify two reasons why globalisation has increased.
questions.model_answer: Improvements in transport, such as faster flights, container shipping and refrigerated delivery, allow goods to move around the world more quickly and cheaply. [1] The internet and global media, such as online video and social media, enable even very small businesses to reach customers worldwide at very low cost. [1] (Other valid answers include: removal of trade barriers; growth of multinational companies.)

knowledge_max_2: Transport improvements enabling faster/cheaper movement of goods [1]
Communication and internet/global media enabling worldwide reach [1]

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why globalisation has helped a small business like Emberglaze reach foreign customers.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Global media can give small firms worldwide exposure at almost no cost. [k] One cooking video posted by Priya was viewed 4.8 million times, creating instant global awareness of the brand. [app] Reason 2: The internet allows businesses to sell directly to customers in other countries. [k] The website now takes orders from 30 countries through a global delivery firm. [app]

knowledge_max_2: Global media/social media provide cheap worldwide exposure [1]
Internet enables direct selling across borders without foreign offices [1]
application_max_2: Cooking video posted by Emberglaze viewed 4.8 million times, creating instant global awareness
Website takes orders from 30 countries via a global delivery firm

questions.question_text: Explain two opportunities exporting creates for Emberglaze Sauce Co.
questions.model_answer: Opportunity 1: Exporting dramatically increases the potential customer base. [k] Distributors in Country N and Country R have offered to stock Emberglaze in 400 shops abroad. [app] Covering 400 shops would spread fixed costs over far more bottles and lift profits. [an] Opportunity 2: Exporting early builds a defensible brand position. [k] Copycat sauces have already appeared in foreign markets since the video went viral. [app] Establishing Emberglaze first would make it harder for imitators to capture the overseas market. [an]

knowledge_max_2: Exporting opens far larger markets / customer base [1]
Early entry builds brand position ahead of rivals [1]
application_max_2: Distributors in Country N and Country R offering stock in 400 shops
Copycat sauces already appearing in foreign markets after the viral video
analysis_max_2: 400 shops spread fixed costs over more bottles, improving margins and profit
First-mover advantage makes it harder for copycat brands to gain distribution

questions.question_text: Do you think Priya should make exporting Emberglaze's main focus? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Exporting could transform Emberglaze's growth. [k] The distributor offers would place the sauce in 400 shops across Country N and Country R, and the website already ships to 30 countries. scenario_stem:
Dallow Farm Supplies Ltd is a private limited company selling animal feed, seed and machinery to 900 farms, employing 31 staff. Revenue was $3.3 million. Its statement of financial position shows current assets of $425,000: inventories $260,000, receivables $135,000 and cash $30,000.

scenario_stem:

scenario_stem:
Peregrine Bookshop is an independent partnership with 4 staff, stocking 25,000 titles. Sales are $190,000, but revenue fell 12% as a national chain and an online retailer discount bestsellers by 25%.

The owners compare a community hub with readings and a loyalty stamp card for $3,000, against matching the 25% discount on 40 bestselling titles at $18,000. A decision is due before summer holidays.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'marketing mix'.

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why matching the 25% discount may not save Peregrine Bookshop.

Reason 2: An online retailer can sustain discounting far better than a small shop [k], so a price war Peregrine cannot afford could drag on regardless of the 12% revenue fall already seen [app].

Advantage 2: A loyalty stamp card encourages repeat custom [k], building lasting relationships with the local market rather than one-off bargain hunters [app], creating a defensible position the online retailer cannot easily copy at any discount [an].

Argument against: matching the 25% discount [k] could win back price-driven buyers quickly and stem the 12% revenue decline [app], but it costs an estimated $18,000 in lost margin and teaches customers to buy only on discount [an]. scenario_stem:
Eldertree Furniture Co is a partnership making sofas and dining sets with $700,000 sales. Customer complaints rose 35%, and 3 of every 100 sofas were returned for broken frames or loose joints, while profit margin slipped to 7%.

Two big retailers paused orders until quality improves. The partners must choose between $28,000 quality assurance—redesigning the frame-gluing process and training staff to prevent faults—and $12,000 for stronger end-of-line quality control, adding a final inspection bench and two-person repair team. scenario_stem:
Alderheath Pharmacies Ltd is a private limited company operating 8 community pharmacies. Revenue was $9.5 million. Its statement of financial position shows non-current assets of $1,250,000 and current assets of $980,000, including inventories of $620,000.

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Alderheath's board would compare debt and equity before financing the expansion.

scenario_stem:
Baltica Mart Plc is a public limited company supermarket chain with 210 stores in 9 countries, planning to enter Country X's $900 million grocery market. Country X chain Castleton Retail Co has offered a joint venture using its 25 stores and distribution depot.

The board must choose between this venture and 12 stand-alone megastores. Castleton would hold 40%, and Country X competition authorities review it. Megastores could close 40 local shops; the venture keeps 480 staff and local purchasing but halves Baltica's market share gains.

questions.question_text: Define 'ethical issue'.
questions.model_answer: A situation in which a decision involves a conflict between making profit and doing what is considered morally right [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Baltica Mart Plc of choosing the joint venture with Castleton Retail Co.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Baltica would gain immediate access to Country X [k], entering through Castleton's 25 stores and distribution depot rather than building stores from scratch [app]. Benefit 2: Baltica would protect its reputation [k], as the joint venture would keep Castleton's 480 staff and local purchasing, avoiding accusations that it forces 40 local shops to close [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Baltica Mart Plc could face if it opens the 12 stand-alone megastores.

Problem 2: Competition authorities may block or restrict the stores [k], because the plans are being reviewed by Country X competition authorities [app], so Baltica could waste money on a launch that is delayed or not allowed [an].

questions.model_answer: The megastores would let Baltica set its own prices, layouts and range [k], giving it full control of a share of Country X's $900 million grocery market [app], which could maximise long-term profit if the stores win customers quickly [an]. However, opening 12 megastores could force 40 local shops to close [k] and puts the plans under review by competition authorities [app], risking conditions, delays or a blocked launch, plus reputational damage that slows sales [an]. scenario_stem:
Ironfen Brewery is a craft brewery partnership founded by Tom and Bess Riley, employing 16 staff, brewing 9 cask ales and earning $700,000. It has a strong local following among pubs and restaurants, with orders doubling since 2023, and dreams of national distribution.

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages to Ironfen Brewery of growing internally with a bigger brewhouse.

Advantage 2: No commission is paid on sales [k], unlike the 12% per sale under the distributor deal, so they retain more of the $700,000 revenue [app].

scenario_stem:
Brackenmoor Textiles Ltd is a private limited company garment factory with 120 machinists, $5.2 million revenue. Amina, with 4 years' service, was dismissed after performance dipped on pregnancy-related sick leave, without formal warnings.

The owner calls it fair, but her union representative claims unfair dismissal: two male colleagues with similar records kept theirs. A tribunal claim risks 12 months' pay. Option one: settle for $18,000, reinstate Amina with retraining. Option two: defend, with $25,000 in legal fees.

scenario_stem:

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Fenhallow's bank would insist on a recent statement of financial position before lending more money.

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Varello Steel Plc, a Country Y steel multinational having supplied Country X for 6 years, sells 90,000 tonnes a year there for $40 million. Country X proposes a 22% tariff to protect its 3 mills with 1,150 workers.

The board must choose: absorb the tariff, cutting its margin on Country X sales by 22%, or build a $12 million mini-mill in Country X with 150 workers on wages 20% below average. The trade minister wants local investment; a decision is needed before 1 January.

questions.question_text: Define 'import tariff'.
questions.model_answer: A tax placed on goods brought into a country, which raises the price of imports and makes domestic products more competitive [2].

knowledge_max_2: a tax on goods imported from abroad

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Varello Steel Plc of building the mini-mill in Country X.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Varello would avoid the proposed tariff entirely [k], as steel made inside Country X pays no 22% import duty on $40 million of sales [app]. Benefit 2: Varello would gain secure, low-cost local production [k], with 150 workers on wages 20% below the industry average and no risk of being shut out of the market [app].

knowledge_max_2: avoiding tariffs by producing inside the market
secure market access with lower local costs
application_max_2: 22% import duty on $40 million of sales avoided
150 workers on wages 20% below the industry average

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Varello Steel Plc could face if it builds the mini-mill in Country X.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Building the mill is a large investment [k], at $12 million it commits cash that could be used elsewhere [app], so Varello faces higher financial risk if Country X steel demand falls [an]. Problem 2: Varello may be seen as a rival to local mills [k], competing against 3 mills employing 1,150 workers [app], which could provoke demands for even tougher protection or higher taxes on its new plant [an].

new foreign plants may provoke backlash from protected local firms

3 remaining Country X mills employ 1,150 workers

questions.model_answer: Absorbing the tariff keeps Varello's options open [k], requiring no $12 million outlay on a market it has served for 6 years [app], which protects short-term cash flow if Country X demand is uncertain [an]. However, the 22% tariff would cut the margin on $40 million of sales [k], costing Varello roughly $8.8 million a year [app], so profits would be heavily squeezed every year the tariff remains [an]. Overall, Varello should build the mini-mill, because avoiding about $8.8 million a year of tariff costs soon recovers the $12 million investment and secures its Country X position [eval], while creating 150 local jobs would please the trade minister and reduce political risk [eval].

evaluation_max_2: clear, justified recommendation on building the mini-mill

scenario_stem:
Finch & Marlowe Print Co is a private limited printing company established 18 years ago by Colin Marsh, employing 25 staff on offset presses. Revenue was $780,000, down from $1.1 million five years ago, as customers switch to digital marketing and online printing.

Colin can spend $200,000 on digital printing presses and a design studio to win work back within 18 months, or cut to 10 staff serving loyal clients. The $200,000 opportunity cost is forgoing a smaller, safer but shrinking business.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'opportunity cost'.
questions.model_answer: The value of the next best alternative foregone when a choice is made [2].

knowledge_max_2: value of next best alternative
foregone when a choice is made

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why established printing businesses like Finch & Marlowe might fail.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Disruptive technology, as customers switching to digital marketing and online printing leaves offset presses underused [k], reflected in revenue falling from $1.1 million to $780,000 over five years [app]. Reason 2: Failure to adapt products and services [k], such as operating with no digital printing or design studio despite 18 years in the market [app].

knowledge_max_2: disruptive technology replacing old methods
failure to adapt products/services
application_max_2: revenue fell from $1.1 million to $780,000
no digital printing or design studio despite 18 years trading

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of investing $200,000 in digital printing presses and a design studio.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Digital capability meets the demand customers now expect [k], letting Finch & Marlowe win back work from online printers and recover part of the $320,000 of revenue lost over five years [app], restoring growth [an]. Advantage 2: A design studio differentiates the firm from commodity print shops [k], bundling design with digital printing for local businesses [app], raising added value per order [an].

knowledge_max_2: meets new customer demand
differentiation from commodity competitors
application_max_2: win back work from online printers (recover part of $320,000 lost)
design studio bundled with digital printing
analysis_max_2: restores revenue growth
raises added value per order

questions.question_text: Do you think Colin should invest $200,000 in digital equipment rather than reduce the workforce to 10 staff? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Investing $200,000 in digital presses and a design studio gives Finch & Marlowe a future [k], letting it win back customers switching to digital marketing and online printing, potentially recovering the $320,000 lost over five years [app], saving most of the 25 jobs [an]. Cutting the workforce to 10 staff keeps fixed costs low and protects loyal clients [k], but locks in the decline from $1.1 million to $780,000 with no path to recovery [app], and the $200,000 opportunity cost passes with no asset gained [an]. Overall, investing is the better choice because survival requires meeting digital demand [eval], although the decision relies on the 18-month win-back forecast holding true [eval].

knowledge_max_2: investment creates a path to recovery
downsizing protects cash but locks in decline

25 to 10 staff while revenue fell from $1.1 million to $780,000
analysis_max_2: saves jobs and restores revenue growth
shrinks the firm with no recovery asset gained
evaluation_max_2: weighs investment risk against managed shrinkage; justified recommendation
conditional on the 18-month win-back forecast

scenario_stem:
Oxbrow Steel Co is a private limited company steel components factory with 88 workers and $3.8 million revenue. 7 workers suffered injuries on two ageing pressing machines, and a guard was found missing.

The health and safety authority issued a prohibition notice giving 8 weeks. Option one stops both machines to fit modern safety guards and emergency stops at $22,000 each, costing $9,000 per week in lost output. Option two keeps them running, paying $4,000 for risk assessments.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'health and safety'.
questions.model_answer: The legal duty of employers to protect the welfare of employees at work, including safe machinery, proper training, equipment and working conditions [2].

knowledge_max_2: legal duty to protect employee welfare at work
covers safe machinery, training, equipment and conditions

questions.question_text: Explain two consequences for Oxbrow Steel Co if it fails to comply with the health and safety notice.
questions.model_answer: Consequence 1: The authority can keep the machines stopped [k], halting output estimated at $9,000 per week on the two pressing machines [app]. Consequence 2: The company may face prosecution and fines [k], putting the $3.8 million annual revenue and 7 injured workers' claims at risk [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Oxbrow Steel Co of fitting modern safety guards.

Benefit 2: Compliance with the prohibition notice protects production [k], avoiding an 8-week shutdown that could cost up to $72,000 [app], safeguarding the $3.8 million revenue stream [an].

compliance avoids prohibition and fines

analysis_max_2: fewer injuries, claims and lost working days

questions.question_text: Do you think Oxbrow Steel Co should fit modern safety guards rather than rely on risk assessments alone? Justify your answer.

Argument against: risk assessments cost only $4,000 [k], satisfying the authority at its follow-up visit while the machines keep running and revenue holds near $3.8 million [app], but relying on paperwork alone leaves operators exposed to further injury and prosecution [an]. Overall, fitting the guards is the responsible and ultimately cheaper choice [eval], because it removes the root cause of the injuries and keeps the factory legally operating [eval].

scenario_stem:
Whiteoak Creamery is a partnership ice-cream maker near Tarnley. It sells through 15 local shops, employs 6 staff and took $85,000. A supermarket chain will stock it in Marisport (220,000 people) if it supplies 30,000 tubs yearly at $2.20 against a $4 direct price.

The owners compare a supermarket deal for 2 years worth $66,000 a year with the home market: a new flavour, tastings and a $4,000 loyalty card. A decision is due 31 May.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'niche market'.

questions.question_text: Explain two opportunities for Whiteoak Creamery from signing the supermarket deal.
questions.model_answer: Opportunity 1: Supplying 30,000 tubs a year would massively increase production volume [k], lifting revenue towards $66,000 a year from the 220,000-person Marisport market [app]. Opportunity 2: Listing in national supermarkets would raise national brand awareness [k], helping Whiteoak reach far beyond its 15 local shops without paying for advertising [app].

Benefit 2: Tastings and a loyalty card build relationships and repeat custom [k], deepening loyalty among existing buyers near Tarnley [app], which suits a small firm employing 6 staff that may not yet guarantee 30,000 tubs a year [an].

knowledge_max_2: direct selling keeps the full price and margin
tastings and loyalty schemes strengthen relationships and repeat purchase

questions.question_text: Do you think Whiteoak Creamery should sign the supermarket supply deal rather than focus on the home market? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Argument for: the national supermarket deal [k] offers 30,000 tubs a year at $2.20, roughly $66,000 of new revenue from a 220,000-person market [app], approaching the $85,000 earned last year through just 15 local shops [an]. Argument against: the $2.20 price halves Whiteoak's direct $4 margin [k] and commits it to 30,000 tubs a year for 2 years [app], which could strain a 6 staff team and undermine the farm-fresh quality on which the home market depends [an]. Overall, focusing on the home market first is the wiser strategy for a small creamery, because protecting margin and quality builds the brand before scaling up [eval], although the owners should revisit the supermarket offer once capacity and cash flow allow [eval].

evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation based on margin, capacity and brand risk

scenario_stem:
Poppet & Pine Toys Ltd, a private limited company making toys, employs 36 workers producing 12,000 toys monthly. New safety rules demand a 1.5 metre drop test; certified plastic at $0.85/kilo, uncertified at $0.70, saving $21,600 yearly.

Cheaper plastic cracks in 4% of drop tests versus under 1% for certified. The director must choose: switch supplier with end-of-line quality control or keep certified plastic, spending $18,000 yearly on continuous improvement teams under total quality management. A national toy retailer audit happens in 4 months.

questions.question_text: Define 'continuous improvement'.
questions.model_answer: Continuous improvement is the ongoing effort by all employees to make small, regular improvements to processes, products and quality over time [2].

knowledge_max_2: ongoing effort to make small regular improvements
involves employees and covers processes, products and quality

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Poppet & Pine Toys Ltd of involving all workers in continuous improvement.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Workers spot small faults and waste that managers miss [k], helping reduce the 4% drop-test failures of the cheaper plastic [app]. Reason 2: Involving staff raises motivation and ownership of quality [k], supporting a total quality management culture across the 36 workers [app].

employee involvement raises motivation and ownership
application_max_2: reducing 4% drop-test failures of the cheaper plastic
total quality management culture across 36 workers

questions.question_text: Explain two trade-offs between quality and cost facing Poppet & Pine Toys Ltd.

Trade-off 2: Keeping the certified plastic protects safety and reputation [k], essential under the new 1.5 metre drop test rules [app], but it raises input costs and squeezes margins [an].

higher-quality inputs protect safety and reputation

However, the cheaper supplier would save $21,600 a year [k], tempting for a business only 4 years old with 12,000 toys made monthly [app], though failures in the 4-month retailer audit could end the account [an]. Overall, Poppet & Pine should keep the certified plastic and invest $18,000 a year in continuous improvement teams, because safety and reputation outweigh $21,600 in savings [eval], provided the teams genuinely cut waste to offset the extra material cost [eval].

scenario_stem:
Wentworth Sports Ltd is a private limited company running 5 sports goods stores. Revenue was $5.6 million. Its statement of financial position shows current assets of $680,000, including inventories of $470,000 and cash of $150,000.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'retained profit'.

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Wentworth's shareholders want to see its statement of financial position.

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity

scenario_stem:
Alderley Opticians Ltd is a private limited company running 4 optician practices. Revenue was $840,000, cost of sales $504,000, gross profit $336,000 and profit $92,400, with capital employed $660,000; last year revenue $720,000, gross profit $237,600, profit $57,600, capital employed $576,000.

The owner plans to invest $150,000 in digital measuring equipment for premium lenses, or hold prices for budget-conscious customers. Rival Clearglass Opticians has a 45% gross profit margin and 17% ROCE. The bank wants latest accounts before approving a loan.

questions.question_text: Define 'gross profit margin'.
questions.model_answer: Gross profit margin is the ratio of gross profit to revenue, expressed as a percentage (gross profit / revenue x 100), showing how much of each $1 of sales remains after the cost of sales has been deducted. It indicates how efficiently a business buys or makes its goods. [2]

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Alderley Opticians' gross profit margin may have risen from 33% to 40%.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: The owner could have raised retail prices or shifted the product mix towards premium lenses, which carry higher mark-ups than standard lenses [k]. Selling more premium lenses within revenue of $840,000 (up from $720,000) supports the rise in gross profit to $336,000, a 40% margin [app]. Reason 2: The firm may have reduced its cost of sales, for example by renegotiating supplier terms or bulk-buying lens blanks more cheaply [k]. A lower cost of sales of $504,000 against higher revenue lifts gross profit from $237,600 to $336,000 and explains the improvement from 33% last year [app].

Lower cost of sales (cheaper suppliers, bulk buying, better trade terms)

questions.question_text: Explain two uses of profitability ratios for the bank when deciding whether to approve the loan.
questions.model_answer: Point 1: Return on capital employed shows how effectively profits are earned on capital, helping the bank judge whether the business can generate enough surplus to repay interest and principal [k]. Alderley's ROCE rose to 14% from 10% ($92,400 on $660,000, up from $57,600 on $576,000), supporting its application to borrow $150,000 [app]. This means the bank can see rising returns on capital rather than relying on the balance sheet alone, reducing default risk [an]. Point 2: Profit margin shows how much profit remains from each $1 of sales after expenses, indicating whether the business generates enough surplus to cover new finance costs [k]. The profit margin improved to 11% from 8% ($92,400 profit on $840,000 revenue), so the bank can expect healthy cover for loan repayments if the trend continues [app]. The bank should still compare these ratios with rival Clearglass Opticians at 17% ROCE to judge competitive risk [an].

Profit margin shows profit per $1 of revenue, indicating cover for finance costs

questions.question_text: Do you think Alderley Opticians should invest $150,000 in the digital measuring equipment? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: I believe Alderley should invest in the $150,000 digital measuring equipment. Premium lenses carry higher mark-ups, so the equipment would lift the gross profit margin above the current 40% and improve the profit margin above 11%, generating the cash to service a bank loan [k]. The firm's returns are already improving, with ROCE up from 10% on $576,000 capital employed to 14% on $660,000, which gives the bank confidence to lend and funds the investment [app]. Stronger margins would also give Alderley an advantage against Clearglass Opticians, protecting market share in premium lenses and reducing reliance on price competition [an]. However, keeping current prices would protect the budget-conscious customers who generate reliable footfall, and $150,000 is a heavy commitment when Clearglass Opticians still leads on a 45% gross profit margin and 17% ROCE [k]. If premium demand disappoints, Alderley would face higher interest costs with no guarantee of extra sales, whereas price stability preserves the volume that underpins revenue of $840,000 [app]. Although the safer option protects existing trade, it locks in the gap to the competitor and slows margin growth [an]. Overall, I recommend the investment, because the improving trend suggests premium lens demand exists and, provided the loan terms are manageable, the reward outweighs the risk of defending prices alone [eval]. The main risk is over-committing to debt, so the board should agree stage payments with the bank and track premium lens sales monthly [eval].

scenario_stem:
Ravensworth Creamery is a private limited company in Country X making mature cheddar in two maturing rooms. It exports 420,000 kilograms a year to Country W at $15 a kilogram, earning $6,300,000; the dollar has appreciated from $1.50 to $1.25 per euro.

Carla Jimenez must set export prices. Option A cuts the price to $12, so Country W buyers pay €9.60. Option B keeps $15, accepts falling orders and seeks domestic listings. It employs 38 workers and has $500,000 of bank loans due this year.

questions.question_text: Define 'appreciation'.
questions.model_answer: Appreciation is an increase in the value of one currency against other currencies, so the currency buys more of a foreign currency than it did before [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the appreciation on Ravensworth Creamery.
questions.model_answer: First, appreciation makes exports more expensive for buyers abroad [k]. At $1.25 per euro, the same $15 kilogram now costs Country W supermarkets €12 instead of €10, so they may baulk at renewing the contract or demand discounts [app]. Second, demand for exports may fall as buyers switch to cheaper locally produced cheddar [k]. The 420,000 kg Country W order book, worth $6,300,000 a year, could shrink if supermarkets delist Ravensworth in favour of domestic suppliers [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Ravensworth Creamery might face if it chooses Option A.
questions.model_answer: First, cutting the price shrinks the revenue earned on every kilogram [k]. At $12 instead of $15, Ravensworth forgoes $3 per kilogram across 420,000 kilograms, about $1,260,000 a year of lost revenue [app]. That leaves less cash to repay the $500,000 bank loans this year, raising the risk of refinancing at worse terms or missing repayments [an]. Second, a sharp price cut can provoke rival suppliers into cutting prices too [k]. Country W rivals may match the €9.60 shelf price to defend their own listings [app]. Margins then stay permanently lower across the category, so Ravensworth struggles to fund the two maturing rooms and its 38 workers even after winning orders back [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Ravensworth Creamery should cut the export price to $12 (Option A)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A cuts the price by 20% to $12 a kilogram [k]. At the new rate Country W buyers pay €9.60, below the €10 they paid before the appreciation, so the 420,000 kg order book worth $6,300,000 is far more likely to hold [app]. Keeping the Country W contract fills both maturing rooms, protects the jobs of 38 workers, and avoids the slow, risky push into delicatessens in Country X where volumes are much smaller [an]. However, Option B holds the $15 price [k]. Refusing to discount avoids forgoing $1,260,000 a year, keeping cash flow stronger for the $500,000 bank loan repayments, and it bets on higher-margin delicatessen listings instead [app]. The danger is that Country W supermarkets, now facing €12 per kilogram, delist Ravensworth altogether and leave it with idle capacity and falling sales [an]. Overall, I think Ravensworth should choose Option A [eval]. The appreciation was driven by currency markets, not by anything Ravensworth failed to do, so protecting volume and shelf space in Country W matters more than squeezing the margin per kilogram, and the price can be reviewed if the dollar weakens next season [eval].

questions.question_text: Define 'profit margin'.
questions.model_answer: Profit margin (net profit margin) expresses the profit a business makes as a percentage of its revenue, calculated as profit / revenue x 100. It shows how much profit remains from each $1 of sales after all costs, expenses and tax have been deducted. [2]

With profit rising from $39,200 on $980,000 revenue to $69,000 on $1,150,000, the margin improved from 4% to 6% [app]. With profit margin up from 4% to 6% and gross profit margin up from 24% to 30% ($345,000 of $1,150,000), the owners can see their current approach is working [app]. This evidence helps them justify continuing margin-focused decisions when agreeing supplier contracts [an]. Use 2: Profitability ratios highlight relative performance and guide future investment decisions [k]. Comparing their own 30% gross profit margin against the 35% achieved by ValueBuilt Homes shows where improvement is still possible, guiding the decision on whether to switch suppliers [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Dovetail Kitchens should switch to premium German appliance suppliers? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: I think Dovetail Kitchens should switch to premium German appliance suppliers. Premium ranges carry higher selling prices and mark-ups, which would lift the gross profit margin above the current 30% ($345,000 of $1,150,000) towards the 35% achieved by ValueBuilt Homes, improving the profit margin above 6% [k]. Improved margins would strengthen return on capital employed beyond 15% ($69,000 on $460,000), justifying the owners' plans and helping fund future growth [app]. Higher-quality kitchens can also differentiate the business from the national chain, winning customers who value design over lowest price [an]. However, the owners could instead keep the value ranges, because switching carries risks: premium stock costs more to hold, and if sales volumes fall, revenue growth could slip back from the $1,150,000 level achieved this year [k]. Keeping the value offer protects price-sensitive customers and avoids being undercut on price by ValueBuilt Homes, whose appeal is high volume at keen prices [app]. A wrong switch could dent the 6% profit margin if premium demand proves weak, whereas the current strategy already delivered an improvement from 4% [an]. Overall, I recommend the switch, but phased: trial premium lines in a small number of projects first and track gross profit margin monthly, since the upward trend and stronger ROCE suggest the premium market is reachable [eval]. The main risk is demand uncertainty, so supplier agreements should protect Dovetail against unsold premium stock [eval].

scenario_stem:
Marston Fish Smokery Ltd is a private limited company smoking salmon and mackerel. Revenue was $950,000, gross profit $304,000 and profit $76,000, with capital employed $475,000; last year revenue $880,000, gross profit $264,000 and profit $61,600 on $440,000 capital. Gross margin rose 30% to 32% and ROCE 14% to 16%.

Rival Clifftop Smokehouse reports 36% gross margin but 12% ROCE. Marston plans to borrow $180,000 for a second kiln to serve a supermarket contract, or continue small-batch artisan production for direct customers.

questions.question_text: Define 'capital employed'.
questions.model_answer: Capital employed is the total long-term funds invested in a business, usually calculated as non-current assets plus working capital (current assets minus current liabilities). It represents the capital base that generates the business's profit and is the denominator of the ROCE ratio. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Non-current assets plus working capital (current assets minus current liabilities)
Equals total assets minus current liabilities; the base that generates profit

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Marston Fish Smokery's ROCE rose from 14% to 16%.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Profit rose from $61,600 to $76,000, a proportionally larger increase than capital employed, lifting the return [k]. Return on capital employed is profit / capital employed x 100, so Marston's ROCE rose from 14% ($61,600 / $440,000) to 16% ($76,000 / $475,000) [app]. Reason 2: The gross profit margin improved from 30% to 32% ($304,000 of $950,000), showing tighter control of production costs relative to prices [k]. This extra profit flows directly into ROCE, which is calculated on the $475,000 capital employed [app].

knowledge_max_2: Profit rising faster than capital employed raises ROCE
Higher gross profit margin (cost control) raises the profit feeding ROCE
application_max_2: ROCE rose from 14% to 16%; profit $61,600 to $76,000; CE $440,000 to $475,000

questions.question_text: Explain two uses of profitability ratios for Marston's managers.
questions.model_answer: Use 1: Profitability ratios show managers how efficiently the firm converts sales into profit, guiding pricing and cost decisions [k]. Marston's profit margin rose from 7% to 8% ($76,000 on $950,000), with gross profit at 32% ($304,000 of $950,000), confirming the artisan strategy is adding value [app]. This evidence supports continuing to focus on premium direct customers rather than discounting [an]. Use 2: ROCE helps managers assess whether investments earn satisfactory returns [k]. The 16% ROCE (up from 14%) and the comparison with Clifftop Smokehouse's 12% show Marston is using its $475,000 capital more productively than its rival [app]. This supports expansion decisions, such as whether to build the second smokehouse kiln [an].

knowledge_max_2: GPM/PM track pricing and cost-control performance
ROCE assesses returns on investment decisions
application_max_2: ROCE 14% to 16% vs Clifftop Smokehouse 12%; capital employed $475,000
analysis_max_2: Confirms artisan premium strategy and supports its continuation over discounting
Strong relative ROCE supports the expansion decision on the second kiln

questions.question_text: Do you think Marston Fish Smokery should borrow $180,000 to build a second smokehouse kiln? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: I think Marston should proceed with the second smokehouse kiln. Building the kiln would let Marston serve the supermarket contract and lift revenue beyond the current $950,000, while its 16% ROCE already beats Clifftop Smokehouse's 12%, showing it uses new capital productively [k]. Profit rose to $76,000 (8% profit margin) this year, so a larger output base should raise the cash available to service loan repayments [app]. Extra capacity also diversifies Marston beyond local delicatessens and online sales, reducing reliance on its limited direct-customer base [an]. However, staying artisan keeps costs low and avoids new debt entirely [k]. Local delicatessens and online customers give predictable cash flow, and borrowing $180,000 adds repayment pressure if supermarket volumes or payment terms disappoint, squeezing the 8% margin [app]. The rival comparison is instructive: Clifftop Smokehouse earns a 36% gross profit margin at only 12% ROCE, suggesting scale alone does not guarantee strong returns on capital [an]. Overall, I recommend borrowing for the kiln, because the improving trend (margins and ROCE all rising) indicates Marston can profit from extra capacity, provided the loan is tied to the supermarket contract [eval]. The board should phase the build and monitor ROCE and profit margin quarterly so the expansion can pause if returns fall below 14% [eval].

knowledge_max_2: New capacity enables volume/revenue growth; loan funds it
Staying artisan avoids debt and protects healthy margins and cash flow
application_max_2: ROCE 16% vs Clifftop 12%; profit $76,000 (8% PM) on $950,000; GPM 32%
$180,000 loan adds repayment pressure; rival GPM 36% at only 12% ROCE
analysis_max_2: Diversification beyond direct customers reduces reliance risk
Scale alone does not guarantee returns - Clifftop evidence
evaluation_max_2: Recommendation weighs trend against debt risk; conditional on contract
Phased build with quarterly ROCE monitoring set as a safeguard

scenario_stem:
Holmfirth Surgical Instruments is a private limited company in Country X exporting bone drills to Country W hospitals. It sells 320 sets yearly at €2,400 each, worth €768,000. Rates swung between $1.20 and $1.50 per euro, moving receipts from $921,600 to $1,152,000, a $230,400 gap.

Yusuf Rahman must set next year's prices. Option A invoices in dollars at $3,000 a set, shifting risk to buyers. Option B invoices in euros at €2,400, carrying the uncertainty. The firm employs 17 machinists.

questions.question_text: Outline what is meant by 'exchange-rate fluctuation'.
questions.model_answer: Exchange-rate fluctuation is when the value of one currency against another rises and falls over time rather than staying fixed, so the price of foreign currencies changes frequently [2].

knowledge_max_2: The value of one currency against another changes over time
Rates are not fixed / they move up and down frequently

questions.question_text: Explain two problems the fluctuation creates for Holmfirth Surgical Instruments.
questions.model_answer: First, export earnings in dollars become unpredictable [k]. The 320 sets sold each year at €2,400, worth €768,000, can yield $921,600 at the low point of the range or $1,152,000 at the high point, a swing of $230,400 on identical orders [app]. Second, the firm finds budgeting and cash-flow planning difficult [k]. It cannot fix monthly dollar inflows, making it hard to schedule wages for 17 machinists or to plan equipment purchases with confidence [app].

knowledge_max_2: Fluctuations make foreign-currency earnings unpredictable
Fluctuations make budgeting and cash-flow planning difficult
application_max_2: Reference to $921,600 at the low point and $1,152,000 at the high point
Reference to the $230,400 gap / 320 sets / €768,000 a year

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of choosing Option A, to invoice in Country X dollars at $3,000 a set.
questions.model_answer: First, dollar invoicing removes the exchange-rate risk from Holmfirth entirely [k]. At $3,000 a set the firm knows it will receive about $960,000 a year for 320 sets, whatever happens between $1.20 and $1.50 [app]. Predictable receipts let it budget wages, materials and the clearing-bank account without guessing each month's conversion, cutting financial stress and borrowing costs [an]. Second, invoicing in the home currency simplifies bookkeeping and management reports [k]. All 320 export invoices are written and collected in dollars, so no conversion work or foreign-currency bank charges apply to each deal [app]. Management can compare monthly performance directly against equivalent euro figures, improving control and the speed of decision-making [an].

knowledge_max_2: Invoicing in the home currency removes exchange-rate risk for the seller
Invoicing in the home currency simplifies bookkeeping and administration
application_max_2: $3,000 x 320 sets is about $960,000 a year regardless of the rate between $1.20 and $1.50
Reference to 320 sets a year / Country X clearing bank
analysis_max_2: Chain from fixed dollar receipts to reliable budgeting to lower stress and borrowing costs
Chain from dollar invoicing to simpler administration to faster, better-informed decisions

questions.question_text: Do you think Holmfirth Surgical Instruments should invoice 2027 orders in dollars at $3,000 (Option A)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A invoices in Country X dollars at $3,000 per set, fixing annual revenue at about $960,000 for 320 sets [k]. It removes the $230,400 swing between the low and high points of the dollar-euro range, making wages for 17 machinists and loan repayments easy to plan, and it spares the firm conversion fees and extra paperwork [app]. The trade-off is that Country W hospitals face a euro price that moves with the rate — at $1.50 the price is €2,000 and at $1.20 it is €2,500 — so buyers may push back or compare rival quotes, which could cost Holmfirth orders [an]. However, Option B invoices in euros at €2,400 per set [k]. Buyers see a stable euro price, which they prefer, and it may help Holmfirth win and keep hospital contracts against rival suppliers whose quotes also move with the rate [app]. The cost is that Holmfirth carries the full currency risk itself, so a year of adverse rates could cost $230,400 of margin, out of earnings of between $921,600 and $1,152,000 [an]. Overall, I think Holmfirth should choose Option A [eval], because the swing is worth about $230,400 a year — too large to gamble on hospital loyalty, and the firm can discount individual deals if a buyer complains, whereas it cannot recover euro invoices already written; it should review the $3,000 price each quarter as the rate moves [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Option A: dollar invoicing at $3,000 fixes revenue at about $960,000
Option B: euro invoicing at €2,400 gives buyers price stability but Holmfirth carries the risk
application_max_2: Reference to $921,600–$1,152,000 range and the $230,400 gap
Reference to 320 sets / €2,400 / $3,000 / 17 machinists / Country W hospitals
analysis_max_2: Chain from dollar invoicing to revenue certainty to easier wages and loan planning
Chain from euro invoicing to buyer price stability but $230,400 of currency risk for Holmfirth
evaluation_max_2: Clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B
Weighs both options using stem figures and proposes quarterly price review

scenario_stem:
Redhill Stationery Wholesalers Ltd is a private limited company supplying schools and offices. This year revenue was $5,200,000, cost of sales $4,160,000, gross profit $1,040,000 and profit $156,000, with capital employed $1,300,000; last year revenue $4,800,000, gross profit $960,000 and profit $240,000. questions.question_text: Calculate the profit margin for Redhill Stationery Wholesalers Ltd. Show your working.
questions.model_answer: Profit margin = profit / revenue x 100 = $156,000 / $5,200,000 x 100 = 3%. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Profit $156,000 divided by revenue $5,200,000

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why profit fell from $240,000 to $156,000 despite revenue rising.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Sharp increases in warehouse energy prices and staff wages pushed up operating expenses, so more of the extra revenue was absorbed by running costs [k]. Revenue rose to $5,200,000 from $4,800,000, yet profit fell by $84,000, meaning expenses grew faster than sales [app]. Reason 2: Cost of sales stayed proportional at 80% of revenue ($4,160,000 of $5,200,000), reflecting little room to raise wholesale prices in a competitive market [k]. scenario_stem:
Brayford Marine Engines is a private limited company in Country X importing outboard motors from Country W at €3,100. It sells 240 yearly at $5,400, earning $1,296,000. The dollar fell from $1.25 to $1.50 per euro, raising the bill from $930,000 to $1,116,000, an extra $186,000.

Mark Davison must set spring prices. Option A raises them 20% to $6,480, adding $259,200. Option B holds $5,400, absorbing the $186,000 rise from the $260,000 reserve. The firm employs 9 fitters and uses 4 dealers.

questions.model_answer: First, imported motors become more expensive in local currency [k]. The 240 motors a year rise from a $930,000 to a $1,116,000 import bill, an extra $186,000 a year for the same stock [app]. Second, margins are squeezed if prices are held at $5,400 [k]. questions.question_text: Explain two problems of choosing Option A, to raise prices by 20% to $6,480.
questions.model_answer: First, a 20% price rise may drive fishing crews to rival importers or the used-motor market [k]. Moving from $5,400 to $6,480 adds $1,080 to each motor, and crews working on tight margins may simply delay replacing engines [app]. Every ten motors lost cuts $64,800 of revenue, so losing more than forty motors a year would wipe out the $259,200 gain from the rise [an]. Second, the rise may trigger retaliatory discounting across the small-engine market [k]. Brayford's nine fitters could be left with idle workshop hours if demand falls away [app]. Idle capacity spreads fixed workshop costs over fewer units, pushing up unit costs and eroding the very margin the price rise was meant to protect [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Brayford Marine Engines should raise retail prices by 20% (Option A)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A raises the retail price by 20% to $6,480, adding $1,080 per motor and about $259,200 a year at 240 motors [k]. That more than covers the extra $186,000 import cost and would rebuild the profit reserve, a strong position if the dollar falls further [app]. The margin of safety is also comfortable: Brayford can lose about forty motor sales a year, roughly one sixth of volume, before the rise loses its benefit [an]. However, Option B holds the $5,400 price and absorbs the $186,000 rise from the $260,000 profit reserve [k]. Holding prices protects goodwill with fishing crews and ferry operators who buy on reputation and aftercare, keeping the order book and workshop utilisation stable [app]. The risk is that the reserve falls to about $74,000, leaving almost no cover if the rate weakens again or if warranty claims arrive, which could force an emergency loan at painful interest [an]. Overall, I think Brayford should choose Option A [eval], because the price rise stays well ahead of the reserve cushion even after realistic customer losses, and absorbing a permanent $186,000 cost into a $74,000 reserve would be reckless; it should monitor weekly orders and soften the rise if sales collapse [eval].

scenario_stem:
Chippendale & Rose Auctioneers Ltd is a private limited company running a saleroom. questions.question_text: Calculate the return on capital employed (ROCE) for Chippendale & Rose Auctioneers Ltd. Show your working.
questions.model_answer: ROCE = profit / capital employed x 100 = $225,000 / $1,500,000 x 100 = 15%. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Profit $225,000 divided by capital employed $1,500,000

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why ROCE fell from 20% to 15% even though revenue and gross profit rose.
