Because ROCE = profit / capital employed x 100, the $475,000 extra capital dilutes the ratio to 15% despite a higher profit [app]. Reason 2: The new premises generate little immediate auction income, so in the short term they add capital without adding returns [k]. Gross profit margin actually improved to 70% ($630,000 of $900,000), so the fall reflects the timing of the investment, not weaker trading [app].

This lets partners hold management accountable for restoring ROCE before committing more capital [an]. Benefit 2: Ratios help the partners benchmark efficiency against rivals when planning strategy [k]. Bramley Auction House achieves a 72% gross profit margin and 18% ROCE, against Chippendale's 70% and 15%, showing the firm is competitive on margins but behind on capital efficiency [app]. Second, imported inputs become more expensive for the partnership [k]. The €700,000 fertiliser and tractor parts bill rises from $910,000 to $1,092,000, an extra $182,000 a year [app].

With 9,000 tonnes a year, the partnership is guaranteed $3,780,000 in each of the two years, regardless of how the rate moves [app]. Predictable inflows make it far easier to plan cash for the higher fertiliser bills and tractor-part purchases, cutting the risk of short-term borrowing [an]. Second, it removes the risk of an unfavourable move in the exchange rate against the partnership [k]. If the dollar rebounds towards $1.30, euro-quoted revenue under Option B would shrink, but Option A pays out the agreed $420 per tonne in dollars [app]. Certainty also strengthens the partnership's case for credit with suppliers and its bank, easing investment across its 2,600 hectares [an].

scenario_stem:
The Arncliffe Bay Hotel is a private limited company with 120 rooms generating $2.6 million. Carla Jensen wants to know why occupancy fell from 74% to 61% last year.

Option 1 is an online survey to 2,000 past guests, expecting 15% response (300 replies) for $300. Option 2 is observation with short interviews of 120 departing guests over 4 weeks for $1,900, but captures mostly leisure guests. Carla uses a table and bar chart.

questions.question_text: Define 'observation'.
questions.model_answer: Observation is a method of primary research in which researchers watch how people behave rather than asking them questions [1]. It records real behaviour, such as what customers choose or how they move around a business [1].

knowledge_max_2: researchers watch how people behave rather than asking questions
records real behaviour to inform decisions

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the expected 15% response rate matters.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: A low response rate shrinks the sample [k], so only about 300 of the 2,000 emailed guests may reply, which weakens the reliability of the findings [app]. Reason 2: A low response rate may bias the results [k], as only guests motivated enough to reply answer, so their views may not represent all past guests of the Arncliffe Bay Hotel [app].

knowledge_max_2: low response rate reduces the effective sample size
respondents may be unrepresentative, introducing bias
application_max_2: about 300 of 2,000 emailed guests expected to reply
Arncliffe Bay Hotel's 120 rooms and falling occupancy

questions.question_text: Explain two factors that could affect the accuracy of either option.
questions.model_answer: Factor 1: Sample size affects reliability [k], so 300 online replies give more data than 120 departing-guest interviews, though the smaller sample allows deeper questions [app], influencing how confidently the owners interpret the fall from 74% to 61% [an]. Factor 2: Who is included affects accuracy [k], as the interviews capture mainly leisure guests while the online survey hears only from past guests bothered to reply [app], so both samples are biased in different ways and neither fully represents everyone who might book [an].

knowledge_max_2: larger samples generally give more reliable findings
biased samples distort findings and do not generalise
application_max_2: 300 online replies versus 120 departing-guest interviews
interviews mostly capture leisure guests
analysis_max_2: sample size shapes confidence in interpreting the 74% to 61% fall
each option is biased differently, so neither is fully representative

questions.question_text: Do you think Carla should use the online survey instead of observing and interviewing departing guests? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The online survey is far cheaper and reaches more people [k]: 300 replies from 2,000 past guests at a cost of $300 would give a broad spread of views on why occupancy fell [app], letting the owners analyse trends across room types and seasons before the summer [an]. However, option 2's observation of departing guests shows real, immediate behaviour and detail [k], interviewing 120 leisure guests would reveal in depth why they rated the hotel as they did [app], whereas the 15% online response rate risks hearing only from already-disappointed guests and misdiagnosing the 74% to 61% drop [an]. Overall, Carla should use the online survey [eval], because 300 responses at $300 give the widest and cheapest evidence, and the owners can always commission follow-up interviews if the table and bar chart raise questions [eval].

knowledge_max_2: online surveys are cheap and reach large numbers
observation and interviews yield richer but narrower evidence
application_max_2: 300 replies expected from 2,000 past guests, costing $300
120 departing leisure guests observed over 4 weeks, costing $1,900
analysis_max_2: online breadth supports trend analysis across the whole past customer base
low response rate risks hearing only from disappointed guests
evaluation_max_2: weighs breadth and cost of online data against depth of interviews
recommendation justified with stem figures and practical follow-up

scenario_stem:
Kingsmead Family Butchers Ltd is a private limited company operating 3 butchers' shops. Revenue was $1,600,000, gross profit $560,000 and profit $48,000, with capital employed $400,000; last year revenue $1,500,000, gross profit $540,000 and profit $75,000. Wholesale meat costs rose 12% and gross margin eased from 36% to 35%.

Wellworth Supermarkets discounts meat, reporting 28% gross margin and 18% ROCE. The directors consider investing $70,000 in an in-store kitchen for higher-margin ready meals, or cutting counter prices to match it and defend footfall.

questions.question_text: Identify two stakeholders who might use profitability ratios.
questions.model_answer: Owners and shareholders use profitability ratios to judge the return on their investment, such as profit margin and ROCE. Banks and other lenders use them to assess whether Kingsmead can generate enough profit to repay loans and interest. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Owners/shareholders judge returns on their investment
Banks/lenders assess ability to repay loans and interest

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Kingsmead Family Butchers' profit margin fell from 5% to 3%.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Wholesale meat costs rose by 12%, so the cost of sales climbed faster than the prices Kingsmead could charge [k]. Gross profit margin eased to 35% ($560,000 of $1,600,000) from 36% ($540,000 of $1,500,000), squeezing the profit remaining after costs [app]. Reason 2: Nearby Wellworth Supermarkets discounts meat prices, forcing Kingsmead to keep prices competitive and limiting its ability to pass on cost increases [k]. Profit fell to $48,000 from $75,000 even though revenue grew, confirming that margins rather than demand were the problem [app].

knowledge_max_2: Input cost inflation (meat +12%) outpaces price increases
Supermarket price competition prevents passing on cost increases
application_max_2: Profit fell from $75,000 to $48,000 (PM 5% to 3%) despite revenue growth

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why comparing Kingsmead's profitability ratios with Wellworth Supermarkets is useful.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Comparison shows whether Kingsmead's weakness is sector-wide or specific to Kingsmead [k]. Wellworth achieves a 28% gross profit margin at scale, while Kingsmead matches a solid 35% locally, showing its product economics are healthy and price competition is the pressure point [app]. This directs managers towards differentiation, such as ready meals, rather than a price war [an]. Reason 2: Benchmarks help set targets and evaluate strategic options [k]. Wellworth's 18% ROCE on supermarket scale shows what disciplined volume can deliver, while Kingsmead's smaller 12% ROCE ($48,000 on $400,000) is reasonable for 3 shops [app]. Comparing ROCE helps the directors judge whether investing $70,000 in a ready-meals kitchen is realistic [an].

knowledge_max_2: Distinguishes industry-wide weakness from firm-specific problems
Benchmarks set targets and assess feasibility of strategy options
application_max_2: Wellworth 28% GPM at scale vs Kingsmead 35% locally
Wellworth 18% ROCE vs Kingsmead 12% ($48,000 on $400,000); $70,000 kitchen option
analysis_max_2: Points towards differentiation rather than a price war
Benchmark quantifies headroom for the ready-meal investment decision

questions.question_text: Do you think Kingsmead Family Butchers should invest $70,000 in the in-store kitchen? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: I think Kingsmead should invest the $70,000 in the in-store kitchen. Ready meals carry higher margins than fresh meat, so the kitchen would lift the gross profit margin above the current 35% and the profit margin above 3%, reversing the fall from 5% last year [k]. Profit fell to $48,000 from $75,000 and ROCE slipped to 12% from 15%, so a margin-rich range is what Kingsmead needs to rebuild returns [app]. Differentiated artisan ready meals also give customers a reason to choose Kingsmead over Wellworth Supermarkets on quality rather than price [an]. However, cutting counter prices to match the supermarket would defend customer numbers and protect revenue of $1,600,000 in the short term [k]. But matching a supermarket's discounting would typically force margins below 3% and risk deeper losses, since Kingsmead cannot buy meat at Wellworth's scale [app]. A price war would erode ROCE further and delay any recovery towards the 15% achieved last year [an]. Overall, I recommend the $70,000 kitchen investment, because differentiation is more sustainable than chasing prices down against a supermarket, and improved margins would strengthen both profit and ROCE [eval]. The board should pilot 6 popular ready-meal lines first and track gross profit margin weekly before scaling up [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Ready meals carry higher margins than fresh meat
Price cuts defend volume but compress margins further
application_max_2: GPM 35%, PM 3% (down from 5%); profit $48,000; ROCE 12% (down from 15%)
Wellworth 28% GPM/18% ROCE scale benchmark; revenue $1,600,000
analysis_max_2: Differentiation protects margin from a supermarket price war
Pilot approach de-risks the decision and tracks GPM before scaling
evaluation_max_2: Recommendation justified against both options with figures
Phased pilot acknowledged as risk control

scenario_stem:
Amberfell Instruments is a private limited company in Country X building laser levels for Country W construction firms. It exports 1,500 units at $380 each, worth $570,000. The dollar swung between $1.25 and $1.60 per euro, making profit hard to forecast.

Lena Kovac must invoice 2027 orders. Option A bills in dollars at $380, shifting risk to buyers. Option B bills in euros at €304: $570,000 at $1.25 or $729,600 at $1.60. The firm employs 24 specialists and buys €96,000 of lenses.

questions.question_text: Calculate the dollar revenue at $1.25 and $1.60 per euro if 1,500 units are invoiced at €304 each.

knowledge_max_2: Correct calculation at $1.25 per euro: $570,000
Correct calculation at $1.60 per euro: $729,600

questions.question_text: Explain two problems the exchange-rate swing creates for Amberfell Instruments.
questions.model_answer: First, it makes annual revenue unpredictable [k]. Invoicing in euros could yield $570,000 at $1.25 per euro or $729,600 at $1.60 per euro — a difference of $159,600 on exactly the same sales of 1,500 units [app]. Second, the firm finds costing and pricing very difficult [k]. It cannot set firm budgets for wages for 24 specialists or for imported lenses when the payout for identical orders can swing by six figures in a single year [app].

knowledge_max_2: Exchange-rate swings make revenue unpredictable
Exchange-rate swings make budgeting and pricing decisions difficult
application_max_2: Reference to $570,000 at $1.25 vs $729,600 at $1.60 per euro
Reference to the $159,600 swing / 1,500 units / 24 specialists

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of choosing Option B, to invoice in euros at €304.
questions.model_answer: First, euro invoicing appeals strongly to Country W buyers [k]. A fixed €304 per unit removes currency risk for the construction firms, so their purchasing departments can approve orders without worrying about monthly rate moves [app]. Lower buyer risk should win repeat orders against rivals who quote in volatile currencies, keeping the workshop fuller [an]. Second, if the dollar weakens further, euro invoices convert to more dollars [k]. At $1.60, 1,500 units at €304 yield $729,600 — $159,600 above the $570,000 floor — while the imported lenses at €96,000 a year also cost more dollars at the same time [app]. This partial natural offset protects margin without any special financial instruments [an].

knowledge_max_2: Invoicing in the buyer's currency removes buyer risk and can win orders
A weaker dollar raises the local-currency value of foreign earnings
application_max_2: Reference to €304 fixed unit price appealing to Country W construction firms
Reference to $729,600 at $1.60 vs $570,000 at $1.25 and €96,000 lenses rising in dollar terms
analysis_max_2: Chain from buyer price certainty to more repeat orders and fuller capacity
Chain from euro invoicing to revenue and lens costs moving together to protected margin

questions.question_text: Do you think Amberfell Instruments should invoice 2027 orders in euros at €304 (Option B)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option B invoices in euros at €304 per unit, so Country W buyers face a stable price and no currency risk [k]. That should help Amberfell win and keep contracts in a market where buyers prefer simplicity, and at $1.60 the same invoices yield $729,600, comfortably covering the €96,000 lens cost and lifting margin well above the $570,000 floor [app]. The trade-off is that if the dollar strengthens towards $1.25, Amberfell receives only $570,000 from the same orders, with zero upside if the dollar weakens further [an]. However, Option A invoices in dollars at $380, fixing Amberfell's annual revenue at $570,000 whatever happens to the rate [k]. That gives complete certainty for budgeting 24 specialists' wages and removes the $159,600 swing, but it pushes all currency risk onto buyers: at $1.60 they would pay just €237.50, while at $1.25 they pay €304, which buyers will resist [app]. The risk is losing price-sensitive orders to suppliers who quote in euros [an]. Overall, I think Amberfell should choose Option B [eval], because revenue and lens costs are both priced in euros, so euro invoicing creates a natural balance that a dollar invoice cannot match; it should monitor the rate monthly and raise the €304 price if the dollar strengthens persistently [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Option B: euro invoicing at €304 gives buyers price certainty
Option A: dollar invoicing at $380 fixes revenue but shifts risk onto buyers
application_max_2: Reference to $570,000 at $1.25 and $729,600 at $1.60 per euro
Reference to $380 dollar price / €96,000 lenses / 24 specialists / Country W buyers
analysis_max_2: Chain from euro invoicing to buyer certainty to more orders and natural offset of euro costs
Chain from dollar invoicing to fixed $570,000 but buyers resisting a swinging euro price
evaluation_max_2: Clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B
Weighs both options using stem figures and proposes monitoring the rate monthly

scenario_stem:
Talbot & Graves Solicitors Ltd is a private limited company of solicitors. Revenue was $2,500,000, gross profit $1,875,000 and profit $500,000, with capital employed $2,500,000; last year revenue $2,000,000, gross profit $1,600,000 and profit $360,000. Gross margin fell 80% to 75% after hiring 2 junior solicitors at higher salaries, while smaller premises lifted profit margin 18% to 20%.

Brereton & Co reports 82% gross margin and 25% ROCE. Partners weigh a $600,000 second office in Thelwall or $200,000 on case-management software to cut overtime.

questions.question_text: Define 'profit'.
questions.model_answer: Profit is the surplus remaining after all costs and expenses have been deducted from a business's revenue (Profit = Total Revenue minus Total Costs). It is the reward to the owners, which can be retained in the business or distributed as dividends, and it is the starting point for calculating profitability ratios. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Revenue minus all costs and expenses (Total Revenue minus Total Costs)
Surplus reward to owners; retained or distributed (dividends)

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Talbot & Graves' gross profit margin fell from 80% to 75%.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: The firm hired 2 junior solicitors at higher salaries, raising its direct fee-earner costs, so more of each $1 of fees is absorbed before overheads [k]. Direct costs rose against revenue of $2,500,000, producing gross profit of $1,875,000 (75%) versus $1,600,000 on $2,000,000 (80%) the previous year [app]. Reason 2: Increasing salaries in a fixed-fee environment means each additional instruction adds cost faster than fee income [k]. Profit still rose to $500,000, so the fall in the gross profit margin reflects cost inflation at fee-earner level rather than weaker demand [app].

knowledge_max_2: Higher direct/fee-earner salaries raise the cost of delivering fees
Cost inflation at fee-earner level outpaces fee income
application_max_2: Profit still rose to $500,000 (PM 20%) despite the margin fall

questions.question_text: Explain two uses of profitability ratios for the partners of Talbot & Graves.
questions.model_answer: Use 1: Profitability ratios help partners judge how hard each dollar of capital is working [k]. ROCE held at 20% ($500,000 on $2,500,000, the same as last year), telling partners growth so far has not diluted returns, a key test before committing $600,000 to a second office [app]. If planned investment fails to lift ROCE above 20%, it should not proceed [an]. Use 2: Comparing ratios with competitors highlights strategic gaps [k]. Brereton & Co achieves an 82% gross profit margin and a 25% ROCE, so Talbot & Graves can see its 75% GPM and 20% ROCE trail a rival, prompting action on fees or costs [app]. This benchmarking supports the choice between a second office and case-management software [an].

knowledge_max_2: ROCE measures capital efficiency; a test for new investment
Competitor benchmarking highlights strategic gaps
application_max_2: Brereton & Co 82% GPM / 25% ROCE vs Talbot 75% GPM / 20% ROCE; $600,000 second office option
analysis_max_2: ROCE threshold discipline for committing to major investment
Gap prompts fees/costs review and informs the office-vs-software choice

questions.question_text: Do you think Talbot & Graves Solicitors should open a second office in Thelwall? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: I think Talbot & Graves should not open the second office yet, and should invest in case-management software instead. A second office would capture conveyancing work in Thelwall and lift revenue beyond $2,500,000, spreading management costs over a larger client base [k]. The firm has grown profit from $360,000 to $500,000 while holding ROCE steady at 20%, so it can digest expansion investment efficiently if fees hold [app]. A local presence could also win referral work from estate agents in Thelwall, deepening the pipeline rather than relying on one town [an]. However, spending $200,000 on case-management software could cut overtime and lift the profit margin above 20% without the risk of a new office [k]. Software is cheaper, quicker and lower risk, and it reduces fee-earner hours per matter, letting the same team handle more client work [app]. Opening an office commits $600,000 to fit-out, rent, recruitment and marketing, and unproven local demand could drag ROCE below 20% while Brereton & Co leads on 25% ROCE and an 82% gross profit margin [an]. Overall, I recommend case-management software first, because it is lower-cost and addresses the direct-cost squeeze that cut the gross profit margin from 80% to 75%, strengthening margins to fund a later Thelwall office from profits rather than new debt [eval]. If software delivers the promised efficiency gains within 12 months, the board can revisit the second office with stronger evidence [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Second office lifts revenue and spreads costs over a larger client base
Software is cheaper and lower risk; cuts overtime
application_max_2: Profit $360,000 to $500,000; ROCE held at 20%; revenue $2,500,000
$600,000 office vs $200,000 software; GPM 80% to 75%; Brereton 25% ROCE / 82% GPM
analysis_max_2: Thelwall referral pipeline diversifies the client base
Fixed costs plus unproven demand risk dragging ROCE below 20%
evaluation_max_2: Software-first recommendation justified; phased revisit option set out
Both options weighed against figures; direct-cost squeeze identified as root issue

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Larkhill Brewery Co is a private limited company in Country X brewing craft ale. It exports 30% of 480,000 litres to Country W at $6 a litre: 144,000 litres, $864,000, importing €320,000 of hops; the dollar fell $1.30 to $1.56 per euro.

Sofia Almeida must set 2027 strategy. Option A expands exports: ale is €3.85 a litre to Country W, not €4.62. Option B raises domestic prices 4% on $2,016,000 of sales, gaining $80,640 against dearer hops. It employs 14 and made $290,000 profit.

questions.question_text: State two effects of a depreciation on a business that imports its raw materials.
questions.model_answer: Imports become more expensive in the local currency, so raw material costs rise [1]. Profit margins are squeezed because prices cannot always be raised to cover the higher input costs [1].

knowledge_max_2: Imports become more expensive in local currency
Profit margins are squeezed / input costs rise

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the depreciation on Larkhill Brewery Co.
questions.model_answer: First, its ale exports become cheaper for Country W buyers [k]. At $6 a litre, the 144,000 litres exported now cost buyers about €3.85 a litre instead of €4.62, making the push into Country W more competitive without cutting the dollar price [app]. Second, imported hops become more expensive for the brewery [k]. The €320,000 hop bill rises from $416,000 to $499,200 a year, an extra $83,200 of cost [app].

knowledge_max_2: A depreciation makes exports cheaper for foreign buyers
A depreciation makes imported raw materials more expensive
application_max_2: Reference to €3.85 vs €4.62 per litre / 144,000 litres / $864,000 export revenue
Reference to the €320,000 hop bill rising from $416,000 to $499,200 (extra $83,200)

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of choosing Option A, to expand exports.
questions.model_answer: First, expanding exports exploits the weaker currency immediately [k]. With ale effectively cheaper at €3.85 a litre, Larkhill can pitch to new Country W pubs and bottle shops without cutting its $6 price [app]. Winning accounts now locks in demand before rivals adjust, spreading fixed brewhouse costs over more litres and lifting profit beyond the $290,000 of last year [an]. Second, growing beyond the 30% export share reduces reliance on Country X pubs [k]. Increasing output past the 144,000 litres now shipped abroad diversifies the customer base across two countries [app]. Diversification protects revenue if domestic pub closures or duty changes hurt the home market, and export success can later support stronger negotiating positions with distributors [an].

knowledge_max_2: A weaker currency lets the business expand exports without cutting price
Export growth reduces dependence on the domestic market / diversifies risk
application_max_2: Reference to €3.85 a litre / $6 price / pitching to new Country W pubs
Reference to 30% export share / 144,000 litres / $290,000 profit last year
analysis_max_2: Chain from cheaper ale abroad to locked-in demand to fuller capacity and higher profit
Chain from diversification to protected revenue if the home market weakens

questions.question_text: Do you think Larkhill Brewery Co should expand exports (Option A)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A expands exports while ale is cheap for Country W buyers at about €3.85 a litre [k]. The existing 144,000 litres already earn $864,000, and each extra litre sold at $6 adds margin while the dollar stays weak, so expanding now is the highest-return use of the brewery's capacity [app]. Success would spread fixed costs further and could lift profit well above the $290,000 achieved last year [an]. However, Option B raises domestic pub prices by 4% on $2,016,000 of sales, gaining $80,640 [k]. That almost covers the $83,200 extra cost of imported hops, protecting margins with no overseas risk, no new working capital and no sales effort in a foreign market, and pubs usually accept modest rises more easily than large ones [app]. The danger is that 4% may still put some price-sensitive drinkers off, and it does nothing to capture the cheap-ale window or to cut dependence on the 70% domestic share [an]. Overall, I think Larkhill should choose Option A [eval], because the depreciation is temporary and only Option A converts it into lasting market position and profit growth; the brewery should keep domestic prices under review and apply Option B if export orders disappoint or the dollar rebounds [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Option A: expand exports while the ale is cheap for Country W buyers
Option B: 4% domestic price rise on $2,016,000 of sales, gaining $80,640
application_max_2: Reference to €3.85 vs €4.62 a litre / $6 price / $864,000 export revenue
Reference to $80,640 vs $83,200 extra hop cost / $290,000 profit / 144,000 litres / 70% domestic share
analysis_max_2: Chain from cheaper ale abroad to growing export volume to spread fixed costs and higher profit
Chain from 4% domestic rise to covered hop costs but lost share and untapped export opportunity
evaluation_max_2: Clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B
Weighs both options using stem figures and proposes keeping Option B under review

scenario_stem:
Northpoint Automation Ltd is a private limited company making precision components for packaging machines. It employs 28 technicians, runs 4 automated pressing lines costing $2.4 million, and reports $6.2 million revenue with $5.1 million capital employed.

A rival employs 210 workers with $1.8 million revenue. For a government manufacturing award, directors must claim leadership by employees, value of output or capital employed. They also weigh a $400,000 investment to hire 60 assembly workers against remaining highly automated.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'capital employed'.
questions.model_answer: The total value of the long-term finance invested in a business, equal to non-current assets plus working capital (current assets minus current liabilities) [2].

knowledge_max_2: total value of long-term finance invested in the business
non-current assets plus working capital (or shareholders' equity and long-term liabilities)

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the number of people employed may be a misleading measure of business size for Northpoint Automation.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: It ignores automation [k], because Northpoint's 28 technicians run 4 pressing lines costing $2.4 million yet produce $6.2 million in revenue while the rival's 210 workers produce just $1.8 million [app]. Reason 2: It ignores capital employed [k], because Northpoint has $5.1 million tied up in assets and pressing lines which the headcount never reveals [app].

knowledge_max_2: number employed ignores productivity / automation
number employed ignores capital / assets invested
application_max_2: 28 technicians run 4 automated pressing lines
$6.2 million revenue vs rival's 210 workers producing $1.8 million
$5.1 million capital employed / $2.4 million pressing lines

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of using value of sales to measure business size.
questions.model_answer: Limitation 1: Value of sales says nothing about profit or efficiency [k], because Northpoint reports revenue of $6.2 million but sales figures reveal nothing about what it keeps after costs [app], so two firms with equal sales can differ greatly in financial strength [an]. Limitation 2: It hides production and asset scale [k], because the $2.4 million of pressing lines and $5.1 million of capital employed would never appear in a sales figure [app], so a capital-intensive firm can look small beside a labour-intensive rival [an].

knowledge_max_2: sales value excludes profit / costs
sales value ignores unsold output / assets / capital employed
application_max_2: $6.2 million revenue not the same as profit
$5.1 million capital employed in pressing lines
analysis_max_2: equal-sales firms can differ greatly in financial strength
capital-intensive firms appear small beside labour-intensive rivals

questions.question_text: Do you think Northpoint Automation Ltd should invest $400,000 in hiring 60 assembly workers instead of keeping its automated operation? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Investing in 60 workers would make Northpoint appear larger by the employment measure [k], strengthening its award entry and adding labour capacity it does not currently have [app], which could win larger contracts and push revenue beyond $6.2 million [an]. However, wages would add greatly to costs and reduce productivity [k], because the business's real strength is 28 technicians running $2.4 million of automated pressing lines [app], and 60 extra staff would raise unit costs and slow automated throughput [an]. Overall, Northpoint should keep its automated operation rather than hire 60 workers for appearance [eval], because capital employed, value of output and efficiency are truer indicators of its size than raw headcount [eval].

knowledge_max_2: larger headcount improves ranking on the number-employed measure
extra staff raise wage costs / reduce automation advantage
application_max_2: $400,000 investment and 60 assembly workers
28 technicians running $2.4 million of pressing lines
$6.2 million revenue
analysis_max_2: bigger headcount may win contracts / award but dilutes productivity
wages erode the automation cost advantage and margins
evaluation_max_2: weighs employment-measure gains against automation productivity in this capital-intensive context

scenario_stem:
Alderfen Supermarkets is a private limited company with 14 branches and 4,800 people. Four regional directors each oversee 3 or 4 branches, and each branch manager supervises 5 department supervisors. A weekly written report reaches the chief executive via the regional layer.

The board proposes removing the regional director layer, delayering from six levels to five and widening the operations director's span of control from 4 to 14. Decision due before winter, when weekly sales reach $9.6 million.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'span of control'.
questions.model_answer: The number of subordinates directly supervised and answerable to one manager on a given level of the organisation [2].

knowledge_max_2: the number of employees directly supervised by one manager
can be wide (many subordinates) or narrow (few subordinates) depending on the work

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why widening the operations director's span of control from 4 to 14 might help Alderfen.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Fewer layers speed up decisions [k], because branch stock problems currently travel through a regional director before reaching the operations director, and removing that layer shortens the business from six levels to five [app]. Reason 2: A wider span cuts management costs [k], because four regional director posts would be removed, saving salary across 14 branches that already generate $9.6 million in weekly winter sales [app].

knowledge_max_2: fewer management layers mean quicker decisions and a shorter chain of command
removing a layer reduces management salary costs
application_max_2: chain shortens from six levels to five
14 branches under one operations director generating $9.6 million weekly

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Alderfen may face if it removes the regional director layer.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: The operations director may become overloaded [k], because instead of reviewing 4 regional reports she would now receive a weekly written report from each of the 14 branches [app], so urgent stock decisions could still be delayed across $9.6 million of weekly winter sales [an]. Problem 2: Branch managers lose local support and guidance [k], because regional directors currently visit the 3 or 4 branches they each oversee and understand local conditions [app], so branch-specific problems could go unnoticed until they damage branch performance [an].

knowledge_max_2: a manager supervising too many staff becomes overloaded / span too wide
removing a layer removes local support, coaching and quality checks
application_max_2: operations director would review reports from all 14 branches instead of 4 regions
regional directors currently oversee 3 or 4 branches each and know local conditions
analysis_max_2: overload slows urgent decisions and errors slip through
loss of local support lets branch problems grow before being noticed

questions.question_text: Do you think Alderfen should remove the regional director layer to create a flatter structure? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Removing the regional director layer would shorten the chain from six levels to five and cut management costs [k], since one operations director could receive the weekly written report from each of the 14 branches directly [app], so decisions on winter stock reaching $9.6 million could be faster and cheaper [an]. However, a span of 14 is very wide compared with today's 4, and the operations director may miss problems in individual branches [k], especially as regional directors currently know local conditions across the 3 or 4 branches they each visit [app], so service and stock control could slip during the busiest season [an]. Overall, Alderfen should keep the regional director layer through the winter at least [eval], because protecting branch performance across $9.6 million of weekly winter sales matters more than the salary saving from delayering [eval].

knowledge_max_2: delayering shortens the chain of command / cuts management costs
a span of 14 is too wide / risks overload and loss of local knowledge
application_max_2: from six levels to five with reports from all 14 branches
$9.6 million weekly winter sales and 3 or 4 branches per regional director
analysis_max_2: faster, cheaper decisions versus slower branch problem detection
salary savings versus protection of sales during peak season
evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation tied to peak winter trading and branch supervision

scenario_stem:
Redfield Energy Drinks is a private limited company founded by twin sisters, making a mango and lime drink sold in 1,800 convenience stores. Revenue was $3.6 million, up 8%, with 9% of the youth market.

The director has $120,000 and chooses between sponsoring the national basketball league for $100,000, or social media costing $110,000 for 18-24 year-olds. A trial raised awareness 14%.

questions.question_text: Define 'sponsorship'.
questions.model_answer: A business paying to support an event, team or individual in exchange for displaying its name or logo to a wide audience, gaining publicity and brand awareness [2].

knowledge_max_2: paying to associate the business name with an event, team or individual
gaining publicity and brand awareness from the association

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Redfield Energy Drinks of sponsoring the national basketball league rather than running social media adverts.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Sponsorship provides repeated exposure of the Redfield name [k] to 18-24 year-old basketball fans through courtside boards and team shirts across one season [app]. Benefit 2: Association with the national league gives the drink a healthy, energetic image [k] that appeals to the young buyers it must win over from two multinational rivals [app].

knowledge_max_2: sponsorship gives repeated, wide exposure to the brand name
association with an event or league builds a positive image
application_max_2: courtside boards and team shirts reaching fans across a season
winning young buyers from two multinational rivals

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why sponsorship may not increase sales for Redfield Energy Drinks.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: The $100,000 fee uses most of the $120,000 budget [k], leaving only $20,000 for everything else that drives purchase decisions [app], so awareness may rise without enough in-store support to convert it into sales [an]. Reason 2: Sponsorship reaches mainly basketball fans [k], a narrower audience than the 1,800 convenience stores across Country X [app], so many young buyers outside the sport never see the logo and buying habits do not change [an].

knowledge_max_2: sponsorship consumes most of the promotional budget
sponsorship reaches a limited, self-selected audience

basketball fans are narrower than 1,800 convenience stores nationwide

questions.question_text: Do you think Redfield Energy Drinks should sponsor the national basketball league? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The sponsorship would build positive brand awareness [k] among 18-24 year-old fans through courtside boards and shirts all season [app], helping Redfield close the gap on two multinational rivals at 9% market share [an]. However, the $110,000 social media campaign [app] would reach 18-24 year-olds precisely for six months with clicks and sales tracked directly [k], converting awareness into purchases faster [an]. Overall, Redfield should sponsor the basketball league [eval] because the 14% awareness lift shown in the trial is hard evidence rather than speculation, and an image built over a season outlasts a six-month advert run [eval].

knowledge_max_2: sponsorship builds brand awareness and positive image
social media advertising allows precise targeting and measurable results
application_max_2: courtside boards and shirts reaching 18-24 year-olds all season
$110,000 six-month social media campaign targeting 18-24 year-olds
analysis_max_2: awareness may help Redfield take share from two multinational rivals
tracked clicks and sales may convert awareness into purchases faster
evaluation_max_2: weighs trial evidence of a 14% awareness lift against social media measurability
justified recommendation to sponsor the league based on durable image and hard evidence

scenario_stem:
Kelwick Knitwear Ltd is a private limited company in Country X making school jumpers and cardigans for 9 retail chains. Its 180 machinists earn $1,150 a month, a $2.48 million wage bill. A rival in Country Y pays $420 a month.

Directors weigh a $3.2 million Country Y factory, where 180 machinists cost $907,200 a year, against upgrading 40 machines in Country X. Orders are steady at 620,000 garments a year, and two buyers demand lead times under 6 weeks.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'variable cost'.
questions.model_answer: A cost that varies directly with the level of output produced, such as raw materials or piece-rate wages [2].

knowledge_max_2: a cost that varies with the level of output
examples include raw materials or piece-rate wages

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why wage costs influence where Kelwick Knitwear locates production.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Lower wages abroad cut production costs [k], because Country Y pays $420 a month compared with $1,150 in Country X, reducing the wage bill from $2.48 million to $907,200 [app]. Reason 2: Lower labour costs free up cash [k], because the $1.58 million annual saving could fund part of the $3.2 million factory [app].

labour cost savings improve competitiveness or free cash

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Kelwick Knitwear may face if it relocates to Country Y.

Problem 2: Distance threatens delivery times [k], because two buyers insist lead times stay under 6 weeks for orders from 9 retail chains [app], so freight delays could cost Kelwick contracts [an].

scenario_stem:
Braeburn Valley Wholesale Ltd is a private limited company supplying frozen and dry goods to 14 shops. Revenue was $1.15 million and profit $92,000. Current assets are $180,000 (inventories $96,000, receivables $64,000, cash $20,000); current liabilities $120,000 (payables $72,000, overdraft $48,000).

FreshMart offers $260,000 a year but needs more stock and 45 days to pay; Karen must choose between this and supplying the 14 shops. Delta Produce gives 30-day credit.

questions.question_text: Define 'current ratio'.
questions.model_answer: Current assets divided by current liabilities; it shows whether a business can pay its short-term debts when they fall due, expressed as x:1 [2].

knowledge_max_2: current assets divided by current liabilities
shows ability to pay short-term debts, expressed as x:1

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Karen should study the acid test ratio before accepting the FreshMart contract.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: The acid test is a stricter measure of liquidity than the current ratio [k]; Braeburn's acid test is 0.7:1, that is ($180,000 - $96,000) / $120,000, well below the 1.5:1 current ratio [app]. Reason 2: The acid test ignores inventories, which can be slow to sell [k]; Braeburn holds $96,000 of inventories within $180,000 current assets, and the FreshMart deal needs still more stock plus 45 days for FreshMart to pay [app].

knowledge_max_2: acid test measures ability to pay short-term debts without relying on inventories
acid test is stricter than the current ratio, useful for judging stock-heavy businesses
application_max_2: Braeburn's acid test is 0.7:1 from ($180,000 - $96,000) / $120,000 against a 1.5:1 current ratio
inventories are $96,000 of the $180,000 current assets and FreshMart wants 45 days to pay

questions.question_text: Explain two uses of Braeburn's final accounts for its stakeholders.
questions.model_answer: Use 1: The bank can use the final accounts to judge whether to lend or renew the $48,000 overdraft [k]; with working capital of only $60,000 ($180,000 - $120,000) and an acid test of 0.7:1, the bank can see cash is tight, so it may demand security or restrict the facility [app][an]. Use 2: Delta Produce can use the final accounts to set credit terms before the FreshMart deal [k]; trade payables of $72,000 against current assets of $180,000 show how much Braeburn already owes suppliers, so Delta Produce can decide whether to keep 30-day terms or tighten them [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: banks and lenders use accounts to judge ability to repay before lending
suppliers use accounts to decide whether to offer or tighten credit terms
application_max_2: acid test of 0.7:1 and working capital of $60,000 ($180,000 - $120,000); overdraft $48,000
trade payables of $72,000 against current assets of $180,000; $1.15 million revenue
analysis_max_2: tight cash cover means the bank may restrict or secure the overdraft before renewal
suppliers may tighten credit if the FreshMart deal stretches payables further

questions.question_text: Do you think Karen should accept the FreshMart contract? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Accepting the contract could lift profit [k]. FreshMart offers $260,000 a year of extra sales and Braeburn earned $92,000 profit on $1.15 million last year, so the contract could raise revenue and profit significantly [app][an]. However, the deal would stretch an already weak liquidity position [k]; the acid test is just 0.7:1 and FreshMart wants 45 days to pay, so trade payables of $72,000 and the $48,000 overdraft could swell with the extra stock [app][an]. Overall, Karen should accept the FreshMart contract but phase the stock build-up over two quarters [eval], because the extra sales are large relative to $1.15 million revenue, provided Delta Produce keeps 30-day credit and collections stay tight [eval].

weak acid test leaves little room to fund extra stock and credit
application_max_2: $260,000 a year of extra sales against revenue of $1.15 million; profit $92,000
acid test of 0.7:1 with 45 days allowed to FreshMart, overdraft $48,000 and payables $72,000

the profit opportunity is significant relative to last year's $92,000
evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation to accept with a phased stock build-up, weighing the 0.7:1 acid test against $260,000 extra sales

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Ashvale Ceramics Ltd is a private limited company importing and wholesaling glazed wall tiles in Country X, with $3,400,000 annual revenue. Some 60% of stock, worth $400,000 yearly, comes from Country Z outside the Celestra Trade Bloc; domestic suppliers provide 40%.

The import tariff on Country Z tiles rises from 10% to 25% next quarter. Management must choose between switching to domestic suppliers or keeping imports and passing the extra $60,000 annual cost to retail customers paying $45 per box.

questions.question_text: Define 'import tariff'.
questions.model_answer: A tax placed on goods or services brought into a country, increasing their price to buyers [2].

knowledge_max_2: A tax on imports / goods brought into a country
Raises the price of the imported good / protects domestic industry

questions.question_text: Explain two impacts on Ashvale Ceramics Ltd of the tariff rising from 10% to 25%.
questions.model_answer: Impact 1: Raised import costs [k], adding about $60,000 a year to the $400,000 of Country Z stock Ashvale buys annually [app]. Impact 2: Improved price competitiveness of domestic tiles [k], allowing Ashvale to sell more of the 40% domestic stock it already handles [app].

knowledge_max_2: Tariff raises the cost/price of imports
Tariff makes domestic goods relatively more competitive
application_max_2: $400,000 of Country Z stock; the 15 percentage point rise adds about $60,000 a year

scenario_stem:
Redburn Village Stores is a family partnership running 2 convenience stores. Revenue was $1.4 million, profit $88,000. Current assets are $210,000 (inventories $150,000 of chilled lines, receivables $15,000, cash $45,000); current liabilities $105,000 (payables $85,000, overdraft $20,000). Last year assets were $180,000 (inventories $130,000), liabilities $90,000.

A new supermarket opens 10 minutes away in March. The Whitmore family must choose a third store near the railway station, costing $350,000 funded by a $250,000 loan plus $100,000 savings, or refurbish the 2 stores for $90,000.

questions.question_text: State two limitations of comparing ratios over time.
questions.model_answer: Ratios are based on historic figures, so they may not predict future performance; and comparisons over time can be distorted by inflation, changes in accounting methods or changes in the business, making the trend look better or worse than it really is [2].

questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Ratio analysis shows whether Redburn could take on a $250,000 loan [k]; revenue of $1.4 million and profit of $88,000 with working capital of $105,000 (current assets $210,000 minus current liabilities $105,000) suggest the business could service a loan but not comfortably fund $350,000 outright [app]. Reason 2: Ratio analysis reveals the trend in liquidity [k]; the current ratio has held at 2.0:1 in both years while the acid test has barely moved from 0.56:1 to about 0.57:1, signalling steady but stock-reliant trading rather than growing cash headroom [app].

Limitation 2: Historic figures ignore the new supermarket opening in March [k]; the steady 2.0:1 current ratio reflects the 2 stores trading as usual, but the third store decision depends on future footfall near the railway station, which past ratios cannot show [app][an].

scenario_stem:

scenario_stem:

scenario_stem:
Aldercombe Footwear Ltd is a private limited company manufacturing leather shoes in Country X, employing 75 workers to make 85,000 pairs a year with $5,200,000 revenue. Its best-seller retails at $65, above the $58 price of Country F rivals.

A 22% tariff now puts those imports at about $71 at the border. The tariff is temporary, reviewed after 3 years, and some ministers warn protection breeds inefficiency. Directors must choose between $1,100,000 in new lasting machines to cut costs or relying on the tariff.

questions.model_answer: Any government measure that restricts international trade, such as a tariff or quota [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of the 22% tariff for Aldercombe Footwear Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Removes price undercutting [k], as imported rivals from Country F will now retail at about $71, above Aldercombe's $65 price [app]. Benefit 2: Higher sales volumes [k], as price-sensitive shoppers shift to the domestic 85,000 pairs Aldercombe can supply with 75 workers [app].

knowledge_max_2: Tariff raises import prices so domestic goods win on price
Domestic firms gain market share / higher sales volumes
application_max_2: Country F imports now about $71 vs Aldercombe's $65

questions.model_answer: Drawback 1: Complacency risk [k], as shelter from competition may let inefficient working practices persist [app], weakening the firm before the government reviews the tariff after 3 years [an]. Drawback 2: Reduced consumer choice may shrink the market [k], as shoppers face higher prices and fewer imported styles [app], cutting total footwear demand in Country X and Aldercombe's own sales [an].

Tariffs raise consumer prices and reduce choice

questions.question_text: Do you think the 22% import tariff is likely to benefit Aldercombe Footwear Ltd in the long run? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The 22% tariff lifts Aldercombe Footwear Ltd above Country F imports, which now retail at about $71 against Aldercombe's $65 [app], lifting orders and protecting $5,200,000 revenue and 75 jobs in the short term [an]; tariffs are designed to protect domestic producers from cheaper foreign competition [k]. However, shelter can breed inefficiency, letting firms delay cutting costs [k]; the tariff is temporary, facing a review after 3 years [app], so Aldercombe could struggle if protection ends while its costs stay high [an]. Overall, the tariff will benefit Aldercombe in the long run only if it invests the $1,100,000 in new lasting machines during the 3-year protection [eval], because protection will expire and competition from Country F imports will return [eval].

evaluation_max_2: Clear overall judgement on long-term benefit

questions.question_text: Define 'cost-plus pricing'.
questions.model_answer: Cost-plus pricing sets a price by adding a fixed percentage mark-up to the cost of making a product. The business calculates unit cost first and then adds an amount meant to cover overheads and profit. Giltspur's unit cost of $18 with a 130% mark-up would give a price of $41.40.

Point one: A selling price must cover costs and leave a contribution towards fixed costs and profit [k]. Giltspur's $42 price gives $24 per pair over its $18 cost, whereas matching the rival at $35 would leave only $17 [app].

Point two: Firms should consider rivals' prices because customers can switch to cheaper substitutes [k]. The rival's cut to $35 has already reduced Giltspur's orders by 15%, so the $42 price is under pressure [app].

questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A lower price reduces the contribution each pair makes towards fixed costs and profit. At $42 Giltspur earns $24 per pair over its $18 cost, but at $35 that falls to $17 on 4,500 pairs. Profit could drop by about $31,500 a year even if the lower price wins back the 15% of lost orders.

Point 2: Matching a rival's price may start a price war that neither firm can win. The rival has already cut to $35, so matching it invites a further cut and leaves both selling below $42. Giltspur's independent shop customers may then expect permanent discounts, making future price rises difficult.

scenario_stem: Underharrow Umbrellas Ltd is a private limited company selling 8,400 folding umbrellas a year at $14. Its shop staff notice that customers open and test umbrellas but often leave without buying. The manager plans to observe 150 shoppers for two Saturdays, recording how many open a canopy and how many reach the till. This observation study would cost $420 in staff time. The manager must decide whether it will answer the real question.

questions.question_text: Define 'observation' as a method of market research.
questions.model_answer: Observation is a research method in which a researcher watches and records how customers behave without questioning them directly. It can show what shoppers actually do, although it cannot explain the reasons behind their actions. Underharrow's plan to watch 150 shoppers open canopies is observation research.

knowledge_max_2: Observation is a research method in which a researcher watches and records how customers behave without questioning them directly.
It can show what shoppers actually do, although it cannot explain the reasons behind their actions.

questions.question_text: Outline two drawbacks of using observation for Underharrow Umbrellas Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: Observation records behaviour but not the reason behind it [k]. Underharrow's staff will see how many of the 150 shoppers open a $14 canopy, but not why they leave without buying [app].

Point two: A short observation period may be unrepresentative [k]. Two Saturdays may bring unusual weather or crowds, which would distort the picture for a firm selling 8,400 umbrellas a year [app].

knowledge_max_2: Observation shows what customers do but not why.
A short observation period may not represent normal trade.
application_max_2: Watching 150 shoppers will not reveal why they leave without buying a $14 umbrella.

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why observation may help Underharrow Umbrellas Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Observation records actual behaviour rather than what customers say they do. Watching 150 shoppers shows how many really open a $14 umbrella's canopy, not how many claim they would. The company can see whether testing at the stand is followed by a purchase or by leaving the shop.

Point 2: Observation can reveal a problem at the point of sale. If many shoppers open the canopy but few reach the till, the fault may be price, display or a lack of staff help. Underharrow can then change the display or price rather than guess why 8,400 annual sales are not higher.

knowledge_max_2: Observation records actual behaviour rather than what customers say they do.

questions.question_text: Consider whether Underharrow Umbrellas Ltd should rely on observation to explain why shoppers leave without buying. Do you think the manager should use it? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:

Against: Observation cannot explain why a shopper leaves, so the firm may see the problem without finding the cause [k]. evaluation_max_2: Use observation plus a short till-side question.

scenario_stem: Vantleby Glass is a partnership blowing 720 glass vases a year, sold at $64 to florists. questions.question_text: Define 'sample'.
questions.model_answer: A sample is a small group of people selected from the whole population to take part in market research. Point 2: Bigger samples allow more detailed comparisons between groups. With 600 responses, the partners can compare colour choices by age or by market location, not just overall. That detail helps them plant the colours that sell at each market rather than one average mix.

Products are usually standardised and priced low, with heavy promotion to reach many buyers. The 12,000 toy drones at $140 would be aimed at a mass market, unlike Draycott's 900 survey drones.

questions.question_text: Outline two differences between the survey drone and toy drone markets for Draycott Drones Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: A niche market has fewer buyers but higher margins [k]. Draycott sells just 900 survey drones a year at $1,850 to construction firms, earning a 34% margin [app].

Point two: A mass market has high volume but lower margins and high entry costs [k]. The toy drone could sell 12,000 units at $140 but needs $260,000 for a new line and earns only 12% [app].

Point 2: Serving a niche requires less capital than entering a mass market. A toy line would need $260,000 for a production line, more than the company currently invests in 900 survey drones. scenario_stem: Elversham Eyewear is a partnership making 1,600 pairs of wooden-framed glasses a year, sold at $135. questions.question_text: Define 'qualitative market research'.

Point 2: Discussion can reveal unexpected issues. One buyer's comment about frame weight may prompt others to describe a problem the partners had not considered. That insight can shape the next design of the 1,600 pairs more usefully than 120 ticked boxes.

scenario_stem: Fableford Fudge is a sole trader making 2,800 boxes of sea-salted fudge a year, sold at $12. The printed tins cost $3,400 and each box uses $2 more ingredients. The owner must choose an introductory pricing approach.

questions.question_text: Define 'price skimming'.
questions.model_answer: Price skimming sets a high introductory price for a new product and lowers it later. It aims to earn high revenue from early buyers willing to pay more before competitors enter. Fableford's plan to charge $22 for the first month before falling to $16 is price skimming.

knowledge_max_2: Price skimming sets a high introductory price for a new product and lowers it later.

questions.question_text: Outline two factors Fableford Fudge should consider when setting the introductory price.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: A new price should cover the extra costs of the product [k]. Fableford's limited-edition box uses $2 more ingredients and printed tins costing $3,400, so the price must allow for these [app].

Point two: A high price can signal exclusivity for a limited edition [k]. Launching at $22 for the first month suggests a premium gift, rather than the $14 mass-market option [app].

knowledge_max_2: A new price should cover the extra costs of the product.
A high introductory price can signal quality for a limited edition.
application_max_2: Printed tins cost $3,400 and each box uses $2 more ingredients.
The $22 price applies for the first month before falling to $16.

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why price skimming may suit Fableford Fudge.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Early buyers of a limited edition may pay more because supply is scarce. A printed tin and sea-salted recipe make the $22 box different from the usual $12 fudge, so fans may buy at once. The owner recovers part of the $3,400 tin cost before the price falls to $16.

Point 2: A high price can signal quality for a small producer. Charging $22 suggests the limited edition is a premium gift, which suits buyers who want something special. That impression may support the later $16 price better than launching at $14 ever could.

analysis_max_2: The owner recovers part of the $3,400 tin cost before the price falls to $16.

questions.question_text: Consider whether Fableford Fudge should launch the limited edition at $22. Do you think the owner should do this? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Skimming at $22 earns $6 more per box than $16 and helps repay the $3,400 spent on printed tins [k]. Fableford sells 2,800 boxes of $12 fudge a year, so fans may accept a high price for a scarce limited edition [app]. A high price also signals quality for a gift product [an].

Against: At $22 the box may look expensive beside the usual $12 fudge, and buyers may wait for the price to fall to $16 [k]. The extra $2 of ingredients plus $3,400 of tins raise costs, so unsold boxes would be costly [app]. Launching at $14 might win customers faster in the first month [an].

Point 2: Influencer posts can be shared at no extra cost, so $15,000 may produce far more views than tastings and can be tracked through discount codes [an]. Codes show Silverfen which influencer brought buyers, allowing the next $15,000 to be spent where it works.

scenario_stem: Corrimore Bike Hire is a partnership with three shops that hires out 1,900 bikes a month at $18 a day to tourists. questions.question_text: Define 'mass market'.

Point two: Segment by time of day or season, such as quiet weekdays versus busy weekends [k]. This lets the partnership use idle bikes for the hotel contract without reducing tourist hires [app].

application_max_2: Tourists at $18 a day versus 500 hotel guests at $26 a day

scenario_stem: Mirevale Garden Centre is a private limited company with 1,200 loyalty-card customers. It is testing later opening hours and selected 80 customers at random from the card list; 52 said they would shop after 7pm. Extending hours would cost $2,400 a month in wages and lighting. The manager must decide whether to extend or to survey 300 customers at a cost of $1,900 first.

questions.question_text: Define 'random sampling'.
questions.model_answer: Random sampling gives every member of the population an equal chance of being selected for the sample [2]. Mirevale picked 80 customers at random from its 1,200 loyalty-card holders.

knowledge_max_2: Every member has an equal chance of selection
Sample drawn without bias from the whole population

questions.question_text: Outline two questions Mirevale Garden Centre should ask in a survey of 300 customers about later opening.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: Ask which days and times customers would actually visit after 7pm [k]. Mirevale Garden Centre has 1,200 loyalty-card customers, and 52 of 80 sampled said they would shop late [app].

Point two: Ask about likely basket size or spending to test whether sales cover $2,400 a month [k]. With $1,900 available for a wider survey, this gives the manager stronger evidence than the 65% figure alone [app].

knowledge_max_2: Surveys should ask about actual behaviour, not only intentions
Questions on spending help test whether extra costs can be covered
application_max_2: Preferred days after 7pm from 1,200 card holders, with 52 of 80 in favour
Basket value needed to cover $2,400 a month before paying $1,900

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why a random sample of 80 may give Mirevale reliable evidence.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Because every one of the 1,200 card holders had an equal chance of selection, the 80 should include busy workers, retired gardeners and families rather than only the manager's acquaintances [an]. That reduces the risk of a result that reflects one type of customer.

Point 2: A sample of 80 is large enough to show a clear majority, and 65% saying they would shop after 7pm is a margin the manager can act on without asking all 1,200 [an]. The saving in time and cost matters for a single garden centre.

knowledge_max_2: Random selection avoids choosing only convenient customers
A sample can represent a larger population at lower cost
application_max_2: 80 chosen from 1,200 card holders
52 of 80, or 65%, would shop after 7pm

questions.question_text: Consider whether Mirevale should extend its opening hours now or spend $1,900 on a survey of 300 customers first. Do you think the manager should extend the hours straight away? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: The random sample already shows 65% support, a clear majority, and extending costs $2,400 a month, which can be reviewed after one month [k]. Waiting for another survey delays a decision that could win sales from rivals who close at 6pm [app]. A four-week trial gives real takings quickly [an].

Against: Saying they would shop after 7pm is not the same as doing it, and 80 replies leave uncertainty about basket size [k]. A survey of 300 costing $1,900 could ask about spending and preferred days, making the decision safer for 1,200 card holders [app]. That reduces the risk of losing $2,400 a month [an].

Conclusion: Extend for a four-week trial rather than paying $1,900 for more opinions [eval]; real takings will show demand more reliably than another survey [eval].

evaluation_max_2: Run a four-week trial of later hours
Real takings are more reliable than another survey

scenario_stem: Dunvane Furniture is a partnership that makes sofas and sells 340 a year at $1,150 through two own showrooms. questions.question_text: Define 'distribution channel'.

questions.question_text: Outline two ways Dunvane Furniture could reduce the risk of relying on the online retailer.

Point two: Negotiate limits on discounting and review the 25% commission [k]. At 340 sofas the commission is $97,750 a year, so a lower rate or capped volume protects profit against the $140,000 showroom option [app].

Point 2: Control over how sofas are presented is also important. Own showrooms let customers sit on the sofa and meet staff, whereas an online retailer decides the photographs and may discount, weakening the $1,150 price [an].

scenario_stem: Elmhallow Interiors is a partnership that completes 45 office design projects a year at $3,200 each in Marland. scenario_stem: Dunsterly Home Bakery is a sole trader selling 620 loaves a week at $2.90 from one shop. Her regulars have bought from her for over ten years.

questions.question_text: Define 'customer loyalty'.
questions.model_answer: Customer loyalty is when customers keep buying from the same business because they are satisfied with its products or service [2]. Dunsterly's regulars have bought its loaves for over ten years despite a new rival nearby.

knowledge_max_2: Repeated buying from the same business
Based on satisfaction and trust

questions.question_text: Outline two ways a new rival could attract Dunsterly Home Bakery's customers.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: Charge a lower loaf price and advertise it prominently [k]. Dunsterly Home Bakery sells 620 loaves a week at $2.90, so a rival 300 metres away could pull price-sensitive buyers [app].

Point two: Offer greater choice or fresher products and a welcoming shop [k]. Even with ten-year regulars, a new bakery can win custom by offering something Dunsterly does not [app].

Point 1: Loyal customers do not switch on price alone, so ten years of regular buying may protect much of the 620-loaf volume even if the rival charges less [an]. That gives the owner time to respond instead of losing 93 loaves a week immediately.

Point 2: Loyal customers also recommend the shop. In a small catchment a reputation for fresh bread brings new buyers without advertising, which matters because a sole trader cannot match a rival's promotion budget [an].

application_max_2: 620 loaves a week and a rival 300 metres away

Against: A 40-cent price cut is immediate and visible to shoppers comparing the two shops, while a loyalty card may take months to change habits [k]. At $2.50 the bakery still earns a margin and keeps volume, whereas $3,600 is a fixed cost whatever sales do [app]. A rival 300 metres away may act before the card works [an].

scenario_stem: Ryehollow Bakery is a private limited company with 3,100 customers and wants to test a breakfast range. questions.question_text: Define 'quota sampling'.

questions.model_answer:
Point one: The interviewer chooses who to approach, so the sample may reflect personal preference rather than the customer base [k]. Ryehollow Bakery has 3,100 customers and wants 120 in the survey, with 30% under 35 [app].

Point two: Only customers visiting at that time are included, so busy working groups may be missed [k]. That weakens the breakfast research and makes the $2,800 agency random sample of 300 more attractive [app].

application_max_2: 120 customers from 3,100 with 30% under 35 chosen by the owner

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why quota sampling may suit Ryehollow's breakfast research.

Point 1: The quotas force the survey to include under-35s, who are only 30% of customers but may be the group most likely to buy breakfast on the way to work [an]. A simple shop survey might otherwise fill up with retired customers who have more time to talk.

Point 2: Quota sampling is cheap and quick because the owner can stand in the shop and fill each group, leaving the $2,800 agency fee for ingredients or promotion [an]. For a small bakery testing a range, speed matters more than a perfect sample frame.

questions.model_answer:
For: The quota sample is free, quick and guaranteed to include the under-35 group that matters for breakfast [k]. The owner can ask about price and portion size directly and start baking test batches within a week [app], which suits a bakery with 3,100 customers [an].

Against: Quota sampling can be biased because the interviewer chooses who to approach, and 120 customers is small against 3,100 [k]. scenario_stem: Carrowdore Cider is a partnership producing 8,400 bottles a year at $6.80, sold through farm shops. Sales have been flat and the partners have $7,500 for promotion. The partners must decide whether to cut their price to $20 or spend $4,000 on recipe cards and farm stories that emphasise local produce.

questions.question_text: Define 'market segmentation'.
questions.model_answer: Market segmentation means dividing a market into groups of customers with similar needs or characteristics [2]. Wykeham could group its 640 box customers by household size or by how much they value organic food.

knowledge_max_2: Dividing a market into groups of buyers
Groups share similar needs, incomes or tastes

questions.question_text: Outline two ways Wykeham Organics could respond to the supermarket's $18 box.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: Wykeham could cut its price from $22 to $20, narrowing the gap with the supermarket's $18 box that has already taken 9% of its customers [k]. A lower price may win back price-conscious households [app].

Point two: It could spend $4,000 on recipe cards and farm stories that stress local produce [k]. This gives shoppers a reason to choose Wykeham that a national supermarket cannot copy [app].

knowledge_max_2: Cut price to narrow the gap
Differentiate using local produce
application_max_2: $22 to $20 versus the $18 box; 9% of customers lost
$4,000 recipe cards and farm stories

questions.question_text: Explain two ways the supermarket's $18 organic box may affect Wykeham Organics.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: The $18 box undercuts Wykeham's $22 price, so price-conscious households switch and the 9% loss of customers may continue [k]. Each lost household removes $22 of weekly revenue and the partners still pay for packing and delivery to fewer doors [app]. To respond, Wykeham would have to accept a lower price or spend more on promotion, both of which thin its margin [an].

Point 2: The supermarket's national advertising may make organic boxes feel ordinary rather than special [k]. Wykeham can no longer rely on being the only organic box in town, so it must prove that its local produce and recipe support are worth $4 more [app]. If it cannot, volume falls and the fixed cost of its van and packing shed is spread over fewer boxes, raising unit cost [an].

knowledge_max_2: Rival price cuts reduce a business's sales
Competition erodes differentiation
application_max_2: $18 supermarket box against $22 Wykeham box
9% of customers switched
analysis_max_2: Forces a price response or extra promotion spending
Lower volume raises unit cost

questions.question_text: Consider whether Wykeham Organics should cut its price to $20. Do you think the partnership should cut the price? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: A cut to $20 narrows the gap with the $18 supermarket box, which may win back some of the 9% of customers who switched and keep 640 boxes moving each week [k]. Volume protects the partners' revenue while the $4,000 local-produce campaign is prepared [app]. Keeping volume spreads fixed costs [an].

Against: However, $20 still leaves a $2 gap and the supermarket can cut again because it buys at national scale [k]. Each box would earn $2 less, so 640 boxes give $1,280 less weekly revenue [app]. The business still has no clear reason for shoppers to choose it [an].

Conclusion: Overall, Wykeham should not cut to $20 [eval]. The price cut is easily matched and sacrifices revenue, whereas $4,000 on farm stories and recipe cards creates a genuine difference that supports the $22 price [eval].

Spend on local produce stories to support $22

scenario_stem: Shelbourne Eyewear Ltd is a private limited company in Marland that makes 1,800 pairs of children's glasses a year and sells them at $95. The directors want evidence before launching a new range. They can post a questionnaire to a random sample of 300 parents drawn from a list of 2,500 past customers for $2,200, or buy a national children's eyewear report for $700.

questions.question_text: Define 'primary research'.
questions.model_answer: Primary research is data collected first-hand for a specific purpose [2]. Shelbourne's questionnaire posted to 300 parents would produce new data about children's glasses.

knowledge_max_2: Data collected first-hand by the business
Collected for the specific decision being made

questions.question_text: Outline two advantages of a random sample for Shelbourne Eyewear Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: A random sample of 300 from the 2,500 past customers gives every parent an equal chance of being chosen, so the results should represent Shelbourne's buyers [k]. The $2,200 questionnaire can be tied to its own frames [app].

Point two: Random selection avoids the directors choosing only favourable parents [k]. This gives more reliable evidence for the $95 price than a general report [app].

knowledge_max_2: Random sample gives equal chance and representativeness
Random selection avoids bias
application_max_2: 300 from 2,500 past customers at $2,200
Children's glasses at $95 and the $700 national report

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages to Shelbourne Eyewear Ltd of using primary research rather than the $700 report.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Primary research can ask exactly the questions Shelbourne needs [k]. The questionnaire can show photographs of the proposed frames and ask 300 parents about the $95 price, which a national report about eyewear in general cannot do [app]. The directors therefore get evidence tied to their own design decision rather than broad industry averages [an].

Point 2: Shelbourne knows who answered and when the data was collected [k]. Because the sample is drawn from its own list of 2,500 past customers, the results reflect families who already buy its glasses and may trade up [app]. This makes the findings more current and more relevant than a report that may describe the market a year earlier [an].

knowledge_max_2: Questions can be designed for the exact decision
Data is current and owned by the business
application_max_2: 300 parents asked about the new frames and $95 price
Sample from 2,500 past customers
analysis_max_2: Evidence fits the design decision, not general trends

questions.question_text: Consider whether Shelbourne Eyewear Ltd should pay $2,200 for the questionnaire. Do you think the company should pay it? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: The questionnaire is tailored to Shelbourne's frames and $95 price, and a random sample of 300 from 2,500 customers should represent its buyers quite well [k]. Spending $2,200 gives the directors data they own and can reuse when the range is reviewed [app]. Specific evidence supports the launch [an].

Against: However, $2,200 is more than three times the $700 report, and posted questionnaires often get few replies, so 300 may become 60 [k]. The national report covers a far larger market and may reveal a fall in children's eyewear demand that Shelbourne's own customers cannot show [app]. A poor response would waste money and weeks before launch [an].

Conclusion: Overall, Shelbourne should pay the $2,200 only if it telephones non-responders to protect the sample [eval]. The specific price and design evidence is worth more than the general report, provided the response rate is managed [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Questionnaire is tailored to the new range

scenario_stem: Marrable Furnishings is a partnership in Marland that makes 340 oak tables a year and sells them at $280. Each table costs $190 to produce. The partners are adding a dining chair that costs $60 to make and are choosing between cost-plus pricing with a 40% mark-up and a competitive price of $79 charged by two local rivals. Their showroom is in one town and chairs would be displayed beside the tables.

questions.question_text: Define 'cost-plus pricing'.
questions.model_answer: Cost-plus pricing sets the price by adding a fixed percentage mark-up to the unit cost [2]. Marrable would add 40% to the $60 cost of making a chair.

knowledge_max_2: Price built from unit cost plus a mark-up

questions.question_text: Outline two factors Marrable Furnishings should consider when pricing its new chair.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: Marrable must cover the $60 cost of making each chair; a 40% mark-up gives a cost-plus price of $84 [k]. This keeps a margin on every chair sold beside the $280 tables [app].

Point two: Two local rivals sell similar chairs at $79, so buyers can compare prices directly [k]. A price much above $79 may lose the add-on sale [app].

knowledge_max_2: Cover cost plus a mark-up

application_max_2: $60 cost, 40% mark-up = $84 on 340 tables

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Marrable Furnishings might choose competitive pricing at $79 for its new chairs.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Customers can compare the chair directly with rivals' chairs at $79 [k]. Two local shops already sell at that price, so a higher figure may make Marrable look expensive beside them, even though its tables cost $280 [app]. Matching $79 keeps the new chair on the same shopping list as the rivals [an].

Point 2: A competitive price supports the chair's role as an add-on to the table [k]. Buyers who have just paid $280 for a table may buy chairs at the same time, and a price they recognise reduces the chance of losing the whole order [app]. Marrable still earns $19 on each chair at $79, which covers its selling costs and brings customers into the showroom [an].

knowledge_max_2: Buyers compare prices in a local market
