application_max_2: Rivals at $79 against a $84 cost-plus price
Tables at $280 create a bundle opportunity
analysis_max_2: Matching avoids appearing overpriced
$19 margin still contributes to overheads

questions.question_text: Consider whether Marrable Furnishings should use cost-plus pricing at $84 rather than competitive pricing at $79. Do you think the company should use $84? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Cost-plus guarantees a 40% mark-up on every chair, giving $24 above the $60 cost instead of $19 at the rival price [k]. A handmade chair sold beside $280 tables should look premium, and $84 is consistent with that quality image [app]. The higher margin supports the business [an].

Against: However, $84 is $5 above two local rivals, and chairs are easy for shoppers to compare [k]. At $79 Marrable still earns $19 a chair, and every table buyer who adds four chairs brings $76 of contribution that might otherwise go to a rival [app]. A premium price may also make customers question the $280 table [an].

Conclusion: Overall, Marrable should use the competitive $79 price [eval]. The $5 difference is highly visible, the $19 margin is still positive, and chairs are sold as an add-on to the table rather than as a stand-alone luxury [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Cost-plus guarantees a 40% mark-up
Competitors at $79 make $84 look expensive

evaluation_max_2: Use the competitive $79 price

scenario_stem: Pentire Pottery is a private limited company in Marland that produces 8,400 ceramic pieces a year and sells them at $19 each. Three gift wholesalers account for 60% of sales, and repeat orders from them fell 6% last year. With a marketing budget of $12,000, directors are choosing between a trade fair costing $7,000 and a new website with professional photography costing $11,000.

questions.question_text: Define 'marketing strategy'.
questions.model_answer: A marketing strategy is a plan for using the marketing mix to meet the needs of a target market and achieve marketing objectives [2]. Pentire's choice of how to spend $12,000 is part of that plan.

knowledge_max_2: Plan combining the elements of the marketing mix
Aims at a target market and marketing objectives

questions.question_text: Outline two benefits of a website for Pentire Pottery.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: A website gives Pentire direct contact with buyers, reducing its dependence on three wholesalers for 60% of 8,400 pieces [k]. It can show the full range at $19 itself [app].

Point two: Orders could be taken all year, unlike a one-off trade fair, and the $11,000 site leaves $1,000 of the $12,000 budget [k]. That supports ongoing promotion [app].

knowledge_max_2: Direct selling reduces wholesaler dependence
Online orders are continuous and budget remains
application_max_2: 60% of 8,400 pieces via three wholesalers; $11,000 of $12,000
$19 pieces and $1,000 left

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why relying on three gift wholesalers may be a weakness for Pentire Pottery.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: The three wholesalers buy 60% of 8,400 pieces, so each one is powerful [k]. If one cuts its order, Pentire loses a large share of sales at once, and the 6% fall in repeat orders shows this risk is already real [app]. The directors would then have to cut output or hold unsold stock, raising the cost of each piece [an].

Point 2: Selling only through wholesalers keeps Pentire away from the final customer [k]. It never learns why shoppers pay $19 or which designs sell, because the wholesaler controls that information [app]. That makes it harder to plan new ranges and leaves Pentire unable to build a brand that would attract buyers directly [an].

knowledge_max_2: Concentration of sales in few buyers

questions.question_text: Consider whether Pentire Pottery should spend $11,000 on the website and photography. Do you think the company should choose the website? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: A website gives Pentire direct contact with buyers, which reduces the 60% dependence on three wholesalers and lets it show the full range at $19 [k]. The $11,000 leaves $1,000, and online orders can be taken all year rather than only when a trade fair runs [app]. Direct selling tackles the fall in repeat orders [an].

Against: However, the trade fair costs $7,000 and puts the pottery in front of many wholesale buyers in a few days [k]. Ceramics are tactile, so buyers often want to handle a piece before ordering, and the website may attract only small retail orders [app]. Spending $11,000 leaves almost no budget for promotion, while the fair leaves $5,000 [an].

Conclusion: Overall, Pentire should choose the website [eval]. The 6% fall in wholesale repeat orders shows the current channel is weakening, and direct selling addresses that cause rather than adding more wholesale buyers [eval].

evaluation_max_2: Choose the website and photography
Direct selling addresses the 6% fall in orders

scenario_stem: Mullion Mugs is a sole trader in Marland who throws and glazes 380 mugs a month, selling them at $16 each. Tourists generate 70% of sales between May and September. questions.question_text: Define 'niche market'.

questions.question_text: Explain two ways competition from the $11 online shop may affect Mullion Mugs.
questions.model_answer:

The owner may have to hold the price and accept lower volume, or cut it and lose part of the margin on every mug [an].

Point 2: Online selling lets the rival reach customers all year, while Mullion depends on tourists for 70% of sales [k]. scenario_stem: Veryan Vinegars is a partnership in Marland that fills 5,000 bottles of fruit vinegar a year and sells them at $7.50. The partners want to test a new quince flavour. questions.question_text: Define 'quota sampling'.

Point two: Existing customers already know Veryan's vinegar and can compare quince with the $7.50 flavours [k]. Email lets the partners show the label and ask several questions at low cost [app].

Point 2: The researcher can make the 200 shoppers match the age or sex profile of typical deli customers [k]. This avoids a sample dominated by one type of shopper and gives a fairer picture than whoever happens to answer an online link [app]. scenario_stem: Colbythorne Dairy is a partnership in Marland that bottles 18,000 litres of milk a week and sells them at $1.10 a litre to local shops. questions.question_text: Define 'penetration pricing'.

Point 2: Colbythorne has 4,000 litres of spare capacity each week [k]. Low pricing can fill that space without new machinery, so the fixed cost of the dairy is spread over more litres [app]. The owner is deciding whether to supply two supermarkets at $2.45 a pie or protect quality and keep selling only to cafes. Ingredients cost $1.30 a pie.

questions.question_text: Define 'customer loyalty'.
questions.model_answer: Customer loyalty is when buyers repeatedly choose the same business or brand [2]. Porthleven's twelve cafes have stayed with the baker despite the rival's four outlets.

knowledge_max_2: Repeat purchasing from the same business
Built through satisfaction and trust

questions.question_text: Outline two ways in which supplying two supermarkets could affect Porthleven Pies.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: A new large customer can replace lost volume and fill spare capacity [k]. Two supermarkets could take far more than the 1,500 pies a week lost through an 8% order fall [app].

Point two: A lower selling price reduces margin per unit and may harm quality image [k]. At $2.45 against $3.20, a pie earns $1.15 over $1.30 ingredients instead of $1.90 [app].

knowledge_max_2: A large new customer can replace lost volume
A lower price cuts margin and may harm image
application_max_2: More than 1,500 pies a week after an 8% fall
$2.45 versus $3.20 with $1.30 ingredients

questions.question_text: Explain two ways the rival chain's four outlets may affect Porthleven Pies.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Four nearby outlets give cafe owners and shoppers an alternative supplier [k]. Porthleven's orders have already fallen 8%, which is about 120 pies a week at 1,500 [app]. Losing that volume leaves the baker with the same oven and delivery costs spread over fewer pies, raising unit cost [an].

Point 2: The chain can charge prices Porthleven cannot match because it buys ingredients in bulk [k]. Porthleven may be forced to hold its $3.20 price and accept lower sales, or cut the price and reduce the $1.90 margin on each pie [app]. Either way, the owner has less money to invest in quality or new recipes [an].

knowledge_max_2: Rival outlets take existing customers

application_max_2: 8% fall equals about 120 fewer pies a week
$3.20 price against a bulk buyer
analysis_max_2: Fixed oven and delivery costs spread over fewer pies

questions.question_text: Consider whether Porthleven Pies should supply two supermarkets at $2.45. Do you think the owner should do this rather than keep selling only to cafes? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Supermarkets can replace the 8% volume lost and may order more than 1,500 pies weekly [k]. At $2.45 with $1.30 ingredients, each pie adds $1.15, better than an idle oven [app]. Bulk orders spread the bakery's fixed costs [an].

Against: However, $2.45 gives a thinner margin than $3.20, so more pies must be sold for the same profit [k]. Supermarkets can delist a small supplier and may make the twelve cafes question quality [app]. Concentration on two big buyers replaces one risk with another [an].

Conclusion: Overall, Porthleven should supply the supermarkets while keeping the cafe range [eval]. The 8% fall shows cafes alone cannot fill capacity, and $1.15 per pie is better than unused ovens [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Supermarkets can replace the 8% lost volume

analysis_max_2: Bulk orders spread fixed costs over more pies

evaluation_max_2: Supply the two supermarkets
Keep the cafe range at $3.20

scenario_stem: Nancarrow Nursery Ltd is a private limited company in Marland that grows 14,000 garden plants a year and sells them at $9 each. It is considering opening a cafe beside its plant sales area, which has space for 40 seats. Managers can observe 400 visitors over four weekends or survey a random sample of 300 holders of its loyalty card at a cost of $1,100.

questions.question_text: Define 'observation' as a method of market research.
questions.model_answer: Observation is a research method that records what customers actually do rather than what they say [2]. Staff could count how many of the 400 visitors sit down and for how long.

knowledge_max_2: Records actual customer behaviour
Does not rely on asking questions

questions.question_text: Outline two advantages of observing 400 visitors rather than surveying 300 loyalty-card holders.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: Observation records actual behaviour rather than stated intentions [k]. Staff can count how many of the 400 visitors use the seating area beside the $9 plant sales [app].

Point two: Observation includes all visitors, not just existing card holders [k]. Casual day-trippers who may use the 40 cafe seats are missed by a loyalty-card list [app].

knowledge_max_2: Observation records actual behaviour rather than intentions
Observation includes all visitors, not just card holders
application_max_2: 400 visitors counted over four weekends
40 cafe seats beside $9 plant sales

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages for Nancarrow Nursery Ltd of observing visitors rather than surveying loyalty-card holders.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Observation records what visitors really do, not what they claim they would do [k]. Staff can count how many of the 400 visitors use the seating area or carry plants to the till [app]. That evidence is more reliable than opinions about a cafe that does not yet exist [an].

Point 2: Observation includes every visitor, not only loyalty-card holders [k]. Day-trippers and casual gardeners may be the people most likely to buy a drink, and they are invisible in a loyalty list [app]. It also avoids the cost and low response of a survey, so managers get evidence within four weekends [an].

knowledge_max_2: Shows actual behaviour rather than stated intent
Covers all visitors, not just loyal customers
application_max_2: 400 visitors over four weekends
Loyalty list misses casual gardeners
analysis_max_2: Better evidence for a cafe that does not exist yet
Fast and avoids survey non-response

questions.question_text: Consider whether Nancarrow Nursery Ltd should observe visitors. Do you think observation is better than surveying 300 loyalty-card holders? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Observation shows whether visitors linger and use the 40 seats, which decides cafe demand [k]. Counting 400 visitors over four weekends gives real behaviour at the site [app]. It costs little and can use existing staff [an].

Against: However, observation cannot show what customers would pay for a coffee [k]. The 300 loyalty-card holders visit often and would use a cafe regularly, and the $1,100 survey can ask about prices [app]. Four weekends may not represent quieter months [an].

Conclusion: Overall, Nancarrow should survey the 300 loyalty-card holders [eval]. Spend per visit decides success, and observation may miss off-season patterns [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Observation shows real use of the 40 seats
A survey can reveal what buyers would pay
application_max_2: 400 visitors counted over four weekends
300 loyalty-card holders and a $1,100 survey
analysis_max_2: Observation is cheap but gives no price evidence
Four weekends may not reflect other months
evaluation_max_2: Survey the 300 loyalty-card holders
Use observation as a supplementary check

scenario_stem: Wrenbury Toys Ltd is a private limited company in Marland that makes 48,000 wooden toys a year and sells them at $14 each through independent toy shops. Can promote the product and carry information

questions.question_text: Outline two benefits of redesigning the packaging for Wrenbury Toys Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: A window lets shoppers inspect the product before buying [k]. Parents paying $14 can see the wooden toy's finish through the window in an independent toy shop [app].

Point two: Recycled card can appeal to environmentally conscious buyers and retailers [k]. The new card adds $0.35 to each of 48,000 toys and may win more shelf space [app].

knowledge_max_2: A window lets shoppers inspect the product
Recycled card can appeal to green buyers and retailers
application_max_2: Parents paying $14 in independent toy shops
48,000 toys with $0.35 added packaging cost

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why better packaging may increase Wrenbury Toys Ltd's sales.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A window lets shoppers see the wooden toy, which matters in a shop where many boxes look alike [k]. Parents buying at $14 want to check the finish and colour before paying, and a window answers that without opening the box [app]. Better presentation can justify the price against cheaper plastic toys [an].

Point 2: Recycled card appeals to buyers who care about the environment [k]. Independent toy shops increasingly favour suppliers with less plastic, and staff are more willing to give shelf space to a range that matches their values [app]. The packaging also protects the toy in transit, reducing damage and returns [an].

questions.question_text: Consider whether Wrenbury Toys Ltd should absorb the $0.35 packaging cost. Do you think the price should stay at $14 rather than rise to $14.60? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Keeping $14 avoids persuading shops and shoppers to accept a rise [k]. The $16,800 extra cost is small against revenue from 48,000 toys at $14 [app]. Independent shops dislike repricing and may keep the range prominent [an].

Against: However, absorbing $16,800 cuts profit for a feature buyers may not value [k]. Raising to $14.60 adds $0.60, above the $0.35 cost, adding $0.25 per toy [app]. Wooden-toy buyers are less sensitive to a small rise [an].

Conclusion: Overall, Wrenbury should raise the price to $14.60 [eval]. The rise covers the packaging and protects profit on 48,000 toys [eval].

analysis_max_2: Existing shops may resist a price change

evaluation_max_2: Raise the price to $14.60

scenario_stem: Boscawen Boats Ltd is a private limited company in Marland that builds 210 sailing boats a year and sells them at $4,800 each. Includes online ordering and payment

questions.question_text: Outline two benefits of opening showrooms outside the region for Boscawen Boats Ltd.

application_max_2: A $4,800 boat with only 9% of sales outside the region

questions.model_answer:

Showrooms outside the region give distant customers somewhere to inspect a $4,800 boat, which the current local site cannot do [app]. Only 9% of sales come from outside, so there is clear room to grow [an].

Point 2: Local showrooms build trust and provide servicing and advice [k]. Buyers of sailing boats often want a nearby dealer for repairs, and a physical presence answers that concern before purchase [app]. Two new sites also put the brand in front of people who have never heard of it, unlike a website alone [an].

questions.model_answer:

Against: However, $120,000 is $35,000 more than the configurator and brings rent and staff costs [k]. A website reaches buyers beyond two towns for $85,000 [app]. If distant demand is weak, two showrooms may sit empty while the brand stays unknown [an].

scenario_stem: Harlyn Hats Ltd is a private limited company in Marland that makes 7,200 sun hats a year and sells them at $24 each, mostly at summer festivals. questions.question_text: Define 'brand image'.
questions.model_answer: Brand image is the impression customers have of a brand, built from its products, promotion and reputation [2]. Harlyn's image is of colourful hats sold at summer festivals.

knowledge_max_2: The impression a brand creates in customers' minds
Built through product, price and promotion

questions.question_text: Outline two ways in which the school contract could affect Harlyn Hats Ltd.
questions.model_answer:

Point two: A lower-priced product can weaken an established brand image [k]. Plain $15 hats under the Harlyn name may make buyers question the $24 colourful festival range [app].

A cheaper product can weaken an established image

If the supplier changes terms or moves to a cheaper maker, Harlyn loses a large share of sales at once [app]. scenario_stem: Rosevear Rugs is a partnership in Marland that weaves 480 wool rugs a year and sells them at $210 each through galleries. Each rug costs $135 in wool and labour. questions.question_text: Define 'market research'.
questions.model_answer: Market research is the collection and analysis of information about customers, rivals and markets to support marketing decisions [2]. Rosevear's choice between statistics and interviews is market research.

knowledge_max_2: Gathering information about customers and markets
Used to support marketing decisions

questions.question_text: Outline two advantages of interviewing 60 overseas gallery owners for Rosevear Rugs.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: Interviews can test a specific price and explain buyers' reasons [k]. Gallery owners can say whether they would pay $260 for the larger rug rather than $210 [app].

Point two: Direct feedback from actual buyers is more relevant than broad statistics [k]. The 60 owners are the people who would stock rugs made with $135 of wool and labour [app].

knowledge_max_2: Interviews can test a specific price and give reasons
Feedback from actual buyers is more relevant than totals
application_max_2: Owners asked about $260 rather than $210

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of using government export statistics for Rosevear's decision.
questions.model_answer:

Point 2: Government data is usually published months after collection and groups countries together [k]. By the time it appears, tastes and competitors' prices may have moved, and it cannot explain why buyers choose one rug over another [app]. Rosevear needs reasons, not totals, before committing $6,000 of materials and time [an].

Against: However, $6,000 is a large sum for a partnership selling 480 rugs at $210 [k]. Owners may say they would pay $260 without placing an order [app]. The $400 statistics cover many countries cheaply and show whether wool-rug demand is growing [an].

Its fixed costs are $154,000 a year, variable cost is $11 a unit and selling price is $25 a unit. The furnaces are hot and dangerous, and the directors are considering a $260,000 robot to lift and shape the bottles.

questions.question_text: Define 'robot'.
questions.model_answer: A robot is a programmable machine that can carry out physical tasks automatically, often replacing or assisting human workers [2]. At Colbury it would lift and shape hot bottles that are dangerous for people to handle.

knowledge_max_2: A machine that can be programmed to perform tasks
It operates automatically, often replacing human effort

questions.question_text: Outline two drawbacks for Colbury Glassworks of using a robot in its production.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: [k] A robot has a high capital cost and adds fixed costs [app] The $260,000 robot is almost four times the $70,000 profit, and maintenance adds to the $154,000 fixed costs, pushing break-even above 11,000 bottles at Colbury Glassworks.

Point two: [k] Robots are less flexible than skilled glassworkers [app] Changing bottle shape needs costly reprogramming, and a breakdown stops the line making 16,000 bottles for drinks makers.

knowledge_max_2: robots involve high capital and running costs
robots lack flexibility and can halt production
application_max_2: $260,000 robot against $70,000 profit
16,000 bottles for drinks makers at Colbury

questions.question_text: Explain two drawbacks for Colbury Glassworks of using robots in its production.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: The robot costs $260,000, which is almost four times the $70,000 profit earned at 16,000 bottles [k]. Buying it would add loan interest and maintenance to the $154,000 of fixed costs, so break-even rises above 11,000 bottles and the company needs stronger sales just to stand still [an].

Point 2: Robots are less flexible than skilled glassworkers [k]. A change in bottle shape may need expensive reprogramming, and if the robot breaks down the line stops while specialists are called; staff may also fear for their jobs, reducing morale and willingness to help the change succeed [an].

knowledge_max_2: High purchase, maintenance and interest costs
Reduced flexibility and reliance on specialists
application_max_2: $260,000 against $70,000 profit
$154,000 fixed costs and 11,000 break-even
analysis_max_2: Higher fixed costs raise break-even
Breakdowns and staff fear disrupt production

questions.question_text: Consider whether Colbury Glassworks should spend $260,000 on the robot. Do you think the board should approve it? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Safety is a strong benefit [k]. Removing workers from hot, dangerous furnaces cuts accident risk and insurance, and less breakage could save $3 a bottle, or $48,000 a year, on 16,000 bottles [app]. That helps recover the $260,000 over time [an].

Against: Payback is long and demand is seasonal [k]. Five and a half years is a long wait for a company earning $70,000, and maintenance or reprogramming could stretch it further [app]. Seasonal orders from drinks makers may leave the robot idle while the loan is repaid, and skilled staff may leave before the change is complete [an].

Conclusion: Colbury should invest only if safety rules make the change unavoidable or a grant reduces the $260,000 cost [eval]. On cost savings alone the case is weak at current output of 16,000 bottles [eval].

knowledge_max_2: robots can improve safety and reduce breakage
cost recovery is slow and demand is seasonal
application_max_2: $48,000 saving from 16,000 bottles at Colbury
$260,000 outlay against $70,000 profit
analysis_max_2: fewer accidents lower insurance and disruption
idle seasonal capacity delays cost recovery
evaluation_max_2: invest if safety rules require it or a grant helps
the cost-saving case alone is weak

chapter: 4.3 Sustainable production of goods and services
scenario_stem: Ryehill Bakery is a sole trader in Egypt that produces 85,000 loaves a year for village shops. Its fixed costs are $48,000 a year, variable cost is $1.45 a unit and selling price is $2.25 a unit. About 6,000 loaves a year are unsold, and the owner is considering a $14,000 freezer to turn this waste into breadcrumbs for sale.

questions.question_text: Define 'waste minimisation'.
questions.model_answer: Waste minimisation means reducing the amount of material, energy or finished output that is lost or thrown away during production [2]. Ryehill would do this by turning its 6,000 unsold loaves into breadcrumbs instead of binning them.

knowledge_max_2: Reducing materials, energy or output that is wasted
Fewer resources are lost in production and distribution

questions.question_text: Outline two benefits Ryehill Bakery could gain from reducing the number of unsold loaves.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: [k] Less waste saves variable cost [app] Cutting the 6,000 unsold loaves saves part of the $8,700 wasted at $1.45 a loaf, money the owner can use towards the $48,000 fixed costs at Ryehill Bakery.

Point two: [k] A responsible image supports sales [app] Selling breadcrumbs or donating loaves builds goodwill with village shops, protecting the $2.25 price and their shelf space.

knowledge_max_2: reducing waste saves materials and labour
responsible practices protect reputation and sales
application_max_2: 6,000 unsold loaves wasting $8,700
village shops paying $2.25 at Ryehill

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Ryehill Bakery of reducing the number of unsold loaves.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Every unsold loaf wastes $1.45 of flour, energy and labour [k]. Cutting the 6,000 unsold loaves saves part of the $8,700, which is money the sole trader can keep as profit or use to cover the $48,000 of fixed costs when village shop orders are quiet [an].

Point 2: Shops and villagers notice when a bakery throws food away [k]. Selling breadcrumbs or donating unsold loaves builds a responsible image that supports the $2.25 price and may persuade shops to keep shelf space for Ryehill rather than a supermarket brand, although the owner must keep records to prove the food was safe [an].

knowledge_max_2: Saves materials, energy and labour already paid for
Builds a responsible image with shops and customers
application_max_2: $8,700 wasted variable cost
6,000 loaves at $2.25 and $48,000 fixed costs
analysis_max_2: Saved cost adds directly to profit
Reputation protects shelf space and price

questions.question_text: Consider whether Ryehill Bakery should buy the $14,000 freezer. Do you think the owner should go ahead? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Waste becomes a product [k]. The freezer turns an $8,700 annual loss into saleable breadcrumbs and could repay the $14,000 in under two years [app]. It also lets the owner bake slightly ahead of demand without throwing food away, protecting supplies to village shops [an].

Against: The outlay is large and demand for crumbs is limited [k]. $14,000 is 70% of the $20,000 profit and electricity adds to the $48,000 fixed costs [app]. Not every unsold loaf can become breadcrumbs, few village buyers may want them, and a breakdown could spoil a large batch [an].

Conclusion: Ryehill should buy the freezer only after village shops and caterers agree to buy the breadcrumbs [eval]. Without buyers, the $14,000 would freeze the problem rather than solve it [eval].

knowledge_max_2: the freezer can turn waste into a saleable product
the outlay is large and crumb demand is uncertain
application_max_2: $8,700 wasted on 6,000 loaves at Ryehill
$14,000 freezer against $20,000 profit
analysis_max_2: breadcrumb sales could recover the freezer cost
limited local demand may leave the freezer unused
evaluation_max_2: buy only with committed buyers for the crumbs
without buyers it does not solve the waste problem

chapter: 4.4 Costs, scale of production and break-even analysis
scenario_stem: Stonebury Marble is a partnership in the Philippines that produces 1,320 stone worktops a year for kitchen fitters. Its fixed costs are $162,000 a year, variable cost is $620 a unit and selling price is $800 a unit. A developer offers 1,300 extra worktops at $740 each, which would need a second shift adding $70,000 to fixed costs.

questions.question_text: Define 'diseconomies of scale'.
questions.model_answer: Diseconomies of scale are the rise in average cost per unit that can happen when a business grows too large to manage efficiently [2]. Stonebury could suffer them if a second shift made supervision and coordination of 2,620 worktops harder.

knowledge_max_2: Average cost per unit rises as output grows
Caused by difficulties in managing and coordinating a larger business

questions.question_text: Outline two effects on costs of accepting the developer's order at Stonebury Marble.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: [k] A special order adds contribution towards fixed costs [app] The 1,300 worktops at $740 earn $120 each above the $620 variable cost, or $156,000, at Stonebury Marble.

Point two: [k] A second shift adds fixed and labour costs [app] The $70,000 added to the $162,000 fixed costs, plus higher pay for scarce stonemasons, can erode the $120 margin on each worktop.

knowledge_max_2: special orders generate contribution
extra shifts increase fixed and labour costs
application_max_2: 1,300 worktops at $740 and $620 at Stonebury
$70,000 second shift added to $162,000

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Stonebury Marble's average cost per worktop might rise if it doubles its output.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Managing 2,620 worktops needs more supervisors and paperwork [k]. The two partners cannot watch every cut and polish, so mistakes and rework grow, and the cost of coordinating the extra shift is spread over units that may already carry the $162,000 of fixed costs without a matching gain in efficiency [an].

Point 2: Skilled stonemasons are scarce, so a second shift may need higher pay or agency staff [k]. If the variable cost rises above $620, the $180 contribution falls, and the partnership may also pay overtime and storage costs for extra slabs, both of which push average cost up rather than down [an].

knowledge_max_2: More supervision and coordination are needed
Scarce skilled labour commands higher pay
application_max_2: 2,620 worktops and $162,000 fixed costs
$620 variable cost and $180 contribution
analysis_max_2: Coordination problems raise rework and overhead
Higher wages and storage lift average cost

questions.question_text: Consider whether Stonebury Marble should accept the developer's offer of 1,300 extra worktops at $740 each. Do you think the partners should agree? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: The gain is large [k]. At $120 contribution each, 1,300 worktops add $156,000, and after the $70,000 shift cost about $86,000 remains, more than the $75,600 profit [app]. It uses existing skills and premises to grow the business [an].

Against: The price and staffing create risk [k]. $740 is $60 below the normal $800 and may set a precedent the developer expects again [app]. Two partners stretched by a second shift may pay more than $620 for scarce stonemasons or see quality slip, threatening the 1,320 worktops sold at $800 [an].

Conclusion: Stonebury should accept if it can staff the shift at the current $620 variable cost and keep the $740 price confidential [eval]. The $86,000 gain is too large to refuse on those terms [eval].

knowledge_max_2: a special order can greatly increase contribution
a lower price and second shift create risks
application_max_2: $156,000 contribution less $70,000 at Stonebury
$740 against $800 and $75,600 profit
analysis_max_2: the remaining gain exceeds current profit
scarce labour or falling quality could damage existing sales
evaluation_max_2: accept if staffing holds at $620 and the price is confidential
the $86,000 gain justifies it under those conditions

scenario_stem: Fennick Audio is a private limited company in Ecuador that produces 7,200 speakers a year for music venues. Its fixed costs are $140,000 a year, variable cost is $37 a unit and selling price is $65 a unit. About 288 speakers a year are rejected at final inspection, and the directors are considering $60,000 of automatic testing equipment.

questions.question_text: Define 'quality assurance'.
questions.model_answer: Quality assurance is a system that builds quality into every stage of production so that faults are prevented, rather than relying on checking finished items [2]. Fennick would set standards for each assembly step instead of rejecting speakers only at final inspection.

knowledge_max_2: Quality is built into each stage of production
The aim is to prevent faults before the finished item is checked

questions.question_text: Outline two ways poor quality could affect Fennick Audio.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: [k] Faulty products lose customers and reputation [app] A speaker that fails during a performance may push music venues to stop buying the 7,200 speakers at $65 from Fennick Audio.

Point two: [k] Rejects waste materials and add replacement cost [app] The 288 speakers rejected at final inspection waste $10,656 at $37 each and may need free delivery, weakening the $65 price.

knowledge_max_2: poor quality loses customers and reputation
rejects waste materials and add replacement cost
application_max_2: music venues buying 7,200 speakers at Fennick
288 rejects costing $10,656

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why poor quality could damage Fennick Audio.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Music venues depend on sound equipment working during performances [k]. A speaker that fails may force a venue to cancel or borrow replacements, so it will stop buying from Fennick; losing even a few venues would cut sales below 7,200 units and leave the $140,000 of fixed costs spread over fewer speakers [an].

Point 2: Replacing faulty speakers costs $37 of variable cost each and may also require free delivery and fitting [k]. The 288 rejects already waste $10,656, and repeated complaints can damage the company's reputation, making it harder to charge the $65 price against rival brands that venues trust [an].

knowledge_max_2: Customers lose confidence when equipment fails
Replacement and reputational costs rise
application_max_2: 288 rejects and $10,656 wasted
7,200 units, $65 price and $140,000 fixed costs

questions.question_text: Consider whether Fennick Audio should spend $60,000 on automatic testing equipment. Do you think the directors should invest? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Testing protects customers [k]. It catches faults that manual inspection misses and gives recorded evidence of quality, helping keep contracts and the $65 price [app]. Fewer failures during performances protect the 7,200-speaker trade with music venues [an].

Against: The cost is almost all the profit [k]. $60,000 is nearly the $61,600 profit and would add maintenance to the $140,000 of fixed costs [app]. Testing finds rather than prevents faults, so the 288 rejects may continue when a 4% fault rate could be attacked more cheaply by improving one assembly step [an].

Conclusion: Fennick should not spend $60,000 yet; it should first identify why the 288 speakers fail and fix that cause [eval]. Testing equipment can wait until output and profits are larger [eval].

the equipment cost is very high relative to profit

scenario_stem: Oakhurst Cider is a partnership in Bangladesh that produces 25,000 cases of cider a year for pubs. questions.question_text: Define 'just-in-time production'.

Point two: [k] Less handling reduces breakage and stale stock [app] Fresher bottles support the $9.20 price with pubs, though the partners become dependent on suppliers delivering on the agreed day.

chapter: 4.4 Costs, scale of production and break-even analysis
scenario_stem: Skerryford Nets is a sole trader in India that produces 6,000 fishing nets a year for boat owners. Its fixed costs are $92,400 a year, variable cost is $31 a unit and selling price is $53 a unit. The owner pays a courier $9,000 a year and is considering a $40,000 van to make deliveries instead.

questions.question_text: Define 'fixed cost'.
questions.model_answer: A fixed cost is a cost that does not change with the level of output in the short run, such as rent or insurance [2]. Skerryford's $92,400 of fixed costs must be paid whether 6,000 nets or fewer are made.

knowledge_max_2: A cost that does not vary with output
It must be paid even when output is zero

questions.question_text: Outline two factors the owner of Skerryford Nets should consider before buying a van.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: [k] Compare the purchase cost with current delivery spending [app] The $40,000 van replaces a $9,000 courier, so on that figure alone recovery takes about four and a half years at Skerryford Nets.

Point two: [k] Running costs and reliability matter [app] Insurance, fuel and servicing add costs the courier price already covers, and a breakdown could stop deliveries of the 6,000 nets to boat owners.

knowledge_max_2: compare purchase cost with existing delivery spending
allow for running costs and reliability
application_max_2: $40,000 van versus $9,000 courier at Skerryford
6,000 nets delivered to boat owners

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Skerryford Nets' fixed cost per net falls as output rises.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: The $92,400 of fixed costs is shared across more nets [k]. At 6,000 nets the fixed cost is $15.40 a net, but at 8,000 it falls to $11.55, so the owner keeps more of the $22 contribution on each extra net even though total fixed costs have not changed [an].

Point 2: The workshop, tools and insurance are already paid for, so extra nets use capacity that would otherwise be idle [k]. Rising output therefore lowers average total cost and makes the $53 price more profitable, but only until the workshop becomes crowded and the owner must rent more space or work longer hours [an].

knowledge_max_2: Fixed costs are spread over more units
Existing capacity is used more fully
application_max_2: $22 contribution per net
analysis_max_2: Average fixed cost falls as output grows
Gains stop when capacity is exhausted

questions.question_text: Consider whether Skerryford Nets should buy the $40,000 van instead of using the courier. Do you think the owner should go ahead? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: The van could save money and improve service [k]. Replacing the $9,000 courier could pay back the $40,000 in about four and a half years if running costs were ignored [app]. The owner could deliver at short notice and carry extra nets to boat owners [an].

Against: Running costs eat the saving [k]. Insurance, servicing, fuel and depreciation are included in the courier price, so real recovery could stretch past six years [app]. $40,000 is a large sum for a sole trader and a breakdown would leave customers without their 6,000 nets [an].

Conclusion: Skerryford should keep the courier unless the van can win enough extra deliveries to cover its running costs [eval]. On the $9,000 saving alone, the four-and-a-half-year wait is not attractive [eval].

scenario_stem: Hollowdean Candles is a partnership in Tunisia that produces 18,500 scented candles a year for gift shops. Its fixed costs are $65,000 a year, variable cost is $7 a unit and selling price is $12 a unit. About 925 candles a year are returned cracked, and the partners are considering $16,000 of training in pouring and cooling techniques.

questions.question_text: Define 'quality'.
questions.model_answer: Quality means how well a product meets the standards and expectations that customers have for it [2]. For Hollowdean, a quality candle should burn evenly, look attractive and arrive without cracks.

knowledge_max_2: How well a product meets customer expectations

questions.model_answer:
Point one: [k] Better technique can prevent cracks at source [app] Training should cut the 925 candles returned cracked, which waste $6,475 at $7 each at Hollowdean Candles.

Point two: [k] Fewer returns protect the brand [app] Gift shops judging a supplier by returned goods are more likely to keep the $12 price and shelf space for reliable candles.

knowledge_max_2: training can remove the cause of defects
fewer returns protect reputation and sales
application_max_2: 925 cracked candles costing $6,475
gift shops paying $12 at Hollowdean

questions.question_text: Explain two ways poor-quality candles could affect Hollowdean Candles.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Each cracked candle wastes $7 of wax, wick and labour and must be replaced [k]. The 925 returns already cost $6,475, and replacements use capacity that could make saleable candles, so the partnership loses twice and the $65,000 of fixed costs is spread over fewer sound units [an].

Point 2: Gift shops judge a supplier by what customers bring back [k]. Repeated cracks damage Hollowdean's reputation, so shops may reduce shelf space or demand a lower price than $12; because gifts are bought on appearance and trust, a rival with reliable packaging could take the order [an].

knowledge_max_2: Materials and labour are wasted on faulty units

questions.question_text: Consider whether Hollowdean Candles should spend $16,000 on staff training. Do you think the partners should agree? Justify your answer.

For: Training attacks the cause of defects [k]. Pouring and cooling techniques should reduce the 925 cracked returns, saving much of the $6,475 and protecting the reputation with gift shops [app]. Better skills may also raise output of the 18,500 candles [an].

Against: The cost is high and the cause is uncertain [k]. $16,000 is 58% of the $27,500 profit and cannot guarantee control of wax and workshop temperature [app]. A cheaper thermometer or cooling adjustment might fix the problem, and trained staff may leave for other work [an].

Conclusion: Hollowdean should spend on training only after identifying why the candles crack [eval]. If temperature control is the cause, a cheaper fix is better than a $16,000 course [eval].

scenario_stem: Marrowbrook Jam is a private limited company in Bulgaria that produces 72,000 jars of jam a year for delicatessens. Its fixed costs are $55,000 a year, variable cost is $1.90 a unit and selling price is $3 a unit. A unit beside an orchard would cost $8,000 more rent but save $11,000 in fruit transport, and the directors are deciding whether to move.

questions.question_text: Define 'external economies of scale'.
questions.model_answer: External economies of scale are cost savings that come from the business being located near other firms in the same industry, such as shared suppliers or skilled labour [2]. A food-processing area near the orchard might offer Marrowbrook shared cold storage and experienced staff.

knowledge_max_2: Cost savings arising from the location of the business
Nearby firms provide shared suppliers, skills or infrastructure

questions.question_text: Outline two factors Marrowbrook Jam should consider before moving to the orchard site.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: [k] Transport and rent determine total cost [app] Saving $11,000 in fruit transport but paying $8,000 more rent gives a net $3,000 gain on the 72,000 jars made at Marrowbrook Jam.

Point two: [k] Distance to customers affects delivery and freshness [app] Being nearer fruit means longer journeys to delicatessens, which may raise delivery costs and risk the $1.10 contribution on each jar.

knowledge_max_2: compare transport savings with extra rent
distance to market affects delivery cost and service
application_max_2: $11,000 transport saving and $8,000 rent at Marrowbrook
72,000 jars sold to delicatessens

questions.question_text: Explain two factors Marrowbrook Jam should consider when choosing between its current site and the orchard site.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Fruit transport and rent determine total cost [k]. The orchard saves $11,000 of haulage but adds $8,000 of rent, a net $3,000 gain that lowers the cost of each of 72,000 jars and makes the $1.10 contribution go further [an].

Point 2: Distance to delicatessens affects freshness and delivery [k]. Moving closer to fruit means longer journeys to customers, so jars may arrive later and delivery costs may rise; the directors must weigh the $3,000 saving against the risk of losing delicatessens that value quick, regular supplies [an].

knowledge_max_2: Transport and rent costs differ between sites

application_max_2: $11,000 saving versus $8,000 extra rent

questions.question_text: Consider whether Marrowbrook Jam should move to the orchard site. Do you think the directors should go ahead? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Costs fall and fruit is fresher [k]. The net $3,000 saving repeats every year, and fruit picked nearby can be processed sooner, improving flavour and reducing spoilage [app]. Buying fruit at short notice in a good harvest also becomes easier [an].

Against: The gain is small and the move disruptive [k]. $3,000 is only 12% of the $24,200 profit and could be wiped out by higher delivery costs to delicatessens [app]. Moving disrupts production of 72,000 jars, and the company may lose staff who cannot travel to a rural site [an].

Conclusion: Marrowbrook should move only if delivery costs stay unchanged and the workforce is retained [eval]. The $3,000 gain is too small to justify a move that risks the delicatessen trade [eval].

scenario_stem: Tarnwick Upholstery is a partnership in Costa Rica that produces 1,400 bespoke sofas a year for private clients. Its fixed costs are $150,000 a year, variable cost is $280 a unit and selling price is $430 a unit. A hotel offers to buy 250 identical sofas at $380 each, which would mean pausing bespoke work for six weeks.

questions.question_text: Define 'job production'.
questions.model_answer: Job production means making a single, unique item to a customer's order, with the work completed before the next item begins [2]. Tarnwick's bespoke sofas are job production because each is made to one client's design and size.

knowledge_max_2: One unique item is produced at a time
The product is made to the individual customer's requirements

questions.question_text: Outline two ways the hotel order could affect Tarnwick Upholstery's production.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: [k] A large order adds contribution towards fixed costs [app] The 250 sofas at $380 earn $100 each above the $280 variable cost, or $25,000, at Tarnwick Upholstery.

Point two: [k] Identical work changes the method of production [app] Pausing bespoke work for six weeks moves the partnership towards batch work, so private clients expecting $430 sofas may cancel.

knowledge_max_2: special orders add contribution

application_max_2: 250 sofas at $380 and $280 at Tarnwick

questions.question_text: Explain two ways accepting the hotel's order could affect Tarnwick Upholstery's production.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: The order would bring $25,000 of contribution, which is 42% of the $60,000 profit at 1,400 sofas [k]. That money could cover the $150,000 of fixed costs during a quiet period and may lead to further hotel contracts if the sofas are delivered on time [an].

Point 2: Producing 250 identical sofas moves the partnership towards batch working and away from bespoke job production [k]. Jigs and repeated cutting may speed the work, but private clients must wait six weeks, and some may cancel; the partners also risk losing the design skills and premium $430 price that depend on individual work [an].

questions.question_text: Consider whether Tarnwick Upholstery should accept the hotel's order of 250 sofas at $380 each. Do you think the partners should agree? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: The money is useful [k]. $25,000 of contribution uses the same premises and staff and may lead to further hotel contracts [app]. It helps pay the $150,000 of fixed costs while private orders are quiet [an].

Against: Bespoke clients may be lost [k]. Six weeks of delay could cost private orders worth $150 contribution each, and the hotel may expect $380 again rather than $430 [app]. Volume work could dilute the design skills behind the premium price [an].

Conclusion: Tarnwick should accept only if the order can be scheduled around existing clients or temporary staff are hired [eval]. If bespoke clients must wait, $25,000 is not worth losing the personal-service reputation [eval].

chapter: 4.2 Technology and production of goods and services
scenario_stem: Caldbourne Instruments is a private limited company in Oman that produces 4,600 pressure gauges a year for chemical plants. Its fixed costs are $208,000 a year, variable cost is $85 a unit and selling price is $150 a unit. Each new gauge design needs a jig that takes three weeks to make, and the directors are considering an $85,000 three-dimensional printer.

questions.question_text: Define 'three-dimensional printing'.
questions.model_answer: Three-dimensional printing means building a solid object layer by layer from a computer design, rather than cutting or moulding it [2]. Caldbourne would print the jigs used to hold gauge parts during assembly.

knowledge_max_2: An object is built up layer by layer

questions.question_text: Outline two benefits Caldbourne Instruments could gain from a three-dimensional printer.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: [k] Printing speeds up tool making [app] A jig that takes three weeks by hand could be printed in days, letting the company quote for new gauge designs sooner at Caldbourne Instruments.

Point two: [k] Complex shapes can be changed easily [app] Editing a design file reduces wasted metal on jigs for the 4,600 gauges, although operators and materials add cost.

knowledge_max_2: rapid prototyping speeds new designs
design changes reduce waste and rework

questions.model_answer:

Point 2: Printing allows complex shapes that are difficult to machine and can be changed by editing the design file [k]. That reduces wasted metal and rework, lowering the $85 variable cost, although the printer needs skilled operators and its material costs must be watched [an].

questions.question_text: Consider whether Caldbourne Instruments should spend $85,000 on the three-dimensional printer. Do you think the directors should buy it? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Faster jigs can win orders [k]. New designs reach production sooner, pushing output beyond 4,600 gauges and spreading the $208,000 of fixed costs [app]. If jig costs fall by $25,000 a year, the printer is recovered in under four years [an].

Against: Usage may be too low [k]. $85,000 is almost the $91,000 profit and new designs are only occasional, so the printer may stand idle [app]. Materials and skilled operators add cost, and a printed jig may wear faster, producing inaccurate gauges for chemical plants [an].

chapter: 4.3 Sustainable production of goods and services

Point one: [k] Certification meets shop sourcing requirements [app] Health shops asking suppliers to prove responsible sourcing may keep stocking the 110,000 bars at $1.45 from Wraybrook Soap.

Point two: [k] A credible claim differentiates the brand [app] Wraybrook can stand out from cheaper soap and may win new shops, provided audits confirm the certificate covers the whole supply.

Point 2: A credible sustainability claim helps Wraybrook stand out from cheaper soap brands [k]. scenario_stem: Elderford Crates is a private limited company in Croatia that produces 10,500 wooden crates a year for fruit growers. questions.model_answer: A variable cost is a cost that changes directly with the level of output, such as the timber and nails used in each crate [2]. Elderford's $38 a crate is variable because it is only incurred when a crate is made.

Point two: [k] The machine shifts cost from variable to fixed [app] Servicing and insurance must be paid even if fruit growers order fewer crates, so average cost per crate rises at low output.

Point 2: The machine shifts cost from variable to fixed [k].
