unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Wrenfield Sports Ltd is a private limited company in Indonesia making sportswear, exporting 1,200,000 shirts a year to the United States at $18 each. The US has imposed a 20% tariff on Indonesian clothing, and the rupiah has fallen 6% against the dollar. Directors must decide whether to build a factory in Vietnam for $4,000,000 or keep exporting from Indonesia.

questions.question_text: Define 'trade barrier'.
questions.model_answer: A trade barrier is any government measure that restricts imports or exports [2]; the 20% US tariff on Wrenfield Sports Ltd's shirts is one example.

knowledge_max_2: A government measure restricting trade
Examples: tariffs, quotas, embargoes

questions.question_text: Outline two reasons why Wrenfield Sports Ltd might build a factory in Vietnam.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: It avoids the US tariff [k]. Shirts made in Vietnam face lower US duty than the 20% on Indonesian clothing, taking the landed price below $21.60 [app].

Point two: It spreads risk across countries [k]. A second site means a problem in Indonesia cannot stop all 1,200,000 shirts [app].

knowledge_max_2: Locating abroad can avoid tariffs on exports
A second site spreads operational risk across countries
application_max_2: Vietnam shirts avoid 20% duty, landed price below $21.60
1,200,000 shirts no longer depend on Indonesia alone

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Wrenfield Sports Ltd might build a factory in Vietnam instead of exporting from Indonesia.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: It avoids the US tariff [k]. Shirts made in Vietnam face a lower US duty than the 20% now charged on Indonesian clothing [app], so the landed price falls below $21.60 and orders are easier to win [an].

Point 2: It spreads risk across countries [k]. A second site means a flood, strike or new tariff in Indonesia cannot stop all 1,200,000 shirts [app], protecting revenue for US customers [an].

knowledge_max_2: Production inside a country facing lower tariffs
Spreading operations reduces country risk
application_max_2: 20% US tariff on Indonesian shirts
Current output of 1,200,000 shirts from one country
analysis_max_2: Lower landed price wins US orders
Supply continues if one country is disrupted

questions.question_text: Consider whether Wrenfield Sports Ltd should spend $4,000,000 on a factory in Vietnam. Do you think the directors should build it? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: A Vietnamese plant escapes the 20% US tariff and cuts the landed price from $21.60 towards $18 [k]. That could restore US orders across 1,200,000 shirts and reduce reliance on Indonesian trade policy [app]. More stable orders protect revenue [an].

Against: $4,000,000 is a large commitment when the rupiah has fallen 6%, which already makes Indonesian costs cheaper in dollars [k]. Building abroad means managing a new workforce and risks losing quality control [app]. The outlay is high relative to current margins [an].

Conclusion: Do not build yet [eval]. The weaker rupiah offsets part of the tariff, so renegotiate US prices and test Vietnamese production through a local partner first [eval].

knowledge_max_2: A Vietnam factory avoids the 20% US tariff
A weaker rupiah already lowers Indonesian dollar costs
application_max_2: $21.60 to $18 landed price; 1,200,000 shirts
$4,000,000 cost; 6% weaker rupiah; new workforce
analysis_max_2: Restored US orders protect revenue
New-site management may damage quality and is costly
evaluation_max_2: Do not build yet
Renegotiate prices and test Vietnam via a partner first

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Ashcombe Cycles Ltd is a private limited company in Norway assembling e-bikes, selling 12,000 units a year at $1,450. The central bank's interest rate is 4.5% and inflation is 3.2%, while GDP growth has slowed to 0.8%. A $1,800,000 assembly line would replace imported frames costing $640 each. Directors must decide whether to borrow for the line or keep importing.

questions.question_text: Define 'recession'.
questions.model_answer: A recession is a period when gross domestic product falls for two successive quarters [2]; with Norwegian GDP growth down to 0.8%, Ashcombe Cycles Ltd faces cautious household spending.

knowledge_max_2: Two successive quarters of falling GDP
Falling output, income and employment

questions.question_text: Outline two effects of a 4.5% interest rate on Ashcombe Cycles Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: Borrowing for the line is relatively cheap [k]. Interest on $1,800,000 is $81,000 a year, which frame savings can cover [app].

Point two: Customers delay big purchases [k]. E-bikes at $1,450 are often bought on credit when GDP growth is only 0.8% [app].

knowledge_max_2: Low interest reduces the cost of borrowing for investment
Higher borrowing costs can discourage customer credit purchases
application_max_2: $1,450 e-bikes bought on credit; GDP growth 0.8%

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of a 4.5% interest rate on Ashcombe Cycles Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Borrowing for the line is relatively cheap [k]. Interest on $1,800,000 is $81,000 a year [app], which the saving on 12,000 imported frames can cover if assembly costs fall [an].

Point 2: Customers still delay big purchases [k]. E-bikes at $1,450 are often bought on credit, and higher repayments discourage buyers when GDP growth is only 0.8% [app], so sales may fall just as new capacity arrives [an].

knowledge_max_2: Lower interest makes investment cheaper
Consumer credit becomes more costly
application_max_2: $1,450 e-bikes and 0.8% GDP growth
analysis_max_2: Frame savings can cover the interest
Weaker demand leaves new capacity underused

questions.question_text: Consider whether Ashcombe Cycles Ltd should borrow $1,800,000 for the assembly line. Do you think the directors should borrow? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: At 4.5% the loan costs $81,000 a year, while importing 12,000 frames at $640 costs $7,680,000 [k]. Assembling in Norway cuts freight and import exposure and gives control over quality and delivery [app]. Local assembly could reduce total frame costs [an].

Against: GDP growth of 0.8% and inflation of 3.2% suggest cautious buyers, so 12,000 sales at $1,450 are not guaranteed [k]. A fixed interest charge and a large loan could strain cash if demand dips [app]. Unsold capacity would add to costs [an].

Conclusion: Borrow, but phase the line so capacity matches demand [eval]. The $81,000 interest is manageable against $7,680,000 of frame purchases provided sales hold [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Loan interest is small relative to frame import costs
Weak growth creates demand risk for e-bikes
application_max_2: $81,000 interest vs $7,680,000 for 12,000 frames at $640
GDP growth 0.8%; inflation 3.2%; 12,000 sales at $1,450
analysis_max_2: Local assembly cuts freight and may lower total costs
Fixed interest on unsold capacity raises unit costs
evaluation_max_2: Borrow but phase the investment
Manageable interest if 12,000 sales hold

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Vellacott Motors plc is a public limited company in Spain making car parts, using 6,000 tonnes of steel a year at EUR 700 a tonne. An EU carbon border levy of 22% now applies to imported steel, while EU-made steel costs EUR 820 a tonne. Directors must decide whether to switch to EU steel or keep importing and pay the levy.

questions.question_text: Define 'regulation'.
questions.model_answer: Regulation means rules set by government that businesses must follow [2]; the EU carbon border levy forces Vellacott Motors plc to account for the emissions in its 6,000 tonnes of imported steel.

knowledge_max_2: Rules set by government or public bodies
Businesses must comply or face penalties

questions.question_text: Outline two ways the carbon border levy could affect Vellacott Motors plc.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: Imported steel becomes more expensive [k]. The 22% levy adds EUR 154 a tonne, taking imported steel to EUR 854 against EUR 820 for EU steel [app].

Point two: It changes where the firm buys [k]. EU steel is now cheaper per tonne for the 6,000 tonnes of car parts [app].

knowledge_max_2: The levy raises the price of imported steel
It may encourage switching to cheaper domestic (EU) steel
application_max_2: 22% levy = EUR 154 per tonne; EUR 854 vs EUR 820
6,000 tonnes of steel for Spanish car parts

questions.question_text: Explain two ways the carbon border levy could affect Vellacott Motors plc.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Imported steel becomes more expensive [k]. The levy adds EUR 154 a tonne, taking the cost to EUR 854 against EUR 820 for EU steel [app], so the 6,000 tonnes now cost EUR 924,000 more than before [an].

Point 2: It changes where the firm buys [k]. EU steel is now cheaper per tonne [app], but switching may lengthen delivery times and require new supplier checks for car-part quality [an].

knowledge_max_2: Levy raises the price of imported steel
Favours local suppliers inside the levy area
application_max_2: EUR 700 + EUR 154 = EUR 854 vs EUR 820
6,000 tonnes a year
analysis_max_2: EUR 924,000 extra cost across the year
Switching suppliers risks delays and quality checks

questions.question_text: Consider whether Vellacott Motors plc should switch to EU steel at EUR 820 a tonne. Do you think the directors should switch? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Imported steel now costs EUR 854 a tonne once the EUR 154 levy is added, so EU steel saves EUR 34 a tonne, or EUR 204,000 across 6,000 tonnes [k]. Local supply also avoids future levy rises and shortens delivery distance [app]. The saving recurs each year [an].

Against: A saving of EUR 34 a tonne is only about 4% and could be lost if EU mills raise prices [k]. Existing imported steel may be tailored to the car parts already in production, and new supplier checks are needed [app]. Quality may suffer [an].

Conclusion: Switch most of the 6,000 tonnes to EU steel, keeping a small import share until quality is proven [eval]. The EUR 204,000 saving is real but too small for a complete immediate change [eval].

knowledge_max_2: EU steel is cheaper after the levy, saving EUR 204,000
The margin is small and quality may be affected
application_max_2: EUR 854 vs EUR 820; EUR 34 per tonne over 6,000 tonnes
Tailored imported steel; new EU supplier checks for car parts
analysis_max_2: Recurring annual saving and shorter delivery distance
A small saving could be erased by price rises or quality issues
evaluation_max_2: Switch most tonnage to EU steel
Keep a small import share until quality is proven

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Saltire Marine Ltd is a private limited company in Italy making yacht fittings, winning US orders worth $1,200,000 a year. The dollar has strengthened 10% against the euro to $1.20, while Italian inflation is 2.9%. Directors must decide whether to invoice US clients in dollars or in euros, knowing the exchange rate may move again.

questions.question_text: Define 'appreciation of a currency'.
questions.model_answer: An appreciation is a rise in the value of one currency against another on the foreign exchange market [2]; the dollar's 10% rise to $1.20 means each dollar now buys more euros.

knowledge_max_2: Rise in a currency's value against another
Makes imports cheaper and exports dearer

questions.question_text: Outline two effects of the stronger dollar on Saltire Marine Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: Dollar orders convert into fewer euros [k]. At $1.20, the $1,200,000 of US orders is worth EUR 1,000,000 [app].

Point two: Italian fittings look dearer to US buyers [k]. The same euro price now costs American clients more dollars [app].

knowledge_max_2: A stronger dollar reduces the euro value of dollar receipts
It makes the exporter's goods dearer in the buyer's currency
application_max_2: Yacht fittings dearer for US clients in Italy

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the stronger dollar on Saltire Marine Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Dollar orders convert into fewer euros [k]. At $1.20, the $1,200,000 of US orders is worth EUR 1,000,000 [app], so revenue measured in euros is lower than before the 10% rise [an].

Point 2: Italian fittings look dearer to US buyers [k]. A stronger dollar means the same euro price costs American clients more dollars [app], which may push them towards local suppliers [an].

knowledge_max_2: Stronger domestic currency cuts export revenue in home currency
Stronger domestic currency makes exports dearer abroad
application_max_2: 10% dollar rise against the euro
analysis_max_2: Euro revenue falls despite unchanged dollar orders
US buyers may switch to domestic suppliers

questions.question_text: Consider whether Saltire Marine Ltd should invoice US clients in dollars. Do you think the directors should invoice in dollars? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Invoicing in dollars matches the customer's own currency and removes their exchange-rate risk [k]. With $1,200,000 of US orders, winning repeat business matters more than protecting each euro receipt [app]. Simpler quotes help retain US clients [an].

Against: Dollar invoicing leaves Saltire exposed [k]. The 10% rise has already cut the euro value of $1,200,000 to EUR 1,000,000, and a further dollar fall would reduce euro income while Italian wages and materials stay in euros [app]. Costs are fixed in euros [an].

Conclusion: Invoice in dollars but add a currency clause allowing quarterly price review [eval]. That keeps US clients comfortable without accepting unlimited exchange-rate risk [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Dollar invoicing suits the customer and removes their risk
It leaves the exporter exposed to currency movements
application_max_2: $1,200,000 orders; repeat US business
10% rise; EUR 1,000,000; Italian wages and materials in euros
analysis_max_2: Simpler quotes help retain US clients
Euro-denominated costs stay fixed as dollar receipts fall
evaluation_max_2: Invoice in dollars with a currency clause
Allow quarterly review to limit exchange-rate risk

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Nordhaven Logistics Ltd is a private limited company in Canada running 180 lorries, using 2,400,000 litres of diesel a year. Fuel duty has risen by 9 cents a litre and the bank rate is 5.25%. Directors must decide whether to raise haulage rates by 4% or borrow $6,000,000 to replace 30 lorries with electric models.

questions.question_text: Define 'indirect tax'.
questions.model_answer: An indirect tax is a tax on spending, collected by sellers and passed to government [2]; the 9 cents a litre fuel duty raises the cost of Nordhaven Logistics Ltd's 2,400,000 litres of diesel.

knowledge_max_2: A tax on goods and services, not income
Collected by the seller and paid to government

questions.question_text: Outline two effects of higher fuel duty on Nordhaven Logistics Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: Operating costs rise on every journey [k]. With 2,400,000 litres used, the 9 cent duty adds $216,000 a year [app].

Point two: Older lorries become less viable [k]. The 30 least efficient of the 180 lorries may be retired early [app].

knowledge_max_2: Fuel duty raises operating costs per litre
It makes older, less efficient vehicles uneconomic
application_max_2: 2,400,000 litres x 9 cents = $216,000 a year
30 least efficient of 180 lorries at Nordhaven in Canada

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of higher fuel duty on Nordhaven Logistics Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Operating costs rise on every journey [k]. Diesel use of 2,400,000 litres means the 9 cent duty adds $216,000 a year [app], which must be recovered from customers or taken from profit [an].

Point 2: Older lorries become less viable [k]. With fuel taking a larger share of cost, the 30 least efficient vehicles may be retired early [app], pushing the firm towards the $6,000,000 electric replacement [an].

knowledge_max_2: Fuel duty raises running costs
Accelerates replacement of inefficient vehicles
application_max_2: 2,400,000 litres at 9 cents adds $216,000
180 lorries, 30 candidates for replacement
analysis_max_2: Higher rates or lower profit
Early retirement of old lorries

questions.question_text: Consider whether Nordhaven Logistics Ltd should borrow $6,000,000 to replace 30 lorries with electric models. Do you think the directors should borrow? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Electric lorries would remove diesel duty from 30 vehicles, saving a share of the $216,000 annual bill and shielding the firm from future duty rises [k]. At a 5.25% bank rate finance cost is predictable, and the vehicles cut emissions for green clients [app]. Savings grow as duty rises [an].

Against: $6,000,000 is heavy debt for a haulier [k]. Electric lorries have limited range on long Canadian routes, and charging points and driver retraining add cost before savings appear [app]. Cost recovery is slow [an].

Conclusion: Replace only the 30 lorries on short urban routes [eval]. That captures fuel savings where range is not a problem, leaving long-haul work on diesel until charging improves [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Electric lorries cut diesel duty and future exposure
High debt and limited range are significant drawbacks
application_max_2: 30 vehicles; $216,000 duty; 5.25% bank rate
$6,000,000; Canadian routes; charging points and retraining
analysis_max_2: Savings increase if duty rises further
Range and infrastructure delays reduce real savings
evaluation_max_2: Replace only short-route lorries
Keep long-haul diesel until charging improves

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Quillmark Couriers Ltd is a private limited company in Australia delivering 9,000,000 parcels a year for online retailers from six depots. Business clients now ask for carbon-neutral delivery, which costs $0.35 a parcel in offsets, and the bank rate is 4.35%. Directors must decide whether to buy offsets or spend $4,800,000 on 120 electric vans.

questions.question_text: Define 'sustainability'.
questions.model_answer: Sustainability means meeting present needs without compromising future generations [2]; Quillmark Couriers Ltd must cut the emissions from 9,000,000 parcel deliveries to keep its Australian clients.

knowledge_max_2: Meeting needs without harming future generations
Reducing pollution, waste and resource use

questions.question_text: Outline two reasons why Quillmark Couriers Ltd's business clients prefer a low-emission courier.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: Their own green targets depend on suppliers [k]. Australian firms reporting emissions must count deliveries made for them by Quillmark's 9,000,000 parcels [app].

Point two: Reputation with their customers [k]. Shoppers increasingly judge brands on delivery waste and air quality from the six depots [app].

knowledge_max_2: Clients' environmental targets include their suppliers' emissions
A green courier protects the client's brand reputation
application_max_2: Clients count Quillmark's 9,000,000 Australian parcels
Shoppers judge delivery waste from six depots

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Quillmark Couriers Ltd's business clients prefer a low-emission courier.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Their own green targets depend on suppliers [k]. Australian firms reporting emissions must count deliveries made for them [app], so using Quillmark's 9,000,000 parcels with offsets helps them meet published targets [an].

Point 2: Reputation with their customers [k]. Shoppers increasingly judge brands on delivery waste and air quality [app], so a low-emission courier protects the client's image and may justify a higher delivery charge [an].

knowledge_max_2: Clients must report supply-chain emissions
Green delivery protects the client's brand
application_max_2: 9,000,000 parcels and carbon-neutral option
$0.35 per parcel offset cost
analysis_max_2: Helps clients hit published emission targets
Supports premium pricing and customer loyalty

questions.question_text: Consider whether Quillmark Couriers Ltd should spend $4,800,000 on 120 electric vans. Do you think the directors should buy the vans? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Electric vans cut emissions at source rather than paying $3,150,000 a year for offsets [k]. Over time the vans lower running costs and give Quillmark a genuine green service Australian clients can advertise [app]. Real emissions cuts strengthen the offer [an].

Against: $4,800,000 is a large outlay against a $3,150,000 annual offset bill, and at 4.35% the finance charge is significant [k]. Van range and charging time may disrupt 9,000,000 deliveries a year from six depots [app]. Operations could suffer [an].

Conclusion: Start with offsets and buy vans gradually [eval]. Offsets keep the service green immediately, while a smaller electric fleet can prove the economics before the full $4,800,000 is committed [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Electric vans cut emissions at source and lower running costs
Large outlay and range concerns create operational risk
application_max_2: 9,000,000 parcels from six depots; charging time
analysis_max_2: A genuine green service strengthens the client offering
Range and charging may disrupt daily deliveries
evaluation_max_2: Start with offsets, buy vans gradually
Prove a smaller fleet's economics before full commitment

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Rosemullion Hotels Ltd is a private limited company in Japan running business hotels, selling 6,000 room-nights a year to overseas visitors at $120 a night. The yen has weakened 18%, from 127 to 150 yen per dollar, while Japanese inflation is 3.1%. Directors must decide whether to raise dollar room rates by 10% or hold them.

questions.question_text: Define 'exchange rate'.
questions.model_answer: An exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another [2]; Rosemullion Hotels Ltd converts its $120 room rate at 150 yen per dollar, up from 127.

knowledge_max_2: Price of one currency expressed in another
Determined by currency supply and demand

questions.question_text: Outline two effects of the weaker yen on Rosemullion Hotels Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: Japan becomes cheaper for foreign guests [k]. At 150 yen per dollar instead of 127, a $120 room brings more yen revenue, so 6,000 room-nights earn 108,000,000 yen [app].

Point two: Imported supplies cost more [k]. Food, wine and linen bought abroad need more yen while inflation is 3.1% [app].

knowledge_max_2: A weaker currency attracts more foreign visitors
A weaker currency raises imported supply costs
application_max_2: 6,000 room-nights at $120 = 108,000,000 yen at 150
Imported food, wine and linen; 3.1% Japanese inflation

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the weaker yen on Rosemullion Hotels Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Japan becomes cheaper for foreign guests [k]. At 150 yen per dollar instead of 127, a $120 room costs the same in dollars but more yen revenue [app], so 6,000 room-nights bring in 108,000,000 yen [an].

Point 2: Imported supplies cost more [k]. Food, wine and linen bought abroad need more yen for the same invoice [app], trimming the gain from extra tourist bookings while inflation runs at 3.1% [an].

knowledge_max_2: Weaker currency attracts foreign tourists
Weaker currency raises imported supply costs
application_max_2: Rate moves from 127 to 150 yen per dollar
$720,000 of rooms at $120 a night
analysis_max_2: Room revenue rises to 108,000,000 yen
Imported food and linen cost more yen

questions.question_text: Consider whether Rosemullion Hotels Ltd should raise its dollar room rate by 10%. Do you think the directors should raise rates? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Demand from overseas visitors is strong while the yen is 18% weaker, and a 10% rise lifts the $120 rate to $132 [k]. The extra dollars convert at 150 yen, adding revenue without losing Japan's price advantage [app]. Yield per room rises [an].

Against: Competitors in Seoul and Bangkok target the same travellers [k]. A 10% rise may fill fewer of the 6,000 room-nights, and empty rooms cannot be stored, so occupancy matters more than rate [app]. Lost bookings hurt reputation with tour operators [an].

Conclusion: Hold the $120 rate this season [eval]. The weaker yen already raises yen revenue to 108,000,000, and filling rooms protects the hotel's reputation with tour operators [eval].

knowledge_max_2: A rate rise increases revenue per occupied room
Higher rates may reduce occupancy in a competitive market
application_max_2: $120 to $132; 18% weaker yen; 150 yen conversion
Seoul and Bangkok rivals; 6,000 room-nights; 108,000,000 yen
analysis_max_2: Extra dollars convert at a favourable 150 yen
Empty rooms cannot be stored, so occupancy matters more
evaluation_max_2: Hold the $120 rate this season
Prioritise occupancy and tour-operator relationships

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Tarnbrook Catering Ltd is a private limited company in India supplying 4,000,000 school meals a year. Food inflation is 6.7% and the bank rate is 6.5%, while its current contract fixes the meal price for three years. Food now costs $1.80 a meal. Directors must decide whether to accept a new fixed-price deal at $2.10 or demand an index-linked $1.95.

questions.question_text: Define 'inflation'.
questions.model_answer: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level [2]; India's 6.7% food inflation means Tarnbrook Catering Ltd pays more for rice, pulses and cooking oil every month.

knowledge_max_2: Sustained rise in average prices
Reduces what money can buy

questions.question_text: Outline two effects of 6.7% food inflation on Tarnbrook Catering Ltd under a fixed-price contract.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: Costs rise while revenue is fixed [k]. Food costs $1.80 a meal and the contract price cannot change for three years [app].

Point two: Quality may be reduced to protect profit [k]. Directors could use cheaper ingredients across 4,000,000 meals [app].

knowledge_max_2: Rising costs with fixed revenue squeeze margins
The firm may cut quality to protect profit
application_max_2: $1.80 food cost and a three-year fixed price
Cheaper ingredients across 4,000,000 school meals in India

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of 6.7% food inflation on Tarnbrook Catering Ltd under a fixed-price contract.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Costs rise while revenue is fixed [k]. Food costs $1.80 a meal and the contract price cannot change for three years [app], so each 6.7% rise cuts the margin on 4,000,000 meals [an].

Point 2: Quality may be reduced to protect profit [k]. Directors could use cheaper ingredients or smaller portions [app], but schools may then end the contract or complain to the Indian education authority [an].

knowledge_max_2: Fixed prices with rising costs squeeze margin
Pressure to cut ingredient quality
application_max_2: $1.80 food cost across 4,000,000 meals
Three-year fixed contract
analysis_max_2: Margin falls with every price rise
Poorer meals risk losing the school contract

questions.question_text: Consider whether Tarnbrook Catering Ltd should accept the fixed-price deal at $2.10 a meal. Do you think the directors should accept it? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: At $2.10 the margin over the $1.92 food cost is $0.18 a meal, or $720,000 across 4,000,000 meals [k]. A fixed price gives certainty and may win the contract against rivals demanding indexation [app]. Budget certainty is valuable [an].

Against: Food inflation of 6.7% compounds over three years, so costs could pass $2.10 before the deal ends [k]. An index-linked $1.95 protects the margin even though the starting price is lower [app]. A fixed margin will shrink each year [an].

Conclusion: Demand indexation at $1.95 [eval]. Three years is too long to carry 6.7% inflation, so a smaller but protected margin is safer than a fixed $2.10 that may become unprofitable [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Fixed $2.10 gives a $0.18 margin now and certainty
Indexation protects against compounding food inflation
application_max_2: 6.7% inflation over three years; index-linked $1.95
analysis_max_2: Budget certainty helps win and run the contract
A fixed margin erodes as food costs keep rising
evaluation_max_2: Demand index-linked $1.95
A protected margin is safer than fixed $2.10 over three years

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Yarrow Cafes Ltd is a private limited company in Nigeria running 38 coffee shops, selling 2,400,000 cups a year with beans costing $0.85 a cup. questions.question_text: Define 'fair trade'.

Often includes social and environmental standards

questions.question_text: Outline two benefits to Yarrow Cafes Ltd of fair-trade certification.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: It differentiates the brand [k]. With 38 shops selling 2,400,000 cups, a fair-trade mark gives customers a reason to choose Yarrow [app].

Point two: It protects long-term supply [k]. An 18% premium encourages farmers to keep growing coffee despite the 24% price rise [app].

knowledge_max_2: Certification differentiates the brand from cheaper cafes
Fair-trade premiums help secure long-term coffee supply
application_max_2: 38 shops and 2,400,000 cups in Nigeria
18% premium to farmers amid a 24% world coffee price rise

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Yarrow Cafes Ltd of fair-trade certification.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: It differentiates the brand [k]. With 38 shops selling 2,400,000 cups, a visible fair-trade mark gives customers a reason to choose Yarrow over cheaper cafes [app], supporting sales and allowing a higher price [an].

Point 2: It protects supply in the long term [k]. Paying farmers an 18% premium encourages them to keep growing coffee despite the 24% price rise [app], reducing the risk of shortages that would close shops [an].

knowledge_max_2: Differentiates the brand from competitors
Supports farmer incomes and future supply
application_max_2: 38 shops and 2,400,000 cups a year
18% premium against a 24% world price rise
analysis_max_2: Higher sales or prices at the same volume
More secure bean supply

questions.question_text: Consider whether Yarrow Cafes Ltd should become fair-trade certified. Do you think the directors should certify? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Certification gives 38 shops a clear ethical story and may justify a higher cup price [k]. Paying the 18% premium, about $367,200 a year, also helps secure supply while world coffee prices have risen 24% [app]. Supply security protects sales [an].

Against: Total cost is $367,200 plus $45,000 certification, over $412,000 a year [k]. Nigerian customers may care more about price than ethics, and cheaper blends would protect margins in a cost-of-living squeeze [app]. Volume could fall at higher prices [an].

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Coppervale Electronics Ltd is a private limited company in South Korea making 90,000 memory chips a month, exporting 70% to Japan at $34 each. The won has depreciated from 1,100 to 1,265 won per dollar, and Japan has imposed a 12% tariff on imported chips. Domestic rivals have cut prices by 5%. Directors must decide whether to cut the dollar price to $30 to hold market share or keep $34 and accept lower export volumes.

questions.question_text: Define 'depreciation' of a currency.
questions.model_answer: A depreciation is a fall in the value of one currency against another, such as the won moving from 1,100 to 1,265 per dollar for Coppervale Electronics Ltd [2].

knowledge_max_2: A fall in a currency's value against another currency
It takes more of the currency to buy one unit of foreign currency

questions.question_text: Outline two effects of the won's depreciation on Coppervale Electronics Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: A depreciation increases home-currency earnings from exports [k]. Each $34 chip converts to about 43,010 won rather than 37,400 won for Coppervale Electronics Ltd in South Korea [app].

Point two: A depreciation raises the cost of imported components [k]. Silicon and circuit boards from Japan cost more won across 90,000 chips a month [app].

knowledge_max_2: Depreciation raises home-currency export earnings.
Depreciation raises the cost of imported components.
application_max_2: A $34 chip converts to 43,010 won instead of 37,400 won in South Korea.
Japanese components cost more won across 90,000 chips.

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the won's depreciation on Coppervale Electronics Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Higher revenue in won [k], because each $34 chip now converts to 43,010 won instead of 37,400 won [app], so the same exports earn more home currency [an].

Point 2: Dearer imported components [k], as silicon and circuit boards bought from Japan cost more won [app], raising costs on 90,000 chips a month and limiting the gain [an].

knowledge_max_2: A depreciation raises the home-currency value of exports
Imported inputs become more expensive
application_max_2: 90,000 chips a month; 12% tariff in Japan
analysis_max_2: Export earnings rise in won terms
Imported component costs erode the competitive gain

questions.question_text: Consider whether Coppervale Electronics Ltd should cut its dollar price to $30. Do you think it should? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: A lower price can restore competitiveness after a tariff [k]. The 12% tariff lifts a $34 chip to about $38 and rivals have cut 5%, so $30 protects the 70% of output exported to Japan [app], and the weaker won keeps a workable margin [an].

Against: Cutting price loses revenue on every unit [k]. Dropping to $30 loses $4 a chip, or $252,000 a month on 63,000 chips [app], and dearer imported components squeeze profit too [an].

Conclusion: Do not cut to $30 for all buyers [eval]. Hold $34 where there is no tariff and discount only where Japanese rivals are strongest [eval].

knowledge_max_2: A lower price can restore competitiveness after a tariff.
A price cut reduces revenue on every unit.
application_max_2: 12% tariff lifts $34 to about $38; rivals cut 5%.
$4 less on 63,000 chips loses $252,000 a month.
analysis_max_2: A $30 price protects 70% export volume to Japan.
Dearer components and lower price squeeze profit together.
evaluation_max_2: Do not cut to $30 for all buyers.
Discount selectively where Japanese rivals are strongest.

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Rosemark Builders Ltd is a private limited company in Turkey building 140 houses a year, with an overdraft of $2,400,000. The central bank has raised interest rates from 9% to 14% to fight inflation of 38%, and mortgage rates have doubled, cutting buyer enquiries by 30%. Timber costs have risen 24% and 12 finished houses are unsold. Directors must decide whether to pause construction of 40 houses or cut prices by 10% to sell the finished stock.

questions.question_text: Define 'interest rate'.
questions.model_answer: An interest rate is the cost of borrowing money, expressed as a percentage, such as the 14% rate now charged on Rosemark Builders Ltd's $2,400,000 overdraft [2].

knowledge_max_2: The price charged for borrowing money
Expressed as a percentage of the amount borrowed

questions.question_text: Outline two effects of higher interest rates on Rosemark Builders Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: Higher interest rates raise the cost of overdraft finance [k]. The $2,400,000 overdraft costs $120,000 more a year after the rise from 9% to 14% for Rosemark Builders Ltd in Turkey [app].

Point two: Higher mortgage rates reduce demand for houses [k]. Buyer enquiries are down 30%, leaving 12 finished houses unsold and cash tied up [app].

knowledge_max_2: Higher interest rates raise overdraft costs.
Higher mortgage rates reduce housing demand.
application_max_2: $2,400,000 overdraft costs $120,000 more after 9% to 14%.
Enquiries down 30% with 12 finished houses unsold in Turkey.

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of higher interest rates on Rosemark Builders Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Higher finance costs [k], as the $2,400,000 overdraft now costs $120,000 more a year [app], reducing profit on only 140 houses [an].

Point 2: Fewer buyers [k], because doubled mortgage rates cut enquiries by 30% [app], leaving the 12 finished houses unsold and cash tied up [an].

knowledge_max_2: Higher rates raise business borrowing costs
Higher mortgage costs reduce demand for housing
application_max_2: $2,400,000 overdraft costs $120,000 more a year
Mortgage rates doubled; enquiries down 30%; 12 unsold houses
analysis_max_2: Profit falls as finance costs rise on fixed output
Unsold stock reduces cash flow and raises holding costs

questions.question_text: Consider whether Rosemark Builders Ltd should pause construction of 40 houses. Do you think it should? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Stopping work can protect cash when demand is weak [k]. Enquiries are down 30% and 12 houses are unsold, while the overdraft costs $120,000 more [app], so building 40 more risks tying up cash during 38% inflation [an].

Against: Pausing work leaves fixed costs and idle labour [k]. Skilled site workers would be idle while a 10% price cut on finished stock in Turkey could sell houses faster [app], protecting revenue and recovering cash [an].

Conclusion: Pause the 40 houses only after discounting finished stock [eval]. Clearing 12 unsold houses restores cash without abandoning the build programme [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Stopping work can protect cash when demand is weak.
Pausing leaves fixed costs and idle labour to pay.
application_max_2: Enquiries down 30%, 12 unsold houses and $120,000 extra overdraft interest.
A 10% price cut could sell finished houses in Turkey.
analysis_max_2: Pausing protects liquidity while inflation is 38%.
Idle workers and fixed costs raise unit costs and delay revenue.
evaluation_max_2: Pause the 40 houses after discounting stock.
Clearing 12 unsold houses restores cash without ending the programme.

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Kestrelmoor Timber Ltd is a private limited company in Finland felling 260,000 cubic metres of timber a year from 650 hectares of forest. The government has raised the felling licence fee by 35% and requires 20% of each harvested area to be replanted within two years. Environmental groups have blockaded two forest roads, halting deliveries for nine days. Directors must decide whether to buy 4,000 hectares of certified forest for $7,800,000 or cut output by 15%.

questions.question_text: Define 'sustainable development'.
questions.model_answer: Sustainable development means meeting present needs without damaging the ability of future generations to meet theirs, such as Kestrelmoor Timber Ltd replanting 20% of every harvested area [2].

knowledge_max_2: Meeting today's needs without harming future generations
Using resources so they remain available long term

questions.question_text: Outline two effects of the road blockades on Kestrelmoor Timber Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: Blockades disrupt deliveries to customers [k]. Nine days without road access stops timber reaching builders from Kestrelmoor Timber Ltd's 260,000 cubic metres in Finland [app].

Point two: Environmental protests can harm reputation [k]. The dispute publicises the felling of 650 hectares and may deter builders who need certified timber [app].

knowledge_max_2: Blockades disrupt deliveries and revenue.
Protests can harm a firm's reputation with buyers.
application_max_2: Nine days without access halts deliveries of 260,000 cubic metres in Finland.
Builders needing certified timber may be deterred by the protest.

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the road blockades on Kestrelmoor Timber Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Lost deliveries and revenue [k], as nine days without access stops timber reaching builders [app], so orders may be cancelled and 260,000 cubic metres of annual output cannot be sold on time [an].

Point 2: Reputational damage [k], because the protest publicises the environmental dispute [app], which may deter builders who need certified timber for their own contracts [an].

knowledge_max_2: Blockades stop production and deliveries
Protest publicity can damage a firm's reputation
application_max_2: Nine days of halted deliveries
260,000 cubic metres a year; 650 hectares felled
analysis_max_2: Cancelled orders cut revenue and cash flow
Builder customers may switch to certified suppliers

questions.question_text: Consider whether Kestrelmoor Timber Ltd should buy 4,000 hectares of certified forest for $7,800,000. Do you think it should? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Owning certified forest can secure supply and buyer confidence [k]. Buying 4,000 hectares for $7,800,000 would support 260,000 cubic metres of output in Finland [app], answering protesters and keeping builders who demand certified timber [an].

Against: A large purchase may be unaffordable for a mid-sized firm [k]. Cutting output by 15% still meets the 20% replanting rule at far lower cash cost [app], avoiding strain on cash flow while deliveries are disrupted [an].

Conclusion: Buy the forest only if it can be financed without straining cash flow [eval]. Certification is becoming a condition of trade rather than a luxury [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Certified forest can secure supply and buyer confidence.
A large purchase may be unaffordable.
application_max_2: 4,000 hectares for $7,800,000 supports 260,000 cubic metres in Finland.
Cutting output 15% still meets the 20% replanting rule.
analysis_max_2: Certification answers protesters and keeps builders.
A big outlay could strain cash while deliveries are disrupted.
evaluation_max_2: Buy only if financing is secure.
Certification is becoming a condition of trade.

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Driftwood Furniture Ltd is a private limited company in Vietnam making 24,000 wooden tables a year, exporting 80% to China at $150 each. China has cut its import quota from 30,000 to 18,000 tables a year and the dong has depreciated 7% against the dollar. Freight costs have risen 16%. Directors must decide whether to open a factory in China to avoid the quota or target new markets in Australia.

questions.question_text: Define 'import quota'.
questions.model_answer: An import quota is a limit on the quantity of a good that may be imported, such as China's 18,000 table limit on Driftwood Furniture Ltd [2].

knowledge_max_2: A physical limit on the volume of imports
Set by government to protect domestic producers

questions.question_text: Outline two effects of the quota cut on Driftwood Furniture Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: An import quota limits export volume [k]. China's quota falls from 30,000 to 18,000 tables, leaving 1,200 tables worth $180,000 unable to enter for Driftwood Furniture Ltd [app].

Point two: Surplus stock and higher freight squeeze margins [k]. Tables must be sold elsewhere or discounted while freight has risen 16% on each $150 table [app].

knowledge_max_2: A quota limits the volume a firm can export.
Surplus stock and higher freight squeeze margins.
application_max_2: Quota cut from 30,000 to 18,000 tables leaves 1,200 worth $180,000.
Freight up 16% on $150 tables from Vietnam.

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the quota cut on Driftwood Furniture Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Lost sales [k], as the quota falls from 30,000 to 18,000 tables [app], leaving 1,200 tables worth $180,000 unable to enter China each year [an].

Point 2: Pressure on price and costs [k], because surplus tables must be sold elsewhere or discounted [app], while freight costs have risen 16%, squeezing the margin on each $150 table [an].

knowledge_max_2: A quota restricts export volume
Surplus output must be sold in other markets
application_max_2: Quota 30,000 to 18,000; 19,200 tables exported
$180,000 of exports above quota; freight up 16%
analysis_max_2: Lower volume cuts revenue and spreads fixed costs
Discounting surplus stock and higher freight cut margins

questions.question_text: Consider whether Driftwood Furniture Ltd should open a factory in China. Do you think it should? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Producing inside a market avoids import quotas [k]. A Chinese factory would avoid the 18,000 table quota and the 16% freight rise for Driftwood Furniture Ltd [app], keeping access to its main market [an].

Against: A new factory is a large, hard-to-reverse commitment [k]. The dong's 7% depreciation already makes Vietnamese costs lower than Chinese costs [app], so a new plant may be uncompetitive [an].

Conclusion: Test Australian buyers before committing to a factory [eval]. A fixed investment is risky while the quota may change and the weaker dong supports exports [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Local production avoids import quotas.
A new factory is a costly, hard-to-reverse commitment.
application_max_2: A factory avoids the 18,000 table quota and 16% freight rise.
The dong has depreciated 7% against the dollar.
analysis_max_2: Local production keeps access to the main Chinese market.
The new plant may cost more to run than Vietnam.
evaluation_max_2: Test Australia before building a factory.
A fixed investment is risky while the quota may change.

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Sableford Hotels Ltd is a private limited company in Egypt running 6 hotels with 1,800 rooms, earning $54,000,000 a year from European tourists. Inflation has risen to 29% and the Egyptian pound has depreciated 22% against the euro, while the government has cut fuel subsidies, raising electricity bills by 40%. Occupancy is 68%. Directors must decide whether to raise room prices by 15% or cut staff numbers by 120.

questions.question_text: Define 'subsidy'.
questions.model_answer: A subsidy is a payment by government to a business to reduce its costs, such as the fuel subsidy whose removal raised Sableford Hotels Ltd electricity bills by 40% [2].

knowledge_max_2: A government payment to reduce business costs
It lowers prices or helps firms stay viable

questions.question_text: Outline two effects of the pound's 22% depreciation on Sableford Hotels Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: A weaker currency makes holidays cheaper for foreign visitors [k]. A euro now buys 22% more Egyptian pounds, making rooms at Sableford Hotels Ltd's 6 hotels cheaper and lifting occupancy above 68% [app].

Point two: A weaker currency raises the cost of imported supplies [k]. Imported food, drink and spare parts cost more pounds while inflation is 29% [app].

knowledge_max_2: A weaker currency makes holidays cheaper for foreigners.
A weaker currency raises imported supply costs.
application_max_2: A euro buys 22% more pounds for 1,800 rooms in Egypt.
Imports cost more pounds with inflation at 29%.

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the pound's 22% depreciation on Sableford Hotels Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: More European tourists [k], because a euro now buys 22% more Egyptian pounds [app], making Sableford's rooms and meals cheaper and lifting occupancy above 68% [an].

Point 2: Dearer imported supplies [k], as imported food, drink and spare parts cost more pounds [app], adding to costs when inflation is already 29% [an].

knowledge_max_2: Depreciation makes a country cheaper for foreign visitors
Imported supplies become more expensive
application_max_2: 22% depreciation against the euro; occupancy 68%
Inflation at 29%; electricity bills up 40%
analysis_max_2: Higher visitor numbers raise room revenue
Import costs and inflation squeeze profit margins

questions.question_text: Consider whether Sableford Hotels Ltd should raise room prices by 15%. Do you think it should? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: A price rise can cover higher operating costs [k]. A 15% rise adds $8,100,000 a year at 68% occupancy for Sableford Hotels Ltd, covering electricity up 40% and inflation of 29% [app], while the 22% weaker pound keeps European guests able to pay [an].

Against: Higher prices may deter price-sensitive tour operators [k], and cutting 120 staff would reduce service quality [app], which could deter them more than a modest rise [an].

Conclusion: Raise prices, but by less than 15% [eval]. The depreciated pound allows a higher margin while still undercutting euro-zone rivals [eval].

knowledge_max_2: A price rise can cover higher operating costs.
Price-sensitive tour operators may be deterred.
application_max_2: 15% adds $8,100,000 at 68% occupancy against 40% higher electricity.
Cutting 120 staff would reduce service quality in 6 hotels.
analysis_max_2: The 22% weaker pound keeps rooms affordable for Europeans.
Poor service could deter operators more than a modest rise.
evaluation_max_2: Raise prices by less than 15%.
The weaker pound allows margin while undercutting euro-zone rivals.

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Lanternhill Brewing Ltd is a private limited company in Germany bottling 24,000,000 bottles of beer a year, of which 40% are returned for reuse. A new deposit return scheme charges $0.25 per bottle and the government has raised the packaging tax to $1,200 per tonne, while energy costs have climbed 31%. Supermarkets refuse any price increase. Directors must decide whether to buy a $4,500,000 bottle-washing line or switch to aluminium cans.

questions.question_text: Define 'external cost'.
questions.model_answer: An external cost is a harmful effect of production felt by third parties, such as the packaging waste from Lanternhill Brewing Ltd's 24,000,000 bottles [2].

knowledge_max_2: A cost of production borne by third parties
Harm such as pollution not paid for by the firm

questions.question_text: Outline two benefits of the deposit return scheme for Lanternhill Brewing Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: Returned bottles can be reused, reducing material costs [k]. Some 9,600,000 of the 24,000,000 bottles can be refilled instead of buying new glass, with packaging tax at $1,200 per tonne [app].

Point two: Recycling can improve a firm's image with retailers [k]. German supermarkets refuse price rises, so a greener image may help Lanternhill Brewing Ltd win shelf space [app].

knowledge_max_2: Reused bottles reduce glass purchase costs.
Recycling improves image with customers and retailers.
application_max_2: 9,600,000 returned bottles refilled instead of new glass at $1,200 per tonne tax.
German supermarkets refuse price rises, valuing a green image.

questions.question_text: Explain two ways the deposit return scheme might benefit Lanternhill Brewing Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Cheaper glass supply [k], because 9,600,000 returned bottles can be washed and refilled instead of buying new ones [app], saving money when the packaging tax is $1,200 per tonne [an].

Point 2: Greener brand image [k], as customers see the firm acting on waste [app], which may win shelf space and loyalty in German supermarkets that refuse price rises [an].

knowledge_max_2: Reuse reduces raw material purchases
Environmental action can strengthen brand image
application_max_2: 9,600,000 bottles returned; $0.25 deposit
Packaging tax $1,200 per tonne; energy up 31%
analysis_max_2: Lower material costs offset the packaging tax
Green image supports sales where prices cannot rise

questions.question_text: Consider whether Lanternhill Brewing Ltd should buy the $4,500,000 bottle-washing line. Do you think it should? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Reusing packaging can cut costs over several years [k]. Refilling 9,600,000 bottles limits exposure to the $1,200 per tonne packaging tax in Germany [app], and the deposit scheme guarantees returns while supporting a green image where prices cannot rise [an].

Against: A large fixed cost is risky when energy prices rise [k]. Energy is up 31% and washing uses hot water and power [app], while aluminium cans avoid the deposit scheme and are lighter to transport [an].

Conclusion: Buy the washing line [eval]. Reuse spreads the one-off $4,500,000 over years, unlike exposure to metal prices [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Reuse can cut packaging costs over time.
A large fixed cost is risky when energy rises.
application_max_2: Refilling 9,600,000 bottles limits the $1,200 per tonne tax in Germany.
Energy up 31% makes washing expensive.
analysis_max_2: The deposit scheme guarantees a steady supply of returns.
Cans avoid the scheme and are lighter to transport.
evaluation_max_2: Buy the bottle-washing line.
Reuse spreads $4,500,000 over years of avoided tax.

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Elmswood Toys Ltd is a private limited company in Poland making 1,200,000 wooden puzzles a year, exporting 55% to Germany at $12 each. Germany has imposed a 12.5% tariff on imported toys and the zloty has appreciated 8% against the dollar. A German rival sells similar puzzles at $13. Directors must decide whether to cut their price so importers still pay $12 or keep $12 and let importers pay the tariff.

questions.question_text: Define 'tariff'.
questions.model_answer: A tariff is a tax on imported goods, such as the 12.5% charge Germany now adds to Elmswood Toys Ltd puzzles priced at $12 [2].

knowledge_max_2: A tax on imported goods
It raises the price paid by importers

questions.question_text: Outline two effects of the zloty's 8% appreciation on Elmswood Toys Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: An appreciation reduces home-currency earnings from exports [k]. Each $12 puzzle earns fewer zloty for Elmswood Toys Ltd, affecting 55% of its 1,200,000 puzzles sold to Germany [app].

Point two: An appreciation lowers the cost of dollar-priced imports [k]. Imported wood and paint cost fewer zloty, partly offsetting the 12.5% tariff [app].

knowledge_max_2: Appreciation reduces export earnings in home currency.
Appreciation lowers the cost of dollar imports.
application_max_2: $12 puzzles earn fewer zloty on 55% of 1,200,000 units to Germany.
Wood and paint cost fewer zloty against the 12.5% tariff.

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the zloty's 8% appreciation on Elmswood Toys Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Dearer puzzles in dollars [k], because each $12 puzzle now needs fewer zloty to make the same margin [app], so Elmswood must charge more or accept lower profit on 55% of its 1,200,000 puzzles [an].

Point 2: Cheaper imported wood and paint [k], as inputs bought in dollars cost fewer zloty [app], which partly offsets the tariff pressure at $12 a puzzle [an].

knowledge_max_2: Appreciation makes exports less price competitive
Imported inputs become cheaper
application_max_2: 8% appreciation against the dollar; $12 price
55% of 1,200,000 puzzles exported to Germany
analysis_max_2: Higher dollar prices risk losing market share
Cheaper inputs cushion the effect on margin

questions.question_text: Consider whether Elmswood Toys Ltd should cut its price to $10.67. Do you think it should? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Cutting price can keep the landed price competitive [k]. At $10.67 the border price stays $12 for German importers despite the 12.5% tariff, against a rival's $13 [app], so holding volume on 660,000 puzzles protects factory capacity use [an].

Against: A price cut permanently lowers revenue per unit [k]. The $1.33 cut plus the 8% appreciation squeezes margin [app], and buyers may accept $13.50 since it is close to the $13 German rival [an].

Conclusion: Keep the $12 price [eval]. A permanent cut is worse than a temporary tariff, so compete on quality instead [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Cutting price can keep the landed price competitive.
A price cut permanently lowers unit revenue.
application_max_2: $10.67 keeps the border price at $12 against a $13 rival.
A $1.33 cut plus 8% appreciation on 660,000 puzzles.
analysis_max_2: Holding volume protects factory capacity use.
Buyers may accept $13.50 as close to the rival's $13.
evaluation_max_2: Keep the $12 price.
Compete on quality rather than accept a permanent cut.

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Thistledown Bakeries Ltd is a private limited company in Kenya baking 90,000 loaves a day, sold at $0.60 each. questions.question_text: Define 'minimum wage'.

Set by government and binding on employers

questions.question_text: Outline two effects of the 28% rise in wheat prices on Thistledown Bakeries Ltd.

knowledge_max_2: A key ingredient price rise raises costs.
Firms may reduce product size to protect margin.
application_max_2: Wheat is up 28% on 90,000 daily loaves in Kenya with a $0.65 price cap.
Loaf cut from 800 to 700 grams.

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the 28% rise in wheat prices on Thistledown Bakeries Ltd.
questions.model_answer:

knowledge_max_2: Raw material costs are a large part of food costs
Firms may reduce quantity to avoid raising price
application_max_2: Wheat up 28%; 90,000 loaves a day at $0.60
Supermarkets cap price at $0.65
analysis_max_2: Margin squeezed between rising costs and capped prices
Shrinking the loaf risks customer goodwill

questions.question_text: Consider whether Thistledown Bakeries Ltd should raise the price to $0.70 a loaf. Do you think it should? Justify your answer.

Fines reduce cash available for investment.
application_max_2: 3 restaurant chains stopped buying 15,000,000 portions in Paraguay.
The $900,000 fine reduces funds for a $5,400,000 plant.

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the pollution fine and boycott on Millbrook Poultry Ltd.

Fines are an unavoidable cost that reduces profit
application_max_2: 3 restaurant chains boycotting
analysis_max_2: Lost restaurant contracts cut volume and cash flow
Fine reduces internal funds for environmental investment

Inflation has reached 8.2% and leather prices are rising faster than wages. Directors must decide whether to raise boot prices by 5% or hold prices and accept a lower margin on export orders.

questions.question_text: Define 'inflation'.
questions.model_answer: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level, so money buys less over time [2]; Romania's 8.2% rate is raising Carpathia Footwear Ltd's leather and wage costs.

knowledge_max_2: Sustained rise in average prices
Reduces purchasing power

questions.question_text: Outline two effects of 8.2% inflation on Carpathia Footwear Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: Material costs rise [k]. An 8.2% rise on EUR 1,400,000 adds EUR 114,800 a year, and leather is climbing faster than wages [app].

Point two: Export contracts become risky [k]. Prices agreed months ahead no longer cover costs at 8.2% inflation, so Carpathia Footwear Ltd may lose money on accepted boot orders [app].

knowledge_max_2: Inflation raises material costs
Fixed-price contracts become loss-making
application_max_2: EUR 114,800 added to EUR 1,400,000 of leather materials
Romanian boot exports with prices agreed in advance

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of 8.2% inflation on Carpathia Footwear Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Materials costs rise [k]. An 8.2% rise on EUR 1,400,000 adds EUR 114,800 a year [app], and because leather is rising faster than wages, the squeeze is worse than the headline rate suggests [an].

Point 2: Export contracts become risky [k]. Prices agreed months ahead with foreign buyers no longer cover costs at 8.2% inflation [app], so the firm may make a loss on orders it has already accepted [an].

knowledge_max_2: Higher input costs
Fixed-price contracts become unprofitable
application_max_2: EUR 114,800 added cost
Export prices agreed in advance
analysis_max_2: Leather rises faster than wages
Losses on orders already signed

questions.question_text: Consider whether Carpathia Footwear Ltd should raise boot prices by 5%. Do you think the directors should raise prices? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: A 5% rise recovers much of the EUR 114,800 cost increase and protects margin on boots in Romania [k]. Export buyers expect periodic increases when inflation is 8.2% [app]. Price rises can be phased to spread the impact [an].

Against: Five per cent still leaves part of the cost uncovered, and export buyers may switch to cheaper Asian suppliers [k]. Holding prices could win volume that spreads 260 wages over more pairs [app]. Lower margins remain a risk [an].

Conclusion: Raise prices by 5% and add an inflation clause to export terms, because absorbing EUR 114,800 is unaffordable [eval]. Review prices if input costs keep climbing [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Price rise recovers rising material costs
Rivals and cost gaps limit the rise
application_max_2: 5% rise against EUR 114,800 on EUR 1,400,000
260 employees making leather boots in Romania
analysis_max_2: Higher volume would spread labour costs
Asian suppliers may undercut export prices
evaluation_max_2: Raise by 5% with an inflation clause
Protect margins against further cost rises

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Rila Rose Ltd is a private limited company in Bulgaria distilling rose oil, buying 12,000 kilograms of petals a year from small growers. questions.question_text: Define 'ethical trading'.

knowledge_max_2: Fair treatment of workers and suppliers
Often verified by independent standards

questions.question_text: Outline two effects of joining the fair trade scheme on Rila Rose Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: Costs rise but a contract follows [k]. Paying $18 more per kilogram on 12,000 kilograms adds $216,000, which secures a $2,000,000 cosmetics contract [app].

Point two: Supply becomes more reliable [k]. Guaranteed premiums encourage the small growers who supply petals in Bulgaria to keep producing during the short harvest [app].

knowledge_max_2: Premium payments secure a large contract
Fair trade terms support supplier loyalty
application_max_2: $216,000 premium for a $2,000,000 rose oil contract
12,000 kilograms of petals from small growers in Bulgaria

questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Costs rise but a large contract follows [k]. Paying $216,000 more to growers secures a contract worth $2,000,000 a year [app], which is nearly ten times the extra payment [an].

Point 2: Supply becomes more reliable [k]. Guaranteed premiums encourage the small growers who supply 12,000 kilograms to stay in production [app], protecting Rila Rose from shortages of petals during the short harvest [an].

knowledge_max_2: Higher payments to suppliers
More secure supply and customer contract
application_max_2: $216,000 premium
$2,000,000 contract
analysis_max_2: Contract value far exceeds the premium
Loyal growers secure petal supply

questions.question_text: Consider whether Rila Rose Ltd should join the fair trade scheme. Do you think the directors should join? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:

Against: The premium is paid whether or not the buyer renews after year one, leaving a permanent cost [k]. Audits and record keeping add administration for a small distiller in Bulgaria [app]. A non-renewal would leave the scheme with little benefit [an].

Conclusion: Join, because the contract value makes the $216,000 easy to justify [eval]. Seek a longer commitment from the buyer before the second year [eval].

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Morava Berry Ltd is a private limited company in Serbia freezing raspberries, exporting 4,000 tonnes a year at EUR 2,200 a tonne to the European Union. The EU has cut Serbia's quota to 3,200 tonnes, and no other buyer will take the surplus. Directors must decide whether to build cold storage for the surplus or reduce growers' contracts.

questions.question_text: Define 'trade barrier'.
questions.model_answer: A trade barrier is any measure that restricts international trade, such as a tariff, quota or licence [2]; the EU quota limiting Morava Berry Ltd to 3,200 tonnes is a barrier to its exports.

knowledge_max_2: Measure restricting trade between countries
Includes tariffs, quotas and regulations

questions.question_text: Outline two effects of the EU quota cut on Morava Berry Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: Export revenue falls [k]. Losing 800 tonnes at EUR 2,200 removes EUR 1,760,000, leaving the Serbian freezing plant below capacity [app].

Point two: Growers face uncertain contracts [k]. With only 3,200 tonnes sellable, Morava Berry Ltd may cut purchases, and growers could switch to other crops [app].

knowledge_max_2: Quota cuts export revenue and capacity use
Suppliers face reduced demand for their crop
application_max_2: 800 tonnes at EUR 2,200 loses EUR 1,760,000
Raspberry growers in Serbia selling to the European Union

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the EU quota on Morava Berry Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Export revenue falls [k]. Losing 800 tonnes at EUR 2,200 removes EUR 1,760,000 of sales [app], so the Serbian freezing plant runs below capacity while its fixed costs remain [an].

Point 2: Growers face uncertain contracts [k]. With only 3,200 tonnes now sellable, Morava may cut purchases from its growers [app], and they may switch to other crops, reducing future supply [an].

knowledge_max_2: Lower export sales

questions.question_text: Consider whether Morava Berry Ltd should build cold storage for the surplus rather than cut growers' contracts. Do you think the directors should build storage? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Cold storage keeps 800 tonnes in condition until another buyer is found, protecting EUR 1,760,000 of potential sales [k]. Keeping growers loyal avoids a shortage if the European Union quota rises again [app]. The plant can keep using its freezing capacity [an].

Against: Storage costs money and raspberries lose quality, so the surplus may sell at a discount [k]. The quota may be permanent, making storage an ongoing cost for Morava Berry Ltd [app]. No other buyer has yet been found [an].

Conclusion: Build limited storage for one season, because holding 800 tonnes buys time to find buyers [eval]. Keep growers on side while the quota is reviewed [eval].

evaluation_max_2: Use temporary storage for one season
Preserve grower relationships meanwhile

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Saaremaa Plywood Ltd is a private limited company in Estonia making birch plywood, with sales of $6,400,000 a year and 300 workers. National unemployment has reached 9.6% and construction orders are falling, so sales are expected to drop 14%. questions.question_text: Define 'unemployment'.

knowledge_max_2: People without work but seeking it
Measured as a percentage of the labour force

questions.question_text: Outline two effects of rising unemployment on Saaremaa Plywood Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: Demand for plywood falls [k]. With unemployment at 9.6% and sales down 14%, the Estonian mill loses $896,000 of revenue and cannot use all its capacity [app].

Point two: Wage pressure eases [k]. High unemployment means 300 workers are less likely to demand large rises, and vacancies are easier to fill [app].

knowledge_max_2: Lower demand reduces sales and capacity use
Higher unemployment reduces wage pressure
application_max_2: Sales down 14% removes $896,000 at Saaremaa Plywood Ltd
300 workers with unemployment at 9.6% in Estonia

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of rising unemployment on Saaremaa Plywood Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Demand for plywood falls [k]. With unemployment at 9.6% and sales down 14%, the firm loses $896,000 of revenue [app], leaving the mill with capacity it cannot use [an].

Point 2: Wage pressure eases [k]. High unemployment in Estonia means 300 workers are less likely to demand big rises and vacancies are easier to fill [app], which partly offsets the lost revenue [an].

knowledge_max_2: Lower demand for building materials
Weaker wage pressure
application_max_2: $896,000 lost sales

Easier recruitment and lower pay pressure

questions.question_text: Consider whether Saaremaa Plywood Ltd should make 60 of its 300 staff redundant. Do you think the directors should make redundancies? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Cutting 60 jobs matches the 14% fall that removes $896,000 of sales and protects cash [k]. Paying 300 workers for hours not needed is more costly than a smaller workforce [app]. Cash is preserved while construction is weak [an].

Against: Plywood skills take time to learn, and rehiring when construction recovers is costly [k]. Reduced hours for all 300 keep the Estonian mill ready to raise output quickly [app]. Morale suffers less when jobs are shared [an].

Conclusion: Use reduced hours first, because the fall looks cyclical and $896,000 of sales should return [eval]. Reconsider redundancies only if orders stay low [eval].

Review if the decline lasts

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Kurzeme Peat Ltd is a private limited company in Latvia extracting peat for bagged garden compost, taking 240,000 cubic metres a year from protected bogs. questions.model_answer:
Point one: Extraction becomes much costlier [k]. The levy of $4.50 a cubic metre on 240,000 cubic metres adds $1,080,000 a year [app].

Point two: Restoration raises the cost of staying [k]. The $600,000 bog restoration is needed before the Latvian licence is renewed for five years [app].

Point 2: Restoration raises the barrier to staying [k]. The $600,000 bog restoration must be funded before the licence is renewed [app], so total compliance costs $1,680,000 in the first year and may make the site unviable [an].

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Colonia Dairy Ltd is a family-owned private limited company in Uruguay making powdered milk for export, with sales of $12,000,000 a year. Usually has headquarters in a home country

Point two: The partner brings export experience [k]. An Argentine dairy multinational can open markets for Colonia Dairy Ltd's powdered milk beyond Uruguay [app].

A multinational partner brings expertise and market access
application_max_2: $4,000,000 avoids $380,000 interest at 9.5%

Point 2: Control is shared [k]. A 40% share values the whole company at $10,000,000 but gives the multinational a strong say in pricing and exports [app], which may limit the family's independence [an].

Against: Giving up 40% of a company worth $10,000,000 surrenders future dividends and control [k]. A loan keeps family ownership intact at Colonia Dairy Ltd, and interest may fall if rates ease [app]. The partner may push its own pricing policy [an].

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Bergslagen Batteries Ltd is a private limited company in Sweden making lithium battery packs, with sales of $14,000,000 and 220 employees. questions.question_text: Define 'interest rate'.
questions.model_answer: An interest rate is the percentage charged for borrowing money over a period, set largely by central bank policy [2]; Sweden's 4.5% rate sets the annual cost of Bergslagen Batteries Ltd's $9,000,000 loan.

knowledge_max_2: Percentage cost of borrowing
Influenced by central bank policy

questions.model_answer:
Point one: Borrowing for the second line costs more [k]. Interest on $9,000,000 is $405,000 a year, $112,500 more than at 3.25% [app].

Point two: Customers delay purchases [k]. Swedish hauliers and builders facing 4.5% rates postpone battery conversions, weakening demand for Bergslagen Batteries Ltd's packs [app].

knowledge_max_2: Higher rates raise financing costs
Higher rates reduce customer demand

Point 2: Customers delay electric conversions [k]. Swedish hauliers and builders facing 4.5% rates postpone battery purchases [app], weakening demand just as Bergslagen considers expanding capacity [an].

Against: Borrowing at 4.5% costs $112,500 more than before, and customers are delaying orders [k]. Building capacity as demand slows could leave the line idle while interest is still due [app]. Swedish hauliers may wait for cheaper finance [an].

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Marrowgate Steel Ltd is a private limited company in Peru rolling reinforcing bars for builders, earning $64,000,000 a year from 96,000 tonnes. Inflation has reached 7.4% and the central bank has raised interest rates to 9.25%. questions.model_answer:

Point two: Dearer credit reduces customers' spending on construction [k]. Peruvian builders facing 9.25% finance costs may cut orders for the $64,000,000 of steel output [app].

Point 2: Builders who buy steel on credit cut orders [k]. Higher repayments squeeze Peruvian construction firms [app], so demand for reinforcing bars falls just as Marrowgate needs volume to cover its fixed costs [an].
