unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Quillhaven Paper Ltd is a private limited company in Norway recycling waste into office paper, producing 42,000 tonnes a year at $780 a tonne. A carbon levy of $46 a tonne now applies to its gas dryers, while a European scheme pays $18 a tonne for paper collected. The board must decide whether to spend $3,600,000 converting the dryers to electric heat.

questions.question_text: Define 'external cost'.
questions.model_answer: An external cost is a cost of production borne by a third party rather than the business [k]. Quillhaven's gas dryers emit carbon that Norwegian residents pay for through climate damage, which is why the $46 levy exists [app].

knowledge_max_2: Cost of an activity paid by a third party
Not included in the firm's private costs

questions.question_text: Outline two ways in which the carbon levy may affect Quillhaven Paper Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: A carbon levy raises the cost of each tonne produced [k]. At $46 a tonne on 42,000 tonnes, Quillhaven Paper Ltd pays $1,932,000 a year while selling paper at $780 a tonne [app].

Point two: Payments for collected paper give the business extra revenue [k]. The European scheme pays $18 a tonne for paper collected by Quillhaven, which helps offset the levy [app].

knowledge_max_2: A carbon levy raises the cost per tonne produced
Payments for collected paper give revenue to offset green costs
application_max_2: $46 a tonne on 42,000 tonnes adds $1,932,000 at Quillhaven
$18 a tonne is paid for collected office paper

questions.question_text: Explain two ways the carbon levy may affect Quillhaven Paper Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Costs rise on every tonne dried [k]. The $46 levy adds $1,932,000 a year to a business charging $780 a tonne [app], and because paper buyers can switch supplier easily much of that cannot be passed on, so the margin on each tonne shrinks [an].

Point 2: Investment in electric dryers becomes more attractive [k]. The $18 a tonne paid for collected paper offsets part of the $3,600,000 conversion [app], reducing exposure to future carbon taxes and strengthening the recycled brand [an].

knowledge_max_2: Levy raises operating costs
Levy rewards cleaner technology
application_max_2: $1,932,000 a year on 42,000 tonnes at $46
$18 a tonne received for collected paper
analysis_max_2: Buyers resist higher prices so margins fall
Conversion cost is partly offset by recycling income

questions.question_text: Consider whether Quillhaven Paper Ltd should spend $3,600,000 converting its dryers to electric heat. Do you think the board should go ahead? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Removing the levy saves a recurring annual cost [k]. Quillhaven Paper Ltd pays $46 on each of 42,000 tonnes, or $1,932,000 a year, and sells paper at $780 a tonne [app]. That saving covers much of the $3,600,000 conversion within two years and protects the business if Norway raises carbon taxes [an].

Against: The conversion needs a large upfront outlay and creates a new dependency [k]. Quillhaven must find $3,600,000 while earning $780 a tonne, and the $18 a tonne collection scheme is small beside it [app]. If electricity prices rise or Norway cuts the levy, the expected saving shrinks and cash is tied up [an].

Conclusion: Convert, but only if finance is secure [eval]. Spread the $3,600,000 over several years rather than paying it from one year's reserves [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Removing the levy saves a recurring $1,932,000 a year
Conversion requires a large $3,600,000 outlay and new energy dependency
application_max_2: A $46 levy on 42,000 tonnes costs Quillhaven $1,932,000
The $18 a tonne collection scheme partly offsets the $3,600,000 cost
analysis_max_2: The annual levy saving repays much of the conversion within two years
Higher electricity prices or a lower levy reduce the net benefit
evaluation_max_2: Convert provided finance is secure
Spread the outlay instead of using one year's reserves

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Bluewren Seafoods plc is a public limited company in Sri Lanka freezing prawns for export, shipping 5,400 tonnes a year at $6,200 a tonne to buyers in Japan. The government has imposed a 12% export levy, and freight costs have risen by 9%. The board must decide whether to absorb the levy or raise its dollar price to Japanese importers.

questions.question_text: Define 'export'.
questions.model_answer: An export is a good or service sold to a buyer in another country [k]. Bluewren's frozen prawns leave Sri Lanka for Japan and earn $6,200 a tonne in foreign currency [app].

knowledge_max_2: Good or service sold abroad
Earns foreign currency for the seller

questions.question_text: Outline two ways in which the 12% export levy may affect Bluewren Seafoods plc.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: Absorbing the levy cuts the margin on every tonne [k]. A 12% levy on a $6,200 tonne of prawns takes $744 from Bluewren Seafoods plc, leaving $5,456 [app].

Point two: Raising the price risks losing buyers [k]. Japanese importers comparing offers on 5,400 tonnes may switch from Bluewren to Thai suppliers if its dollar price rises [app].

knowledge_max_2: Absorbing a levy reduces revenue kept per tonne
Passing costs to buyers can lose price-sensitive export orders
application_max_2: 12% of $6,200 takes $744 per tonne from Bluewren
Japanese importers buying 5,400 tonnes compare Thai suppliers

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the 12% export levy may reduce the competitiveness of Bluewren Seafoods plc.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Absorbing the levy cuts the margin on every tonne [k]. At $6,200 a tonne the levy takes $744, so Bluewren keeps $5,456 [app]; with freight already up 9%, the price it can offer Japanese buyers is squeezed against rival suppliers [an].

Point 2: Raising the price risks losing orders [k]. Japanese importers buying 5,400 tonnes compare offers closely [app], so a higher dollar price may send them to Thai exporters, leaving Bluewren's cold stores half empty [an].

knowledge_max_2: Margin per tonne falls
Higher prices lose price-sensitive importers
application_max_2: $744 on every $6,200 tonne
Freight costs up 9% on 5,400 tonnes
analysis_max_2: Costs cannot be passed on without losing volume
Empty capacity raises unit fixed costs

questions.question_text: Consider whether Bluewren Seafoods plc should raise its price to Japanese importers. Do you think it should pass on the levy? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: A higher price protects the margin on each tonne [k]. Bluewren Seafoods plc loses $744 on every $6,200 tonne if it absorbs the 12% levy, and freight is already up 9% [app]. Recovering part of the levy across 5,400 tonnes restores profit that would otherwise be lost [an].

Against: Japanese importers can switch to cheaper suppliers [k]. They buy 5,400 tonnes of prawns and can turn to Thai exporters if Bluewren raises its dollar price [app]. A full pass-through may cut volume and leave the cold stores half empty [an].

Conclusion: Raise the price by only part of the levy [eval]. Recovering about half keeps Bluewren close to rivals while limiting the loss per tonne; a full rise is too risky [eval].

knowledge_max_2: A higher price protects margin lost to the levy
Japanese buyers can switch to Thai suppliers
application_max_2: A 12% levy takes $744 from each $6,200 tonne
Buyers of 5,400 tonnes in Japan compare rival exporters
analysis_max_2: A partial recovery across 5,400 tonnes restores lost profit
A full rise may cut volume and idle cold stores
evaluation_max_2: Raise by only part of the levy
A full pass-through is too risky in a price-sensitive market

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Harlowmoor Cement Ltd is a private limited company in Morocco producing bagged cement, selling 1,300,000 tonnes a year at $84 a tonne. The economy has entered recession with unemployment at 13.6%, and the government has cut infrastructure spending by 15%. The board must decide whether to reduce output by 200,000 tonnes or hold output and cut the price by 8%.

questions.question_text: Define 'recession'.
questions.model_answer: A recession is a period when a country's output falls over two successive quarters or more [k]. Morocco's downturn has pushed unemployment to 13.6%, so Harlowmoor's builders buy fewer bags of cement [app].

knowledge_max_2: Fall in national output over two quarters
Unemployment usually rises

questions.question_text: Outline two effects of the recession on Harlowmoor Cement Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: A recession reduces demand from construction customers [k]. Infrastructure spending is down 15% and unemployment is 13.6%, so Moroccan builders delay projects that would use Harlowmoor Cement Ltd's bagged cement [app].

Point two: Discounting reduces revenue per tonne [k]. An 8% cut takes the $84 price to $77.28 on 1,300,000 tonnes of cement [app].

knowledge_max_2: Recession reduces demand from construction customers
A price cut reduces revenue per tonne sold
application_max_2: Infrastructure spending down 15% with unemployment at 13.6%
An 8% cut takes the $84 price to $77.28 on 1,300,000 tonnes

questions.question_text: Explain two ways the recession may affect Harlowmoor Cement Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Demand from construction falls [k]. With infrastructure spending down 15% and unemployment at 13.6%, Moroccan builders delay projects [app], so the 1,300,000 tonnes sold at $84 may not find buyers [an].

Point 2: Discounting damages revenue [k]. An 8% cut takes the price to $77.28 [app], lowering income by $8,736,000 even if volume holds, while kiln costs cannot be reduced quickly, so profit falls faster than sales [an].

knowledge_max_2: Construction demand falls
Price cutting reduces revenue
application_max_2: Spending cut 15%, unemployment 13.6%
8% cut takes the price to $77.28
analysis_max_2: Fewer buyers for 1,300,000 tonnes
Fixed kiln costs cannot be cut quickly

questions.question_text: Consider whether Harlowmoor Cement Ltd should cut output by 200,000 tonnes rather than cut its price by 8%. Do you think this is the better choice? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Holding the price protects the margin needed to cover kiln costs [k]. Harlowmoor Cement Ltd avoids the $8,736,000 revenue loss from discounting 1,300,000 tonnes from $84 to $77.28 [app]. Keeping the price preserves profit on the tonnes still sold when infrastructure spending is down 15% [an].

Against: Lower output raises the fixed cost per tonne [k]. Cutting 200,000 tonnes leaves kilns underused in a country where unemployment is 13.6% [app]. Importers may take the shelf space that Harlowmoor gives up, and jobs are lost just when demand is weak [an].

Conclusion: Cut output rather than price [eval]. With infrastructure spending down 15%, defending the $84 price matters more than defending volume because margins are too thin for an 8% discount [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Cutting output protects the price and margin
Lower output raises unit fixed costs and may lose market share
application_max_2: Discounting 1,300,000 tonnes from $84 to $77.28 loses $8,736,000
Cutting 200,000 tonnes with unemployment at 13.6%
analysis_max_2: A stable price preserves profit on remaining sales
Underused kilns and importers raise costs and lost share
evaluation_max_2: Cut output rather than discount
Defend the $84 price while infrastructure demand is down

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Silverbeck Laundry Ltd is a private limited company in New Zealand washing linen for 60 hotels, processing 2,800,000 kilograms a year at $1.45 a kilogram. The regional council has doubled its water discharge charge to $0.06 a kilogram and set a water use limit of 2,400,000 kilograms. Directors must decide whether to install a $640,000 water recycling unit.

questions.question_text: Define 'sustainable production'.
questions.model_answer: Sustainable production means making output while conserving resources and limiting harm so future generations can meet their needs [k]. Silverbeck must cut water use to 2,400,000 kilograms, well below its 2,800,000 kilogram throughput [app].

knowledge_max_2: Conserves resources for future generations
Limits waste and environmental damage

questions.question_text: Outline two effects of the water charge and limit on Silverbeck Laundry Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: The doubled discharge charge raises operating costs [k]. At $0.06 a kilogram on 2,800,000 kilograms, Silverbeck Laundry Ltd pays $168,000 a year on linen washed at $1.45 a kilogram [app].

Point two: The water limit caps the volume that can be processed [k]. The 2,400,000 kilogram limit leaves 400,000 kilograms from Silverbeck's 60 hotels unprocessed [app].

knowledge_max_2: A higher discharge charge raises cost per kilogram
A water use limit caps the volume that can be processed
application_max_2: $0.06 on 2,800,000 kilograms costs Silverbeck $168,000
The 2,400,000 kilogram limit affects 400,000 kilograms from 60 hotels

questions.question_text: Explain two ways the water charge and limit may affect Silverbeck Laundry Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: The doubled charge raises operating costs [k]. At $0.06 a kilogram on 2,800,000 kilograms Silverbeck pays $168,000 a year [app], and hotels compare laundry prices closely, so most of it must be absorbed and the margin on each kilogram falls [an].

Point 2: The 2,400,000 kilogram limit caps output [k]. Silverbeck can no longer process 400,000 kilograms of linen sent by its 60 hotels [app], so it must turn work away or spend $640,000 on recycling equipment [an].

knowledge_max_2: Charge raises operating costs
Limit caps throughput
application_max_2: $168,000 a year at $0.06 a kilogram
400,000 kilograms above the limit
analysis_max_2: Hotels resist price rises so margin falls
Growth is blocked with the 60 hotels

questions.question_text: Consider whether Silverbeck Laundry Ltd should install the $640,000 water recycling unit. Do you think it should? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: The unit keeps the business within the limit and retains contracts [k]. Silverbeck Laundry Ltd can process the 400,000 kilograms above the 2,400,000 kilogram limit and keep all 60 hotels [app]. Reusing water also avoids part of the $168,000 annual charge and protects against further council increases [an].

Against: The equipment is costly and contracts may be short [k]. The $640,000 unit equals almost four years of the current $168,000 charge, and the 60 hotels may not stay [app]. If the council relaxes the limit, the recycling unit becomes unnecessary and cash is tied up [an].

Conclusion: Install the unit, but phase the work [eval]. Protecting 400,000 kilograms of throughput and 60 hotel contracts is worth more than the $168,000 charge [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Recycling keeps output within the water limit
The $640,000 unit is a large cost against current charges
application_max_2: Silverbeck must protect 400,000 kilograms and 60 hotels
The unit costs almost four years of the $168,000 charge
analysis_max_2: Keeping contracts preserves revenue beyond the charge saved
A relaxed limit would leave the equipment unused
evaluation_max_2: Install the unit but phase the work
Revenue from hotels matters more than the charge

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Kestrelford Cycles plc is a public limited company in Bangladesh assembling bicycles, making 480,000 bikes a year at $95 each for buyers in Germany. A new trade bloc tariff of 14% has replaced duty-free access, and the taka has depreciated by 6% against the euro. The board must decide whether to build a factory inside the bloc or keep exporting.

questions.question_text: Define 'tariff'.
questions.model_answer: A tariff is a tax on imported goods [k]. The 14% tariff adds $13.30 to a $95 bicycle, raising the price German buyers pay [app].

knowledge_max_2: Tax on imports
Raises the price of imported goods

questions.question_text: Outline two effects of the 14% tariff on Kestrelford Cycles plc.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: A tariff raises the landed price of exports [k]. The 14% tariff adds $13.30 to each $95 bicycle that Kestrelford Cycles plc sends to Germany [app].

Point two: Currency depreciation makes exports cheaper abroad [k]. The 6% fall in the taka lowers the euro price of Kestrelford's 480,000 bicycles and offsets part of the tariff [app].

knowledge_max_2: A tariff raises the price of exports in the importing market
Depreciation makes exported goods cheaper abroad
application_max_2: 14% adds $13.30 to each $95 bicycle sold in Germany
A 6% taka fall helps 480,000 bicycles exported to Germany

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the 14% tariff on Kestrelford Cycles plc.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Each bike becomes dearer in Germany [k]. A $95 bicycle carries $13.30 of tariff [app], so German buyers comparing it with European-made bikes switch, and Kestrelford sells fewer of its 480,000 units [an].

Point 2: Building inside the bloc avoids the barrier [k]. A German factory would sell tariff-free but must match Bangladeshi costs [app]; the 6% depreciation of the taka already helps exports, so the business must weigh that against moving [an].

knowledge_max_2: Export price rises
Local production avoids the tariff
application_max_2: $13.30 on every $95 bike
Taka down 6% against the euro
analysis_max_2: Higher price cuts German demand
Moving loses low wage costs

questions.question_text: Consider whether Kestrelford Cycles plc should build a factory inside the trade bloc. Do you think it should? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: A factory inside the bloc removes the tariff [k]. Kestrelford Cycles plc would avoid the $13.30 duty on each $95 bicycle and protect access to the German market that takes much of its 480,000 output [app]. Local production also shortens delivery time and improves service [an].

Against: Moving production abroad gives up existing advantages [k]. A German plant loses low Bangladeshi wages and the 6% depreciation that already helps its exports [app]. The investment is large and the tariff may be removed by a future trade deal [an].

Conclusion: Do not build the factory yet [eval]. Keep exporting while the 6% currency fall offsets part of the $13.30 tariff and press for a trade agreement first [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Local production avoids the 14% tariff
A foreign factory loses low wages and a currency advantage
application_max_2: Avoiding $13.30 on each $95 bicycle protects 480,000 units
A 6% depreciation already supports exports from Bangladesh
analysis_max_2: Tariff-free local production improves access and delivery
A trade deal could make the investment unnecessary
evaluation_max_2: Keep exporting for now
Wait for a trade agreement before building abroad

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Tanager Confectionery Ltd is a private limited company in Uruguay making chocolate bars, with revenue of $27,500,000 a year and 310 staff. Inflation has risen to 8.9% and the government has increased the minimum wage by 11%, while cocoa prices are up 17%. Directors must decide whether to hold prices and accept lower margins or raise prices by 6%.

questions.question_text: Define 'minimum wage'.
questions.model_answer: A minimum wage is the lowest rate an employer may legally pay a worker [k]. Uruguay's 11% rise lifts Tanager's wage bill on top of 8.9% inflation [app].

knowledge_max_2: Lowest legal pay rate
Set by government and raises costs

questions.question_text: Outline two effects of rising costs on Tanager Confectionery Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: Rising input costs squeeze margins if prices are held [k]. Inflation of 8.9%, an 11% minimum wage rise and cocoa up 17% raise costs for Tanager Confectionery Ltd's 310 staff behind $27,500,000 of revenue [app].

Point two: A price rise may not cover the full cost increase [k]. Moving the chocolate bar from $2.50 to $2.65 recovers only part of an 11% wage rise, while shoppers facing 8.9% inflation may trade down [app].

knowledge_max_2: Rising wages and material costs squeeze margins
A small price rise may not cover the cost increase
application_max_2: Wages up 11% and cocoa up 17% with 8.9% inflation at Tanager
A 6% rise takes a $2.50 bar to $2.65

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of rising costs on Tanager Confectionery Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Margins are squeezed [k]. Inflation at 8.9%, an 11% wage rise and cocoa up 17% all raise unit costs [app], so unless the $2.50 bar price rises, profit on the output behind $27,500,000 of revenue falls [an].

Point 2: A 6% rise may not be enough [k]. Moving the bar to $2.65 recovers only part of an 11% wage increase [app], and shoppers facing 8.9% inflation may trade down to cheaper brands, so volume falls as well as margin [an].

knowledge_max_2: Unit costs rise
Price rise is smaller than cost rise
application_max_2: 8.9% inflation, 11% wages, cocoa up 17%
6% rise takes the bar to $2.65
analysis_max_2: Profit per bar falls if prices hold
Demand may fall at higher prices

questions.question_text: Consider whether Tanager Confectionery Ltd should raise its prices by 6%. Do you think it should? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: A price rise protects the margin on existing sales [k]. Tanager Confectionery Ltd faces inflation at 8.9%, wages up 11% and cocoa up 17%, so moving the bar to $2.65 recovers part of that on $27,500,000 of revenue [app]. Some recovery is better than accepting lower margins on every bar [an].

Against: Consumers facing 8.9% inflation are price-sensitive [k]. Shoppers may switch to rival bars rather than pay $2.65, leaving factory costs spread over fewer units [app]. A 6% rise is smaller than the 11% wage rise, so profit may still fall [an].

Conclusion: Raise prices by less than 6% after cutting waste [eval]. A smaller rise plus efficiency savings balances cost recovery against the risk of losing volume [eval].

knowledge_max_2: A price rise helps recover rising costs
Price-sensitive shoppers may switch to rivals
application_max_2: Costs rise from 8.9% inflation, 11% wages and 17% cocoa
A $2.65 bar is offered to shoppers under 8.9% inflation
analysis_max_2: Partial recovery is better than a fully squeezed margin
Lost volume spreads fixed factory costs over fewer bars
evaluation_max_2: Raise less than 6% and cut waste
Balance cost recovery against volume loss

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Ridgecombe Tannery Ltd is a private limited company in the Philippines curing leather for shoe makers, treating 18,000 tonnes of hides a year. questions.question_text: Define 'external cost'.

knowledge_max_2: Cost paid by a third party
Damage not charged to the producer

questions.question_text: Outline two ways the pollution may affect Ridgecombe Tannery Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: Pollution leads to a direct cost through the levy [k]. The proposed $34 a tonne on 18,000 tonnes of hides costs Ridgecombe Tannery Ltd $612,000 a year [app].

Point two: Pollution can damage reputation and orders [k]. Shoe makers audit suppliers' water records, and evidence that Ridgecombe's effluent kills fish in the river could cost contracts [app].

Pollution can damage reputation and customer orders
application_max_2: $34 a tonne on 18,000 tonnes costs Ridgecombe $612,000
Effluent kills fish in the river near the tannery

questions.question_text: Explain two ways the pollution may affect Ridgecombe Tannery Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: The business faces direct penalties [k]. A $34 levy on 18,000 tonnes costs $612,000 a year [app], a large sum for a tannery selling to price-sensitive shoe makers, so profit falls sharply [an].

Point 2: Reputation and orders are at risk [k]. Shoe brands audit their suppliers' water records [app], so evidence that effluent kills fish could lose Ridgecombe contracts worth more than the levy itself [an].

Reputation and contracts at risk

questions.model_answer:
For: The plant removes both the levy and the pollution [k]. Ridgecombe Tannery Ltd would stop paying $612,000 a year on 18,000 tonnes and recover the $1,900,000 in about three years [app]. Cleaner effluent also protects orders from shoe brands that audit water records [an].

Against: The plant is a heavy outlay with extra running costs [k]. Ridgecombe must find $1,900,000 on uncertain export demand, and the $34 levy may never be fully enforced [app]. Chemicals and power add costs after installation [an].

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Waxwing Optics plc is a public limited company in the Czech Republic grinding lenses for microscope makers, exporting 260,000 units a year at EUR 41 each. The koruna has appreciated by 11% against the euro, and a rival in Vietnam now charges EUR 35 a unit. The board must decide whether to cut its euro price or move assembly to Vietnam.

questions.question_text: Define 'appreciation'.
questions.model_answer: An appreciation is a rise in the value of a currency against another [k]. The koruna's 11% rise makes Waxwing's EUR 41 lenses dearer in euro terms for its microscope customers [app].

knowledge_max_2: Rise in a currency's value
Makes exports dearer abroad

questions.question_text: Outline two effects of the 11% appreciation on Waxwing Optics plc.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: Appreciation raises export prices in foreign currency [k]. An 11% appreciation makes the EUR 41 lens dearer unless Waxwing Optics plc accepts a lower margin, and the Vietnamese rival at EUR 35 is already EUR 6 cheaper [app].

Point two: Appreciation makes imported inputs cheaper [k]. Glass blanks and coatings bought abroad cost fewer korunas for Waxwing's 260,000 lenses [app].

knowledge_max_2: Appreciation raises the foreign-currency price of exports
Appreciation reduces the cost of imported inputs
application_max_2: EUR 41 lenses compete with a Vietnamese rival at EUR 35

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the 11% appreciation on Waxwing Optics plc.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Export prices rise in foreign currency [k]. An 11% appreciation makes each EUR 41 lens cost more euros unless Waxwing accepts a lower margin [app], and with the Vietnamese rival at EUR 35 the gap is already EUR 6 [an].

Point 2: Imported inputs become cheaper [k]. Glass blanks and coatings bought abroad cost fewer korunas [app], which softens the squeeze but is small beside the loss of competitiveness on 260,000 lenses [an].

Imported inputs cheaper
application_max_2: EUR 41 against a rival price of EUR 35

questions.question_text: Consider whether Waxwing Optics plc should cut its euro price to match the Vietnamese rival. Do you think it should? Justify your answer.

Against: Matching the rival destroys margin [k]. Waxwing Optics plc cannot match Vietnam's costs permanently, and an 11% appreciation already limits what it can earn [app]. A full cut may start a price war that only the lowest-cost producer wins [an].

Compete on precision and delivery from the Czech plant

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Dunlarkin Quarry Ltd is a private limited company in Ecuador extracting granite, selling 220,000 tonnes a year at $38 a tonne. A new royalty of 7% has been imposed on sales, and diesel prices have risen 22% after a subsidy cut. questions.question_text: Define 'royalty'.
questions.model_answer: A royalty is a payment to a government or resource owner for the right to extract a material [k]. Ecuador charges Dunlarkin 7% of the value of every tonne of granite sold [app].

knowledge_max_2: Payment for the right to extract
Usually a percentage of sales value

questions.question_text: Outline two effects of the new royalty on Dunlarkin Quarry Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: A royalty reduces profit on every tonne sold [k]. A 7% royalty on $8,360,000 of granite sales takes $585,200 from Dunlarkin Quarry Ltd [app].

Point two: A price rise can recover a royalty but may deter buyers [k]. Moving from $38 to $41 would add $660,000 on 220,000 tonnes, but diesel is up 22% and builders can switch quarry [app].

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Orinoco Cocoa is a co-operative in Ghana processing 8,000 tonnes of cocoa beans a year, with 320 member farmers, a wage bill of $3,600,000 and revenue of $19,200,000. unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity

Payment leaves the importing country

questions.question_text: Outline two effects of the 10% tariff and weaker pound on Rivenhall Pumps.

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Ostrova Glassworks is a private limited company in Estonia making 14,000,000 glass bottles a year, with 280 staff and revenue of $19,600,000. The economy has entered recession, with GDP falling 2.4% and unemployment rising from 6.1% to 8.3%, so orders are expected to fall 12%. Directors must decide whether to cut output and 40 jobs or hold output and build inventory.

questions.question_text: Define 'recession'.
questions.model_answer: A recession is a period when a country's GDP falls for two consecutive quarters or more [2]. Estonia's 2.4% fall in GDP is cutting demand for Ostrova Glassworks' bottles.

knowledge_max_2: Sustained fall in national output
Usually brings rising unemployment

questions.question_text: Outline two effects of the recession on Ostrova Glassworks.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: A recession reduces demand for a firm's products and its revenue [k]. Orders are expected to drop 12%, cutting revenue by $2,352,000 from $19,600,000 [app].

Point two: Rising unemployment reduces household spending and orders from customers [k]. With unemployment up from 6.1% to 8.3%, drink makers order fewer bottles [app].

knowledge_max_2: A recession reduces demand for a firm's products and its revenue.
Rising unemployment reduces household spending and orders from customers.
application_max_2: A 12% order drop costs Ostrova $2,352,000 of its $19,600,000 revenue.
Ostrova has 280 staff and makes 14,000,000 bottles in Estonia.

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the recession on Ostrova Glassworks.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Demand falls [k]. Orders are expected to drop 12%, cutting revenue by $2,352,000 from $19,600,000 [app], leaving 14,000,000 bottles of capacity underused [an].

Point 2: Unemployment weakens household spending further [k]. With unemployment up from 6.1% to 8.3% [app], drink makers order fewer bottles, so the downturn reinforces itself and price cutting becomes likely [an].

knowledge_max_2: Falling demand reduces output
Rising unemployment cuts consumer spending
application_max_2: 12% fall equals $2,352,000
Unemployment 6.1% to 8.3%
analysis_max_2: Underused capacity raises unit costs
Weak demand encourages price competition

questions.question_text: Consider whether Ostrova Glassworks should cut 40 jobs or hold output and build inventory. Do you think directors should cut jobs? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Removing 40 staff quickly lowers wage costs when revenue may fall $2,352,000 [k]. It protects the business if recovery is uncertain [app]. Cutting output matches capacity of 14,000,000 bottles to demand [an].

Against: Holding output keeps skilled workers ready for recovery [k]. Unsold bottles tie up cash and may become obsolete for a firm on $19,600,000 [app]. With unemployment up to 8.3%, redundant staff may be hard to rehire [an].

Conclusion: Cut fewer jobs and shorten hours rather than 40 [eval]. Store only fast-selling lines while the recession lasts [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Job cuts reduce costs quickly when demand and revenue fall.
Holding output keeps skills but ties up cash in unsold stock.
application_max_2: Ostrova may lose $2,352,000 as orders fall 12% with 280 staff.
Unemployment has risen from 6.1% to 8.3% in Estonia's recession.
analysis_max_2: Lower costs help survive an uncertain downturn.
Unsold bottles risk obsolescence and cash strain on $19,600,000 revenue.
evaluation_max_2: Cut fewer than 40 jobs and shorten hours.
Store only fast-selling lines until demand recovers.

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Zambezi Sugar is a private limited company in Zambia refining 250,000 tonnes of sugar a year, with 3,200 staff and revenue of $110,000,000. A carbon levy of $12 a tonne applies to 18,000 tonnes of emissions, and a labour audit found unpaid overtime. Directors must decide whether to invest $900,000 in bagasse power or pay the levy and settle wage claims.

questions.question_text: Define 'fair wage'.
questions.model_answer: A fair wage is pay that reflects the work done and allows employees a reasonable standard of living [2]. Zambezi Sugar's audit found overtime that was not paid at all.

knowledge_max_2: Pay that is just for the work performed
Covers basic needs and legal entitlements

questions.question_text: Outline two benefits to Zambezi Sugar of investing in bagasse power.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: Using a by-product for power avoids a carbon levy on emissions [k]. Burning bagasse could avoid the $216,000 levy on 18,000 tonnes [app].

Point two: Environmental and ethical improvements answer criticisms from buyers and staff [k]. Cleaner power and action on unpaid overtime answer criticisms [app].

knowledge_max_2: Using a by-product for power avoids a carbon levy on emissions.
Environmental and ethical improvements answer criticisms from buyers and staff.
application_max_2: Bagasse power could avoid the $216,000 levy on 18,000 tonnes of emissions.
Zambezi has 3,200 staff and $110,000,000 revenue refining 250,000 tonnes.

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Zambezi Sugar of investing in bagasse power.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: It cuts both energy costs and the carbon levy [k]. Burning bagasse instead of coal could avoid the $216,000 annual levy on 18,000 tonnes [app], lowering costs on $110,000,000 of revenue [an].

Point 2: It improves ethical standing after the labour audit [k]. Cleaner power and action on unpaid overtime answer the criticisms [app], protecting contracts with buyers who check supplier standards and the jobs of 3,200 staff [an].

Improves ethical reputation
application_max_2: $216,000 levy on 18,000 tonnes
$900,000 investment
analysis_max_2: Lower energy costs raise margin
Ethical credibility protects buyer contracts

questions.question_text: Consider whether Zambezi Sugar should invest $900,000 in bagasse power or pay the levy and settle wage claims. Do you think directors should invest? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: Bagasse power removes the $216,000 levy and cuts coal costs [k]. Pairing it with settled wage claims rebuilds trust with 3,200 staff and buyers [app]. It lowers costs on $110,000,000 of sugar sales [an].

Against: $900,000 is over four times the annual levy [k]. The money could clear unpaid overtime immediately and avoid legal action [app]. With 250,000 tonnes to refine, a large outlay may strain cash [an].

Conclusion: Settle wage claims first [eval]. Invest in bagasse afterwards, funded partly from the $216,000 annual saving [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Investing in cleaner power cuts levies and energy costs while improving ethics.
Urgent wage claims and legal risk may deserve priority over capital spending.
application_max_2: The $900,000 bagasse plant compares with a $216,000 levy on 18,000 tonnes.
Zambezi employs 3,200 staff on $110,000,000 revenue.
analysis_max_2: Settling claims and cutting emissions protects buyers and 3,200 staff.
Delayed wage payments risk legal action that outweighs the levy saving.
evaluation_max_2: Settle the unpaid overtime claims before investing.
Fund bagasse power later from the $216,000 saving.

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Mekelle Leather is a private limited company in Ethiopia making 300,000 leather bags a year, with 700 staff and revenue of $15,000,000. Directors must decide whether to accept.

questions.question_text: Define 'globalisation'.
questions.model_answer: Globalisation is the growing integration of world markets for goods, services, capital and labour [2]. The global brand would link Mekelle Leather to buyers in 20 countries.

knowledge_max_2: Increasing worldwide economic integration
Free movement of trade, investment and ideas across borders

questions.question_text: Outline two effects of the global brand's offer on Mekelle Leather.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: A lower selling price reduces revenue on each unit sold [k]. Selling 180,000 bags at $38 rather than $50 loses $2,160,000 [app].

Point two: Training and market access can build long-term capability and diversify buyers [k]. Entry to 20 countries could raise future orders for 700 staff [app].

knowledge_max_2: A lower selling price reduces revenue on each unit sold.
Training and market access can build long-term capability and diversify buyers.
application_max_2: Selling 180,000 bags at $38 instead of $50 loses Mekelle $2,160,000.
Mekelle makes 300,000 bags with 700 staff and $15,000,000 revenue.

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the global brand's offer on Mekelle Leather.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Revenue per bag falls [k]. Selling 180,000 bags at $38 rather than $50 loses $2,160,000 [app], which is hard to absorb on $15,000,000 of revenue and with a 15% export tax [an].

Point 2: Training and market access build capability [k]. Design skills and entry to 20 countries could raise quality and future orders [app], reducing dependence on a few local buyers and protecting 700 jobs [an].

knowledge_max_2: Lower unit price reduces revenue

analysis_max_2: Margin loss threatens short-term profit

questions.question_text: Consider whether Mekelle Leather should accept the global brand's offer. Do you think directors should accept? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: The brand buys 60% of output and opens 20 countries [k]. Design training could transform Mekelle into a recognised exporter with 700 jobs [app]. It reduces dependence on a few local buyers [an].

Against: $38 against $50 loses $2,160,000 a year [k]. The 15% export tax cuts the return further on $15,000,000 of revenue [app]. Dependence on one buyer grows across 180,000 bags [an].

Conclusion: Accept only for a limited period and volume [eval]. Gain skills and contacts without locking 60% of output into a low price [eval].

knowledge_max_2: A large contract with training and market access can build an exporter.
A low price and export tax reduce returns and create buyer dependence.
application_max_2: The brand's $38 price loses $2,160,000 on 180,000 bags against $50.
Mekelle has 700 staff and $15,000,000 revenue with a 15% export tax.
analysis_max_2: New skills and 20-country access can diversify Mekelle's customers.
A 15% tax on top of a $12 price cut deepens the revenue loss.
evaluation_max_2: Accept the offer only for a limited period and volume.
Avoid locking 60% of output into $38 long term.

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Sargasso Plastics is a private limited company in Barbados moulding 25,000,000 food containers a year, with 180 staff and revenue of $12,500,000. questions.question_text: Define 'rate of interest'.
questions.model_answer: The rate of interest is the percentage charged for borrowing money, usually expressed per year [2]. Barbados' 7.5% rate would cost Sargasso Plastics $225,000 on a $3,000,000 loan.

knowledge_max_2: Percentage cost of borrowed funds
Also the return earned by savers

questions.question_text: Outline two ways in which Sargasso Plastics could reduce the impact of higher oil prices on its costs.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: Sargasso Plastics could invest in the $3,000,000 recycling line [k]. Recycled resin reduces dependence on oil-based feedstock and the $750,000 added to resin costs by the 22% oil price rise [app].

Point two: Sargasso Plastics could raise container prices by 6% [k]. This passes the $750,000 increase on to customers, protecting margin on 25,000,000 food containers [app].

knowledge_max_2: Invest in recycling to cut reliance on oil-based resin
Raise selling prices to pass increased costs to customers
application_max_2: The $3,000,000 recycling line reduces use of oil-based resin at Sargasso Plastics
A 6% price rise recovers the $750,000 resin cost on 25,000,000 food containers

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the 22% rise in oil prices on Sargasso Plastics.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Resin costs increase [k]. Oil-based plastic feedstock adds $750,000 to costs [app], which is 6% of $12,500,000 revenue and must be recovered through prices or efficiency [an].

Point 2: A recycling line becomes more attractive [k]. Higher virgin resin prices improve the saving from recycled material [app], but borrowing $3,000,000 at 7.5% adds $225,000 of interest [an].

knowledge_max_2: Raw material costs rise with oil prices
Recycling becomes relatively cheaper
application_max_2: $750,000 added cost
$225,000 interest at 7.5%
analysis_max_2: Cost increase pressures margin
Recycling offsets exposure to oil prices

questions.question_text: Consider whether Sargasso Plastics should borrow $3,000,000 for a recycling line or raise container prices by 6%. Do you think the directors should borrow? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: A recycling line reduces dependence on oil-based resin [k]. This cuts unit costs across 25,000,000 containers and leaves Sargasso less exposed if oil rises again [an].

Against: A 6% price rise needs no borrowing [k]. It recovers the $750,000 directly and avoids adding $225,000 of interest on $12,500,000 of revenue [app]. However, customers in price-sensitive food packaging may switch suppliers, so revenue could fall and the cost would not be recovered [an].

Conclusion: Borrow for the recycling line [eval], but combine it with a modest price rise to protect cash flow [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Recycling reduces reliance on oil-based resin
A price rise recovers costs without taking on debt
application_max_2: The $750,000 resin cost rise and $225,000 loan interest at Sargasso Plastics

analysis_max_2: Lower unit costs on 25,000,000 containers reduce exposure to future oil shocks

evaluation_max_2: Borrowing is preferable because $225,000 of interest is covered by the $750,000 saving
Combine the loan with a modest price rise to protect cash flow

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Kalutara Tea is a private limited company in Sri Lanka growing 9,000 tonnes of tea a year, with 1,500 staff and revenue of $27,000,000. Causes habitat loss and carbon emissions

questions.question_text: Outline two ways in which Kalutara Tea could respond to buyers' demand for certified tea.

knowledge_max_2: Certify existing estates to meet buyer standards
Work with smallholders so sourced leaf is certified
application_max_2: Certification costs $210,000, or $23.33 per tonne, against $27,000,000 revenue

Point 2: It avoids legal and reputational damage [k]. The forest law protects 400 hectares, and buying from smallholders who clear land could bring fines and campaigner criticism [app], threatening the jobs of 1,500 staff [an].

knowledge_max_2: Maintains access to premium buyers
Avoids legal and reputational risk
application_max_2: $210,000 cost equals $23.33 per tonne
400 hectares protected
analysis_max_2: Low unit cost protects sales
Forest clearance risks fines and boycotts

questions.model_answer:

Against: Smallholder leaf may be cheaper and raise volume [k]. Buying it avoids inspection costs and certification paperwork [app]. But buyers rejecting deforestation-linked tea could cancel contracts, putting 1,500 jobs at risk [an].

evaluation_max_2: Certifying the estates is the better long-term choice

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Penang Circuit Boards is a public limited company in Malaysia making 4,000,000 circuit boards a year, with 850 staff and revenue of $52,000,000. questions.question_text: Define 'foreign direct investment'.

Usually involves control of overseas operations

questions.question_text: Outline two ways in which Penang Circuit Boards could respond to the new rival's price competition.

Move upmarket to differentiate from the rival
application_max_2: Automation protects margin on 4,000,000 boards after the 8% price cut
Premium boards can absorb the 4% tariff on US exports

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the multinational rival's new plant on Penang Circuit Boards.

Labour market pressure from a large employer

Borrowing costs are high

It sells each container for $0.50, variable cost is $0.30, and fixed costs are $180,000 a year, with output of 1.2 million containers. A supermarket buyer wants 200,000 containers at $0.38 each. The operations director must decide if the order adds profit and how it changes the break-even calculation.

questions.question_text: Define 'contribution'.
questions.model_answer: Contribution is selling price minus variable cost, the amount left to cover fixed costs [2]. For Tegal Plastics it is $0.20 a container.

knowledge_max_2: Definition of contribution
Selling price minus variable cost

questions.question_text: Outline two ways Tegal Plastics Ltd could increase its contribution per container.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: Raising the price above $0.50 would increase the $0.20 contribution and lower the 900,000-container break-even [k]. Higher prices on 1.2 million containers would cover the $180,000 fixed costs sooner [app].

Point two: Reducing variable cost below $0.30 a container, for example by cheaper resin, also raises contribution [k]. On the 200,000-container order, a lower cost would add more than the $16,000 currently gained [app].

knowledge_max_2: Higher selling price raises contribution per unit
Lower variable cost raises contribution per unit
application_max_2: $0.50 price, $0.30 cost and 900,000 break-even on 1.2 million containers
200,000-container order at $0.38 with $0.30 variable cost

questions.model_answer:
Point 1: At $0.38 a container the order adds $0.08 over the $0.30 variable cost [k]. On 200,000 containers that is $16,000 towards fixed costs [an].

Point 2: Output of 1.2 million already exceeds the 900,000 break-even [k]. The extra order therefore mostly adds profit rather than covering costs [an].

questions.question_text: Consider whether Tegal Plastics Ltd should accept the supermarket buyer's order of 200,000 containers at $0.38. Do you think the order should be accepted? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: At $0.38 the order still exceeds the $0.30 variable cost, adding $0.08 contribution per container [k]. Output of 1.2 million already exceeds the 900,000 break-even, so no extra fixed cost is required [app]. The 200,000 containers would add about $16,000 to profit [an].

Against: A price of $0.38 is well below the normal $0.50 and could undercut other customers [k]. If other buyers demand the same discount, the $180,000 fixed costs must be covered at lower margins [app]. The supermarket may gain leverage and push prices down further [an].

A new trade agreement removes the 12% tariff on those exports, but the Vietnamese dong has weakened 7% against the euro and shipping rates have risen 15%. A rival in Bangladesh offers shirts at $16.50. Directors must decide whether to keep the $18 price to protect margins or cut to $17 to defend market share.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'tariff'.
questions.model_answer: A tariff is a government tax on traded goods that raises their price, such as the 12% tariff previously paid on Tarnside Textiles Ltd's shirts entering Europe [2].

knowledge_max_2: A tax on imports or exports
Raises the price of traded goods

questions.question_text: Outline two effects of the international changes on Tarnside Textiles Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: [k] Removing a tariff improves export competitiveness. [app] The 12% tariff removal makes the $18 shirts cheaper in Europe, potentially lifting sales beyond 640,000 and the $11,520,000 revenue.

Point two: [k] Currency and freight rises squeeze margins. [app] A 7% weaker dong raises imported dyestuff costs and 15% higher shipping rates hurt, while the $16.50 Bangladeshi rival looks stronger.

knowledge_max_2: Tariff removal improves export competitiveness
Currency and freight rises squeeze margins
application_max_2: 12% tariff removed on $18 shirts to Europe, boosting $11,520,000 revenue
7% weaker dong and 15% shipping versus a $16.50 rival

questions.question_text: Explain two ways the international changes could affect Tarnside Textiles Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Removing the 12% tariff makes the $18 shirts more competitive in Europe, potentially lifting volume beyond 640,000 and raising the $11,520,000 revenue.

Point 2: A 7% weaker dong raises the local cost of imported dyestuffs, while 15% higher shipping rates squeeze margins; the $16.50 rival in Bangladesh then looks stronger.

knowledge_max_2: Tariff removal can boost export competitiveness
Currency and freight changes affect costs
application_max_2: 12% tariff removed on $18 shirts in Europe
7% dong fall, 15% freight rise, $16.50 rival
analysis_max_2: Volume gain may offset margin pressure
Bangladesh competitor limits pricing power

questions.question_text: Consider whether Tarnside Textiles Ltd should cut its price to $17. Do you think the business should do so? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: [k] A lower price defends market share. [app] Cutting from $18 to $17 narrows the gap with the $16.50 Bangladeshi rival, and with the 12% tariff gone could win European orders. [an] This could keep volume above 640,000 shirts and protect the $11,520,000 revenue.

Against: [k] A price cut reduces revenue per unit. [app] Cutting to $17 lowers revenue on 640,000 shirts just as shipping rises 15% and the dong falls 7%. [an] With thinner margins, the cut could reduce profit even if volume holds.

Conclusion: [eval] Holding $18 briefly lets the firm use the tariff saving first. [eval] Tarnside Textiles Ltd should cut to $17 only if orders start falling.

knowledge_max_2: A lower price defends market share
A price cut reduces revenue and margins
application_max_2: $17 narrows the gap to the $16.50 rival with the 12% tariff gone
Shipping up 15% and dong down 7% on 640,000 shirts
analysis_max_2: A cut could keep volume and $11,520,000 revenue
Thinner margins could cut profit even if volume holds
evaluation_max_2: Hold $18 and use the tariff saving first
Cut to $17 only if European orders fall

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Wrenford Ceramics Ltd is a private limited company in Stoke-on-Trent, United Kingdom, making 180,000 tiles a month with 120 employees. National unemployment has fallen to 3.9%, forcing wages up 8% to attract skilled kiln operators. A government subsidy of $190,000 is available if the firm trains 30 unemployed people, but training costs $96,000 and takes 140 hours per worker. Energy prices have also risen 22%. Directors must decide whether to take the subsidy or raise tile prices by 6%.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'unemployment'.
questions.model_answer: Unemployment is the situation where people of working age are without a job and seeking work, such as the 3.9% rate facing Wrenford Ceramics Ltd in the United Kingdom [2].

knowledge_max_2: People of working age without jobs
They are actively seeking work

questions.question_text: Outline two effects of falling unemployment on Wrenford Ceramics Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: [k] Low unemployment makes labour scarce and dearer. [app] With unemployment at 3.9%, Wrenford Ceramics Ltd must pay 8% more to attract kiln operators for its 180,000 tiles a month.

Point two: [k] Labour shortages limit output and raise costs. [app] Training 30 workers takes 140 hours each and energy is up 22%, squeezing the 120 employees in Stoke-on-Trent.

knowledge_max_2: Low unemployment makes labour scarce and raises wages
Labour shortages and training reduce short-run output
application_max_2: 3.9% unemployment forces 8% higher wages for 180,000 tiles
30 workers need 140 hours training each with energy up 22%

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the falling unemployment rate on Wrenford Ceramics Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: With unemployment at 3.9%, the firm must pay 8% more to attract kiln operators, raising costs on 180,000 tiles a month in Stoke-on-Trent.

Point 2: The $190,000 subsidy could offset the $96,000 training bill and bring 30 new workers, but 140 hours of training per person reduces short-run output just as energy prices rise 22%.

knowledge_max_2: Low unemployment pushes wages up
Subsidies can encourage recruitment and training
application_max_2: 3.9% unemployment and 8% wage rise
$190,000 subsidy, $96,000 cost, 140 hours
analysis_max_2: Training time reduces output temporarily
Subsidy improves the case for hiring

questions.question_text: Consider whether Wrenford Ceramics Ltd should take the subsidy rather than raise tile prices by 6%. Do you think the business should go ahead? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: [k] A subsidy offsets training costs and adds workers. [app] The $190,000 subsidy covers the $96,000 training bill and brings 30 workers, easing the skilled labour shortage in Stoke-on-Trent. [an] This helps sustain 180,000 tiles a month without passing the 8% wage rise to customers.

Against: [k] Training delays output, while a price rise recovers costs quickly. [app] At 140 hours per worker, training cuts short-run output just as energy rises 22%. [an] A 6% price rise would pass the 8% wage and 22% energy increases to customers sooner.

Conclusion: [eval] The subsidy builds long-term skills for the 120 employees. [eval] Wrenford Ceramics Ltd should take it, and plan a smaller price rise if energy stays high.

knowledge_max_2: A subsidy offsets training costs and adds workers
Training delays output while price rises recover costs faster
application_max_2: $190,000 subsidy covers $96,000 training for 30 workers
140 hours per worker and energy up 22% versus a 6% rise
analysis_max_2: Subsidy sustains 180,000 tiles without passing on 8% wages
Training delays output while a 6% rise recovers 8% and 22% costs
evaluation_max_2: The subsidy builds long-term skills for 120 employees
Take it and plan a smaller rise if energy stays high

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Larkspur Apparel Ltd is a private limited company in Lisbon, Portugal, importing 250,000 cotton T-shirts a year from a supplier in Bangladesh. An audit found the supplier pays below the local living wage and uses 1,800 tonnes of water per tonne of cotton. Ethical campaigners threaten a boycott that could cut sales 18%. Switching to a certified supplier raises each shirt's cost from $6.20 to $7.05 but cuts water use 35%. The board must decide before the autumn contract is signed.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'ethical sourcing'.
questions.model_answer: Ethical sourcing means buying goods from suppliers who meet fair labour and environmental standards, unlike the below-wage supplier used by Larkspur Apparel Ltd in Bangladesh [2].

knowledge_max_2: Buying from suppliers with fair standards
Considers labour and environmental impact

questions.question_text: Outline two benefits of switching to a certified supplier for Larkspur Apparel Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: [k] Certification reduces reputational risk. [app] Switching ends the below-living-wage practice in Bangladesh and helps avoid the threatened 18% sales boycott in Lisbon.

Point two: [k] Certified suppliers can lower environmental impact. [app] The new supplier cuts water use 35% from 1,800 tonnes per tonne of cotton, improving the brand across 250,000 T-shirts.

knowledge_max_2: Certification reduces reputational risk and avoids boycotts
Certified suppliers lower environmental impact
application_max_2: Ends below-wage practice and avoids an 18% boycott in Lisbon
Cuts water 35% from 1,800 tonnes per tonne of cotton

questions.question_text: Explain two consequences of the audit findings for Larkspur Apparel Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Paying below the living wage in Bangladesh risks the threatened 18% sales boycott, which would cut revenue in Lisbon and damage the brand.

Point 2: Using 1,800 tonnes of water per tonne of cotton raises environmental criticism; switching suppliers cuts water use 35% but adds $212,500 a year to costs.

knowledge_max_2: Poor labour practices can trigger boycotts
High water use harms reputation
application_max_2: 18% boycott threat in Lisbon
1,800 tonnes of water and 35% saving
analysis_max_2: Sales loss may exceed the switching cost
Ethical gain must be weighed against $212,500

questions.question_text: Consider whether Larkspur Apparel Ltd should switch to the certified supplier. Do you think the business should go ahead? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: [k] Switching protects reputation and the brand. [app] It ends below-wage pay, cuts water use 35% and avoids an 18% boycott that could far outweigh the $212,500 extra cost. [an] This protects sales of 250,000 T-shirts in Lisbon and the brand's future.

Against: [k] Switching raises unit costs. [app] Paying $7.05 instead of $6.20 on 250,000 shirts adds $212,500 a year, and the boycott may never happen. [an] Higher costs squeeze margins before the autumn contract is signed.

Conclusion: [eval] The 18% boycott risk makes switching worthwhile. [eval] Larkspur Apparel Ltd should switch, since reputational protection and water savings secure the brand more than short-term savings.

knowledge_max_2: Switching protects reputation and avoids boycotts
Switching raises unit costs
application_max_2: $212,500 extra versus an 18% boycott and 35% water cut

analysis_max_2: Protects 250,000 T-shirt sales and the Lisbon brand

evaluation_max_2: The 18% boycott risk justifies switching
Switch for long-term brand security over short-term savings

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Merevale Engineering Ltd is a private limited company in Manchester, United Kingdom, exporting machine parts worth $3,200,000 a year to the United States. Sterling has appreciated 9% against the dollar, and a US competitor has cut its price 5%. The firm holds $800,000 of US customer receipts due in 60 days. A currency hedging contract would fix the exchange rate for a $24,000 fee. Directors must decide whether to hedge, raise dollar prices, or absorb the loss.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'exchange rate'.
questions.model_answer: An exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another, such as the value of sterling against the dollar that affects Merevale Engineering Ltd's $3,200,000 exports [2].

knowledge_max_2: Price of one currency in another
Determines value of foreign receipts

questions.question_text: Outline two effects of sterling's appreciation on Merevale Engineering Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: [k] A stronger currency reduces the value of export receipts. [app] A 9% stronger sterling means the $800,000 of US receipts converts into fewer pounds, cutting the value of the $3,200,000 export trade.

Point two: [k] A stronger currency makes exports dearer abroad. [app] With a US rival cutting prices 5%, raising dollar prices could lose orders for the Manchester firm.

knowledge_max_2: A stronger currency cuts the value of export receipts
A stronger currency makes exports dearer and less competitive
application_max_2: 9% stronger sterling cuts the value of $800,000 receipts
A US rival's 5% cut limits price rises on $3,200,000 exports

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of sterling's appreciation on Merevale Engineering Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A 9% stronger sterling means the $800,000 of US receipts converts into fewer pounds, cutting the value of the $3,200,000 export trade in Manchester.

Point 2: A US rival has cut prices 5%, so raising dollar prices could lose orders; paying a 3% hedging fee protects receipts but uses up $24,000.

knowledge_max_2: Appreciation reduces value of foreign receipts
Stronger currency makes exports dearer
application_max_2: 9% appreciation on $800,000 and $3,200,000
5% rival cut and 3% hedging fee
analysis_max_2: Price rise may lose US orders
Fee is cheaper than an unhedged fall

questions.question_text: Consider whether Merevale Engineering Ltd should pay $24,000 to hedge its US receipts. Do you think the business should go ahead? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
For: [k] Hedging removes exchange rate risk. [app] A $24,000 fee, or 3% of $800,000, fixes the rate for receipts due in 60 days, protecting the $3,200,000 trade from a further sterling rise. [an] This gives budget certainty in Manchester despite a 9% appreciation.

Against: [k] Hedging costs money and may be unnecessary. [app] Sterling may not move further, and a US rival's 5% price cut already threatens exports without an extra $24,000. [an] The fee could be wasted if the rate stays steady.

Conclusion: [eval] The $24,000 fee is small relative to the $800,000 at risk. [eval] Merevale Engineering Ltd should hedge, since certainty is worth more than a possible gain.

knowledge_max_2: Hedging removes exchange rate risk
Hedging costs money and may be unnecessary
application_max_2: $24,000 is 3% of $800,000 due in 60 days
Sterling up 9% and a US rival cut prices 5%
analysis_max_2: Fixing the rate protects the $3,200,000 trade and gives certainty
The fee is wasted if sterling stops rising
evaluation_max_2: The fee is small against $800,000 at risk
Hedge because budget certainty is worth more

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem: Quarrystone Furniture Ltd is a private limited company in Melbourne, Australia, selling 12,000 sofas a year at $860 each. Consumer confidence has fallen and the economy has entered a recession, with household incomes down 4% and unemployment at 6.1%. Sales are forecast to drop 15% next year. questions.model_answer:

Point two: [k] Falling sales make marketing decisions harder. [app] A $520,000 campaign or a 10% discount costing $744,000 in profit may not guarantee a return when households postpone spending.

Point 2: A $520,000 campaign might lift demand 9%, but a 10% discount would cost $744,000 in profit; with tighter budgets neither option guarantees a return.

questions.model_answer:

Against: [k] Advertising may fail in a recession. [app] With incomes down 4% and 1,800 fewer sofas already forecast, a campaign may not work. [an] The $520,000 could be wasted while a discount protects volume immediately.

Conclusion: [eval] Preserving price and brand beats a $744,000 profit loss. [eval] Quarrystone Furniture Ltd should run the campaign only if it is targeted at likely buyers.

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity

It buys beans from 24 suppliers, but an audit found only 9 pay the fair-trade minimum price, leaving 15 suppliers below it. questions.model_answer: Buying materials from suppliers who meet fair standards, such as paying the fair-trade minimum price that only 9 of Bristol Coffee Roasters Ltd's 24 suppliers currently do [2].

questions.question_text: Outline two ways campaigner pressure could affect Bristol Coffee Roasters Ltd.
questions.model_answer:
Point one: A boycott can damage a firm's reputation and sales [k]. Only 9 of 24 suppliers, or 37.5%, pay the fair-trade minimum price at Bristol Coffee Roasters Ltd [app].

Point two: Ethical sourcing may raise input costs [k]. Switching the 15 suppliers below the minimum would raise bean costs by 6% [app].

Point 2: Higher costs [k]. Switching the 15 non-compliant suppliers would raise bean costs by 6% [app], squeezing margins unless prices rise [an].

Against: Higher bean costs may have to be passed to customers [k]. Switching the 15 non-compliant suppliers raises costs by 6% [app]. Passing on that rise could lose price-sensitive customers if the change is not explained [an].
